INTRODUCTION 

by 

CHARLES "CHICK" LEWIS 

I can think of no two practical theatremen better qualified to write a compilation of tried and tested ideas than Bill Hendricks and Howard Waugh. Both have a background in show business and a record of accomplishment second to none, and over a long period of years have learned well their lessons in how to attract public notice to a theatre and its attractions.

Much has been said and still more has been written about how to sell motion pictures to the millions of movie fans the world over. But to attempt to catalogue how to do it is a task that few would even think of, much less succeed in doing. It required years of effort, of filing, of bringing old ideas up-to-date and creating new slants to entice the suspicious patron into the theatre. A mere cursory glance through this book is ample testimony of how difficult this task must have been. 

Every conceivable phase of show-selling has been tabulated and condensed so that the busy men who run theatres and sell the shows can find what they are looking for with a minimum of effort and with a maximum of results. No words or ideas are wasted. Before they could find their way into this volume of ten thousand and one show-selling ideas, they had to pass the acid test of practicability and actual use. 

Wherever the element of doubt existed as to the chances for the success of any idea, it was deliberately left out. 

So, after years of work, Bill Hendricks and Howard Waugh found themselves in a position to produce every one of the ideas so that altogether they constitute this tremendously valuable and important book; a book which, in my opinion, should be on the desk of every theatre manager, district manager, division chief, exploitation and publicity director, circuit executive and all others whose daily work involves them in the problem and task of getting patrons into the theatres.

The job is now done, and it becomes my privilege and pleasure to present it to the thousands of theatremen who are constantly alert and anxious to benefit by the experiences of brother showmen. 

I congratulate Hendricks and Waugh on their accomplishment and predict that with this book their names will go down in history as two of the most aggressive and progressive theatremen this industry has ever known. And for myself, well, I consider that I have been mighty lucky to know them, and I am proud to call them my friends. 

"CHICK" LEWIS.

While my name appears as a co-perpetrator on the cover, my only participation in the volume is the fact that fourteen or fifteen years ago I suggested to Bill Hendricks that if he planned to make theatres his life work, he should commence then to compile data systematically. 

This book is the outcome of that suggestion. 

No attempt is made to claim originality for anything-unless we start with Adam. Nor are we apologizing to anyone for "lifting."

HOWARD WAUGH.

Marching along in the parade of show business for a number of years, we have observed many of the highlights of show-selling, which we have attempted to record here. Some of them date to 

Barnum; some of them, we claim to be original; others have been originated and introduced by you, and you, and you. 

Our efforts have been directed towards organizing the varied methods of merchandising attractions; towards collecting together all the elements of exploitation under one tent. And in a form where instant reference is made easy through a thorough crossindex. 

Naturally, no compilation of merchandising methods can be considered absolutely complete, however comprehensive. And, all ideas won't work in all towns. However, we believe that ideas to be found here will prove adaptable to almost any attraction and any need. Or, at least, that the items presented here will serve to remind of others.

Most important, we offer here a record. Even if the reader is personally acquainted with every stunt and suggestion outlined in this volume, it will, at least, serve as a reminder. We have not tried to chart the course of theatre operation, concentrating our efforts, instead, on the gentle art of ballyhoo called Exploitation. 

To merit use, ideas must be free of risk, must not shock or offend patrons, must be weighed by common sense. And it must be reasonably certain that, as used, any cost will be balanced by business that is attracted. Ideas listed here are subject to any restrictions that may prevail, and in that event, permission of owners is required for use.

BILL HENDRICKS.

Vice-President John N. Garner presents the Quigley Grand 

Award, for the outstanding exploitation campaign of the year, to Bill Hendricks, at the Capitol, in Washington. Looking on are Senators Nathan Bachman, August Lonergan, and Francis 

Maloney, Representative William Citron, Col. A-Mike Vogel, and Bishop Thos. F. Gailor.
