SHOW-SELLING IDEAS

SHOW-SELLING IDEAS 1. TELLING THE WORLD... Telephone is wired into a prominently located window, where an attractive girl, possibly costumed, is seated as center of a display on theatre's attraction, calling numbers from the phone book with a "message" about the show. 

The display carries copy: "Telling the World about (attraction).” 

Amplification can carry voice outside the window, so that girl's conversation in calling numbers is heard by sidewalk crowds. 

Or, the stunt might be adapted to a lobby flash instead, telephone company supplying a regular switchboard (with a single phone connection).

Girl can call those groups to whom the attraction would most likely appeal, or those groups most likely to attend; in connection with a story dealing with office girls, for example, calling all offices, delivering her message to stenographers. And, of course, the telephone calls can be made from theatre office, and not connected with a display. Or, cashier might make the calls in her leisure moments. 

To take the curse off a straight telephoned spiel about an attraction, girl might, immediately the phone is answered, plunge into an intimate line of conversation (to complete message before interruption) addressing the party answering the phone, “Hello Jack (or 'Jane'). How about going with me tonight to see (and into name of attraction and enthusiastic plug)." When told she has the wrong number, she replies with a polite, "I'm sorry," but the message has gone across; and on to the next number. And, even if they catch on, there's no harm done. (For use where unlimited calls are allowed. 

And not too early in the A.M.)

Using a telephone set-up in lobby or foyer, patrons might be invited to leave their phone numbers with the girl, signing them in book provided. . . display panel announcing that certain numbers, to be selected at random when the attraction comes to town, will be called and will receive guest tickets. 

Ad, herald, or announcement might suggest: "Telephone (theatre's number) for an important announcement." Those calling getting a brief message about an attraction. 

(See Photo Section.) 

2. APPEAL ... Every attraction has a definite appeal for some certain class or group. An attraction in which an attorney is the central character, for example, should appeal to lawyers. Or • 1 •

some phase of an attraction might be of vital interest to members of some organization, profession or nationality. 

An attraction might appeal especially to some trade . . . as a story featuring a truck driver would appeal especially to truck drivers. 

The attraction should be brought to the attention of all members of the local union for that particular trade, or those employed in the trade. They might be reached at places of employment, as, in the case of truck drivers, offices of a hauling company and other places using trucks. . . cards being distributed or attached to bulletin boards.

Also, incidents or minor events in attractions might interest certain groups, to whom appeal might be made without publicizing the event, incident or angle in any other way.

Newsreels often carry a definite appeal, showing scenes that certain people would want to see if their attention were called to the showing. 

Mailing lists might be secured from the societies or organizations interested, and their membership contacted by direct mail; or by telephone calls. 

3. TELEGRAMS... Telegraph company will provide sending blanks, to be imprinted with "message" about attraction, perhaps also delivering "telegrams" gratis, house-to-house, if this copy is included: "We are choosing this method of letting you know, because (telegraph) is surer, swifter, safer. . . When in a hurry, always use (telegraph)" (with arrangements made before inserting the line). 

The "telegrams" are inserted, to be more effective, in envelopes (same color as blanks), imprinted: "Delivered by (telegraph) . . . (theatre) Telegram,”-name of Telegraph company and the word "telegram" being set in larger type, other words, on separate lines, in small type.

Distributed house-to-house, telegram-heralds will prove more effective if they can be delivered by uniformed messenger boys. 

Might deliver them to every other house (persons in in-between houses generally making it their business to find out telegram contents). 

Arrangements might be made with telegraph company to deliver special heralds with all telegrams delivered, or to attach imprinted stickers. Tiein copy on herald or insert or sticker sells telegraph service too, though devoting most of space to attraction. 

Jumbo telegrams (large blanks which telegraph company might provide) can be used as heralds, or for display in telegraph company windows. Imprinted copy can include line that "ordinary sized telegram wouldn't do justice to greatness of attraction." Might • 2.

illustrate with scene from attraction. Telegraph boys can deliver the "telegrams," unfolded, house-to-house. Ads of merchants on reverse side can aid in defraying cost. 

Or miniature reproduction of telegram might be effectively used as a herald. . . having cut made up from telegram, in smaller size; or imprinting midget blanks which telegraph company might supply. 

Gigantic wire might be used as a front flash . . . an enlargement of a wire "from star of attraction." Could be used as paneled display for lobby; or a giant banner might be made up, blanketing theatre front (or other space where it will make a flash) . . . with newspaper carrying story about "largest telegram." Banner should be painted in oil (if exposed to weather), and made exact proportions and duplication of telegram. (See photos.)

Copy used in telegram reproduction sells attraction, and might be addressed to "theatre-goers of (city)," and signed by star or stars of the show.

Wires from stars (secured through cooperation of studios), or wires from stars of coming stage attraction, might be used as a lobby flash.

Occasion meriting congratulations would suggest telegrams . . . a theatre opening, or premier showing of an attraction; or just the booking of an outstanding attraction. Telegrams from stars, addressed to theatre or theatre manager, could be attached to panel which carries heading, "Hollywood wires congratulations""

Newspaper or radio contest might be based on best "messages," or "title-grams," made up, telegram-style, using titles of motion pictures (or song titles) and including title of theatre's current attraction. 

Or, long involved "message" about the attraction (from star) might be reproduced, with readers invited to attempt to correctly punctuate it, first so-many winning ducats. 

4. TELEVISION... The effect of television can be produced, for window or lobby display, using an ordinary portable projection machine.

A lettered panel, with small radio (as center of the display), and with a small screen atop the radio, completely covers window (being placed outside the window). Or, in lobby, the projector is hidden behind the panel.

Inside the window, or concealed behind the display, the projection machine is set up, together with sound equipment . . . shooting a picture at close range, focused on the small screen atop the radio. 

Display panel carries copy: "Can these be (and in larger lettering) 

Television Views of (attraction)?" 3.

Speakers, connected with sound equipment, are concealed behind a smaller display panel which stands out from main panel (and which might be boxed over at top and used as a base for the small radio), speakers facing upward, so that sound appears to come from the radio. 

Trailers on attraction are shown, first reversing the titles (scenes are not reversed, and the sound consequently remaining okay); or, the film might be run in regular manner, reversing titles (necessary since picture is focused on screen from behind) by directing the picture into a small mirror, which, in turn, reflects it on the small screen. Several trailers (perhaps on the same attraction) might be connected together to afford a longer flash. Attendant in costume should be in charge of the display, lending additional flash and preventing anyone from tampering with the radio or screen. She might occasionally pretend to tune in or adjust the radio; and might hand out heralds.

Actual television, if available, might be utilized, arranging to have singer present a song number from the attraction, or to dedicate a song to the star . . . or dancer or star of stage show might appear for television. Photographs of the telebroadcast should be good for radio columns of newspaper. 

5. HERALDS... Always effective, and always used, heralds might assume any printed form from a mimeographed circular (a single, unfolded sheet), to an elaborately printed folder. Printing, however, should be neat, clear, effective. "Anything worth printing, is worth printing well."

Proper distribution can reach almost every potential patron. 

Heralds may be distributed house-to-house; placed in parked cars along streets and in parking lots and at plants and factories. They may be placed in pockets of overcoats in check rooms at hotels and night clubs and restaurants and other public places. They might be handed out at busy intersections, police regulations permitting. 

Heralds can be inserted in laundry packages, in loaves of bread, in packages in grocery stores, drug stores, department stores, in market baskets. Inserted in Sunday newspapers on the newsstands, or perhaps in daily papers. Placed in mailboxes in hotels and apartment buildings. In magazines delivered weekly by boys, or even the magazines on the stands. They might be delivered with the milk, the groceries, or the ice. Stores can include them in monthly statements which they mail. 

Heralds might be dropped from a plane, (see No. 201).

Or they can be effectively distributed in street cars, buses, sub- •4•

urban trains, in hotel dining rooms and in restaurants during rush hours.

Arrangements can be made with hotels to place one herald in each room... the maids leaving them, in exchange for a few complimentary tickets. (Especially valuable should hotel be host to a convention.) 

Downtown stores and office buildings shouldn't be overlooked.

Attractive girl handing out the heralds might cause them to receive more than ordinary attention. They might also be handed to employees leaving stores and factories at quitting time. Distributed to schools and playgrounds they will reach the kids (and if attraction is commendable, permission of school principal might be secured to distribute without interference).

Heralds can be effectively distributed to patrons leaving theatre. 

Costumed girl might hand them out, placing her directly in front of a spotlighted panel on the attraction. Or, of course, house staff can take care of the distribution.

Novel ideas for heralds can assume every form from a "rubber check" actually printed on rubber, to a parchment scroll on a roller, depending on the attraction (and, perhaps most expensive forms being only used for distribution to critics and more important publicity contacts).

Heralds can be promoted without cost, or with part of the cost shared by a cooperating store. Merchant's ad can be imprinted on reverse side or on the bottom of the herald (the copy possibly tieing in with theatre's attraction). One or several merchants can cooperate in paying for the heralds in exchange for this space, the theatre taking care of distribution of the heralds. 

Space allotted to merchant might carry an imprinted number, fifteen or twenty numbers being selected and posted at the box office, and heralds bearing a similar number to entitle the holder to a free admission to theatre. Or, the numbers might be posted at the cooperating business place, and the heralds brought there to check numbers (thus bringing persons receiving the heralds into the store). 

Or, instead of numbers, the winning tickets might be based on color of the heralds... which are printed on stock of several different colors, the merchant posting a color instead of numbers . . . and heralds of corresponding colors to be good for admission. Control free admissions by limiting number of heralds of winning color put into circulation. 

Heralds shouldn't be entrusted to a gang of kids in house-to-house distribution unless regular theatre employees supervise them carefully, each employee having several boys under his supervision. • 5 •

6. RUBBER STAMPS... Carrying copy on attraction, a rubber stamp can be made up, and used to stamp newspapers on newsstands, sacks in stores, paper napkins, and other items. 

Back of passes used for several weeks in advance of attraction might even be rubber-stamped with an ad. Almost anything might be rubber-stamped in tieup with business places . . . grocery store tieups might even have eggs stamped, some few of them stamped twice being made good for admissions . . . card in store calling attention to this. Similarly other items. 

7. RADIO BROADCASTS... Cooperation of broadcasting station can prove invaluable. Announcements, interviews, contests can be featured. Events (as grand opening of an attraction) can be broadcast. Personalities can be introduced, interviewed. Sketches can be enacted.

Hollywood chatterer might be featured, presenting daily a program of news about stars and pictures (mostly those coming to theatre). 

Musical numbers might be interspersed. Program might be sponsored by a business place since it is interesting to listeners. Manager · could personally do the gossip-cast, perhaps direct from theatre. 

Musical numbers can be featured (perhaps by orchestras broadcasting regularly), or programs dedicated to theatre's attraction. 

Where attraction's star is featured on a broadcast, announcements of local showing of the attraction can be effectively arranged at beginning and end of the program. Stage show talent can appear on radio programs, including announcements of their appearance at theatre. Innumerable broadcasts direct from theatre are possible. 

Recordings of song hits featured in an attraction should be supplied stations. Announcements accompanying playing of transcriptions should mention theatre's attraction and play dates as well as the song hit. Title of attraction and theatre play dates on a typed sticker should be attached to records supplied radio stations. 

If station has a short-wave broadcast unit, it might be adapted to many stunts... taking station's mobile equipment to desired points and broadcasting to station, where it is rebroadcast. Radio station utilizing short-wave broadcasting cannot use such equipment in a manner that would be too commercial. However, they can, and likely will, tie-up with a great many unusual stunts. Broadcast from a plane might be arranged, perhaps having critics interview a star en route to town, or describing from the air a "grand opening" at theatre below and commenting on attraction (securing special permission to have the station pick up the plane's short-wave). · 6 ·

Contests, features, can be included as part of regular radio programs, making arrangements with the sponsors of the programs; or station might carry them as an interesting feature; or theatre can, of course, purchase the time.

Spot announcements, carefully scheduled, can reach thousands of listeners. Brevity should be the guiding rule in writing copy. 

8. TYPISTS, TYPEWRITERS... Attractive girls as center of a window display, can type "messages" about an attraction, which are handed to those watching by a girl attendant outside window. 

Added angle might be offering of guest tickets to those estimating nearest correct number of words girls will type in specified time. 

Display in window might carry copy: "They're typing an important message for everyone. . . about (and into attraction copy)." 

Stenographers might compete in speed test for "(star) trophy," and perhaps a cash prize. Typewriter company would supply the typewriters, and newspaper might go along for story and photograph of the winners at their typewriters.

Contest, perhaps arranged with cooperation of newspaper or radio station, might be based on best typewriter photos of star of attraction submitted... the "photos" being made up by using a typewriter. 

Several girls might be stationed on a bannered truck, or float, which travels about town. Girls are apparently typing out "message" about attraction (according to copy on banners on truck). 

Actually, quantity of slips of paper have been imprinted with a photo of star of attraction, and copy: "A message about (attraction).”

The "message," too, is printed on the slips, using typewriter style type, however. The girls run the messages thru the typewriters, pretending to type, then pull the "message" out of the machine and hand it to someone along the street. Or another girl, attractively costumed, hands out the "messages." 

Automatic typewriters might be set up in lobby, typing up "messages" on the attraction, which are handed patrons by an attendant. 

9. WINDOWS... Stores are constantly on the look out for attention-winning, crowd-stopping ideas for their windows, and will generally listen to suggestions which will include display material on theatre's attraction combined with their merchandise. 

In outlining a proposed window display to a merchant, a rough pencil-sketch might be prepared in advance, aiding him in visualizing the proposed window tieup, and increasing possibility of favorable reaction.

Window displays should be, as nearly as possible, characteristic of •7•

the store in arrangement. There should be no overcrowding, and at the same time there should be no empty space. They should be well balanced. Built up displays will prove most effective. A well-done job might cost a little more, but if it proves much more effective at the box office, it's worthwhile.

Points to consider include: Promise of attention drawn to window. 

Cleanliness. Point of focus. Centering of attraction. Action. 

Contrasting background. Simplicity. Dramatic presentation and distinctive sales promise. Seasonal. Wide appeal, and especially to women. Theatre name, play dates. Framed stills.

Generally it is necessary to plan ahead and make arrangements for windows in advance, since stores ordinarily plan their windows in advance. Arrangements might be made for displays in the windows of the different stores of a company operating a chain of local stores by contacting the local or regional executive in charge, perhaps arranging at one time for a number of windows. 

10. NEWSPAPER CONTACTS... Constituting one of the most important methods of publicizing an attraction, newspaper angles, stories, ads, cooperative ads, classified ads, contests, features, all are of especial value. Newspaper cooperation is most essential; and can prove mutually advantageous. 

Stories about shows constitute real news. Theatre news, and news of the people of stage and screen carries definite reader interest, and if accorded newspaper space, is of value to both theatre and the cooperating newspaper. The combined circulation of the numerous screen magazines attests eloquently to the interest of the public. 

Newspapers devote full pages to society, to appeal to women; full pages of sports, to appeal to men; theatre news appeals to both sexes. 

Additionally, theatre news is of especial interest to young folks, aiding in establishing them as newspaper's readers. From a commonsense, circulation viewpoint, newspaper consideration of screen news is more than justified.

Theatres, on the other hand, are almost always indebted to newspapers for cooperation. Close cooperation and consideration of the paper and its editors is the only way in which gratitude might be demonstrated.

Good stories submitted an editor, preferably in person, have an excellent chance of registering, if there is any justification at all in their running the story, or the picture; if it can be shown to be of interest. Articles submitted to papers are like bullets . . . if there • 8.

is no scoring, there must be something wrong with the aim or the ammunition.

Stories which papers are requested to use must be clean, legible (no carbon copies); each story should merit a separate sheet of paper (full-size sheets, not scraps of paper). In other words, stories should make a good appearance when presented. Chances of stories landing will be improved.

It must be remembered that newspapers have very definite deadlines . . . and the story, to be printed, must be received in sufficient time. Last minute stories might be phoned, if the deadline is near, generally receiving fair consideration. Flowers should be omitted from copy submitted editors. . . in other words, adjectives should be reserved for other use, and the story should be written as nearly as possible after style in which a newspaper reporter would have written the story. . . the correct information, interestingly written, with due regard to brevity. 

And it doesn't pay to play favorites; newspapers don't like to be scooped; they should all be given an even break. Don't duplicate on stories or photographs-separate stories, exclusive photographs should be handed the different editors. 

Some days are easier than others to crash for space or plant stories. 

Newspapers are less "tight", and space is more easily available on certain days of the week, and on days following a holiday, or a big sale day. This might be considered in planting a story with the paper. (See "Newspaper" classifications.) 

11. GRAND OPENING... "Hollywood Premiere” or gala first night opening of an attraction, would feature ceremonies in theatre lobby, and in front of theatre. Making the program as elaborate as possible, many things can be included. 

Celebrities (local) and visiting (if any) should be invited to attend. 

Also, entertainers from hotels and night clubs and radio stations. 

The event must be announced in advance, in detail; and newspaper ads might carry, for an impression, a listing of celebs who have been invited and who have indicated that they will attend. 

Battery of lights, illuminating front of theatre, might be arranged. 

Possibly fire department has a truck equipped with flood lights, which they might assign to the theatre for the few minutes the "grand opening" is in progress. Or at least, it will be possible to use backstage floodlights and spotlights. Photo floods can be used, a number of them supplying a brilliant illumination. (Photograph supply place can supply them. They burn brightly for about 2 hours.) · 9.

ENCYCLOPEDIA OF EX P L O IT A TI O N 

Radio station should broadcast entire proceedings. . . comment of celebrities, as they arrive and are introduced. A feminine announcer might also be present, perhaps the society editor from newspaper, to describe gowns the ladies wear, or to introduce them. Radio receiving set might be placed nearby, on sidewalk (in charge of an attendant) so that crowds can hear what "celebs" say; or their comment can be sent through public address equipment. And if no radio station is available, amplification equipment might be used instead, and handled exactly as a broadcast. 

Band might be promoted, to march to theatre, play several numbers. Perhaps a high school band might serve; or the band of some local organization. Or, an orchestra might be placed on a band stand (constructed elevation) across street from theatre; or in street in front of theatre; or band could be set up in lobby, or on sidewalk in front of theatre, or even atop the marquee. Both marching band and orchestra might be used. If an orchestra cannot be secured, an accordionist or pianist might supply incidental music for the broadcast. 

Or group of trumpeters (dozen or so trumpet players) might be used, instead of an orchestra. Delivery of film, or arrival at theatre of star of stage show, could be made a highlight of the evening, and trumpeters might sound a blast as this event occurs. 

National Guard, or Cadets, or Naval Reserve, Scouts, American Legion, or other organized group (perhaps attraction will suggest an organization) might march to the theatre, act as a "Guard of Honor." 

Drill squad can perform.

Possibly military organization will agree to fire a salute (with permission of city authorities) as film arrives at theatre, or as highlight of ceremonies.

Group of prominent and good-looking girls in evening gowns might be present, acting as hostesses. 

Carpets (preferably red) should be placed on sidewalk from box office to curbing, with sidewalk man opening doors of cars of guests and patrons as they arrive. Use of canvas canopy might fit into plans.

Group of attractively costumed girls, could "arrive" at theatre during broadcast ceremonies . . . either riding bicycles, or on roller skates, carrying a lettered banner; or each carrying a cutout letter, which, together, spell out name of the attraction. Riding bicycles, the letters are attached to both sides of the bikes. 

Group of motorcyclists might be arranged through cooperation of • 10 •

motorcycle clubs. They might "escort" film, or star to theatre. 

Or motorcyclists might arrive, in single file with the letters attached (possibly each motorcyclist carrying a girl "passenger").

Bathing girls, arriving in individual cars, and mounting a small platform where they model the suits before entering theatre, would add flash and aid in attracting crowds. First girl carries card which ties in "Newest hit of the season, and new styles in swim suits." (And dealer handling the swim suits might buy an ad on the event. 

Possible that suits might be borrowed from a manufacturer.) Night club featuring a floor-show might supply the girls, in return for the announcements and attention which they will receive. 

A "Star Impersonation Contest" might be incorporated as part of the proceedings: Local impersonators of screen favorites, or of the star featured in attraction opening at theatre, arriving in limousines (supplied by a cooperating automobile dealer). Prize might be offered for best impersonation, with the contest presented on stage, or staged quickly out front. (See 172.) ...

The "opening" might be made a costume affair, with public invited to come costumed as attraction suggests . . with prizes offered for best costumes. House staff, in this case, should be costumed, too.

Searchlights, if available, should sweep the skies, and up and down the street. Airport might supply the lights; boat lights might be borrowed; perhaps there's an army or navy unit near which might permit regular anti-aircraft searchlights to be used. 

Moving pictures might be made of the crowd attracted. And perhaps arrangements can be made to have the film developed and printed locally, and shown several hours later on the same night (this being announced in advance, if possible). 

Newspaper columnist or motion picture critic might "sponsor" the grand opening, taking it over as his personal affair, according it news breaks.

Arrangements might be made with airport and pilots to have planes circling overhead during "ceremonies," and dipping a salute. Over public address system, announcer in front of theatre might acknowledge the salute, directing crowd's attention to the planes. 

House might be closed for an hour previous to the premiere, if held in evening (an optional angle and not essential). 

And, with equal success, the grand opening ceremonies might just as easily be arranged for noontime, or morning, when attraction is opening then. · 11 ·

Some member of the staff should be assigned the job of keeping the block, or at least that portion of it in which theatre is located, free of parked cars. Police might cooperate. Space directly across from theatre should, at any rate, be kept clear for band, crowds. 

(See Photo Section.) 12. MUSIC, SONG HITS... Where songs are featured in an attraction, or the music is especially notable, appeal might be made to music schools and societies. Members of musical organizations might be contacted; also Little Theatre and Opera Groups. Telephone might do the trick, or letters or printed cards might be sent them.

Popular music should be featured by music counters. In addition to counter panel and displays, a window display might use sheet music covers, window streamers, theatre display stuff on attraction. Enlargement of sheet music cover, or of a recording, might be used as background for a window display or for lobby display. Music store can distribute heralds, on a musical, with purchases. 

Orchestra and radio stations can feature the tunes. Orchestrations or recordings of the music might be supplied.

Contest for newspaper or radio might be based on submitted parodies on original lyrics from song hit in the show. Or, illustrating a newspaper contest with a scene from the attraction, contestants might be invited to submit a song title that describes the pictured scene.

Cleverest sentence or paragraph submitted using the words that appear in attraction title, or in song hits in the attraction, in combination with other song titles, might win tickets.

Contest could be based on novel, humorous, or clever suggestions for song titles, in connection with attraction that features songs. 

Letter, or card (sent mailing list), might feature a scene from the attraction and a bar or two of music (with the words) from one of the song hits. Made in postcard style, they might be placed on a desk in the lobby, during showing of attraction, with patrons invited to postcard their friends a message about attraction (receptacle being provided for cards, theatre stamping and mailing them).

Singer could be sent to night spots, dance halls, introducing the song hits. Might also appear at luncheon clubs, in lobby, at meetings of ladies' organizations. 

13. BOOK COVERS... Paper jackets for books can be imprinted and supplied schools and libraries. Boxed-in space on front cover carries copy: "This book belongs to (and space for name to • 12 •

be written in)," and copy on theatre's attraction. Additional copy on attraction on back page.

Added imprint of a merchant's ad might help to pay for the covers. 

Similar and simple angle is use of ownership labels. . . imprinted stickers, which carry copy described above, being distributed to students (who paste them in front of their books to identify them). 

14. FLOWERS . . . Several hundred, or several thousand roses might be promoted from cooperating florist, to be distributed at a matinee in advance of opening of attraction. Tag is attached to each rose, imprinted: "A rose from (star)." Ad for florist is carried on reverse side of the tag. Or, instead of using attached tags, the roses might be pinned or stapled to an imprinted card. 

Or, pretty girls might take the roses about town, calling on newspaper critics and prominent local citizens, pinning one of the roses to their lapels. List of people might be handed the girls. Recipients of roses and their friends will naturally discuss the event and the attraction.

Florist might formally name a rose or other flower after star, assuring a window display and possibly getting a newspaper break. 

Baskets of flowers might be promoted for lobby display. Card placed near the flowers, carries the copy: "For (star) for her notable performance in (attraction) (and name of florist)." And of course, a permanent display of flowers for the lobby might be promoted, the flowers being regularly changed, and the cooperating florist receiving a card beside the display. 

Exposition of flowers can be arranged, with display in lobby. 

15. SNAPSHOTS... A candid camera or snapshot contest might be arranged, perhaps with cooperation of newspaper. prize, or guest tickets being offered for the best snapshots of the week. 

All newspaper stories naturally publicize theatre's attraction in connection with which the contest is arranged. 

Or, contest might be arranged in cooperation with a photographer or film developing studio. Photographer or studio to buy newspaper space to publicize the event, and arranging window displays, also placing cards on their branch agencies. Snapshots might be required to be scenes or poses suggested by theatre's attraction. Used as a newspaper contest, the paper would reproduce winning snapshots daily, using at the same time a photograph from theatre's attraction. 

Float, or display on attraction built about a truck, traveling about streets of the city, could feature a man equipped with a camera, with copy on panels inviting girls to pose for a snapshot. With prize • 13 •

or tickets to go to those selected as winners- prettiest girl, most attractive smile, etc. Photos would be displayed in front of theatre, those whose heads are circled to receive free admissions. 

A "See-a-picture, Take-a-picture Week" might be arranged with cooperation of theatre and photographers and film developing places. 

Newspaper might sell a cooperative page, theatre and cooperating business places buying ads. Theatre offering guest tickets for best snapshots of the week. Photographers install window displays. 

Camera stores offer excellent opportunity for window tieups, with displays of stills, or perhaps miniature reproduction of movie set. 

If store wishes, they might reproduce star stills, thus having them for display purposes together with their cameras in same sizes. 

Kodak developing place might agree to insert imprinted cards or heralds in the envelopes in which negatives are returned. Insert should carry an attractive reproduction of a photograph of a scene from the attraction, or its star. Tieup copy would be included. 

Kid camera club might be organized in connection with kiddie club at theatre and with photographer's cooperation, offering prizes for best snapshots each week. 

16. BAKERY . . . Arrangements might be made to place small imprinted inserts in loaves of bread. Generally the inserts must be small enough for the bakery's insert machine to handle. ad or tie-in copy might be carried on the insert. 

Bakery can place streamers or panels on their trucks. Bakery Bakery might buy newspaper space, possibly showing stars eating bread and emphasizing: "bread for vitality, energy" angle; or copy tieing in stars or theme of attraction. 

Limited number of guest tickets might be inserted in bread, or small number of inserts good for admission; bakery buying newspaper ad or window streamers to call attention to the stunt (devoting most of the space to theatre attraction). 

Bakery might supply a quantity of "cookies" for distribution, or as a treat for a kiddie club. If for distribution, they should be inserted in a glassine bag which carries imprinted copy for both bakery and theatre's attraction. 

17. POLICY . . . Having such important bearing on box office and on selling possibilities, correct policy must be considered a show-selling medium. 

Proper opening days must be carefully considered; proper play dates, to get the most out of the various attractions, must be considered and weighed against individual situations, conditions, re- · 14 ·

actions. Opening hours of theatre are of importance. Operation of theatre should take into consideration the box office value of different types of attractions, and the town's reaction on different days of the week. ...

Small policy changes can aid the theatre's grosses materially. 

An early morning opening on Saturday might work out . per- haps at a reduction of matinee prices which prevail for an hour or two. 

Preview of a screen attraction the evening before it is to open (with patrons attending the final showing of the old picture also witnessing preview showing of new show), might prove of definite value at the box office. Using money give-away nights, perhaps patrons attending the matinee, or attending the previous day, might be made eligible to win though not present on night of awarding of prize. . . possibly resulting in build-up in business on matinee, or on day previous. 

Policy changes should be considered carefully in advance, as too frequent changes are confusing to patrons. ... 

18. COMMUNITY COOPERATION. Any civic activity should find the theatre identified with it. The community might be made to almost revolve around the theatre by intelligent cooperation. 

In addition to being prominently represented in any local activity, the theatre might be made the scene of many local events, to the advantage of the house.

Sunday Bible Classes or Sunday Schools might meet in theatre on Sunday morning . . . or additional church cooperation might find 

Holy-Week noonday services being held there. (And see 280, 91, 31.) 

19. DRAWINGS... Using cartoon illustration of scene from attraction, printed on herald, a contest might be based on coloring of the drawing. Generally designed to appeal to kids, the heralds might be distributed into schools and homes, and at playgrounds. 

Or, illustration might be reproduced in newspaper ad or story, or, even regular newspaper comic strip might be used if it ties in with theatre's attraction in any way, as comic strips sometimes do. 

Merchant could sponsor the contest, and carry the illustration and contest information in his newspaper ad. 

Contestants might be invited to draw in a comic face on a picture of a comic character. . . the face being routed out before printing. 

For newspaper or herald. Similarly, a face could be fully reproduced (with no eliminations), with contestants invited to draw on a comic disguise, whiskers, etc. . . . or a comic body.

Or, contestants might merely be invited to draw subject (the com- • 15 •

plete drawing) as suggested by the attraction . . . as an animal in connection with a jungle attraction. 

20. FILLING STATIONS... Generally strategically located, filling stations are usually great spots for displays, or for streamers or cards.

Chain of stations, or group owned by oil company, might be set by contacting their main office in town and arranging the tieup for all their stations.

Oil change reminder stickers, small gummed labels, might be supplied filling stations well in advance of the showing of an attraction. 

Imprinted copy on stickers is: "Your oil was changed last at (underlined space for miles to be written in). Change again at (underlined space for miles). And don't forget to see (attraction, theatre, play dates)." Sufficient space is provided to write in number of miles when oil is changed. 

21. BOOKMARKS... Not to be overlooked, especially if the attraction is based on a well-known book, specially printed bookmarks can list a suggested reading list of books that are similar to or suggested by attraction story . . . or listing other books by the same author. . . and carrying copy on the attraction. 

Arrangements should be made to place the bookmarks in public libraries and libraries in stores, department stores, book stores, for distribution. School and college book shops and libraries shouldn't be overlooked. 

22. MINIATURE DISPLAYS... Especially adaptable to counters in drug stores and cigar stores and hotel desks. . . miniature standees can be made up from stills, or other small illustrations. 

The stills are attached to compo-board, and cutout (outlined) with cut-awl or mat knife. Space is left below the cutout figures, for lettering in title of attraction and play dates.

Often these miniature standees can be effectively placed in spots ordinarily difficult to get.

Miniature billboards might be made up, after style of billboard, with base, so that the display will stand. Display to be so constructed that small cards can be inserted. Illustration from the press-books might be used... the illustration of the 24-sheet ordinarily carried in all press-books, might be clipped out and pasted to a card, which is lettered and inserted in the "billboard." 

With the edges painted, and attached to display panels, cutouts from stills and illustrations might be used effectively for lobby display. 

23. SALE, SPECIAL WEEK... Tieup with grocery, or drug 

16.

store, or with a city-wide chain of stores might make possible arrangements for a "special week" or special sale, at the store, or stores. 

Perhaps title or theme of theatre's attraction might suggest the tieup. 

Store would use pennants and streamers inside store and in, or on, windows. Tieup copy should be carried in newspaper ads. 

Perhaps a city-wide sales event might be promoted, with cooperation of newspapers, merchants' association, Chamber of Commerce, bus and railroad lines. . . dedicating a special day of special values in honor of the star, attempting to draw business from surrounding territory. Much ceremony might be arranged, streets decorated, costumes (in keeping with the attraction worn); and with transportation lines arranging special schedules, perhaps special fares. 

Attraction or star would, of course, have to be outstanding to justify the civic activity . . . which might be called a "greater (town) day," and tieing in "greatest attraction," or "greatest show season" copy in all publicity. 

24. MIRRORS . . . Artist might letter copy on mirrors in restaurants, confectioneries, soda fountains, barber shops, beauty shops, bars, as well as on mirrors in rest rooms of theatre. Similarly, too, artist might go about town lettering copy on windows of business places (with permission, of course). Artist (possibly a girl) should letter the mirrors during rush hours. . . Some special copy for the cooperating business place might also be lettered on. 

A transparent or unopaqued mirror can be effectively used in many displays. The mirror appears as a regular mirror until light behind it is flashed, when it becomes transparent and it is possible to see through it (display or panel behind mirror, illuminated when light is flashed on, then becomes visible through the mirror). 

For an aquatic display in a window, a mirror edged in sand makes a very realistic lake. Small boats might be placed upon it, reflecting as on water. Mirrors make an effective flooring for a window display where small objects are placed on display. Cutout letters, used in connection with a display, and spelling out a title, laid on a mirror flooring, are reflected, and take on the effect of depth. 

25. NEWSPAPER ADS . . . Generally speaking, three 

"W's" form the basis of any newspaper ads, "Where," "When," and "What". . . and in that order ordinarily. 

The important point of layout is, of course, to make the ad attractive, to make it stand out from the other ads on the page. Proper use of white space is of utmost importance. unless a black re- • 17 •

verse ad is used. Idea generally is to do what the others are not doing, to aim at contrast. Ordinarily, however, to be effective, at least a fifth of the ad space should be devoted to clean white space. 

In laying out an ad, it is a good idea to indent - bringing the outside borders in a half inch or an inch . . . or to set type a half inch or so within the outside border. 

Selling angles and appeal should be the first point decided upon in constructing an ad . . . then selecting illustrations and copy in keeping with it. Even the design of the layout might be suggested by the intended appeal. First question, consequently, is "Just what, in the show is being sold . . . and just what appeal is being used to sell it?"

Selling slant should be given careful consideration, since sometimes even the press-books are wrong in this regard; and communities differ, too.

Important point is that the ladies be considered in the ad appeal. 

Illustrations selected for use should be good ones that are definitely attractive. They should look "in." And copy used in the ad should apply or connect up with the illustrations. 

Headlines or catchlines selected for use should demand attention and carry the reader on to the text. The catchline is the barker for an ad . . . and if it is an efficient barker, it will lure newspaper readers into reading the entire ad. It should tease the imagination, and lead on to copy on the attraction.

Catchline type face is important, as a boldface line or a line set in italics, will often lend emphasis to the words, or contrast effectively with the other type. Try to visualize the appearance of the ad in print.

Simple words should generally be used in constructing copy-words that are easy for all readers to understand, yet words that pack a wallop, a forceful appeal. An ad-writer must have a due regard for brevity, condensing thoughts, and with no words wasted. Copy should sell the intriguing and sensational angles; it should be carefully aimed, with appeal as a target. Hackneyed expressions and generalities should be avoided. Instead of long, tiresome copy, it should be bright, sparkling, to the point. Copy should hint, suggest, tickle the curiosity-it shouldn't tell all. 

Avoid commands as "Don't Miss It;" persuade, instead. Existing season or fad or sentiment might be tied to an ad. 

Ad should not be broken into too many units, as it might become confusing. Double-feature ads should be clearly divided, with space allotment depending on the box office value of the individual at- • 18 •

tractions. Short features should receive the billing they deserve, and properly separated from the feature billing. Prices should be given mention if they are an attraction.

Border-lines should hold the ad together. Generally, black borders that suggest the undertakers should be avoided. It is possible that a distinctive border can be used, one that might become identified with the house.

Other points might include: Acquaintance with limitations of the newspapers, and writing ads within these limitations. Acquaintance with styles of type at disposal at paper (proof sheets might be obtained from the papers). Personal acquaintance of the compositor who sets the ads or "lays out" the paper can prove a very valuable contact . . . in more carefully set ads, in better position in the paper. 

Position given the ad in the paper is important, too; outside columns, above the fold, being preferable position. Ads should reflect an occasional change of pace. Occasionally, a variation in design can lend effectiveness to an ad . . . as use of a “stagger" ad-the columns varying in height, with story matter carried above shorter columns to fill out space; or a "skip the gutter" ad-divided into two separate sections, one section on either page and directly across the fold of the paper from each other. Number of small ads might be scattered through the paper perhaps directing attention to the larger theatre-page ad. Letters and telegrams can be sometimes used as ads. (Also see 1001.) ... 

26. FASHIONS. . . Tieups with stores will be suggested by attraction that stresses style or the gowns that the star wears. Or they might be based on naming of a garment or material after star, or the attraction, as: “(name of attraction or star) gown (or dress, or the attraction. Dresses, prints, hats or shoes. Store to install attractive window displays, possibly buying newspaper space. "Perfect Model" contest might be arranged, offering prizes, perhaps a complete outfit to the winner. Elimination contest might be staged first, girls in final contest modeling the gowns (or bathing suits or sport clothes, or other costumes) ... actually creating a style show as well as a girl contest.

Style show might be presented with store's cooperation . . . either on stage, or having garments modeled in lobby or mezzanine floor of theatre. Dresses, furs, coats, lingerie and (or) bathing suit styles might be modeled. Used as a stage attraction, the promenades of fashions should be interspersed with entertainment features. Style promenade for children might be included. Or a lobby style show • 19 •

might have models promenading among patrons, mounting small platform, spotlighted, where they model the garments. Store should publicize both the fashion show and theatre's attraction in their newspaper ads and announcements.

Wedding scene might be a highlight of a fashion show. It could even be a real wedding, but with all those appearing modeling garments.

Girl "pages" traveling about downtown section can carry large hat boxes which are lettered: "We're delivering these to (star), the best dressed woman on screen, at (theatre) in (attraction).” 

27. TRAILERS... One of the most effective methods of selling coming attractions is, of course, the use of "trailers." Actual theatre patrons are naturally the best potential patrons for a coming show.

Prologues to trailers might occasionally effectively build them up (action, suggested by the attraction presented, on the stage or in theatre box at side of stage, and followed immediately by the trailer), (check "prologue" classification).

Trailers might be effectively cut into newsreels. Brief, singleflash trailers can be used well in advance of showing of attraction, by cutting one in after each unit on the program. Each flash different, and selling a different phase of the attraction. Or flash trailers might name previous hits of stars.

Added emphasis might occasionally be lent a trailer by use of color, bringing up colors in footlights or using light gelatine in front of projectors. ... 

28. VALANCES AND FLAGS Adding great flash to a theatre front, flags and valances in any size, made to order, can be obtained from any one of several companies whose advertisements appear regularly in trade papers. Or they might even be made up locally. Valance extending around canopy beneath outer edge, preferably made of silk, or other cloth, with lettering stitched on, or processed on... ... the lettering not transparent and being silhouetted at night.

Or, valance might be made up locally of oil-cloth or silk, with attraction copy lettered on, or letters sewed on. 

Valances might be utilized to sell individual attraction, or special month, or season, policy, or on outstanding show. Or, special valance might be made up and used for event that occurs regularly. 

Summertime valance might carry cool copy, made up in cool colors. 

Valance might sometimes prove effective, too, over doors, as well • 20 •

as around outer canopy. Flag can be used either flat against building, or from flag-pole extending horizontally from building. Banner can be attached against front of building. Pennants, connected in streamer style, might be used to adorn the front of the building. 

Or to be suspended under marquee. Attraction might suggest their use. (See Photo Section.) 

29. POSTING... Highways and prominent posting locations 

(especially larger paper), should be so situated that they are seen by those coming into downtown section, not leaving it. 

24-sheets should be used for highways and fast thoroughfares, and even 24-sheets should carry a minimum of copy. 

Small paper is wasted where the traffic is fast. Smaller posters are useful where pedestrian traffic and slower automobile traffic might read them. 

Where there's local activity, or interest of any kind, or a location that is the object of attention . . . a spot might be found for a poster. 

Billposters should use plenty of white blanking, so that posting appears clean. And poster locations should be scraped regularly, every third to fifth time they are posted, at least. Date strips should be definitely clear. Old paper should never be permitted to live after the attraction has gone.

Billposter might prevent heavy rains from getting under and washing down paper from the top, by placing a small ledge or a piece of molding across the top. For cold weather posting, a pound of calcium chloride added to each ten gallons of paste will prevent freezing; and in diluting, salt water might be used. 

Windows of vacant stores, and even parts of windows of stores that are in use, offer many valuable spots for lithographing. Flat two's, one's, half-sheets or half-sheet upright streamers, will generally prove most effective for lithographing, though occasionally a large window strategically located will offer an ideal location for large paper, even for an occasional 24-sheet. 

Occasional titles offer possibilities of "teaser" posting campaign ... posting quantity of paper (usually 1's, or 3's or smaller paper) carrying just the title, well in advance, then following up as play dates approach with paper carrying rest of information on picture, theatre and play dates.

Group 24's are occasionally possible and effective. Where several 

24-sheet stands are available together, they might be especially painted, all together, as one unit, and used as a group display on one attraction the reading copy spread out over the several stands. 

Upside down posting might be occasionally adapted to an at- • .. • 21 •

traction title, using a prominent location, posting paper well in advance. Adaptable to any paper, though most effective with big paper. Might be covered with correctly placed poster when play dates of attraction come 'round.

Delayed posting might be occasionally used effectively. Selecting a prominent location, well in advance, one sheet of a 24-sheet is posted, adding one additional sheet to the board each day until the entire 24-sheet is up. Date is then posted over space which was previously occupied by a large question mark. Or just a figure is posted, to one side, as that of a girl, rest of poster blanked in; left some several days, rest of poster is added. 

Group of girls, in shorts or attractive costumes, might be assigned to post a 24-sheet, using a poster panel that is prominently located. 

Proceeding leisurely, they attempt to post the display paper. (And a regular billposter can correctly post a 24-sheet over the panel when the girls have finished.) Similarly, the girls might attempt to post a 24-sheet at ball park, before game begins, when they have a large and interested audience. Or billposter might post a 24-sheet during the game, taking his time so that he extends it through duration of game. 

30. CONTESTS... Newspaper contests, with readers competing for theatre guest tickets, or other prizes, make for reader interest and consequently tending to build circulation . . . and are therefore of value to the paper as well as to the theatre. And, generally illustrated with art from theatre's attraction, they can prove of inestimable value to the attraction.

Contests can add interest to a radio program, too, and draw the attention of thousands of listeners to the attraction. And most contests can be adapted to radio broadcasting. Contest might be sponsored by the broadcasting station; or an advertiser buying time over the station might incorporate the contest into his program. 

Many contests can be adapted to tieups with newspaper's classified page. Space assigned theatre's attraction, calling attention to the contest, might be carried on another page if preferred. 

Contests are effective as cooperative page features. 

Usually, in connection with a contest in which it is possible that a large number of the contestants might submit correct answers, it is best to also require something additional (perhaps another contest angle), in which ability or distinctive originality can be used to select a winner. A brief essay on some subject suggested by the attraction would do the trick. • 22 •

Tickets might be used as prizes, perhaps with cash or merchandise prizes for first winners. The more valuable the prizes, the more interest. Cleverest and neatest entries might be awarded tickets. 

Contests should not be too difficult.

Contests might occasionally be effectively adapted to heralds, programs. 

And, of course, windows, stage presentations . . . every sort of advertising might effectively include a contest. Check "Contests" classifications. 

31. LUNCHEON CLUBS . . . Cooperating with a luncheon club, aiding them in arranging programs or contributing to their activities can prove of definite value to a theatre when theatre needs the club's support. 

Introducing talent in connection with a stage program at a luncheon club is, of course, routine, and, occasionally done, will result in publicity, newspaper stories and word-of-mouth; perhaps the program might be broadcast over a radio station. Papers might use photographs of the entertainers and the officials of the club. 

Charity activities of a club might offer an opportunity for theatre cooperation; perhaps a midnight show to raise funds, or members. selling tickets on a percentage basis.

Club can sponsor the arrival of a star or a show in town, forming a "welcome" committee, at depot or airport. (With possibility of subsequent newspaper stories and pictures.) 

Heralds, or imprinted souvenirs or folders, can be distributed to various luncheon clubs. . . preferably by attractive girls. Arrangements might be made to have night letters sent them, calling attention to booking of attraction, read at meeting. Talks "inspired" by theatre's attraction might be made.

Guest tickets might occasionally be supplied luncheon clubs for attendance prizes, with attraction announcements resulting. 

(See Photo Section.) 

32. RACE, SPEED . . . In connection with auto or horse races (or any kind of races or speed tests), arrangements made to have one of the feature races named after the star of theatre attraction, winner to be presented with trophy (loving cup, etc.) (See Photos.)

Program and newspaper mention might be secured, and announcements at the track might be made. Banners announcing the special "(star) Handicap" should be placed in a prominent spot at the track (in advance). 23 ⚫

Picture of pretty girl presenting the trophy might be planted for newspaper space. If playing stage show, girl featured in it might present the trophy.

Race sheets on sale at newsstands might be rubber-stamped with copy on attraction. Display cards will find an interested audience (on a horse-race story) in places where bets are accepted. 

In connection with auto race attraction, perhaps a race-car can be secured for bally, either running it or parking it about town, or mounting it on bannered truck. 

Similarly blanketed race horse (with small signs attached) can be led about town by lad in jockey get-up in connection with racehorse story.

Newspaper contest based on a race story might feature screen stars or local celebs disguised by artist as racers (with helmet and goggles, and possibly drawn into small race automobiles). Contestants to correctly identify them.

Races or speed contest based on whatever industry or produce the town especially specializes in might be promoted-for "world's championship."

Or theme of attraction, or incident in the story might suggest novel race (such as waiters' or waitresses' race, entries carrying loaded tray... the tray containing milk, with dairy cooperating and buying ad on the event and the fact that they supplied the milk) or other liquid, which is not to be spilled. 

Old car, or flivver race, might be staged, in connection with attraction that in any way suggests a race, or old flivvers. Cars to be allowed but one gallon of gasoline. cars to start from newspaper office (or from theatre, if preferred) at a specified time, following an outlined course, obeying all traffic rules. Race is not a speed race, but rather a contest to determine car that will run the nearest to goal (which must have a course of eighteen or twenty miles between same and start) on a gallon of gas.

Display for lobby, front or window can feature miniature racing cars, attached to parallel belts (which are geared to different speeds), the belts bringing the cars into view across an opening in the display, apparently racing. Or a bicycle wheel can be used, with the "cars" attached. Or, a turntable with attached miniature automobiles might be constructed just within an automobile tire for a tire dealer's window, or for a display in lobby with tire dealer buying newspaper space on the display and the attraction. • 24 •

33. KISS... Using reproduction of lips, supposedly those of star of attraction, and in tieup with druggist, or beauty shop, or chain of drug stores . . . tickets are offered girls whose lips are most nearly like star's. Star's lips are printed in store's newspaper ad or on card or herald (imprinting lips in red) ... with space allowed immediately below star's imprint, for girls to make a lipstick imprint of their own lips. Entries to be sent or brought to cooperating store. 

Small copy instructs the girls to apply generous amount of lipstick before making impression. Most of space on ad or herald devoted to attraction copy. Or, large book might be provided, on a pedestal, as center of display in lobby, or rest room, with girls being invited to register their lips and their names with lips nearest like those of star to win tickets. ... 

If kiss, or lips, are important to attraction, stickers with red kiss. imprint (with attraction title lettered on) can be used for windows, windshields, books, correspondence. 

Orchestras and broadcasting stations might feature a program of "kiss" songs (numbers that include the word "kiss" in the title).

Newpaper or radio contest might ask contestants to “define a kiss.” 

Mirrors at cosmetic counters in drug stores, in ladies' rest rooms, might be decorated with red lips (natural size), copy lettered on mirror asking girls if they have lips like those of the star. 

Quantity of small mirrors might be secured cheaply enough for distribution to office girls and shop girls. Small "kiss imprint" can be stenciled on the glass of the mirrors, and sticker attached to back of mirrors.

Candy kisses can be distributed in small envelopes, imprinted with: "A kiss from (feminine star) (and then into copy on attraction).” 

Attractive girls distribute the "Kisses."

Newspaper contest might be based on identification of reproduced lips of screen stars, with, of course, stars of coming attraction included. 

34. POSTER CONTEST... Arrangements might be made with art school, or art department of school, to have students prepare posters on theatre's attraction . . . with prizes offered for the best, tickets for others. Posters can be used for display in windows; or they might be placed on display as a group in prominent windows. 

Life-size cutout figure of star of attraction might be sent to the school, to be used as a model; or, a girl in costume suggested by the attraction, might pose for students. 

Art class might agree to prepare the poster in theatre lobby... • 25 ·

setting up their easels, and using as a model a girl, in costume, who poses as center of a display on attraction. 

35. SUMMERTIME... Hot weather suggests displays that sell the refreshing, cool enjoyment the theatre has to offer. 

Cool colors: greens and blues and whites. Summer trellis, palms, white lattice work with entwining flowers, boxes of shrubbery, fernssuspended under marquee (and watered daily), summery effect generally. Artificial flowers will probably prove most practical, but climbing vines, gourd and morning glory, can be planted in outside boxes.

A summer garden might be a feature of lobby or sidewalk (if sidewalk width permits). Canvas awnings, beach umbrellas and tables, beach chairs, grass mats. Painted summery scenery can be used for background. Tieup with tea company might arrange free ice-tea for patrons resting themselves in the "summer garden," with good looking girl serving the tea.

Lobby display might feature a miniature waterfall, constructed as the center of a display. The water being returned with a centrifugal pump. Or, if only a small amount of water is used, it might be hooked directly into water supply. Tiein with cool copy and displays selling summer hits. Elaboration of the waterfall can have the water falling down the face of a piece of translucent glass . . . and from behind, lantern slides are projected against the glass . . . which are visible (if there is not too much light) from the front, through the glass and the water. Series of slides might be flashed. Side panels should conceal person operating the stereopticon, which is used during rush hours... at other times blue lights flooding the translucent glass from behind. 

Life-size cutout figure of cooling plant engineer might be used as part of a display with copy: "Doc. (name of cooling plant engineer), the (theatre) weather man predicts perfect weather for (theatre) patrons."

Newspaper might use photograph of local weather forecaster, "starting the plant," tieing in angle that theatre makes own weather, quoting him as predicting an even temperature, cool and comfortable at theatre all summer.

Large thermometer might be used on sidewalk (or in some prominent spot removed from theatre), showing correct outside temperature, with lettering on same calling attention to fact that no matter how hot the thermometer might show it to be, that it's always cool in (theatre). • 26 •

Small thermometers, if available cheaply enough, might be attached to imprinted cards and distributed. Copy is to effect that whatever the temperature outside, cool comfort awaits inside theatre. Most of card space can be devoted to a coming attraction. 

Crushed, then straightened out, cellophane can be used to face cutout letters. Made into cones it resembles icicles ("Ambroid" cement will hold it). Green cellophane can be used as frame coverings for stills and to back up displays where letters are cut out. 

Emphasis might be added to the pure air angle by pointing out in newspaper story that the plant removes enough dirt every day (from the outside air which is drawn in) to raise a small garden of vegetables. 

Display in lobby might feature plant growing in flower pot of dirt ... and panel copy to effect that the cooling plant removed the dirt (from outside air) in purifying the air. The plant might be the basis of newspaper story. 

Valances and flags bearing cool copy can be used to add to attractiveness of front.

Refrigerators present a seasonable opportunity to tieup with local dealers and distributors, staging an exposition of refrigerators in the theatre lobby, with one or all dealers represented and buying newspaper space. Newspaper should cooperate, getting out a special page or section, tieing in theatre attractions and refrigerator copy. The affair could be made coincident with the season's first use of the cooling plant, tieing in this angle with the copy . . . perhaps using a photo of a pretty girl in bathing suit “starting" the plant.

Novel herald for hot weather might be based on "weather warning" idea. Folder type herald should be imprinted on the front page: "Weather warning! Hot weather hints! Be very careful this weather. Important information inside." Inside the folder is the copy: "Be very careful this weather. In case of frost-bitten ears, rub the ears with snow. If the nose freezes, lie down in the snow, dig a little hole, and carefully insert said nose. Frozen tootsies should be put in ice water, well salted, and then rubbed briskly with a coarse towel. And remember to shovel the snow from the walk in front of your house. It is very disagreeable to your neighbors to have to wade through the deep snow piled on your walk. Of course your neighbors do not shovel the snow from their walks either, but you can show them what a big kindhearted guy you are. And will they be ashamed of themselves. . . and let you come over and shovel the snow from their walks, too. Take care to wear plenty of warm clothing this weather. Don't go out in blizzards or snow storms unnecessarily. • 27 •

And guard against falling icicles. And, for entertainment, whatever the weather, see (and into copy on theatre attraction).” 

Heralds selling cool comfort of theatre might be distributed by ice company, with the ice. Announcements might be posted in swimming pool dressing rooms. 

An ancient hot weather stunt is the "attempt" to fry an egg on the sidewalk, using girls from stage show, who proceed to place skillets on the sidewalk, in which the eggs are "fried" (the skillets being previously heated in nearby restaurant). Newspaper flash is necessary to justify the stunt, so photographer should be present, or radio station might broadcast it. 

A Bathing Girl Revue, with department store cooperation, might prove an excellent hot weather attraction, for stage or lobby or mezzanine floor.

A good time in the summer to send heralds around to homes is in the evening when (in residential sections) a great many people customarily seat themselves on their porches. Herald might carry copy: "Why sit on the porch when it's so much cooler at (theatre)... and there's a great show tonight— (and into attraction copy).”

Heralds delivered to those found on porches. Sound truck carrying similar copy might be sent around. 

36. FOOTBALL ATTRACTION... Theatre might go in for football atmosphere in front of the house, placing "goal posts" at either end of marquee, so that they span sidewalk . . . and ruling off sidewalk with white lines after fashion of football field. Panels for sidewalk or lobby might be made up in the shape of a football. 

Barker on sidewalk, with megaphone, should be clad in full football regalia. Or girl "cheer-leaders" might be used out front, costumed in short skirts and "cheer-leader" sweaters. Barker spiels the attraction in rah-rah style. A float on the attraction might feature girl "cheer-leaders," who hand out heralds when the truck stops at intersections.

Football team might be secured to run signals down main street at busy time of day (with motorcycle escort to "run interference" for the team). Name of attraction might be used as the signal to "snap" the ball. One or more of the players might carry title of attraction on his back... or each might carry a letter on his back, which, together (when in correct "formation"), spell out attraction title. Or banner might be carried along. 

Herald can be made up after style of a ticket to an important • 28 •

football game, making attraction copy very apparent, however, after first glance. 

Tieup with department store might feature "All-American"

Fashions... including display material on theatre's attraction in their windows. Newspaper or radio station might conduct contest to select city's "All-American" girl. Could be based on submitted photographs. with football team as judges. Clothing store. dummy, in football outfit, can be used for lobby or window display. 

City-wide kicking or passing "championship contest" might be arranged, perhaps with cooperation of sports editor of newspaper or radio sportscaster... presenting trophy named after attraction to the winner. Might be staged just before a big game.

Couple of girls dressed in football costumes, can travel about town, carrying football on which attraction title has been lettered. 

Copy on their backs reads: "Don't pass... (attraction and theatre)." 

Or, "Follow me to (attraction)."

Miniature "football field" might be used as the center of a window display, using small toy "football players." Ads on attraction can be represented by suspending a toy airplane over the field, extending a "banner" behind it (a piece of lettered ribbon kept in straight-out position behind the "plane" by a wire).

Action shots of oustanding football games of the season might be secured from newspaper for an attention-arresting lobby panel. (See 924.) 

37. NAVY, SAILORS, MARINES... Cooperation of Naval units should be secured in connection with an attraction that pictures Navy activities. Naval officers and Naval Reserve should be invited, parading to theatre, with band or drum corps, if available . . . and carrying: "We're on our way to (theatre) to see (attraction),' banners. Cooperation of Sailors, Sea Scouts, and R.O.T.C. might be secured for parades and opening ceremonies at theatre. 

Theatre front displays, if built up, might feature big guns projecting out over the sidewalk (gun frames made of strips covered with painted signcloth with cutout star in ends of each of the "guns" to finish them off). Matboard frames over stills should be made to resemble portholes. "Battleship Grey" color scheme might be featured. Pennants, life-preservers, navy hammocks can be used. (See Photos.)

Crow's nest might be built atop marquee, with gob, or costumed dummy, in same. Naval searchlights might be used.

Arrangements might be made to use Navy's 1-sheet boards which · 29 ·

they have in most towns and which cooperation they will usually extend, carrying tieup copy. 

Navy recruiting office will station a sailor in theatre lobby. 

Similarly, army recruiting. 

Souvenirs, photos, etc., might be borrowed for display in lobby or windows. Stores should feature "navy blue," together with displays. on the attraction, in their windows. 

Comedy angle might be deck-swabbing contest for kids, with swabbers performing out front.

Store can go along for a complete outfit for girl attending opening night in most becoming sailor style outfit. 

Candy life-savers samples might be secured in quantity from the manufacturer. Inserted in small imprinted envelopes and distributed by girls in sailor costumes. Boys distributing heralds should be costumed, too.

On Navy Day (Oct. 28th), arrangements can be easily made to have sailors parade to theatre as highlight of evening (with newspaper photographers on hand).

Quartet, costumed as sailors, might entertain at night clubs and ballrooms; or a couple of girls in sailor outfits. They present numbers from the attraction (if any) and announcements. 

Patriotic groups should be contacted, as they will probably be interested in the attraction. ...

Special appeal should be made to sailors in seaports via handbills, strategically placed cards, banners. Newspapers with attraction copy imprinted on margin might be distributed to ships. (See 861.) 

38. SHORT SUBJECTS. Silent treatment shouldn't be accorded short subjects. The feature attraction is, of course, of major importance; however, short subjects and individual acts often carry very definite value that theatres can capitalize upon, adding materially to the box office appeal of the show. 

A short subject might appeal to a certain group, or class, or nationality; and if this is so, the attention of these people might be directed to it. Often important stars appearing in shorts have a very definite following.

At the least, short subjects should merit mention in front of theatre, and in all newspaper ads. Occasionally, tieups and window displays are possible. Newspaper and radio mention is often justified.

Playing stage attractions, each individual act or performer carries a definite, different, appeal, adding to the appeal of the show as a · 30 ·

whole. They merit and generally receive individual mention, or billing. Short subjects deserve similar consideration, supplementary, of course, to the feature attraction. 

With show-goers shopping for entertainment, attractive short subjects might be supply just the extra pull needed to draw them in. 

39. EDUCATIONAL . . . Attractions of a definitely educa tional nature should merit support and cooperation of schools and colleges, clubs and organizations of all kinds. 

Screening for superintendent of schools and principals would secure their endorsement, and cooperation in arranging for school children to see the attraction. Special group rate could be made students; and with cooperation of teachers, the tickets might be sold in the schools in advance. Or, teachers might bring their pupils in a body to witness an attraction that carries special interest or educational value. Plans might be worked out for use of school buses (where they are used) in transporting the kids to theatre . . . and, additionally, each teacher might collect admissions from her charges, buying the tickets for them, speeding up handling of the children at theatre. 

Schools and colleges might permit posters to be placed on their bulletin boards, or in school libraries or bookstores. Announcements might be made in classes. Imprinted heralds or blotters might be distributed to students. 

Board of Education might agree to dismiss classes early so that students might attend a special matinee. Essay contest, inspired by the feature and based on it, could be arranged in schools. 

And in selling an educational attraction, in routine advertising the entertainment value should be stressed. Sell the educational features to those to whom they will definitely appeal. (See 281, 324, 479, 603.) 

40. LETTERED RIBBONS... Lettered with title of attrac tions, ribbons might be worn in advance by ushers and house staff. 

They could be small, and attached to lapel; or large, and pinned across chest. (See Photos.)

Waitresses in restaurants, soda fountains, might wear them; also, clerks, cashiers in stores.

Small, imprinted ribbons might play an important part in welcome ceremonies, or in connection with appearance of an important stage star... the small ribbons being worn by welcoming committee, or by members of luncheon club where star makes an appearance. Ribbons imprinted: "Welcome (star).” · 31 ·

41. SHORTHAND . . . Appealing to stenographers and secretaries, or in connection with an attraction that appeals especially to them, these angles can be adapted: Blotter or herald, carrying an inscription in shorthand, and distributed to the offices. Message printed twice, since there are two popular brands of shorthand. Written out by hand, an engraving is made up. reproducing the shorthand. Blotters would prove of most value since they will remain on desks for a longer time. A note, in ordinary type, at bottom of shorthand inscribed herald or blotter might offer guest tickets to first so-many girls phoning in correct translations. Or, perhaps the stunt might be reversed, with the "message" carried in correct English, and with the tickets to go to those sending in best translations into shorthand. (Business 

College professor might serve as the judge.) Most of space is devoted to attraction copy. Idea is also adaptable to newspaper or classified page contest. 

A newspaper ad (theatre or cooperating store) might be headed: "Secretaries, stenographers, we speak your language (and then into shorthand 'message')." Guest tickets offered for the best translations (making the offer and including theatre copy in straight English). "Message" in shorthand about unusual values, at stores and at theatre, might be made the center of a cooperative newspaper page. 

Newspaper could feature a series of scenes from a coming attraction, with the captions cut in in shorthand offering guest tickets for first so-many stenographers, secretaries, students to correctly interpret them. ... 

42. BOAT BALLY Where there's a beach or a much frequented river front . . or where a water regatta of any kind is attracting crowds, a sailboat with sails lettered or with banner attached can be used effectively, cruising near the crowds. serve.

If sailboat is unavailable, a lettered or bannered motorboat will Motion pictures being made of a regatta from a bannered speed boat will assure permission generally for the speed boat to travel about where everyone might see it. 

Or a banner might be placed on a buoy, or diving barge, near the shore. 

43. BICYCLES... Can often be used for street bally. 

Cards might be attached to bikes used by messenger boys, delivery boys-triangular card with grommets in each corner tied into frame of bikes. 

Period story would suggest use of old-time high-wheel bike, or a • 32 •
