tandem bike. Bicycle shop might have one. 

Man and woman might ride the bike, dressed in costume suggested by picture. Or used on comedy, with copy: "Funnier than an old-fashioned bike (and into picture copy).' 99 Bike could be set up solidly atop canopy... or atop new automobile ... with girl in shorts and sweater, or costume suggested by picture, pedaling it. Tickets offered to those guessing nearest correct mileage that a register attached to the wheel will show by the time. that (attraction) arrives in town. Used atop canopy, pedaling of bike can be arranged to revolve display behind bicycle, which spells out name of attraction, or lists names of stars. Could also be adapted to lobby display. 

Bike races for kids at playgrounds might be promoted, with tickets or other prize for winners. Perhaps a bicycle for winner. As a playground feature, additional tickets can be awarded for winners of contests-trick-riding, slow-riding, fancy-riding, balancing, prettiest girl cyclist, etc.

Bike parade could be arranged, with bicycles decorated or lettered. 

Bicycle clubs might make arrangements. 

44. TIME... in different cities of the world at the identical time, would make an interesting window for an attraction that deals with travel or with foreign country, or with time. Telegraph company renting clock service might agree to install a number of clocks, each showing the correct time in some part of the world. Display carries copy: "Here's the correct time the world over .. But in (city) it's the right time to see (attraction).” Clocks about town might be lettered, or stickers can be attached, carrying copy: "It's time to see (attraction).”

Where a definite period of time is important to title or theme of an attraction, cooperating department stores could arrange special sales for a similar duration of time. Or a newspaper contest might be based on contestants' suggestions for best and most enjoyable way to spend a similar period of time in (town). Or what contestants would do if they had only the same number of hours to live. 

45. MAGAZINE SLIPS... Small imprinted slips of paper can be attached to the covers of magazines on the newstands, especially screen fan magazines, the slips carrying copy on theatre's attraction. Or a sticker might be used.

Using imprinted slips (not adhesive), space is left to the right of the slip. Blank part of the slip is folded over, and when slip is attached to magazines, the folded under part of the slip is touched · 33 ·

with paste and attached to under side of the cover-thus avoiding pasting to the front of the cover and defacing it. 

46. USHERS, STAFF... On seating patrons, ushers might hand them a small card, which carries imprinted copy: "Pardon me but as a member of the staff of (theatre) it has seldom been my pleasure to address you personally. However, I have a message for you today that justifies my stepping out of character" (and into copy on attraction, adding that usher felt it his obligation to suggest to those patrons whom he seated, that they plan, by all means, to see the picture).

Exploitation possibilities of attractions might be discussed at staff meeting with often excellent results. Various members could be assigned various attractions on which to work up suggestions. In connection with an important campaign on an attraction, each employee could be asked to come through with three advertising stunts which the individual employees would see through to a completion. 

Employees should be sold on the idea that they can aid business in their contacts with patrons. Since they make the contacts, they naturally make the impression for the theatre. They should strive to be cheerful, courteous, patient, considerate, intelligent. 

47. INTERVIEWS... Interviews with star of theatre's at traction by newspapers are, of course, very valuable. Similarly, radio broadcast interviews can reach thousands of people. Both are important; and any personal appearance of a star or important stage or screen personality must be featured by interviews. 

In connection with a screen attraction perhaps newspaper might "interview" the star of the attraction by submitting a list of questions direct to the star at the studio . . . the questions to be answered in regular interview style (and space being provided on the paper carrying the questions where the answers might be inscribed), newspaper publishing questions and answers exactly as a real interview would be handled. Could be adapted to radio, and handled as an interview, with someone doubling for the star (which is announced). Newspaper readers, or radio listeners, could be invited to send in questions they would like to have included in the interview; best ones used. 

Telephone interviews, via long distance, direct with star of attraction have been arranged in the past, and might possibly be worked out with cooperation of the studio. Or star of stage show could be reached at city played previously to local engagement. 

Such a stunt can prove expensive, and this should be checked in advance. Newspaper cooperating, columnist or critic, or newspaper's · 34 ·

editor conducts the "interview"... conversation of both parties being jotted down for newspaper reproduction; and, too, conversation, questions and answers, might be carried through loud speakers into theatre; or the interview could be the highlight of a luncheon, with guests "listening in" with the aid of amplification. Or broadcasting station could conduct the interview, broadcasting it, or a recording of same.

Newspaper critics might be assembled, perhaps at a luncheon, with call to star (previously arranged) put through, and each newspaper representative permitted to talk to the star for several minutes. 

Telephoto of star at phone might be carried by newspaper. 

Arrangements might be made to have star speak or sing, via long distance to orphans or for some charitable organization (perhaps as feature of a charity show or meeting), and with the charity angle, the cost might possibly be reduced. Newspaper critics should, of course, be present.

Imaginary interview with star of the attraction might be made the basis of a contest for newspaper or radio sponsorship . . . with contestants to submit their imaginary interviews, questions and answers, with prizes for cleverest, most accurate. 

Newspaper writer or movie editor can work up a novel feature by "interviewing" manager of theatre on some subject about which he appears (in the interview) to be uninterested, answering each question (which are carried too, question-answer style), with some information about an important coming attraction, or about theatre's cooling plant (if summer), dismissing subject he is being queried about with as few words as possible.

Local character similar to that portrayed in an attraction might be interviewed for a newspaper story; or a person who is interested in a similar business to that pictured in the attraction. Radio interview might be similarly arranged, possibly from person's place of business, as interviewing a cab driver as he sits in his cab (in connection with a story that features a cab driver). 

48. ANIMATION. . . The value of any lobby or front dis play can be very much enhanced if some movement can be secured. 

Motor-driven, a cutout figure might be made to move, or a display of stills to change, or a series of figures attached to a belt made to pass in constant review. Each attraction or front design should suggest some possible animation.

Generally mechanical, animation might also be secured, however, by using persons, possibly attractive girls, in a display, to create · 35 ·

movement. Lights might be made to change or flash. Panels or scenes can be made to revolve or change. 

Mechanical animation is almost always based on use of an eccentric (a wheel with an off-center drive), with use of worm gears for regulation of speed of motor, or through reduction of gears. (From small gear to large decreases speed . . . and large to small gear increases.) 

Ordinary bicycle wheel can be used to reduce speed. (See diagrams in picture section.) 

In addition to eccentric wheel animation, weights and springs can occasionally be used to "return" the object being animated. 

Rocker arm (rocking part of a display from side to side), animated by a couple of dry cell batteries (or in some arrangements, by house current), can be used to add movement to a display. Can cause a cutout figure to wave an arm, or leg of a chorus girl to kick, or other movement as desired. Several devices are in use, and electrical supply house can supply same. Best idea is to secure a unit intact from an electrical store or drugstore where it has been used in connection with a window display. (Commonly used, many national advertisers send the units out with window displays on their product.) 

Animation might be added to a display, without actual movement: as, a scene painted on a scrim (thin cloth), with another scene behind the scrim which becomes visible (through the scrim) when a light flashes on (illuminating the scene behind the scrim), and thereby changing scenes. Or, using scrim, a cutout figure might be attached directly against the scrim (in front), and behind the scrim, a band or belt, moving around a light, reflects light through perforations in the band against the scrim (as moving stars thrown against the scrim), as background for the display in front. 

Push button, outside a window display, might be so arranged that it animates display within the window when pressed. (Center of display in the window could feature transparent mirror . . . with light flashed behind it illuminating display, which shows through, when button is pressed . . . or stills or display can be placed closely behind cloth or paper, showing through same when light is flashed behind them.)

Simple and easily-done animation will often add a hundred per cent to the attention-attracting value of a display. 

A "motion maker," available for a small sum from the American Display Company of Dayton, Ohio, can be utilized to drive almost every type of animation, and at variable speeds. It is a compact unit that is complete, requiring no additional devices or attachments. • 36 •

49. AIRPLANES AND AVIATION . . . In connection with showing of an attraction that features flying, a display of flying equipment and instruments might be arranged in cooperation with aviation manufacturer or a flying service company at airport. Display is set up in lobby, or as center of an elaborate window display, and possibly used in front of theatre when attraction is shown. (All equipment should be carefully guarded, or locked in show cases to prevent theft.) 

An airline might install an elaborate display, including equipment, maps, photographs. Display, using globe of world, or lighted map, could point out hours by air to different points. 

Plane, on exhibition at flying field, might be lettered with attraction copy, especially if crowd is attracted to field. Copy is lettered in water color so that it will wash off. Or, if plane is not to be flown, small banner might be attached to the side of the ship. 

Similarly, lettered plane might possibly be placed in prominent downtown location, in depot, or hotel lobby, or in other enclosed and prominent place. 

Smaller type plane might be placed in theatre lobby, if size of lobby permits, in advance of attraction. Plane should be roped off so that it will not be tampered with, and should be in charge of attendant. Attraction copy on easel panels. 

In placing a plane on display in theatre lobby, some additional publicity could be secured, when transporting the plane to the theatre, by arranging to have a traffic cop give the pilot a "ticket" for parking his plane in front of the theatre (for a newspaper photograph and novel story).

Airplane might be mounted atop marquee, either borrowing an old plane, or building a replica of one. motor, made to revolve. Sound fication system, supplies the roar. be lighted at night, flickering on and off. Flood lights or beacon lights can be used out front.

Toy airplane might be made up, and made to "fly," for a lobby or under marquee flash. Slowly revolving wheel is set up horizontally, with plane fastened by a string or wire to the edge of the wheel. 

As the wheel revolves, the plane will "fly" in a circle. The "plane" should be lettered, or a miniature "banner" (made from ribbon, lettered, extended by means of a wire) might be attached to its tail. 

Or a toy plane could be animated, for a front or lobby flash, by fastening it to a revolving belt which traverses the display, sending the plane around behind the background after it passes in front · • 37 •

of display. Several planes might be used, (so that one or more are always visible). Sound record can carry airplane roar, using house amplification (with the display or independent of it). "Wind-sock," borrowed from airport, could be set up atop marquee, with attraction title lettered on. Might be kept extended by means of a stiff wire. "Orientator," or "Pilots' Vision Test Machine," or miniature "wind-tunnel" might be secured from airport or plane equipment company for a lobby flash.

Airport atmosphere could be given theatre lobby (in addition to display of flying equipment), by setting up a short-wave wireless operator in the lobby, duplicating, if possible, airport radio room. 

Airport might cooperate in supplying equipment and operator. The set might be tuned in on conversations between airports and pilots in the air.

Theatre's amplification system can be used to "broadcast" phony "messages" to and from pilots (sending the "messages" from front of theatre, or in lobby). Sound effect record might carry roar of airplane for background. Plugs for attraction should be frequently announced. "Messages" might be along lines of "Calling Pilot 24.

Visibility excellent. Land at once and come to (theatre) and see (attraction)."

Pilots may be invited to attend, on opening night of attraction, as guests of theatre. And, if town is terminal for airline, stewardesses, or girl attendants might also be invited. Perhaps newspaper will go along for a group picture of the uniformed fliers in front of theatre. 

Local Junior Aviators can conduct a model plane contest for a trophy named after the attraction. They might parade to theatre for a special morning showing. Generally newspaper-sponsored, the paper should go along for a picture of the Junior Fliers in front of the theatre. "Stewardess" might be made a feature of a lobby display in connection with a coming air epic. Costumed as a regular airlines stewardess, the girl serves tea and cookies (promoted) to patrons, and acts generally as a hostess. Air line might supply the girl if she is permitted to hand out airtravel circulars. 

Map of area traveled in attraction could have stills attached at points where action occurred.

Philatelists might be found who have a collection of airmail stamps, who will loan them for lobby or window display . . . surrounded with display copy and stills on attraction. (They should be carefully • 38 •

safeguarded because of their value.) Prize could be offered, perhaps with cooperation of newspaper's stamp-collecting column, for best display of airmail stamps brought to theatre (the stamps to be placed on display).

Best air photographs or best snapshots of aviation subjects might be made basis of a contest, for lobby or newspaper. Or good photographs from the air could be used for newspaper reproduction, accompanying a feature story on the attraction; or used for lobby flash. 

Newspaper contest could be based on defining of aviation terms. 

Or for best yarn written in aviation language, using flying terms and slanguage. Or for best aviation gag, or joke. Aviation questionnaires, listing questions pertaining to flying for a check-up on knowledge of aviation terms, expressions, etc., might be used as the basis of a herald, or for a newspaper contest. Or quiz could be based on questions pertaining to air history. 

Group of girls may be posed about a new plane, holding large cutout letters, which together spell out attraction title, for a photograph (for newspaper). Or the picture can be used as a lobby display. 

Perhaps arrangements can be made to have announcements read over amplification equipment at flying field, at a time when a crowd is present.

Float might be made up as a plane, and perambulated about streets. Or a midget racing plane might be secured and mounted on a large truck, with the truck dressed up with display panels and banners in float style. Pretty girl wearing flying helmet rides in the plane, hands out heralds.

Experiments and endurance tests and flights of various kinds are constantly being made at airports. Congratulations sent those participating might make a newspaper story; or perhaps a trophy (from the star of theatre's attraction) could be presented. 

Travel windows will cooperate with displays calling attention to air travel and to the attraction. And, of course, displays can be placed in airline offices. (See 706, 603.)

Store tieup could be based on "mileage checks". . . slips handed each patron with purchases. (See No. 589.)

For juvenile appeal, small imprinted paper airplanes might be secured cheaply in quantity for distribution.

Old propeller might draw interest in lobby as part of a display. 

Blades could be covered over with scenes from the attraction. 

Small stick-pins, made up after style of wings pins that most aviators wear, might carry name of attraction; and distributed to · 39 ·

patrons they will be gladly accepted and worn. Or they might be used as prizes for radio contest or in connection with kiddie club contests.

History of transportation, from prairie wagons to latest planes, would make an interesting newspaper feature. Or an essay contest arranged in schools could be based on the subject. Perhaps with the aid of miniatures or photographs, a window or lobby display might be arranged. Perhaps cooperation of a museum might be secured. Travel agency should be glad to lend their windows. 

History of flying, "inspired" by attraction, and building up to it, might be made a newspaper feature. 

Department stores featuring toy planes should cooperate with window displays, also permitting display panels in toy department. 

Optical store might emphasize necessity of good sight in flying, going along for window display of goggles and photographs on attraction.

Aviation story magazines on stands reach potential patrons, and small stickers with imprinted copy can be attached to the covers. "Air Day," or "Aviation Week" might be promoted with sponsorship of a civic club. Proclamation of Mayor could start it off. Airlines and airport should lend their support. Broadcasts might feature crack pilots and airline officials. Attraction title can be worked into all stories and announcements. 

If newspaper has an aviation editor, he should be invited to screening or opening night of attraction. His technical review will be appreciated by his readers. 

Night club or dance spot might present an Aviation Number . . with girls dressed in "aviation" costumes.

Anything new in the way of airplane development or construction, receiving more than ordinary attention, would be especially effective for tieup purposes.

Flight maneuvers over city by group of planes, perhaps an army squadron, might possibly be arranged in honor of opening of attraction with subsequent news stories. ...

Old parachute could be used out front, perhaps suspended above marquee. Dummy figure might "ride" it. Parachute, opened, will make an excellent background for a window display. Or man on street, costumed as an aviator and wearing a 'chute can carry sign on his back: "I just bailed out to see (attraction)."

Air picture offers natural opportunity for radio dealer tieups, featuring ads and windows displays that use illustrations from the · 40 ·

attraction, building on the angle that both radio and airplanes span distance, cheat time. Clocks, too, can be tied up on a similar angle. 

50. BEAUTY CONTESTS... Might be handled as a straight newspaper feature, with girls submitting photographs to the paper; and with the contest "inspired" or "suggested" by theatre's attraction, or described as a search for a girl similar to attraction star. 

Local artists, or orchestra leaders can serve as judges. 

Or, the contest might be handled as a stage presentation (possibly with newspaper sponsorship). The contest, in keeping with theatre attraction, or intention in staging it, might be a "Bathing Girl Contest;" or a "Perfect Girl Contest;" or just a straight beauty contest, with the girls appearing in evening gowns. Contest, too, could be limited to blondes, or redheads, or brunettes (as suggested by an attraction or star); or, a winner from each type might be selected.

With newspaper sponsorship, cooperating merchants, who buy newspaper space on the event, can be each "represented" by a girl appearing in the contest. Girls wear ribbons on which names of the various business places have been lettered; however, the ribbons are discarded after the initial promenade, and before final judging. 

Winners decided by vote of judges, or by applause. Judges should consider beauty of face and figure and personality. Title of "Miss (city)" handed the winner, together with a loving cup (from star of a coming attraction), and gifts from the various cooperating merchants; or other prize; perhaps a trip.

With fifteen or twenty girls selected in elimination contests in advance (if in connection with an attraction), they might appear as guests of night-spots and prominent places about town. They could appear in stores (possibly parading styles or bathing suits), inside store or in store window (the store buying newspaper space on the stunt). They might be photographed (for newspapers) at beaches.

College or school might sponsor and stage a beauty contest (with trophy from star of theatre's attraction . . . and with subsequent newspaper stories and pictures). With such a contest based on photographs, perhaps arrangements can be made to have star of a coming attraction act as judge, sending the photos on to him. 

A contest can be tied into some other drive or special event, as, in connection with a "Harvest Month," selecting a “Harvest Queen.”

Contest held on stage, or selection might be decided by votes distributed with purchases by cooperating merchants, and at theatre; votes, to be clipped, also being carried in columns of the newspaper. · 41 ·

Paper also carries daily standings of the entries. Votes to be "cast" at theatre, with attractive receptacle provided as part of a display panel. Stores pay for the "vote tickets" they use.

Photographer should be tied into girl contests to make photographs of all contestants, the pictures being placed on exhibition in his windows, and in theatre lobby. Girls should all be photographed in similar type costumes.

Additional angles for girl contests include competition based on most perfect back, or most beautiful hands, eyes, hair, legs, or lips. (See No. 619 and No. 659.) 

51. EYE-TEST... Herald is set up in graduated type, after style of regular eye-test chart used by oculists, headed: "(Star) 

Eye-Test"... and continues, "If you can read this . . . you'll learn about one of the most entertaining shows in a decade (and into copy on attraction)." First line of type is quite large, final line is smallest possible; length of lines becomes shorter with each decrease in type size, same number of words being used in each line regardless of type variation (adding to resemblance to optometrist's eye-test chart). 

52. GIRL AND CUTOUT LETTERS... As center of a dis play, for lobby or window flash, attractive girls, in costumes or bathing suits, place cutout letters on a panel display, spelling out the attraction title. Or, they might spread them across on the floor. 

Jumbling the letters at first, they rearrange them so that they correctly spell out the title.

Letters are not placed in immediate sequence, first letter being placed, then the last letter, then others filled in at random until the entire name is correctly filled in. Vacuum sweeper could be used in connection with display, attaching it behind cloth background . . . and letters adhering to the cloth when girl places them there (due to suction of vacuum). After placing letters correctly, vacuum sweeper motor is shut off and letters, released, naturally fall to floor; with the stunt then being repeated. Girl could clown the stunt, turning to take a bow as she finishes placing the letters... with the letters then being released. She can include a display of stills in her routine, changing the stills (mounted and on an easel) each time she goes through the routine. 

Cutout letters might be adapted to a billboard display, securing use of a prominently located billboard panel. Attraction copy is lettered against the panel in advance . . . leaving, however, the title space empty. Later, on busy day or opening day of attraction, several costumed girls, working on a platform (sufficiently large and · 42.

safely constructed) which has been built in front of the billboard, attach letters against the panel which spell out attraction title. 

After attaching the letters, they are taken down, and the stunt repeated periodically. Advance copy on panel should be designed to arouse curiosity.

Using small cutout letters (cut from compo board, or other light board, and painted), a couple of costumed girls might travel about town, periodically spilling the letters on the sidewalk (on prominent corners), and then proceeding to rearrange them so that title of attraction is spelled out, together with star's name. The letters might be carried in some container suggested by the attraction, or in a small case which is lettered with catch-lines on the show. 

53. STREET SPANNER Perhaps arrangements can be made to stretch a banner above and across the main street. Okay of city authorities will generally be required. The banner is made secure to ropes at top and bottom. 

Or, a light net (tennis net will serve) might be used, with banners attached to the net; or letters cut from oil cloth, or several smaller banners may be attached. Or cutout star designs. 

Or it may be possible to stretch a steel cable across the street and suspend individual letters spelling out the name of the attraction, the letters outlined with neon, or with globes, for a night-time flash. 

The individual letters might be made from strips of wood, with sockets wired in; and because of weight, cable and letters must be definitely secure.

Using a cable across street, an unique display would feature a cutout life-size figure of a man, or girl, in wire-walking position. 

Banner, heavier than the cutout figure, extends below the cable, with figure riding atop wire, heavier banner portion balancing the display and keeping figure upright above wire. Framework holding banner and figure together is carried on either side of the cable, preventing possibility of figure or banner slipping off cable. 

A banner or display might be kept constantly moving back and forth across street, via cable . . . as a cutout figure of a dirigible, with banner attached beneath. 

54. WINDOW CARDS... Affording an opportunity to economically secure display space in many windows, window cards are definitely effective if the copy is brief and the illustration arrests interest.

Large or small, tall or wide, card layout in any proportion might · 43 ·

be used. A long narrow card, such as the circus uses, sometimes will receive preferred window space. 

Cards might be bent in center in placing, standing alone in windows. 

Or they could be attached to glass, or to backing in window with gummed paper. Or a cardboard easel back can be attached behind them.

In printing cards, if using a border, over-printing two colors, several inches wide, around edge of card, will give the effect of a frame. 

Where cards are used regularly in set locations, they can be more effectively displayed in frames. Also, merchant accepts the card then as routine. 

In addition to use in windows, cards might be placed inside business places, in check rooms, rest rooms, waiting stations, in and on cars and buses, in dance spots and night clubs, and attached to light poles up and down the street. 

Cards for special locations should be specially lettered, with stills attached. The more attractive the card, the better the chances of its landing in an important window. 

55. SMELLING SALTS . . . For distribution in connection with thrill dramas, small bottles of "smelling salts" can be made up, securing a quantity of small vials from a wholesale druggist, placing a few grains of coarse ice cream salt in each bottle, then adding a few drops of ordinary ammonia. 

Small stickers are attached, carrying imprinted copy: "Smelling salts... just in case you can't stand the thrills in (attraction)." 

56. ROADS, HIGHWAYS . . . Posters might be placed advantageously on approaches to city. Or permanent displays might be designed to catch the eye of out-of-towners, driving into town. City limits would be an ideal spot for a permanent panel, either carrying painted institutional copy, or a posted 24-sheet or 

6-sheet. "Welcome" copy could be carried. 

Use of reflecting glass will draw added night attention along busy highways, the reflectors catching the lights of automobiles and outlining the letters at night.

Printed cardboard signs on a coming attraction could be attached back-to-back to fences and cross-fences along the roads leading into town. Type on the cards should be large, bold and brief. 

Message might be divided over a series of small panels, placed consecutively along highway, so that they might be easily read from cars passing at high speed. 

57. RURAL... Smaller town newspapers will often publish a · 44 ·

story sent them on theatre's attraction without charge, if a pair of guest tickets are sent along with the story.

Imprinted heralds or postcards can be mailed all persons on rural routes, merely addressing them to "box holder" (arrangements being made at postoffice). Heralds might be distributed in surrounding smaller towns, and in rural schools. 

Postcard sent rural routes could serve to entitle holder to special reduced price on certain day. Maybe merchant's ad on the card will pay part of the cost. 

Window cards might be sent station agents or postmasters in various towns within drawing radius, together with guest tickets, and request that they place the cards on display in some prominent spot in town. 

See No. 585. 

58. STAR PHOTOGRAPHS... Star stills, or reproductions, used for distribution, might have attached to each photograph a small imprinted slip which carries copy: "See me in (attraction and theatre)." Slip to be attached to back of photo and folded over face of photo (so that it is not defaced and could be framed). 

Store handling fan magazines can give away a photo with each magazine sold. Drug store or soda fountain can present a photograph with each sundae. Displays being placed on counter, in windows, and perhaps mirrors might be lettered. “(Star) Night," at night club could feature presentation of the pictures to patrons. 

Stills (with imprinted ad on reverse side) can be given with any commodity in any kind of tieup . . . restaurants, laundries, shoe stores, cleaners, department stores, etc. 

59. ARTIST... Painting photo of star of attraction, and set up in a prominent window or in lobby, artist will attract much attention. He might use, as a model, a cutout display or a threesheet display panel, which carries copy on the coming show. 

Or, advertising or title of attraction might not be attached to the "model" but to the display which the artist is painting. 

Girl, in costume suggested by the attraction, could be used as a model, posing on a pedestal which is made the center of a display panel on the show.

Those watching the artist would be invited to leave their names, and completed painting to be presented to one of them. (See Photos.) 

60. PAINTED SIDEWALKS Adding attractiveness to a front at any time, and a "natural" for hot weather is the white · • 45 ·

sidewalk. It's cool appearing. Traffic white paint is used, and sidewalk is painted at night, being roped off until paint is dry (with marquee lights kept up as long as ropes remain up). 

Checker-board effect can be used, with green and white, or other color combination. Or other design.

Title of coming attraction might be lettered in huge letters across sidewalk in front of theatre, for an effective flash. Or a giant painted arrow, aiming across sidewalk, toward box office, might carry attraction title. 

61. COMEDY PHOTOGRAPHER .. Couple in costume suggested by attraction, or dressed as country couple, travel about downtown section with comedy photographer. Couple poses on sidewalk, and "photographer" goes to great trouble to set up his camera and get the couple properly posed. Then, when sufficient attention has been attracted, he throws camera cloth forward over camera, revealing copy on theatre's attraction. Then on to another spot. 

62. LETTERED BRICKS... Men, or girls, in appropriate costume, are supplied with a set of lettered bricks. . . the bricks, together, and in proper sequence, spelling out name of theatre's attraction (blank bricks being used for spaces).

Beginning with the bricks some distance from theatre, they line the bricks up on sidewalk so that they spell out the title. then one brick is taken (from end away from theatre) and placed at other end (the end towards theatre). Then next brick similarly. Results in a jumble of letters until bricks reach proper sequence again, when stunt is stopped for several minutes to permit those whose curiosity has been aroused to read. Then beginning again, always working towards theatre. 

63. LETTERED UMBRELLAS . . . Attention getters any time, lettered umbrellas are especially effective in rainy weather. 

Might be lettered (in oil), “Rain or shine, see (attraction and theatre)." Umbrellas might be carried in rain by raincoat-clad girls. 

Lettered parasols present an easy and effective way of getting advertising into a street bally, or into a parade . . . perhaps with good-looking costumed girls carrying the parasols. 

Man wearing a slicker and carrying a lettered umbrella, could stand on sidewalk in front of theatre, or in prominent location, on sunny day, enjoying his own private rain . . . the rain being arranged through use of a hose with spray attachment which extends over edge of marquee, shooting down towards the curb line, or through small · 46 ·

rubber hose that extends up umbrella handle and out through sprinkler nozzle at top. 

Umbrella carries "Rain or Shine" copy. 

64. PARADE... Everybody loves a parade . . . and a parade will command their attention when nothing else will. 

Theatre can arrange its own parades in connection with an attraction, or can participate in other parades. Where an important crowd-attracting parade is scheduled locally, several ushers could be sent out along the parade route, in advance of the parade, carrying banners on which theatre copy is lettered. And, of course, parades might be "tailed" . . . bringing up the rear with a bannered truck or float, or perhaps merely a large banner. 

A band is important to lead a parade. Costumed girls would follow the band carrying banners; or each girl carrying a cutout letter, which, together spell out title of attraction and theatre name (letters can be attached to strips to keep them definitely in line and in order). Or automobile dealer could supply a group of new cars, with girls riding on fenders, and each holding a cutout letter. Cooperating business places might include floats or bannered cars in the parade. Any unusual car or truck or float that might be available could be bannered and included. Group of motorcycles can be arranged, through cooperation of motorcycle clubs, as an escort. Groups of costumed girl skaters or cyclists might be secured to travel along with the parade. Motorcycle police should lead the way.

Airport cooperation might supply a group of planes to fly over the line of march, forming an aerial escort. Serpentine may be distributed in advance to upper office windows along line of march, attached sticker carrying copy, asking that it be saved for the parade, giving time. See "parade" classifications. 

65. MONEY WRAPPERS... Paper or cellophane strips or bands, cut exact size to fold completely around paper money, the ends overlapping to paste down center of reverse side, are imprinted, "A million dollars worth of entertainment (and into attraction copy)." Or, wrapping four one dollar bills, the slips are imprinted, simply: "$4.00 in change. Thank you, and may we suggest that you see (coming show)."

Cashier attaches the slips around paper money in her leisure time, handing the bills out in change in advance of showing. 

66. PHONOGRAPHS... A couple of good looking girls, carrying a portable phonograph and wearing lettered ribbons might stop on street corners and in prominent spots playing records of hit tunes from attraction, and distributing heralds. They can visit · 47 ·

restaurants, or other places where crowds gather. Phonograph is placed on a folding camp stool which they carry along. 

In connection with an attraction which does not feature song hits, any popular record might be used, with card on phonograph carrying copy: "Playing a gay tune... to call your attention to a gay romance (and into attraction copy)."

Exploitation recordings, sometimes available on an attraction, can be used effectively. 

Phonograph might be set up in lobby, as center of a display, with attendant playing hit tunes from a coming musical. 

Where restaurants, other places, feature coin-in-the-slot phonographs, recordings of song hits from attraction might be included among those to be selected from. Card within the machine (and visible) or attached to its face, calls attention to the song hit, and the attraction.

Phonographs might be used to add voice to displays of various kinds, lobby or out of doors. With speakers placed behind the display, a motor-driven turntable carries the recording, sending it through amplification. Record repeater can be used to keep it playing continuously. 

See No 383. 

67. OVERSIZE PASSES. . . Where a number of passes are used in advertising an attraction, as for posting purposes, oversize passes could be specially printed and used. Made 22"x28", or thereabouts, and printed on light cardboard, they carry plenty of large copy on attraction as part of the layout, and possibly a cut. And they carry the line in large type: "Not Good if Folded." Should be made good for one certain day. They will make a great flash as they are brought to the theatre on the set date. 

Gigantic pass (carrying attraction title) might be "delivered" to

Mayor with newspaper photographer present for a picture. 

68. CLUB AND INDUSTRIAL PUBLICATIONS...A check up on fraternal, club and industrial publications might reveal new outlets for publicity. They might go for stories, pictures; and possibly without cost, or on a pass-exchange basis. 

Occasionally industrial publications for public distribution can reach many people, as a folder to be distributed on street cars or buses, or other transportation system. 

Newspapers often print weekly publications which reach their advertisers and prospective advertisers. And they will often use scene-cuts, especially girl pictures. · 48 ·

69. RADIO CELEBS . . . Arrangements might be made to have local radio celebrities appear at theatre, in person, week in advance of opening of attraction. Upon being introduced, they say a few words about the coming show (a different "guest" celebrity each evening). They could do a song from the coming attraction, or dedicate one to it. They might be presented on stage, or introduced from lobby, perhaps as feature of a lobby broadcast. 

70. FRAMES . . . Stores with displays of picture frames will often use attractive star stills in the frames. 

Small sticker, or carefully lettered card carrying copy on attraction can be placed in the corner of each still. 

Jewelers, kodak stores, department stores, photographers, ten cent stores, handle frames. 

71. ARM-BANDS 

As an effective method of getting advertising into football games, or other games where crowds gather, imprinted paper arm-bands might be distributed to entering crowds. 

Arm-bands carry copy (for instance): "Beat (opposition team)”. . . and then, in smaller type: “. . . and go see (attraction) at (theatre) after the game."

Printed on bright colored paper, the bands are distributed with an attached paper-clip, so that they can be fastened around arms. 

If several attractive girls attach the bands as crowds enter, the bands will be better received.

Newsboys and house staff might wear the arm-bands. 

72. DRINKS... A soda fountain tieup is an old reliable, but still effective stunt. A special soda or sundae is named after the star, or the attraction; and display cards placed behind the counter call attention to the special. Cards should also be placed in windows. 

And windows and mirrors behind the counter could be lettered. 

Merchant may mention the special in his newspaper ads. 

Bars might feature a cocktail named after the attraction, or dedicated to its star.

Added angle would be announcement that checks bearing certain listed numbers would receive a free sundae or a guest ticket to see attraction.

If attraction suggests, a small folder herald, to be distributed by a cooperating drink-spot, might feature a number of cocktail recipes. 

Front cover is imprinted: "Special (attraction) Cocktail Recipes," ad is imprinted on back cover. 

73. SHOES... Shoe store can name a shoe after attraction, or star of attraction; as: "(Star) Sandals," installing a · 49 ·

Ad- window display which includes theatre panels on attraction. ditionally, store might buy newspaper ad or radio announcements. 

A Cinderella's Slipper stunt might be worked with cooperation of shoe store... placing small size slipper on display in lobby, as center of display on attraction (mate to the shoe being placed in store window, panel directing attention to the shoe at theatre). Slipper is fastened securely, and is represented as being similar in size to that worn by star or one of the beauties appearing in a coming attraction. 

Store to present pair of fine slippers to first girl whose foot the slipper fits perfectly. 

74. CAR FOR SALE... Cards, (about 11x14 in size), imprinted: "For Sale... must have money to see (theatre's attraction)," are placed on windshields of automobiles (with owners' permission) especially those cars on display on used car lots. ...

Or, words: "This car not" might be added in small type above large words "for sale,” . . . and then the copy: "We will need it to drive to (theatre) to see (attraction).” 

75. FLOATS... Designed as suggested by the attraction, a float might be constructed around a truck, or truck trailer; or float could be constructed over the stripped chassis of an automobile. 

Sides should be paneled or bannered. Attractive girls can be used to adorn the float, in costumes as suggested by attraction. 

An elaborate float can be built over a flat-bed street car, touring lines at rush hours.

Floats can be illuminated for nighttime flash, using flood lamps or neon outlining.

Float should be equipped with a public address outfit, over which records might be played, as it travels about town. If in connection with a musical, the numbers would be those from the attraction. 

Or radio can supply music for the float if no special numbers are desired. Announcements on attraction would be cut in. 

If in keeping with attraction, the girls used aboard the truck might be dancers or singers, and as the float travels about town, it stops at prominent locations, where the girls go through a brief routine of song and dance numbers. Microphone to be used by singers and for announcements of attraction. (See Photos.)

Miniature Grass mat could be used to cover the bed of truck. float, using a small Austin automobile, might prove effective. 

Tractor drawing a float will add to attention value. 

Floats should select their routing so as to reach greatest crowds "making" business sections at noontime, or whenever crowds · 50 ·

are on streets . . . arriving at factories as employees are leaving . . and appearing at schools as they are dismissed. 

76. GUMMED LABELS... Or stickers, can be often used to good advantage.

They can be attached to packages, and sacks in stores, paper napkins in restaurants (small ones used), soap in hotels, matches, automobile windshields, windows. They can be attached to mirrors in eating places, rest rooms, and in bath houses at swim pools. 

Stickers might be attached to local outgoing letters. 

Photographs of stars might be printed up after style of postage stamps (though slightly larger), adding star's name and attraction title. Most effective if special engraving is made up, using clear still of star, with lettering added. 

Can help in any 

77. CHAMBER OF COMMERCE 

problem, and generally are glad to aid. Membership in the association, and close cooperation with the organization will prove a valuable investment.

The Chamber of Commerce can assist in putting over special weeks, or help in arranging welcome festivities for a star or stage show. 

They might aid in lining merchants up on a city-wide stunt, or special sales day, in connection with an attraction. Live mailing lists can be supplied by the association. Convention information is always available there. 

78. GRAPHOLOGY... Mr. Webster defines graphology as: 

"The art of describing character from the handwriting." 

Cuts of the handwriting of stars being made, newspaper offers tickets to persons most accurately or most interestingly describing the star (their character, habits, etc.) from the handwriting. Photo of star illustrates the newspaper story. Or the contest can be adapted to an ad. A fountain pen would be a natural first prize; stationery store might present the pen to the winner. 

Studio might supply a note from screen players for use. Stage show star might be contacted at town to be played previous to local engagement. 

Another angle would be contest for best signature suggestion for star, contestants submitting signed names.

Or, a "message from star," in his handwriting, asks readers to see how closely their handwriting resembles that of the star. 

Perhaps handwriting expert, or graphologist (costumed as an Oriental, or as attraction suggests) can be secured . . . who analyses patron's handwriting gratis in theatre lobby. He would have them · 51 ·

ENCYCLOPEDIA EXPLOITATION 

O F write name of a coming attraction (display panel carrying this copy) for a handwriting specimen. 

79. BALLROOMS AND NIGHT CLUBS ... Can dedicate a certain evening to star of attraction... naming and advertising the dance as "(name of star) Ball." If in connection with stage show, star and entire company should be present. Imprinted photos or stills might be presented to those attending. Perhaps dance spot will buy newspaper space announcing the event. They might make announcements on their radio time. Atmosphere of the ballroom can be made appropriate to theatre attraction. 

Dance contest (for couples) at a ballroom might have a trophy named after star as a prize. Trophy placed on display at ballroom several weeks in advance. 

Display panels can be placed in dance spots. 

Floor show might be named after theatre attraction . . . and if night club produces its own shows, perhaps it can use theme suggested by theatre attraction or its title . . . giving the attraction program credit or announcements.

Dancer or singer might feature a number "inspired" by theatre program, or named after it—a sailor number if the picture is a navy epic; or a jungle dance in connection with jungle attraction. 

Night club's entertainers might present the number, or theatre might supply dancers. Dance spot might give the event billing in newspaper ads, perhaps using a photo of the girl in costume. "Movie" ball might have guest tickets offered to those coming dressed as a screen star, or for those most nearly resembling star of theatre's attraction. Or they might be dressed in costumes suggested by the attraction.

Dance programs might be supplied ballrooms or dance places. 

Made up in card or folder form, the "program" carries spaces for names of dance partners to be written in, with special dance underlined as dedicated to star of theatre's attraction. Or one of the musical numbers from attraction might be especially featured, and so noted on the program. Tieup copy printed on front of the "dance program," ad on reverse side. "Pass-out checks" are often used by ballrooms (readmitting guests who wish to leave the dance before it is over). These checks, (small cards) might be supplied dance places, well in advance of showing of attraction, imprinted: "(Name of ballroom) pass-out checks,' and then devoting most of space to theatre's attraction (or theatre ad might be imprinted on reverse side of the card). 99 · 52 ⚫

80. TALENT TOUR... Float (see No. 75), might be loaded with talent, singers, dancers, girls in costumes, and sent on a tour of neighborhoods; or of the surrounding towns and territory. 

Stopping in each town, and neighborhood center, the entertainers run through a routine of entertainment, using song hits from theatre's attraction (if any), and including attraction announcements. Girls distribute heralds or souvenirs to those attracted when float makes a stop.

Amplification equipment should be added to truck, for use of announcer and entertainers.

Musical accompaniment should be included for the singers, dancers —perhaps an accordionist; or a string trio; or perhaps the attraction will suggest a certain type of music. Records might be played. 

Elaborating on a tour of surrounding towns, a motor cavalcade might be arranged, automobile dealer cooperating to include floats or bannered automobiles or trucks. Radio stations can cooperate by announcing the schedule of towns visited, perhaps dedicating a program to the individual towns, or sending along a mobile short-wave unit. Newspaper might sell cooperative ads to stores.

Band should be included (costumed, perhaps as suggested by attraction), alighting from cars when business sections are reached, and leading a parade. Bathing girls, or girls in costumes, riding in the cars, take places on fenders, or hand out heralds along the line of march. Stopping in center of town, the band plays a concert, entertainers are introduced, heralds distributed; then on to the next town. 

Elaborating on the type of transportation used, a special bus might be arranged in a tieup with a transportation company. Or even a transport plane might be used. Properly bannered, the bus or plane would include in its tour all towns within a drawing radius. 

Entertainers (mostly attractive girls), would present a brief routine of entertainment in each town. Welcome ceremonies arranged in each town should include greeting by Mayor, parade, possibly to a luncheon club as guests and entertainers. Automobile dealers in each town might arrange the parade having cars meet the bus or plane and carry the entertainers to business section of town (and returning them). Newspapers in towns should use photographs of the troup; and visit should be well publicized in advance. Local 

Chamber of Commerce cooperates in arranging the tour, perhaps promoting simultaneously a goodwill tour of local business men; their contact with Commercial clubs in other towns will aid in securing advance notice on the tour. • 53.

Amplification equipment should be carried along, for use of entertainers and for announcements. Using plane, perhaps a group of local fliers might also visit the different towns, forming an "air cavalcade;" or local fliers in each town might present an aerial "welcome." Automobiles would accompany a special bus used in a "talent tour." (See Photos.) 

81. CUTOUTS... Enlargements from photographs and illus trations, painted figures, or lithographs might be mounted on compo-board, and then the figures cut out. These figures might be used to good advantage in connection with lobby displays, front panels and windows.

Cutouts can be coated over with colorless varnish or shellac, if they are to be exposed to weather, but using cheapest quality varnish for back of cutout. Edges might be painted. 

Specially made-up life-size enlargements, or cutouts, might be used in advance of an attraction in the theatre, spotting them in various poses in every available lobby location. Small lettered card might be attached to each cutout, carrying copy: "He's on the way!" If the star is especially well-known no further copy might be required, though title of attraction can be added. In connection with a girl show, or a musical, life-size figures of girls might be used ... either painted figures, or enlargements from photographs, or lithograph cutouts.

Occasionally costumes on cutout figures can be effectively touched up with flitter, applying glue or shellac, and then sprinkling with metallics.

Cutout figures might be animated, by separating the figure into several over-lapping sections, connecting same so that desired movement might be secured. Using lithographs in creating an animated figure, more than one lithograph would be used, so that different parts of the figure overlap. Moving parts generally are attached by a single pivot, so that movement can be secured. . . . perhaps a wriggle to a dancing figure; or other movements. 

Manual training department of a school might be willing, for experience and a few passes, to make up a number of cutout figures, made to design, which are painted and lettered and used for display, or street decorations.

Cutout life-size figures might be made up with strip of wood extending at bottom, made to fit into holes in sidewalk curbings which are generally there for flag-poles. Cutouts might be placed back to · 54 ·

back against the strip to which they are attached. Or they could be wired against light poles.

Life-size cutout figure of a girl, "dressed" as a page, or an usher, might be used in theatre to "direct" crowds. . . the figure being placed so that it points (across self) towards direction patrons are to go. Or figure might hold a frame which is changed each show and carries caption, "Next attraction." (See 34.) 

82. BENEFIT. . . In the event of some local need, or of the public's attention directed to some poor local person who needs a lift in a financial way, a special fund might be started in newspaper, in the name of star of theatre's attraction.

Star's donation, together with that of theatre and theatre employees, turned over to newspaper to start the fund, to which readers are asked to contribute.

A stunt that will break page one if the paper goes for it, besides creating lots of goodwill if handled diplomatically. 

And, of course, in the event of some great need, a benefit show should be arranged, with receipts to go to special fund. Might be set for midnight, or morning, and should be worked out with newspaper cooperation. Film exchanges should supply old film gratis, and talent might be promoted for stage. Staff services would be donated. In connection with a morning matinee, if food is needed, an article of food might be accepted as admission. 

83. SONG COVER DISPLAY... for lobby or front, or for float .. duplicating, in very large size, the sheet music cover of number featured in the picture. 

Several openings placed diagonally up front of "cover" are large enough for a person's head to be seen through, and singers appearing behind the openings, introduce song numbers from the picture. Back of the singers is plush or painted background. Piano, accordion, or guitar, might supply the accompaniment. Could be adapted to window display, using public address system to get the music to the outside. (See Photos.)

During hours when the talent is not appearing, the holes in the display panel can be covered with painted heads of the stars. 

Large reproduction of a sheet music cover makes an excellent background for a window display. 

84. BANDS... Parades, grand openings, any event of importance, can be made more effective by the addition of a band. 

Band on bannered truck, playing song hits (if any) from an attraction will win attention. Musicians might be costumed as sug- · 55 ·

gested by the show. The truck cruising about town, can stop at prominent locations, playing a brief "concert." Perhaps truck can carry sound equipment, and other entertainers, singers, dancers. 

Girls might alight and distribute heralds when truck stops. 

Band might play on over sidewalk balcony or on top of a marquee, somewhere about town, playing number from show, or one suggested by the attraction, then permitting lettered banner to unroll. 

85. STILLS... All stills should be carefully checked before outlining a campaign. They can often suggest many good ideas. 

Star stills, available on pictures, or specially posed in connection with stage attractions, offer many natural tieups. Merchants or business places might use the stills in their ads in newspapers, or for tieup displays in their windows, in connection with sale of some object or service shown or suggested in the picture. Sports goods store would use a still showing star swinging a golf club; or a cleaner will use a still of a girl in a beautiful gown. Mention made of attraction wherever still is used; or tieup copy suggested by attraction might be used. And, mats or cuts made from the stills are often available. Prospects include: Cleaners, laundries, bakers, beauty shops, furriers, radio dealers, furniture stores, in fact, any business place that buys newspaper space. 

Occasionally, studio might arrange to supply a specially posed still if it can be used to command sufficient attention to make it worthwhile. Photo of star reading copy of local newspaper, or the classified page, will generally be assured of space in the paper. 

Stills used for front display should all definitely sell the attraction, and each still should be carefully considered. Some attractions can be sold especially well with stills in lavish display; occasionally, stills don't sell the attraction at all.

Effective layout for lobby panel, or for 1-sheet lobby board, might be arranged by completely covering the panel with stills placed side by side, one row above the other, then attaching cutout letters spelling out the name of attraction across and over stills. Most of stills permitted to be visible. Script type cutout letters might be used, touched with flitter.

Display panel could have stills attached so that they appear to be pouring out of a pictured book, or saxaphone, or something suggested by the attraction.

Cutout or box letters used in front can be effectively faced with stills.

Newspaper fashion editors will use fashion stills. · 56 ·

86. NAMES... Series of "Lucky Names" might be featured during the showing of an attraction . . . each evening placing a different given name (as Joe or Mary or Mike) in the letters in the attraction sign, or posting the name at the box office . . . and the first so-many persons arriving at the theatre who can prove that their name is the same win free admissions.

Persons having same name as star (or title), might be invited as theatre's guests, or as newspaper's guests in tieup with the paper. 

Might check city directory for names, sending invitations; or paper can announce invitation through their columns, requiring some proof. 

Photo of the group, assembled at theatre on opening night ought to make an interesting newspaper feature. "Club" might be organized of the identically-named persons. 

87. INQUIRING ANNOUNCER . . . "Sidewalker Forum," 

might be conducted from the sidewalk in front of theatre, in cooperation with radio station. Announcer appears in front of theatre, at busy hour, with portable microphone. . . stopping persons passing. and asking them each a question (the questions being changed daily). 

Question may pertain to some topical subject, or to theatre's attraction; or listeners-in might be invited to send along their suggestions for questions to be asked. And mention of theatre's current attraction is included in all broadcasts. Radio receiving set might be placed nearby on sidewalk (not too near) and tuned in. 

Stunt is especially effective if it is made a regular feature on a certain day each week, or a certain time each day. 

If no radio station tieup is available, the "inquiring announcer" can be effectively used, with house amplification system, speakers being placed atop canopy, so that comment and answers might be amplified so that everyone might hear. 

88. MEMO PADS... A serviceable gag for office distribution that will find a place on many desks: Small pads (15 or 20 sheets padded together), imprinting at top of sheet, "Memo," with space then left where message might be written in. Attraction copy being imprinted at bottom of the sheet. 

89. TIRES... Safety angle in an attraction, or driving or racing, would suggest a tire dealer tieup. Dealer might buy newspaper space which also includes attraction copy, and installing window display. 

Tire matinee, in early morning, might be set for kids . . . the kids bringing an old tire for admission. Arranged as a tire dealer tieup, · 57 ·

perhaps a dealer who handles old tires will buy the tires brought in by the kids. 

90. MAILING LISTS... Theatre files should contain a prepared list of names of potential customers. Several lists might be included, in addition to a general list of names. . . including a list of lawyers, doctors, ministers, club women. Membership list of prominent women's club might be secured and copied, and similarly list of members might be secured from Better Films Council. 

Names of registered automobile owners or registration lists will present a good list of names; or the telephone directory.

Different attractions suggest different clubs, organizations, groups . . whose membership registers might be secured, their members contacted. 

Newspapers in surrounding small towns could be advantageously added to the files, together with editors . . . with occasional stories being sent them (together with guest tickets),

When letters are returned by the postoffice because of a change of address, they should be immediately removed from the list. 

Heralds can be mailed by imprinting with name of addressee, and holding herald together with postage stamp or a gummed label.

Using envelopes for mailing heralds, perhaps different envelopes can be imprinted economically each week, carrying different copy each time.

Lot mailing permit may be secured from postoffice. Check weight, in this event, carefully.

Mailing list can be best kept as a card system, making changes easier. Addressograph can be used, if expense is not too great.

Organizations might permit use of their stencils to address letters, especially if the attraction carries a special appeal for their membership or their endorsement (the stencils carrying names of their members and being ordinarily used by them in addressing letters). 

Fraternal organizations, unions, clubs might be contacted. 

91. LOBBY EXPOSITION... Where lobby space permits, cooperative exhibits of many types might be arranged. 

Radio dealers might cooperate in a "Radio Exposition," (or "Fair," "Exhibit," or "Show"). Or a single dealer might sponsor it. Dealers buying cooperative newspaper space which sells theatre attraction as well as calling attention to the exhibit of new radios. Radio might be given away in connection with the exhibit. Nightly broadcast over a local radio station can be made a feature. 

With all of leading merchants participating (having lobby suf- • 58 •

ficiently large), displays might be arranged on an elaborate scale. 

Stores to buy newspaper space (large part of which is devoted to attraction), and required to buy a block of tickets (which they might hand to prospects or customers).

Civic organizations might cooperate, with Mayor officially opening the “exposition," clipping a ribbon which extends across lobby. 

Arrangements can include a band, broadcast from lobby, pretty girls serving as hostesses. Cooperating merchants can provide prizes to be given away; and perhaps they will cooperate in buying an automobile (with dealer selling it at cost), which is awarded on final evening. 

Similarly a "Flower Show" might be arranged, or an "Electrical 

Show;" or a "Food Show." Almost any line of business could sponsor an exhibit of some kind Farm Exhibits, or "Country Fair" might be arranged (possibly for Saturday only), offering prizes, blue ribbons, for best farm produce. 

Survival of fittest might be made basis of judging in order to limit amount of stuff on display, those items on display being displaced by any similar item brought in that is larger or adjudged superior. 

92. TELETYPES... Telegraph company to place a teletype machine in theatre lobby, as center of a display which carries copy: "(Telegraph company). . . telling the world about (attraction)." 

Girl operating the teletype machine is constantly preparing "messages" which carry copy about the coming attraction, and which are handed patrons. The "telegrams" addressed "Theatre Patrons," and carrying attraction selling copy, can be signed by the star of coming show. Ordinary sending blanks would be used by the girl in preparing the "messages."

Two machines might be used if desired, one inside theatre, one outside, or in the outer lobby. Patrons invited to "send" a telegram receiving it on entering theatre. Operator "receiving" the telegram would add line about the attraction. 

Another teletype angle requires arrangement with newspaper to install a newspaper teletype machine in the lobby, the machine being connected with regular newspaper service, and news coming in on the machine exactly as it does in a newspaper office. Display would credit the paper for the "hot news," and carry copy: "Read the exciting news in (paper) . . . see the most exciting (and into attraction copy)." 

93. GOLF... Tickets to see theatre's attraction might be offered to golfer turning in best score on certain day, the competition · 59 ·

being publicized in newspaper (on sport page) and on display panels in golf links clubhouse. Might refer to the competition as the "(Star) Golf Tournament." 

Or, tickets can be offered golfers making certain difficult hole in par displays, announcing the stunt, placed in clubhouse and on the green. 

Imprinted score cards might be supplied golfers. 

Driving range might offer guest tickets for best scoring of certain day. A display which has an opening, might be placed on a driving course green at safe distance (design suggested by attraction . . . as a laughing face with wide open mouth). Tickets to those driving a golf ball through the opening in the display. (See Photos.) 

94. CUTOUT LETTERS... Spelling out attraction title, can be used effectively in connection with displays or large front panels. Large cutout letters atop canopy will prove an effective flash.

Orchestra pit, when not in use, and covered over, presents a prominent place for cutout letters display, visible when house or stage lights are brought up.

Giant letters, possibly constructed in third dimension, might be placed across edge of sidewalk... the letters (securely attached) extending, for best flash, from lower edge of marquee to sidewalk, spelling out a brief title or name of star. Or, letters might be cut from cloth, extending from edge of canopy to sidewalk . . . with bottom of letters weighted (using chain) to hold them in position. 

Large letters, cut from compo-board, with stills attached, could be used for advance lobby display . . . arranged with easel backs and placed in correct sequence. 

95. STAIRWAYS, ELEVATORS, ESCALATORS... Much used open stairways offer a great spot for lettered strip cards, tacked to the steps... running them in routine up the stairs. 

Staircases in theatre might be utilized, too, attaching cards closely to the vertical angle in the steps. 

Cards can be placed in elevators in hotels and in important buildings. 

Where stores boast of escalators, they might be lettered, using watercolor. 

96. LETTERED STOOGES... Group of kids, or costumed girls, each carry a cutout letter, which, together, spell out name of attraction. Mixing the letters up as they carry them, they line up correctly on reaching prominent locations. • 60 •

Lettered sweaters might be used, girls in slacks, shorts, or sport skirts, wearing them. Name of theatre can be carried across their collective fronts, the title across their backs. Or lettered umbrellas might be carried. Or items suggested by the attraction, lettered, can be used.

At beaches, a group of girls might have letters attached to their swim suits which, together, spell out the title. 

97. PHYSICAL . . . Where an attraction stars an athletic celebrity, or feminine star famous for physical beauty, or features athletics or acrobatics, a mailing list of those interested in similar gymnastics might be secured from the physical director of a gymnasium. Or, contest (as suggested by the attraction) would have awarded trophy named after star of attraction.

Or, contest might be designed as effort to discover local boy or girl of physical development similar to star of attraction. Figure of star, life-size, might be used in connection with display panel which carries details of contest, and measurements of star. Newspaper might sponsor the contest, with contestants submitting snapshots and measurements Winners to be honor guests at dances, night spots, luncheon clubs, in addition to receiving trophies or prizes Contest might be billed as "(City) (name of star or character in story) search."

Strength testing machines, in lobby as center of display, invite patrons to try their strength. Grip machine, or punching bag setup might be secured.

Boxing in attraction might suggest an exhibition bag-puncher working out in lobby. Set up on slight elevation, as center of a display, expert would punch bag, which is firmly attached. 

Tieup with local food distributor for windows could be based on "strength-giving" qualities of the food. 

Gymnasium might use a photograph of a trim and neat girl from a coming attraction for newspaper ads or mailing pieces . emphasizing in accompanying copy that exercise is the way to acquire the streamline curves, or "Curve Control," the dancers exhibit in (the coming attraction). 

98. TUNE TEST... Organist, or featured orchestra, broadcasting over radio station, might present a radio memory contest . . . playing a series of old musical numbers, song hits of years before, offering guest tickets to first so-many persons phoning the radio station and correctly identifying the broadcast tunes. Attraction announced. • 61

Minus radio broadcast, orchestra appearing in dance spot could feature the stunt, with the award of tickets and attraction mention. 

Radio station can play star's recordings of tunes from previous screen hits . . . with listeners to name pictures in which songs were introduced and star's leading ladies (or men) in the pictures. 

99. PARROT . . . Display for lobby or window features a live parrot (secured from a bird or pet store or zoo). Securely attached to the perch on which the parrot is placed, is an open dictionary (which is attached with the cover in view). Panel carries copy: "He's just learning to talk . . . so he can tell you about a swell show . (and into attraction copy)." ... 

Or... panel could carry the copy: "Let Mr. Parrot tell you about a swell show . . . (and attraction copy). Behind the panel a speaker is placed which is connected through amplification system to concealed microphone (well away from the display) through which brief announcements are made about the attraction, speaking after manner of a parrot. Adapting to a window display, similar arrangement is used, except that additionally a dummy stand microphone is placed in front of the parrot, so that he might be apparently speaking into the microphone . . . and the speaker (through which concealed operator actually speaks) is placed outside the window. 

And, a non-talking bird might be used, with guest tickets offered to first person to make the parrot repeat the name of the coming attraction (naturally making patrons repeat it a good many times, too, in attempts to make the bird talk). 

100. CIRCUS... Front display should feature canvas, or canvas-effect, circus style, across entrance (tent and awning company can supply the canvas . . . ... or paneling might be painted to resemble canvas of circus "front door"). "Main Entrance" should be painted over doorways. Circus style cloth banners might be used to good advantage. Panels over doors might be painted to resemble ends of animal cages. Sawdust on lobby floor. Several clowns. Staff should be dressed as clowns. Perhaps a couple of girls, in shorts or dance costumes, might swing on a "flying trapeze," or flying ladders, under the canopy. Ticket booth covered to resemble a ticket wagon. (See Photos.)

Clown band, in costumes might play out front on opening night, after marching to theatre (accompanying girls carrying lettered banner). Radio broadcast might be featured, and arrival of celebrities, introduction of any circus personalities who should be located. · 62 ·

Clown band might also serve on a float, or bannered truck, touring the town in advance; or play at luncheon clubs. 

Barkers out front on opening night spiel the attraction in circus style. Peanut vender, balloon man and circus pink lemonade add to atmosphere.

Display of animals, alive or stuffed, should be secured for lobby or window display. 

Old-time circus men might be located and contacted. Any number of good stories for newspapers can be secured from them (including their comment on attraction in all newspaper and radio interviews). 

They can prove of much assistance, offering valuable advice. They should be invited as guests of honor on opening night, or for special screening. Perhaps an old circus performer or clown might write a review of the show for newspaper. 

Some people collect circus stuff as a hobby, and perhaps someone might be located who has a miniature circus, or collection of circus souvenirs or curios, or old circus lithographs, photographs, hand bills. Could be displayed in lobby or in store window. 

Heralds modeled after long circus-style handbills might be distributed by boys in clown costumes. Or they hand out imprinted paper sacks, with one or two peanuts inside, carrying copy: "Peanuts for the elephant . . . when you see the circus in (attraction)."

Kid circus can be arranged at school or playground. Playground directors, cooperating, might present guest tickets to winners of contests held in connection with the "circus," or to leading "entertainers," and announcing theatre's attraction, perhaps permitting banners on attraction to be displayed.

Tieup with a dance spot or night club might feature a "Circus 

Dance," or "Clown Dance"... with guest tickets to be presented for best costumes. Orchestra can be dressed as clowns. 

Newspaper contest for best essay on "My First Circus" might be set, illustrating with art from attraction. 

Kids who come dressed as clowns on early showing on opening day could be invited to see attraction Kids might be required to meet at newspaper, parading to theatre, carrying banners . . . perhaps accompanied by clown band. Tumblers, (from school or gymnasium) can work in front of theatre, in costume. Gymnastic or acrobatic contest might be arranged, at gymnasium or swimming pool, or in front of theatre. . . with announcements made, and trophy or tickets as prize.

Kid contest for dogs that can do tricks might be arranged. · 63 ·

A couple of boys inside "animal" costumes (from a costumer), could be "led" about town by a man in clown costume. 

Broadcasting station can feature circus marches, dedicated to the attraction. Dance orchestras might feature a circus number, mentioning the show.

An old calliope, or circus wagon might be located, bannered, and driven about town. 

Circus parade should be arranged, with clown band, girls in costumes carrying cutout letters that spell name of attraction . . . Old circus equipment, balloon hawkers, with clusters of gaily colored balloons. Girls on roller skates. Group of horseback riders (from riding club). Stilt walker, or any circusy bally. Kid circus parade, arranged with playground or paper cooperation, in clown costumes, might be included. (See 64, 344.) 

101. STREET CARS, BUSES, TRANSPORTATION LINES 

. . . Use of street car or bus dashes might be secured, arranging with transportation company to attach cards to front of cars. Frames or card holders are attached, with cards inserted. Window cards might be used. Paper might be pasted to metal or wood dash boards. 

Top lines should read: "Ride the street cars to... (theatre)." Perhaps banners or panels can be attached to sides or top of cars or buses. 

The transportation company should prove agreeable since theatres, in drawing business, cause people to ride the cars. 

Use of a street car or bus might be secured, at least for rush hours, large banners attached to either side, touring the city. Twentyfour sheets might be used, pasting them to a frame over which domestic or sign cloth has been stretched, the frames then being attached securely to sides of the car. Band can be used inside the car; or portable amplification equipment is used, playing records and making announcements. The car might "deliver film" to theatre just before opening, group of costumed girls alighting from the car with the film. (See Photos.)

More elaborate use of street car might be made by transforming it into a float-possibly securing for the purpose a flat work car. 

Construction of float suggested by the attraction. If expense will permit, neon lighting might outline the display (and name of attraction and theatre) for night flash. Attractive girls in costume. ride on the car. Amplification equipment might be also used for music and announcements. Used on opening night of attraction, routing should bring it to theatre at height of opening ceremonies, (if gala premiere opening is staged), or at least at peak hour. Stop · 64 ·

car in front theatre for few minutes, possibly having girls alight. 

Arrangements might be made to have operators of cars stopping in front of, or near theatre, call theatre name as they stop. 

Old couple on street cars, with man feigning deafness, and talking loudly about the attraction, is an old stunt, but still effective. They might do it convincingly, arguing about the attraction, stars, etc., loudly and good-naturedly asking those on street car questions about the attraction. (And, of course, "deaf man" and girl can win attention on street corners and in prominent locations about town, inquiring about attraction.)

Man or girl, riding cars at rush hours, opens up a newspaper, across outside of which is lettered a very large headline about attraction. 

Or title might be lettered on a large "book" which stooge is "reading.' 

Transportation companies often publish a weekly bulletin or folder, which is distributed or made available on their cars. They may use a story or an illustration from attraction.
