Arrangements might be worked out to have theatre ad imprinted on reverse side of weekly passes or transfers. 

102. HOW LONG WILL BATTERY LAST? . . . A No. 6 

dry cell battery, used in a window to attract attention to a display, has a lighted 6 watt lamp attached. The center of globe is soldered to carbon contact (or center terminal). The shell of the lamp has a short piece of wire soldered to it, the wire being connected to the zinc (or negative side of battery, the outside connection). Display carries copy: "How long will this battery last?" Correct answers get tickets to see (attraction)."

The battery, of course, doesn't actually supply the lamp with current. To get the effect, the battery is emptied (from bottom) of all loose carbon. Center pole is insulated from shell. One wire is wrapped around center pole or carbon. Other wire is soldered to zinc shell (or negative). These wires lead off to an extension cord that connects with house current. They are concealed under cloth on which battery is placed, the wires going through the cloth. Paper outside covering of battery must be replaced with the wires penetrating through the bottom of the covering. (See Photos.) (The answer to the question asked in the display is obviously, "As long as the eletricity is turned on”). 

103. MARIONETTES... Miniature stage is made the center of a lobby or window display. Opening is cut in for "stage," and miniature platform built behind the opening for the "stage." 

Seated behind the display, and with head and shoulders visible, ist · 65 ·

the marionette operator (who is costumed according to the attraction), his operation of the puppets being entirely visible. 

The marionettes are made up to resemble characters of stage attraction— small dolls, loosely connected at "joints," with strings leading from feet, hands, back, to crossed sticks which the operator holds in his or her hand and with which the marionettes are manipulated.

Display, of course, carries copy on the attraction. Miniature easels might also be placed against the background on the "stage;" or one of the marionettes might be constructed to carry a lettered "card."

Marionette, made the center of a window or lobby display, might be animated by use of an automobile crankshaft (above and out of sight), which is made to turn continuously. The strings leading from the marionette to the different variations of the crankshaft. The doll might be made to appear to dance, or to jump about. 

104. BROADCAST SKETCH... Highlight, or important episode in a story might be adapted to a five or ten minute radio. sketch, and broadcast over a local station. Members of local 

Little Theatre group, or the radio station staff might enact the roles. 

Or a group can be organized and sponsored by theatre. 

Sketch could be broadcast direct from theatre lobby, or mezzanine; or from stage. Or from store window of the cooperating business place. Scripts for sketches (of brief highlight) are made available on some attractions. On others they might be obtained by having a stenographer shorthand the dialogue from several scenes when screening the picture. 

105. LUCKY PHOTOGRAPHS... Tieup might be made with newspaper, publishing each day a photograph, or several photographs, snapped at random by photographer who travels about town, shooting pictures on the streets, at beaches, dance spots, places where crowds go. Circles drawn about certain heads among those pictured, entitles them to guest tickets to theatre's attraction (which is mentioned), upon identifying themselves at newspaper. 

Or, instead of drawing circles about certain heads, selected figures might be whitened out, leaving just a blank silhouette. Persons correctly identifying themselves (with paper checking against photograph) to get tickets.

Or ringed photographs could be displayed in lobby or windows of cooperating stores, changing them daily. 

Or photographer, might be set up in a store window, with camera, • 66 ·

snapping photographs through window. Pretty costumed girl could serve as the photographer.

Newspaper staff photographer might shoot the pictures. Or local photographer might make them in return for newspaper credit lines in accompanying stories. Similarly, in some situations, engraver may make up cuts for a credit line, if newspaper is not equipped to make them. 

106. INQUIRING REPORTER... Newspaper tieup features a strolling reporter who asks a series of questions, possibly based on attraction theme or title, one question being asked each day. Five or six answers are used daily, these to receive guests tickets to see theatre's attraction (which is mentioned). 

The question and the various answers are carried each day in a single column story in the newspaper. Names of the persons asked, together with their addresses and occupations, and a thumbnail (half column) cut of photo of each person, are carried. Reporter might make the necessary snapshots, using an ordinary camera. 

107. FACTORIES... Employing large numbers of workers, large factories can be effectively circularized. Perhaps heralds might be placed in automobiles, or handed to workers as they depart. 

Sound truck, if used, should arrange its routing so that it arrives at factories as workers are leaving. Similarly any float or outdoors perambulating bally.

Familiar stunt of numbering heralds, with certain numbers posted at theatre box office, and with heralds bearing corresponding numbers to be good for gratis admissions, might be adapted to numbers on employees' badges. Cards or banner announcing the lucky number stunt, inviting workers to check their numbers in theatre lobby, are placed near plant entrance or gate. Numbers in theatre lobby changed daily.

Working with recreation committee of employees' organizations, it might be possible to work up a special evening when all employees will be urged to attend. Special price to be made; or cards are distributed to employees, which they present on attending (and paying regular prices), and percentage (based on the number of cards turned in) to be turned over to employee organization. 

Similarly, large stores, other places employing a great many workers. 

108. "SEE YOUR VOICE” . . . Oscillograph, made part of a display, shows in an opening, when current is supplied, a line, which registers the variations of sound. Connected with a microphone • 67 ·

which is placed in front of the display, and in charge of an attendant, patrons are invited to "see their voices." On speaking into the microphone they witness the variations in the oscillograph line which their voices produce. The microphone is connected through an amplification hookup with the oscillograph. (See Photos.) 

Copy on panel might read: "See your voice! And thrill to the world's favorite singing voice (and into copy on attraction)." 

A switch should be made part of the equipment, and attendant should see that the electricity is not turned on when the oscillograph is not in use (leaving it on at rush hours, however). 

Well known local singer, or singing star of show might be photographed trying his, or her, voice on the oscillograph, watching the results; and the picture ought to be good for newspaper space. 

109. SIDEWALK TWENTY-FOUR SHEET . . . Poster mounted on sign cloth covered frame, might be transported about downtown section during rush hours, being carried by several uniformed or costumed men. Walking at edge of sidewalk, the poster is visible from across the street as a moving billboard. (See Photos.) 

Or, the poster, divided in eight sections, mounted on compo-board panels, might be carried along the street by eight different men, who, at a signal on important corners, assemble, holding the pieces together to form a complete poster. Upper sections might have braces or handles attached so that they can be elevated easily to necessary height. Stunt should be rehearsed so that men know their places, assembling the poster instantly. 

110. FLOWER HORSESHOE . . . Couple of girls dressed as pages, or in costumes suggested by the attraction, carry a large flower horseshoe (made up with cooperation of a florist) through downtown streets. . . card on flowers, large enough to be easily read, carrying copy: "Congratulations to (star) on the finest performance of her career in (attraction) at (theatre)," (or adapt copy to attraction). Or the flower horseshoe might be placed on display in florist's window, or in lobby.

Floral design other than the horseshoe might be suggested by the attraction. 

111. MINIATURE STAGE...Display might be constructed, for lobby or window, with miniature stage as center of display. 

Revolving circular platform might be placed behind the stage opening, as the stage. Platform is separated into several miniature stage settings by dividing upright "walls." As platform revolves, one after another the different stage "scenes" (each set with different • 68 •

display of stills, or figures cutout from stills) come into view. Perhaps mechanism can be arranged so that platform will stop in its turning for an instant as each "scene" arrives before the opening.

Curtain may be made to come down, or close-in, between the different scenes. (See Designs.)

Or panel with stage design might merely feature a "stage," with opening cut where screen should be. Back of the opening a drum is made to revolve, bringing into view a series of stills which are attached to the drum. 

112. HOLIDAY NEWSPAPER FLASH... On July 4th, New 

Year's, Friday the 13th, or any holiday or out-of-ordinary date, newspaper might be willing to use specially posed and unusual art layout in keeping with the date. 

Using photograph of star of attraction, artist might draw in background suggested by the date . . . as seating star on a giant pumpkin on Hallowe'en, or riding a giant skyrocket over a skyline of city for 

New Year's. . . or greeting Santa Claus, for a Christmas photo, etc.

Only actual photo is that of star, rest is drawn in. Playing stage shows, photo of star or one of the girls in the stage revue might be used, or specially posed. 

113. DIGNITY 

... 

An occasional class attraction must be handled with utmost dignity. no tricks, no stunts, no gags. 

Endorsements . . . screenings for Better Films Councils and educators or those who would be interested, perhaps using their comment for newspaper stories; cooperation of editors in carrying straight publicity ... mailing list-all these angles should take the place of hokum.

A committee might be formed to sponsor the showing of the attraction, and these names might serve to add weight to letters, newspaper ads. 

114. SUBMARINE CANARY. . . Effect of goldfish and a live canary, together under water, is obtained by dividing an ordinary square gold fish bowl, or aquarium, into angled compartments, by placing a glass panel diagonally from one corner to the other. the glass being cemented in so that it is water-tight, using aquarium cement, or metal cement or putty. Usual equipment of a gold fish bowl (sand, miniature castles, figures, etc.) is added, making floor of both sections identical (the sand also hiding cement used at bottom of glass dividing panel). (See Photos.)

Water, and the gold fish are placed in front section of the aquarium, a live canary is placed in the other side. Bowl is covered with wire netting (over top). Both ends and top are concealed with dis- • 69 ·

EN CY CLOPEDIA OF EXPLOITATION 

play panels, only a straight forward view being permitted. with the gold fish side facing out, towards those looking at the bowl. 

Used as center of a window display, with panels carrying tiein copy on theatre's attraction. . . as, "(Star's) Amazing Submarine Canary" (and into attraction copy).

Similarly white mice might be used instead of a canary. Hole may be cut in the aquarium floor (on the dry side), so that mice might appear in the aquarium, or go through the opening in bottom into a cage which is attached beneath. Or, instead of a divided aquarium, another small seamless gold fish bowl might be placed upside down in the aquarium, over the hole where the mice emerge (sand being placed equally under the bowl and outside) . . . the bowl within the aquarium being cemented to floor, and covered over with water. 

115. APRONS . . . Cloth aprons, carrying imprinted copy on the attraction, might be supplied newsboys on downtown street corners. Change pockets in the aprons add to their value. Similarly lettered, or imprinted, aprons can be supplied soda dispensers, clerks, butchers. 

116. GIGANTIC INVITATION... Made up after fashion of regular invitation, but lettered on compo-board panel, as large as possible, and in proportions of regular invitation. Or the "invitation" can be lettered on a very large sheet of paper, which is folded once, and inserted in a very large, specially made envelope (both being shown in photographs).

Delivered to Mayor, or other official, or to managing editor of newspaper, the big invitation is photographed with couple of good looking girls "delivering" it . . . (on City Hall steps, if delivered to city official), newspaper carrying the photograph together with a story. The invitation might be delivered to football or baseball team just before start of important game (with photographs of the presentation made, and announcements for crowds).

If used in connection with a stage revue, the girls in the stage show, and perhaps stars as well, can "deliver" the invitation (for photo purposes).

Invitation might be made up in form of gigantic telegram, with star inviting local celeb to witness the attraction as her (or his) guests. 

Invitation to Chief of Police, inviting him and his officers to witness an attraction, might have Chief, or an officer, photographed accepting the "invitation” . . . ... newspaper in reproducing the photograph referring to cops getting a ticket instead of giving one. 

117. ILLUMINATED SHIRT... Night time bally man being 

• 70 •

costumed in full dress, or other costume which includes in the ensemble a stiff-front dress shirt (or "dickey"- a cardboard shirt front). Letters, spelling out the attraction title and theatre, are cut out from the shirt front which is then covered over with white muslin or sign cloth. Flashlight is then arranged under the shirt, so that illumination shines through the letters when the flashlight is lighted. Light is so arranged so that it might be flashed on by man pressing button in pocket. 

118. PERAMBULATING DISPLAY ... Flashy display 

(with name of attraction prominent) being carried about town during rush hours will command considerable attention. Banner, or lettered life-size figure of star, or of girl if attraction is of the “gallossal" variety, might be sent about town. 

Life-size cutout figure might be carried about town by two men (or two girls), holding each arm of cutout figure (one person on either side), and carrying the figure as though walking with a third person, (cutout lettered on reverse side). 

119. BANNERS... Large cloth banner on a coming attraction can be effectively attached to front of theatre, or other prominently located building. Banners, if used regularly, might be attached to a specially constructed frame to which the banner is laced. If star's face is especially well known, large banner across front of theatre might merely carry his picture, no copy, for a onetime stunt. (See Photos.)

Narrow strip banner might be used to carry for a number of stories down the corner of a building. 

Any number of banner manufacturing companies can supply cloth banners of any specified size. Or a local tent and awning company might be capable of constructing the banner. 

Face of an upright sign might be effectively covered with a banner. 

Made of sign cloth, the banner is exact size to cover completely the letters in the upright sign. Name of star or attraction (very brief necessarily), is "cut in"-the background painted black (using oil paint) and the lettering being left the natural white of the sign cloth.

Placed over upright sign, and at night with lights turned on, the lights showing through the unpainted portion of the sign cloth will spell out star or attraction name instead of theatre name.

Where road or street leading to theatre goes over a bridge, banner might be placed conveniently near same, carrying copy: "Cross this bridge to see (attraction)." Where stream flows through down- • 71 ·

town section and main street extends across a bridge, a boat in the stream below might be bannered.

Upright streamer banner might be used effectively out front, the banner extending from the roof of theatre, or top of upright sign, to the marquee. Banner might parallel (on outer edge) the upright sign from top to bottom, being attached at top to an arm or beam extending from top of electric sign. Banner lettered both sides, or two lettered banners, placed together back-to-back, so that it can be read from either direction. Guide wires should carry down sides of banner, through grommets in banner edges, from top to bottom, holding banner securely.

The scene of construction or excavation for a building, is often a great spot for a banner on an adjacent building, since much attention is attracted. Even the steam shovel or excavating machine might possibly be bannered.

Four-sided banner (sign cloth on light wood frame), can be attached around automobile with extreme ease .. being fastened to bumpers in front and rear, and not necessarily touching the car. 

Banner above car might be attached by means of pipe framework to bumpers. 

120. BIGGEST . . . Size of an item (suggested by an attraction) can win attention and possibly merit newspaper space calling it the biggest of its kind (as, if appropriate, the biggest pretzel, or biggest cake), specially made in honor of showing of attraction at theatre.

Window and lobby display might feature the item, and picture of pretty girls grouped about it might make the papers Or where the size of any object will draw attention, there is possibility that it might be adapted to theatre use . . . as a specially large or long truck, used for a float. 

121. COOPERATIVE POSTERS... Billboards bought and specially prepared by some other business might tiein theatre's attraction or star. As, billboards posted for a taxicab company carrying the copy: "Call a (name) cab to call on (star)," and illustrated with photo of the star. Or, a bread company might feature a photograph of one of the girls from a coming attraction, copy carrying message that bread builds glowing health such as these girls have. 

Arrangements should be made well in advance, and might fit into the advertiser's plans, supplying a new approach. Different attractions suggest different tieups. A similar tieup might be made using smaller paper (three-sheets, one-sheets). • 72.

122. CHRISTENING ANIMAL... Arrangements might be made with zoo to formally "christen" a baby animal with name of theatre attraction or star. Local traveler, or explorer, or a pretty and prominent girl, or stage show star, officially performing the "christening." Photographs, for newspapers (arranged in advance). 

Radio station might broadcast the stunt. 

123. REVOLVING DISPLAY... Turning displays for lobby or front are most certain to attract attention. Revolving circular panel might be constructed to bring stills, or a series of illustrations, one after another into view through an opening. Or, circular display or drum revolving behind an opening in a display panel can bring into view the title of attraction, as it turns. (See Diagrams.) 

Animation can be supplied by use of a motor-driven phonograph turntable. . . with stills or other illustrations, attached to edges of the turntable and being revolved behind an opening Effective window display might be adapted from revolving shade display, in which the shade is circular, mounted (on a glass bearing) over a light globe (in center) the heat from the globe rising through angled openings in the top of the shade and causing it to revolve. 

Commonly used in window displays, one of these revolving shades might be secured, and adapted to a shadow-box or window display perhaps a miniature of a billboard, with opening cut for the revolving display to show through. ...

A 24-sheet might be effectively adapted to a revolving display by use of a drum, constructed exact height of a 24-sheet, and covered over with sign cloth. Two hoops made from small rods will serve as top and bottom supports of the drum. . . the circumference of the hoops to be equal to length of the poster (about 240 inches, with added inches if date strip is to be carried between the ends of the poster). 

Join the bottom hoop to a wooden hub, using wire spokes... the hub to revolve on a stationary "axle" placed upright. Top hoop is connected by spokes with a cap that revolves on top of continuance of the axle (axle passing through lower hub and to top of display). 

Drive with motor, using belt which rides in groove cut in lower hub; or chain and gears. Domestic cloth (on which poster is pasted) is sewn tightly over the space between the two hoops. Drum should be illuminated, for night flash, and amplification set-up might be connected, placing speaker under the display, broadcasting music and announcements. Using smaller posters for lobby or window flash, a 6-sheet and date strip might be adapted; or two 6-sheets. 

Or a painted display. • 73 •

124. AUTOGRAPHS... Objects bearing genuine autographs of important or famous people make valued prizes for contests . . . as, in connection with a baseball story, a bat or glove might be autographed by every member of the home team . . . or it might be sent for signature to one of the top-name players (or a football, similarly signed); or suggested object might be sent to studios for stars to sign. Several personally autographed photos might be secured from studio and used for prizes. 

Contest for newspaper or radio can be based on written autographs using the star's name . . . with tickets for best, cleverest “signatures" submitted. 

125. SCREENINGS... Newspaper and radio critics might be invited as special guests at private advance showing of an attraction. Advance stories on the attraction should result. The picture should be one that definitely has merit, or one that will excite controversy.

Newspaper fashion editors should be invited if clothes worn by star are especially attractive.

Local authorities on subject suggested by or dealt with in the show should be invited to witness the screening... if attraction deals with sports, inviting sports editors and leading local players. (And similarly other appeals.) School principals, superintendents, should be invited in connection with an educational feature; if ministers would approve, they might be invited. 

If screening in advance is not possible, those interested might be invited to attend preview, or opening night. (See 435.)

Special screening of attraction might be arranged in surroundings suggested by theme of attraction. A Naval story might be screened for naval officials aboard ship; with consequent newspaper stories, carrying comment. Or screening might be arranged aboard a transport plane, or a railroad train, or a boat, street car or bus. Newspaper support or sponsorship should be secured in advance, with story and photographs assured, and with critics present. 

Screening in jail might be arranged for prisoners in connection with attraction that carries a strong moral that crime does not pay. (With subsequent newspaper stories.) 

126. SCHOLARSHIPS... Appealing to students, perhaps a scholarship of some kind can be promoted, to be awarded as a prize in newspaper contest or essay contest, or other competition. Or scholarship in music school might be presented to winner of singing • 74.

contest, in connection with musical attraction, and with newspaper or radio cooperation. 

Similarly, a business course might be the prize, if attraction suggests (as a story that pictures office girls or secretaries). 

School giving the scholarship should receive credit in all announcements and publicity, both in theatre and through cooperating newspaper or radio station. 

127. SILHOUETTE. 

. . . Attention-arresting silhouette effect can be obtained by using display panel with muslin-covered opening in same light behind the cloth-and figure, or cutout letters, between the light and the cloth. (White paper or translucent glass might be used, instead of muslin.)

Animation might be secured by mounting cutout letters on a light frame, and mechanically making letters (or figure) travel towards the muslin screen, then away from it. . . the silhouetted letters (the shadow of the cutout letters as reflected on the "screen"), from the front, appearing to diminish in size then to become larger, filling up the screen surface. 

Figure, as of a dancer, can be animated, and the dancing silhouette cast on the screen. When the effect of sideways animation is desired (as the silhouette of a hula dancer), figure can be made stationary and the light behind it made to move from side to side. 

The screen should be part of the display (as a clown holding a hoop -the hoop being the screen. Or a pulled-down window shade effect). Etc.

Larger silhouette display (possibly utilizing all or a large section of a window), features a couple of girls in close fitting costumes, posing, dancing, and as part of their routine holding cutout letters. (held together with wire) in front of light so that they cast silhouettes on the screen. Display copy is carried on the panels which mask in the sides of the muslin "screen".

Newspaper contest might be based on correct identification of a series of silhouette drawings of players in coming theatre attraction. 

30-word description of the person whose silhouette is shown might be required additionally. Or, contest might be based on best silhouettes of stars cut from black paper, and submitted. 

128. HOSIERY... Tieups with stores handling hosiery are a "natural" in connection with a girl show; and okay, too, on most feminine stars.

Stores might use leg-art in their ads (photos of girls in brief costumes, or star in leg-revealing pose), and possibly including scenes • 75 •

from the attraction. Stills, too, might be placed in neat display in windows of store, together with hosiery display. And the hose might be named after, or "dedicated to" the star of the show. 

Girls can be featured in a store window, modeling hosiery, as center of a display on an attraction. Window is masked in (or the portion of the window in use) with display panels. An opening in the center of the front panel is just so high that a girl standing behind it will be visible from just above her knees down. A curtain or drape might be used in the window. Girls model hosiery behind this opening. And back of them, a curtain "backs up" the display. 

Display copy is lettered on the outside of the paneled display, or possibly placed on miniature easel display cards within and on either side of the opening. (See Photos.)

One or several girls may be used. In addition to modeling hose, walking across behind the opening, girls might seat themselves on chairs, removing stockings of one color, replacing them with another pair of another color. If they are dancers, they might go through a brief seated tap routine. 

Another angle, would be the use of just one girl, posing behind the curtain, in the midst of several pair of dummy legs, such as hosiery places use to display hose. Girl's legs and the dummy legs are all clothed in same type hose. Girl remains motionless for several minutes at a time . . . and panel copy invites those looking to try and pick the real legs. Another opening in the display panel or curtain (behind which she stands) could, if preferred, permit girl's head and shoulders to show. And to make the task of picking her real legs less easy, she might wear a different type shoe on either foot (two of the dummy legs fitting into similar type shoes). 

Getting away from the curtain idea, girl might be brought "out in the open," having her recline as the center of a window display among several model legs, which extend, in addition to her own, from under the short skirt which she wears. Holding her legs motionless, she occasionally moves them about. Legs (dummy's and girl's), might angle upwards toward back of window. 

Store ought to mention the "girl of many legs" in their ads, and announcing times of girl's appearance. Streamers on window should announce it in advance, too. Tieup copy on the attraction should be included in newspaper ads, as well as in the window. 

Several pairs of dummy legs, in chorus positions might aid, too, in drawing attention to a window which features hosiery, including illustrations of theatre's girl show (screen or stage). 76⚫

Leg or calf contest could be staged in connection with a hosiery tieup (see No. 619). Or an added angle might offer guest tickets to those most nearly estimating correct calf measurements of girl modeling the hose. Another girl, in costume outside the window, might register estimates in a notebook. Stockings might be used as an acceptable prize. · • • 129. CONTROVERSY Often there are angles to an attraction, in story, author, theme, stars or production, about which a controversy of some kind might be stirred up, drawing attention to the attraction. (First weighing the possibility of dangerous consequences.)

Arguments or debates, or conflicting opinions, will naturally result in much word-of-mouth advertising and possible news space. 

Newpspaer stories, or letters-to-the-Editor, might be arranged; newspaper ads may assume the form of a challenge. 

Or a provocative announcement of controversial plans might evoke discussion a statement that conflicts with formula, or a proposed non-conformance with accepted rules. 

Radio commentators might start the ball rolling, giving their opinion, asking listeners if they agree. 

Local authorities might be interviewed as to their opinions. 

Opinion of someone who would be naturally opposed might be requested.

Should all be begun well in advance of showing of attraction to prove effective. And consider consequences first. 

130. COMMISSION. . . As a publicity flash, and good at least for newspaper story and picture, arrangements might be made to have the star of theatre's attraction commissioned as an honorary officer of some kind.

Star might be commissioned an honorary colonel in some local military body, or on the staff of the Governor of the state; or an adjacent state. Or an honorary Chief of Police or Fire Department. 

Stage star could be presented with the commission at a special luncheon in his honor, with newspaper critics and photographers present. Or movie critic might "accept" the commission for an absent motion picture star . . . with subsequent newspaper story. 

Civic organizations, luncheon clubs, etc., might make the star an honorary member of their organization, presenting a special membership card.

Theatre can issue commissions as "Colonels" in theatre's "Army of Show-goers." "Commissions," attractively made up, illustrated ⚫ 77 •

with appropriate scenes, state that "(space for name) is hereby commissioned as 'Colonel' in the great Army of Show-goers whose eager feet bring them regularly to the (theatre) to witness the greatest attractions the show world provides. In recognition of outstanding cooperation and interest in things theatrical, he is duly appointed, this date (and space for date to be typewritten in)." Or attraction might suggest an "organization" sponsored by theatre in which patrons are "commissioned." 

131. TOP MARQUEE ... Where theatre is strategically located, as most of them are, the top of the canopy offers a marvelous spot for an effective display. 

Attraction will suggest type of display. as a jungle scene, perhaps with live "savages" and live monkeys, in connection with a jungle story. Or, backed up by a large banner, attractively costumed girls appearing on constructed platforms (safely constructed so girls cannot fall), carrying letters which spell out title of coming attraction . . . or panels which carry star names or sales copy. Or, giant constructed fan might be the background for a "fashion show," in connection with attraction that deals with fashions, a group of girls modeling gowns, bathing suits, sports outfits. (See Photos.) 

Scene atop marquee should be brightly illuminated at night. 

Attractive girls will add to a constructed atmospheric scene atop the marquee.

Display atop canopy might be built within a giant frame, which is outlined with light globes or neon . . . the "scene" being constructed within a giant "shadow-box" built back of the opening. 

24-sheet might even be posted atop marquee, panel being neatly constructed. 

132. SEE... Copy (lobby, windows, newspaper, radio) might effectively feature "see" angles, as: "See (scene or incident) . See (another scene), etc." Highlights, interesting scenes listed in this fashion.

Panel can feature an opening, behind which a revolving drum, as it turns, brings into view "see" copy (highlights) of attraction.

Word "See" is lettered directly above the opening or to the left of it. 

133. PRIZES . . . Added interest is assured any contest if the prizes are attractive. A trip . . . to Hollywood, Florida, New

York, or to anywhere, can sometimes be promoted through travel agency, railroads, bus lines, airlines. (Theatre should have winner sign a letter of release.) • 78 •

AO 

Attraction may suggest some prize. 

Contest on attraction that is based on a well-known novel might use books as prizes. 

Hotel or night club might entertain winner and a party (of 12 or 

20) without charge, as a prize . . . hotel receiving mention in newspaper stories. Or a season pass to a swimming pool, on the same basis. Or several permanent waves at a beauty shop. Or clothes, stockings (several dozen pairs), etc. And, of course, cash or ticket prizes. 

Additional prize might be presented for cleverest entries.

Newspapers are generally more interested in a contest offering desirable prizes.

Tickets as prizes might secure display space for attraction along boardwalks and midways, in stores, windows, and newspaper ads. 

Several tickets, offered for best scoring in some competition, or to winners of some contest, will often bring many times their value in advertising. 

134. INFORMATION... "Information Booth" in lobby or store offers information about (attraction). Pretty girl in the booth answers questions about the show, schedules, prices; she might hand out heralds.

Typist (possibly costumed)-seated at a table, as center of a display in lobby or store, types and hands out brief "messages" about the attraction. Panel or easel card carries copy (large): "Information (smaller) about (attraction)." 

135. CONVENTIONS... Where city is host to a conven tion, arrangements committee should be contacted. Possibly a block of tickets might be sold them, for their members or their wives. Perhaps announcements can be made at meetings. Heralds can be placed in hotel rooms, or in hotel letter boxes. Stage show stars might be introduced at a meeting. Perhaps theatre might be used in the morning (before opening) for their main meeting (selling them tickets in exchange).

Local "convention," or travesty on a convention might be promoted . . . as a "convention" of local dancers, in connection with attraction that features dancing; or a convention of Santa Clauses at Christmas time, inviting all the sidewalk St. Nicks, tieing in Christmas attraction as theatre's Christmas present. "Convention" should meet (for newspaper photographers) in theatre before house opens, with tea and sandwiches, or coffee, served them. Picture might be screened, with "delegates" as guests of newspaper critic. 

136. RADIUM PAINT... for night display or displays in 

• 79 ·

dark spots, use of luminous paint will draw added attention. Displays (in windows, outdoors) should be placed in darkened location where, however, an occasional light is thrown against it (as by a turning automobile), as luminous paint is "charged" and made to glow by an occasional flash of light. Or it can be made to glow continuously by focusing an invisible UV ray on it (firm supplying luminous paint can supply a slide to be placed over an ordinary spotlight). 

Costumes can be touched with luminous paint for a night time. effect, or for darkened theatre as a man in black suit, with skeleton outlined in luminous paint (for use when attraction suggests). 

137. LETTERED SWIM BALLS... Large rubber balls, distributed well in advance to swimming pools, are inflated, attraction title and copy lettered on, using oil paint. 

138. FANS... Lettered silk ribbon attached to front guard of an electric fan, used as center of a window display. Short length of wire attached to the top of the ribbon keeps it extended. 

Electric fans can be used for animation in a window or lobby display. An enclosed snow scene might have the "snow" (bits of paper) blown about by concealed oscillating fans. Similarly, sand might be blown about (gently) within a glassed-in shadow-box display picturing a desert scene. Or stage money blown about.

Oscillating fans often can be used in animating mechanical displays. 

Fan, swinging, and behind a display, might be arranged to pull an object, which is returned by means of a light spring or rubber band as the fan swings back. Or the fan can make electrical contact at the termination of each swing, ringing a buzzer, or flashing lights, or starting a motor. (See Designs.) 

139. FLOATING HEAD... Magician's illusion of head suspended on ribbons (“Spidora," used around fairs and carnivals), can be used effectively as a window display, lettered: "She laughed her head off at (attraction)."

A public address outfit can be added with “mike" inside window, speaker outside, so girl who appears in the display might speak to persons on the street.

The illusion is simply constructed, consisting of a box, with mirror extending (at an angle, leaning outward) across opening and reaching exactly midway the box (bottom of mirror is at rear bottom of box, top at midway center of box) and reflecting bottom of box and giving illusion of completeness.

Box (square) is lined (all sides) with identical figured material. • 80 •

Over the exact center of the mirror, ribbons cross, extending from back top corners of box, and crossing to front corners of box. Behind mirror, lower half of back of box, there is an opening through which girl thrusts her head (from behind); she rests her head on the mirror edge at the point where the ribbons cross; her body is concealed by the mirror and display panels. 

Small ruffle at point where ribbons cross, as a collar, might further add to the illusion. Curtain should be provided to "close in" on display when desired. Box must be placed sufficiently high. 

After similar fashion illusion of half a girl might be secured, using ordinary kitchen table, with opening cut in same, in which the girl stands, the table reaching to her waist. Short "skirt" comes past her waist, extending slightly over on top of table and concealing edges of opening in table. Under table two angled mirrors extend from a center table leg, to just behind the two rear legs, cloth table cover extends to floor on both sides, though open on front. Mirrors reflect sides and give the illusion of looking through, under table, to table cover extension similar to sides.

141. BANNERED TRUCKS... Constantly cruising about the city, the sides of trucks offer an excellent space for banners. 

Line of copy on banner can mention product represented by truck. 

In connection with newspaper tieup, boards or banners might be placed on the sides of newspaper's delivery trucks. 

Other business places owning trucks that might be bannered include news agencies, ice companies, bakeries, dairies, cleaners, oil companies, laundries, bottlers, department stores. Or any other business owning a fleet of trucks. 

142. SOAP... Tieup might be arranged with distributor of well advertised soap, or with individual stores, to place cards and streamers in store windows, and in stores. Distributor might possibly have special tieup material. 

Placard or streamer might have photo of star attached or reproduced with copy as: "Have a complexion as lovely as (star's) in (attraction). Use (soap)." (No endorsements without approval.)

Prize might be offered for best object modeled, or carved, from a bar of soap. Object to be modeled might be suggested by attraction, • 81 •

or as likeness of star or girl, in connection with girl show animal in connection with jungle story, or a cartoon character.

143. BOTTLERS. . . Distributors have display stuff on many stars. If available, it might be spotted in dealers' windows, possibly with card on attraction attached. 

If nothing available, specially printed paper streamers (to be attached to windows and trucks) might be used. . . copy on streamers carrying a top line tiein with the drink. 

Arrangements might be made to promote a quantity of bottled soft drinks for free distribution to theatre patrons as an ad for drink (handing cards which are redeemed by dealers). 

144. DANCING SHOES . . . Adaptable where dancing is featured in an attraction, a panel for a shoe store window or lobby display features an opening, in which a pair of shoes apparently go through dance steps without human aid. If dancing is not important to story, perhaps the copy might be carried: "You'll be so happy you'll want to dance . . . when you see (attraction).”

Effect of the shoes dancing is achieved by using white shoes, within a shadow-box behind the opening in the display, and backed up with black velvet. Neon or globes outline the opening on the outside (causing a slight glare in the eyes of those watching the display and preventing too close an inspection of the interior of the shadow-boxed opening). A dancer seated behind the display panel, wearing stockings that are black to match black velvet background, is wearing the shoes; as she moves her feet, only the shoes are visible, since the black stockings and the black backing blend together. 

Or, the shoes might be moved by use of black threads which are attached to revolving cam-shaft or eccentric wheel above, and out of sight. 

145. LAUNDRIES. . . Can cooperate by inserting heralds or specially printed inserts in laundry packages. Tieup line, or copy for the laundry might also be carried on the herald, with most of space, however, devoted to theatre attraction. A few guest tickets might help secure insertion of heralds. Or cardboard inserts which many laundries place in laundered shirts, might be imprinted. 

146. HOTELS... Small imprinted stickers can be attached to the small bars of soap used in rooms in hotels. 

Panels and display frames should be placed in hotel lobbies. 

Theatre and attraction should be listed on hotels' bulletin boards. • 82

Morning newspapers delivered to guests, can have a small sticker attached to each paper, the stickers imprinted: "Good morning! 

After you've had your dinner tonight at the (hotel) restaurant, come on over to (theatre) and see (attraction). We're sure you'll like it." Or wording can omit hotel copy. Rubber stamp can be used instead of stickers.

Cards, to be placed in hotel rooms, might carry copy: "Stay over in (town). Why spend a tiresome night on the train when you can rest in comfort here, and attend the showing tonight of (attraction) at (theatre)." Space devoted to theatre attraction, and underlined copy might carry railroad, bus and airline morning schedule. 

Heralds placed in hotel rooms, or in mail boxes. 

Permanent "Rules" cards might be printed and supplied hotels for attaching permanently inside hotel rooms. Necessary information is given, with institutional theatre ad carried at bottom of the card. 

147. MATCHES... Small imprinted gummed stickers might be attached to the inside cover of book matches (usually distributed wherever cigarettes are sold). Or, attached to small boxes of matches. Or, attached around individual matches, where single matches are provided. 

Or, instead of sticker, small rubber stamp might be just as effectively used.

Or, small imprinted card might be inserted in book match folders. 

Imprinted book matches might be supplied restaurants and cigar counters, or distributed to patrons.

150. COFFEE . . . Coffee distributor might be contacted, arranging to print paper streamers, carrying line at top on coffee, devoting most of space to attraction. Streamers to be attached by distributor to windows of places handling the coffee. 

Perhaps it will fit into plans to have coffee served to theatre patrons on matinee, or opening day; and if this is used, a miniature bar might be secured and set up in lobby or on mezzanine floor. 

Bakery will supply sandwiches. Where line of patrons are waiting outside and in lobby to see attraction, arrangements can be made to have coffee served them (especially if the day is cold). 

In connection with a thriller or shock attraction, coffee might be supplied patrons, with display panels and newspaper ads suggesting that the coffee will calm the nerves before and after witnessing the attraction. Coffee concern might buy newspaper space or heralds, also supplying girls to serve the coffee.

153. FRONT AMPLIFICATION... Brief portions (perhaps song highlights) of an attraction can be sent through to front of theatre to speakers concealed behind a display (with panel carrying invitation to listen to attraction highlights or song hits). Effective for occasional use.

Amplification hookup might be connected direct with projection booth; or microphone is used, picking up sound from auditorium when desired. Or, records of song hits from the attraction might be played instead.

And, similarly a portion of theatre's attraction could be broadcast over radio station, direct from theatre. 

Playing song hits, front display might show a radio as part of the painted display, and speaker being concealed behind the panel, so that sound appears to come through the "radio." 

Also, using amplification equipment in front of theatre, microphone might be placed in box office. Cashier's "thank you" and her comment to each patron (in which she mentions a coming attraction), will be amplified for the benefit of those passing. Or she can speak to those passing, plugging the attraction. 

154. LAUGH BROADCAST... In connection with a comedy attraction, a microphone might be used to pick up laughs from the audience (at funniest part of attraction) together with whatever dialogue from attraction that microphone might pick up, for brief period over radio station . . . following up with announcement. ...

Radio announcement might feature recording of hysterical laughter, played for an instant, following with the announcement: "That's a sample of the reception you will receive when you visit the (theatre) to see (attraction).”

Laugh highlights and audience reaction might be carried out front, the speakers being concealed behind a panel which is lettered· "Listen to the crowd roar at (attraction);" or, "Hear 'em laughing 

You'll be laughing, too, when you see (attraction)." Or, laugh record might be used.

Phonograph, as center of front or lobby display, might openly play the laugh record . . . with panel carrying copy: "You'll laugh like this when you see (attraction)." In charge of girl attendant who keeps the record going, or equipped with record repeater, the phonograph might also be placed in prominent spot away from theatre. Or, girl carries a portable phonograph about town, stopping • 85.

155. PRESCRIPTION... Herald printed in shape and form of a regular doctor's prescription, with "Prescription Blank" being imprinted at top. And, then in smaller type: "For patients who need laughs (or 'thrills'). Mix . . . one teaspoonful of thrills every minute . . . 1 dram of special shock drops between each thrill. Add mystery powders, and let dissolve slowly with high tension suspense pills. Stir well with excitement fluid, until thermometer reaches amazing point. Administer until patient's breath comes in gasps ... and while he has chills, keep him bundled in spell-binding atmosphere until limp from awe. Take . . . each dose with tablespoonful of romance to sweeten the prescription. Inject rib-tickling antidote if patient becomes breathless. Signed, Dr. (star of character in attraction)." Or, adapt to suit attraction. 

Or the "Prescription" might be worded simply: "Prescription.

156. COMPARISON... With "Then and Now," "Old and

New" as the theme, current-day stars or celebrities, or articles of any kind, as compared with those of another day, might be made the basis of lobby display, window tieups, parade, or newspaper and radio contests.

A girl show, stage or screen, might inspire a newspaper contest comparing the lovely ladies in the show with famous beauties of history (or literature). Art would use series of photos of both presentday dames and history book girls . . . with modern miss given the break in the art layout. Historical beauties, Cleopatra, DuBarry, Mme. Pompadour, Mary, Queen of Scots . . . and many others, (pictures obtained from the library). Contestants required to identify pictured historical dame and to write (in 100 words or less) a comparison and their preferences. 

Famous lovers might be made basis for contest comparing romantic star of attraction and great lovers of history (or literature) (as Don Juan, Cassanova, Cellini, and others), with today's romanceer getting the edge in art layouts. 

Or, "Famous Sweethearts" can be made basis for contest, if attraction features a team of lovers. Contestants to identify and • 86 •

compare history's famous teams with those portrayed in picture. (Comparisons can be serious, or in rhyme, or humorous.) 

Dancers, or bathing girls in theatre's attraction might suggest other girl comparisons, as girl in modern dress and girl in old costume; or girl in old-style swim suit, and picture of girl in latest, briefest modern suit; dancer in old-style costume might be compared with newest costume. 

Photos of bathing girls, then and now, might be used in window display of bathing suits. Possibly with girls modeling bathing suits, showing old-time suits, bringing them up through the years to present day. (Old-style suits and new ones can be obtained for display purposes from bathing suit manufacturers.)

Automobile dealer might compare newest model automobile with older model for window. Or photograph (for papers) poses girl from stage show with the two cars. Photo might be displayed in dealers window.

Parade might be arranged (see No. 64).

157. CELLOPHANE... Occasionally effectiveness of front or lobby displays can be increased by covering of cellophane. Stills or even entire display panels might be covered over. It can be used in a variety of colors.

Costumes for girls used in connection with front or lobby displays might be covered over with cellophane. Girl might be "delivered" to luncheon clubs or night clubs, introduced as "wrapped in cellophane, untouched by human hands;" covered completely over with cellophane when she enters; or in cellophane covered costume, she does song, or dance routine, suggested by the attraction (with announcements). 

158. SAFETY PINS. . . For distribution, pins might be attached to small cards, which are imprinted: "Just in case you cast aside all restraint . . . and laugh aside all buttons. . . take this 'insurance' with you when you go to see (attraction)." Card (with the attached pin) can be inserted in small envelopes which are imprinted: "(Name of attraction) Insurance Policy." 

159. TROPHIES... Named after star of theatre attraction, 

• 87 •

trophy might be presented to winners of races or contest (which might or might not be actually promoted by the theatre). Might be presented in tieup with newspaper. Or paper might carry stories and picture of good looking girl posed with the trophy. 

Trophy can be an engraved cup; or a plaque; or something suggested by the event, or the recipient (as a baseball glove for a baseball player, the glove possibly autographed by the star of the attraction).

Baseball player on the home team with best batting average for a specified week might be the winner of the trophy, with paper following each day's results on the sport page (mentioning attraction). 

Winner of a dance contest, staged on a special evening dedicated to and named after the star by the cooperating ballroom might receive the trophy.

Winners of races-auto, foot, horse, swimming, bicycle, motorcycle, dog races; any sort of race, can be presented with a trophy. 

Or speed contest might be based on some local industry; for example, in a dairy country, the event promoted might be a cow-milking contest. Or a typing contest might be set for office girls. 

Most valuable player on local football team might receive the trophy, his selection based on decision of appointed judges, or of the players themselves. Presented at end of season, presentation can be made quite an event, with the team assembled on theatre stage, together with cheer-leaders and coach, with Mayor or other local celebrity making the presentation. Or trophy might go to "most popular player." Or to the player making the most touchdowns.

Trophy should be placed on display in advance in a prominent store window, perhaps that of a jeweler.

In connection with an attraction that deals with racing of any kind, local racing organization might loan a display of trophies, to be exhibited in window or in theatre lobby in advance (under lock and key). Perhaps some racing celebrity might appear each evening, or at certain specified time, and discuss the trophies. 

160. HITCH-HIKING... Short-clad girl, standing at busy intersection, pretends to "thumb" a ride from passing automobiles.

She stands near a panel which carries copy: "I'm hitch-hiking a ride to (theatre) to see (attraction)." She hands a herald on the attraction to motorists who stop. 

161. EXERCISE MACHINES... Rowing machine might be set up in lobby or store window, on platform at eye-level, with girl in shorts or bathing suit, "demonstrating" the machine. Panel • 88 •

carries copy: "She's rowing to keep in shape, so that she can withstand the laughs (or thrills) in (attraction)."

Similarly, girl in bathing suit might "demonstrate" an electric reducing machine (borrowed from an electric shop). Or men or girls operating the machine might be costumed as attraction suggests (as clowns in connection with a circus attraction).

Any other type of exercise machine, electric horses, etc., might be similarly adapted. 

162. SEE YOURSELF... Novel display panel, to be placed opposite full length mirror.. carries copy: "See yourself as (star of picture) in (picture)," (or whatever illustration is used). Illustration is on the opposite side of the display . . . a life-size figure, but with the face cut out (an opening being cut through panel... so that persons looking through the opening in the panel will see (reflected in the mirror), their faces framed above the painted figure). Or a life-size lithograph figure (from 3-sheet or 6sheet) could be used, with opening cut in where face should be. 

Ends of panel (space between panel and mirror), taken care of with two small panels set at angle concealing mirror from view except through opening. Stills or copy on end panels. 

Figure used should show costume used in or suggested by the attraction. Best if the costume can win a laugh. Any copy included on the reverse or reflected side of the panel, must be in reverse. 

Panel might carry two identical life-size figures of star, with face of one of them cut out. Panel asks patrons if they think they look like star, inviting them to look and compare. 

Panel might be used first in lobby, later in store or prominent downtown location.

164. STILT WALKER... Good flash when available, a stilt walker wearing costume in line with attraction, will attract attention.

165. LINGO... Type of talk used by characters portrayed in attraction might be made basis of contest for radio or newspaper. 

Circus talk, gangster language, western or stage idiom. 

Many different groups have an intricate language all their own, a trade language or a "slanguage" that isn't ordinarily easily understood by an outsider.

Contest might be based on brief yarn, describing some scene in the attraction, written in the particular slanguage that the attraction suggests, contestants to "interpret it." Newspaper illustrates the contest with scenes from the attraction. Or, various "words" might be listed, with contestants to decipher them, or to write a brief bit of dialogue (suggested by scene pictured) using the lingo. 

166. RADIO OPEN HOUSE... Program to be broadcast, in an informal manner, from stage of theatre, or from mezzanine or lobby, before beginning of day's performances, but after box office opening (sufficiently early to allow time for program before start of show).

Program might include song numbers, or even dance taps (on board, with microphone near) which those present among the audience might care to render (making sure that there are some several "plants" present each broadcast, singers or dancers who can definitely be depended on).

Music can be supplied by organ, pianist, or accordion. 

Those present might be invited to say a few words over the radio; or to call out their favorite song for the pianist to play, and all to sing. Manager or star of stage show might act as master of ceremonies.

Listeners might be invited to send in suggestions for old songs to be played, those selected getting ducats; and guest tickets might be offered to first ten listeners phoning in a correct list of old numbers (or all numbers) played during the program. 

Some guest entertainer could be arranged for each program, some celebrity or entertainer. Plenty of plugs for the attraction should be worked in. • 90 •

Appeal might be made to out-of-town listeners to make the theatre their headquarters while in town, and to attend the broadcast in person when in town, and say a few words over the radio.

167. VOICE TEST... Especially useful where a certain line or expression is identified with star or attraction, or where star has unusual expression or way of speaking, a dictaphone can be made the center of a lobby display, with patrons invited to register their voices, with tickets for voices most nearly resembling that of star. 

Costumed girl attendant should be in charge. 

If attraction features no "saying," or catch-line, on which the stunt might be based, the idea might be adapted to title of attraction or star's name, tickets awarded to those reciting the attraction title, or star's name, with most "expression" or "feeling."

After repeating the required words patron speaks his name and address.

Might be called a "Hollywood Voice Test," with patrons invited to hear their voices, attendant playing back the dictaphone recordings.

Patrons might be asked (on display panels) to discover for themselves if they possess voice like that of star of attraction. 

Another angle uses radio receiving set with microphone connected through to same. Microphone is set up in front of a display panel; and the radio, with which it is connected, is some distance away, also in lobby, however-perhaps across lobby. 

Or, radio station might broadcast the "voice test," from front of theatre or in lobby, with listeners to pick the winners. 

168. ANIMALS, JUNGLE . . . In connection with a zoo, or jungle, or wild animal angle in attraction, live animals from zoo, (as suggested by attraction), or stuffed animals from taxidermists, might be used in lobby or window. Live monkeys (on leash or enclosed) might be used. If alive, precautions taken that they are definitely out of reach of patrons; and where live animals are used in lobby, odor must be considered. Appropriate jungle display should be built around animals. Florist might supply ferns and palms to bank around and behind animal cages, adding jungle atmosphere.

If newspaper will use photo and stories, arrangements might be made to screen a jungle picture (with sound) at the zoo, "to secure the animals' reaction." Or couple of cages of animals (including monkeys) • 91 •

might be brought to theatre for a special screening for zoo keeper, newspaper men, anthropologists, zoologists. 

Radio station might broadcast from zoo on busy day, using portable microphone and extra long extension cords. Announcer talks about animals (interviews visitors), working in announcements for theatre's attraction.

Zoo or menagerie may permit small banners attached near animal cages. 

Photo of girls from stage show "washing an elephant" at zoo might be good for a newspaper flash.

Color cartoon contest might be carried in newspaper (or used on herald). Kids invited to color drawings of animals. Large part of space devoted to theatre's attraction. Or contestants might be asked to submit descriptive "nick-names" for animals and birds. 

Or to identify tracks of different animals (obtainable at library). 

Or, highlights of previous jungle attractions might be made the basis of a several-day newspaper contest . . . with contestants to identify the pictured scenes. Illustration on current jungle attraction also carried. ...

Jungle float, amplification equipped, and carrying girls (costumed in shorts, khaki shirts, tropic helmets), and "savages" dressed in animal skins, painted up and carrying spears, might travel about town. Sound effect record possibly available as an accessory or obtainable from radio station. Animals might be available for a parade. "Savages" Jungle front could feature bamboo and tangle of vines. might be used as front bally, several men costumed in skins, painted up, pounding tomtoms. "Savages" with small animal, or perhaps a snake, might be taken to newspaper office for a visit, with resultant story. ...

Mechanical animals can be constructed or rented-life-size duplicate of a real animal, made to move, and perhaps, using amplification, made to roar or snarl. Or a "roar-box" can be made up by using a small tub or wooden bucket or nail keg . . . with bottom removed and covered over with a piece of old drum-head or tightly stretched skin (other end being left open); string, with a knot in it inserted through center of the drum-head and to be pulled from outside of keg, grasping it with a resined piece of canvas or a canvas glove rubbed with resin. Cutout figure of animal might be animated, the figure being painted up or made up from posters Using cutout figure of a cat (lion or tiger) effectiveness will be in- • 92 •

creased by cutting out the eyes and replacing with green paper, with lights behind, on flashers. 

Theatre artist might go to zoo to "paint or sketch" a picture of (animal suggested by attraction) . . . accompanied by newspaper photographer. Couple of pretty girls might go along, to help the artist (and for the photograph). Or an orchestra might play at the zoo, to secure the animals' reactions to modern jungle rhythms. 

Night club might feature a jungle dancer, pretty girl, who features an aboriginal stomp. (See Photos.) (See 978.) 

169. BOOKS. . . With an attraction based on a popular novel, bookstores will go along for window displays using covers and streamers (generally available from publishers), and display panels. Library exhibit might be arranged. Imprinted book-marks can be distributed by the library. 

Lobby, or window panel might be made up on style of opened book, one side carrying title and cast and selling copy, other side carrying illustrations exclusively . . . and similar layout might be used for newspaper ad. Or a display might picture large replica of the book, slightly opened, and with stills "pouring out"-the stills attached so that they appear to be falling out of the book as it is opened. 

Entrance doors can be covered over with panels made up to resemble book covers. Or panel in front of box office might be made up to resemble the cover of the book; title lettered at top, author's name at bottom... and with opening cut in center, through which tickets are sold. 

Large "book" made from papier mache, or muslin stretched over a light frame, might be made sufficiently large for a man to parade streets with the book over him. 

With attraction based on a well-known book, arrangements may be made to present a copy (or a number of copies) to the local library, making as much of an occasion of the presentation as possible. 

Special and elaborate binding might be placed on the book. It might be sent to the studios for autographs of the stars, or the author. 

Mayor of city might add his autograph, "commemorating the occasion." Prominent citizen, perhaps the Mayor, or a pretty girl, should make the "presentation" to librarian (for newspaper photographs). Copies of the book might be used as contest prizes. 

Copy of book might be presented to visiting or local celeb, with newspaper going along for a picture of the presentation. Newspaper can offer tickets for best suggested greeting to be inscribed in the • 93 •

book to be sent the star (or the author) with the compliments of (city).

Exhibit of author's other work should be displayed by bookstore or library.

Heralds might be made up from a copy, or several copies, of the book from which attraction was adapted. Book is torn apart, into individual pages . . . the pages being overprinted (on both sides): "A page from (copy on story and attraction)." Distribute as regular heralds.

Attention of Literary Societies and educational organizations should be directed to the attraction, if the story is such that they would be interested. Women's clubs might be interested and will discuss the story at a meeting if their attention is called to it. 

Pretty girl, reading the book on which attraction is based might be comfortably seated, clad in lounging pajamas, as center of a window display. Furniture store might prove most logical window. She is selected for her reading voice, and with microphone placed near her, amplification can carry her voice to those outside the window. 

Title of book should be easily seen. Stunt might be built up as a "Marathon Reading Contest." Attendant is dressed as nurse, and periodic radio broadcast from the window can be set. 

Giant book display, for lobby or window (or for float), might feature a cover that carries the attraction title; and several "pages" which carry illustrations, copy on the attraction. The book is placed in an upright "easel" position, and an attractively costumed girl is kept busy turning the pages. Title of attraction is also lettered on the back "page." Used in lobby, the "book" should be placed on a slight elevation. 

Or large display reproduction of book might feature a girl costumed as suggested by the attraction, posed within same. She might be placed behind a lettered scrim, being revealed through the scrim when lights flash on behind same.

Books might be collected and presented to hospital patients, if newspaper sponsorship can be arranged, collecting same type stories as attraction. 

170. DISPLAYS, LOBBY FRAMES... Permanent built-up panels, or frames (for posters, stills, or lithographs), might be shadowboxed for good results. Cutout grill-work could be backed up with colored paper and lights. Where posters are used permanent panels or frames should be made standard size so that in an emergency stock lithographs from the exchanges might be used. Displays should be · 94 ·

arranged with the idea of using them first in the lobby, then advancing to the front when the attraction comes along. Panels should be substantially constructed if they are to last and designed so that they can be changed with a minimum of effort and complication (eliminating necessity of noise, accelerating changes). Variety should be introduced in designs, and display frames and posters should offer some contrast. Panels should conform to some extent with theatre architecture. Electrical displays must be well insulated for protection of patrons, elimination of fire hazards.

Where lobby or front displays call for living talent a painted panel (perhaps cutout figures) should be prepared for use in the display when the live talent is "off duty." (See Animation, Fronts.) 

171. WHAT I KNOW ABOUT WOMEN . . . Folder type herald is imprinted: "What I know about women," adding the name of (male) star, and "See inside pages." Inside the cover there is nothing at all, blank space. Ad on the attraction is printed on the back page of the herald. 

Or, the entire idea might be changed by imprinting on the inner pages, the single word: "Plenty!" 

172. IMPERSONATIONS... Where star, characterization or type, is familiar to everyone, an impersonation contest might be worked out effectively. Judging of entries in the contest should take place in advance of showing of attraction, on stage and immediately preceding trailer; or in window; or at a specified time in front of the theatre on opening day.

Impersonation of any and all motion picture or stage stars, and their arrival at theatre like regular stars, might be made the feature of a "Hollywood Impersonation Contest." Spotlights, cameras (not necessarily using film), band, and all the trimmings, a la Hollywood, should be used. "Stars" to arrive at theatre in individual cars (supplied by an automobile dealer, the cars merely circling the block, picking up a new "star" at rear of theatre each time). "Stars" each say a few words into microphone, either connected with amplification system, with speakers above canopy, or broadcast over a radio station, or both. Clever master of ceremonies in charge of the arrival of "stars" out front can add comedy to the arrivals. Actual contest to be held on stage, as center of a stage revue, with best impersonator to be selected. Used in connection with a stage show, comedians from the show might be conspicuous out front, perhaps "arriving" in a broken-down flivver, or handling the job of master of ceremonies. • 95 •

Impersonator might appear on stage, making brief announcement which is followed by trailer. 

173. WHOM AND WHAT 

Contest for newspaper or radio, in connection with adventure story, might have contestants answer the questions, "What ten articles would you want to take along? (On a cruise or adventure such as attraction pictures).” 

Or, "What ten persons would you like to invite to accompany you ... and why?"

Or contestants might submit a list of ten famous persons that they would like to invite to a dinner party for (star of attraction), if they had the whole world to choose from. . . giving reasons for selection of each person. 

174. COLLEGIATE... Newspaper contest can offer prizes for best college humor, or cleverest "wise-cracks," to illustrate a pictured scene.

Pennants might be printed, in collegiate manner, on paper, and attached to mirrors and windows. Pennants used for display out front might each carry a letter, which, together, spell out name of attraction.

Sidewalk barkers could be dressed as cheer-leaders, performing out front, in collegiate cheering style. 

Stooges, wearing sweaters to which letters are attached, might parade about town, the letters when correctly lined up, spelling out name of theatre's attraction. Pretty girls for this stunt would add to its effectiveness.

Collegiate cars might be used in a parade. Prize could be offered for car lettered with best "collegiate" wise-cracks. 

Appeal should be directed toward schools and colleges. Displays placed in places frequented by college boys and girls. Perhaps school library or cafeteria will permit cards to be displayed. 

Fraternities might have their pledges make speeches about attraction on downtown corners. Ballroom might feature a "collegiate dance," attraction announced, photos of star as prizes. College glee club might appear at theatre on opening night. Perhaps college band, too. Prettiest co-ed contest might be worked out with school or college paper, with trophy for winner. 

175. PARKING... Often very important in its effect on attendance, parking problems of patrons can sometimes be solved by securing permission for patrons to park cars on a nearby vacant lot. 

Should have an attendant in charge and should be kept open until an hour or so after show is over. Or, regular parking station might • 96 •
