OF O make theatre patrons a special price (in return for theatre publicizing the tieup) on presentation of ticket stub from theatre. Perhaps the station will have attendants ride with car to theatre, returning the car after the show.

Special parking rate could be made by garages and parking lots on one special day of each week to aid in attracting people downtown on an off night. 

176. BLOW THE HORN... In connection with a coming musical attraction, an actual trumpet, or other valve musical instrument might be made the center of a lobby display. Copy invites patrons to "press the middle valve down" to hear hit tunes from attraction (or to see a scene from the coming show). Pressing the valve makes a contact that starts a phonograph concealed behind the display (equipped with a record repeater) which plays a recording of the musical numbers; or illuminates a scene behind an unopaqued mirror (the illustration being visible through the mirror when illuminated from behind). 

177. TICKET REPLICAS... Heralds can resemble regular reserve seat tickets for a Broadway show. Might be die-cut, and printed to resemble a couple of tickets protruding from a small envelope. Or "tickets" can be inserted in small envelopes for distribution. Might be used to emphasize the costliness of the production . . . and that an expensive Broadway show might be seen, on the screen, at regular prices. 

Or, in connection with a football attraction, "tickets" might resemble tickets to a football game (copy, when completely read, making it clear that it's an ad on theatre's attraction). ... 

178. SPEAKING CUTOUT . . . Life-size cutout figure of a star of a coming attraction, in lobby (elevated slightly), has a speaker attached behind it, which is connected with amplification system. 

Announcements can be made as entering patrons arrive directly opposite it. (If a feminine star, cashier might make the announcements.) Or a phonograph might supply music, perhaps a recording of the star's voice. 

179. COSMETICS. . . Window displays, for druggist or beauty shop, using attraction stills, can generally be based on cosmetics, and possibly store will buy newspaper space. Might carry copy: "(Name) Cosmetic . . . Choice of many stars of stage and screen." (No endorsement, unless authorized.) 

Cosmetic company may supply sample packages to be presented to ladies attending matinee opening day. Or, placed in imprinted • 97 ⚫

envelopes, distributed in advance. If items to be presented are limited, announcements should say that they will be presented “as long as they last."

Might arrange to have an attractive girl demonstrate make-up in window or lobby. If in window, using amplification so that her voice might be heard. Otherwise, cards placed on an easel carry her message. Make-up expert might give advice and complexion analysis mentioning theatre attraction's star as example. Star of stage show might appear in person at specified time, "waiting" on customers at cosmetic counter . . . selling authographed packages. Photo of star (stage or screen) holding or using cosmetic might be adapted to a newspaper ad, local dealer buying newspaper space, mentioning both the tieup and theatre's attraction. 

Tieup might be based on the angle, “Blonde or Brunette. Which do you think the loveliest?" Using stills of both blonde and brunette stars with copy: "See both (and names) in (attraction)." Copy carries the thought that whether blonde or brunette, the beauty experts and advisors of the store will be pleased to recommend the correct cosmetics. ... 

180. TREASURE Newspaper can cooperate in arrang ing a "treasure hunt," each day picturing locations (in town) where the "treasure" is to be hidden . . a major prize to be concealed at each place, together with lesser prizes. "Treasure hunters" to report to the newspaper office on the morning of the "hunt," receiving large imprinted tags, which they wear -name of the attraction being prominently imprinted on the tags. 

Early on the morning of the hunt, small cards are hidden about the different locations which have been pictured by the paper. . . the locations being guarded to prevent premature search. At each location, one of the concealed cards entitles the finder to a major prize, other cards winning tickets or other prizes. All cards to be exchanged for prizes at newspaper office, or at theatre. 

Number one prize might be a gilded key which opens a treasure chest on display in lobby, which holds promoted prizes. 

Contestants can be routed, the different locations being designated as "location number one," "number two," etc. Or the contestants can be permitted to select locations themselves. But they must start together (at a given signal) from newspaper office. 

In addition to tickets and cash prizes, a number of tags might entitle finders to a bar of candy, or bottled drink (which might be • 98.

EN CY CLOPEDIA OF EXPLOITATI O N 

promoted). Tags can be placed in small packages of candy when concealing them.

Attraction title that mentions money, or treasure, or items of value, might suggest the stunt.

Or a different method of staging a "treasure hunt," in tieup with a number of business places, would have cooperating newspaper announce the names of business places where "treasure slips" might be secured . . . with first so-many "hunters" making the complete rounds getting a slip from each business place to win tickets or prizes. 

Newspaper might publish a map of downtown section of city, with locations of business places indicated. Those engaging in the hunt could start at any point (with business places waiting until an agreed time to distribute slips). Complete sets brought to newspaper office or theatre. Newspaper would sell cooperative ads in connection with the "hunt." Might be adapted to radio. Trade-marks or slogans of places cooperating might be announced, instead of names. 

Adaption of "treasure hunt" to a lobby display, might feature a large container filled with sand, in which small coins and minor prizes are buried. Patrons entitled to a single dig, with a small shovel ... retaining any coin or prize brought up with the scoop. Display in charge of a pretty girl, who supplies the small shovels. Small "nuggets" (small rocks, gilded) might be placed in the sand, and the lucky finders to exchange them for guest tickets.

Or, "treasure chest," covered over with plastic wood, and gilded (wiping the gilt with green) might be placed in the lobby, as center of display on attraction. Inside the chest, guest tickets are placed, or promoted prizes, which go to first person opening the chest. 

Patrons are invited to try their keys. Attractive costumed girls distribute keys about town . . . attached tags explaining that the key might open the "treasure chest." Large quantity of miscellaneous keys, perhaps old keys, might be secured cheaply from a locksmith; and with these, several keys that fit the lock are mixed. "Chest" might be placed in cooperating store (with display on attraction), instead of in lobby. 

181. TRAVELING BOX OFFICE... Tickets might be sold away from the theatre, in advance, establishing a "box office" (a display and table, with attractive girl in charge), in stores, or other downtown locations. Gives the attraction distinction and importance, even if no tickets are sold. Ads on the coming attraction might mention that tickets can be obtained at the special advance box office. 

Best where reserved seats are on sale. • 99 •

EN C Y C L O PEDIA OF EXPLOITATION 

Similarly a truck might be turned into a moving box office ... paneling all sides, and including window in side of truck. Copy on panels sells attraction and calls attention to the fact that tickets are available in advance. Girl is inside the truck, at window; attendant, in uniform, on sidewalk when truck makes a stop. Truck might make a series of downtown stops. "Box office" for street ticket sale (perhaps for charity show), spotted on street corner, might be made up in design as suggested by the attraction: as, in connection with a musical, in the shape of a bass fiddle, or big bass drum. 

182. PIANOS... Piano school might supply one or several pianos and pianists to play song hits from attraction in lobby; or in store window, using amplification. Greater flash if several pianos used, and with attractive girl pianists. Or player-piano in lobby, might play hit tunes from attraction, or numbers suggested by it. 

Using small piano, it might be transported to prominent corners, where pianist plays song hits from attraction. Small truck carries piano, which is lifted off, placed on sidewalk when used. Girl, in costume, might dance. Might also use a singer. Ad copy can be displayed on piano music panel, made up after style of sheet music; or girl can display banner at conclusion of her dance. 

A trip to City Hall and a song number for the Mayor on steps or lawn, might be good for a newspaper flash. Especially adaptable to a stage revue, posing girls from the show for the picture. Or, instead of Mayor if he is not agreeable to the idea, some other local celeb might be used if newspaper will go for the picture. 

Distributor of an electric organ (which merely uses a console and amplification unit) might permit one of the electric organs to be placed on display in theatre lobby, playing hit tunes from a coming attraction. Used out front of theatre (though protected from weather); or in lobby, playing softly; or with console in lobby, speakers in front of theatre. Might be transported to luncheon club meeting where melodies from attraction are introduced and perhaps broadcast. 

183. DISGUISES 

.. 

Drawing or photograph of star is featured in a newspaper ad, herald or program, inviting readers to "disguise" the star. . . using a pencil to draw on the disguise; with tickets for best.

Or photographs of stars might be disguised for a newspaper contest, picturing them with drawn-on beards, or helmet and goggles, or masks (or other "disguise" as suggested by the attraction). Or, • 100 •

star or half mask, or other design might be drawn directly across face of star. Contestants to identify stars, select their favorite, giving reasons.

Localized angle would use disguised photographs of local prominents (with their permission) on which the "disguise" has been drawn, asking contestants to identify them. 

184. SEE WHO... Envelopes, for distribution as heralds, are imprinted: "Look in the envelope. . . See who's going to see (attraction) at (theatre)." Small mirrors, or chips of mirror, are placed inside the envelopes . . . and, of course, on opening the envelopes they see themselves.

Lobby adaption would feature a small window shade as center of a display panel . copy on the shade inviting patrons to raise it, and "see who we expect to have with us next week when (attraction) comes to town." Raising the shade reveals mirror and the reflected face of patron. 

185. BIOGRAPHY . . . In adding selling emphasis to star of picture, life story would be splendid and often acceptable newspaper feature. Radio program might use it. 

Available from press-sheet, or from publicity department of producing company. 

Jumbled biography might form the basis of a contest for newspaper or radio, mixing up the biographies of several stars, so that much of the "information" is in error, with motion picture fans to correct the biographies . . . with guest tickets for first so-many correct ones submitted.

Or a series of biographies of stars might be carried, but without names, inviting readers to identify the star from the biography. 

On another page (to which reader of the biography is directed) star's name and a photograph, story on current attraction, is carried. 

186. BLACKBOARD CARDS... Printed window cards, for distribution to merchants, markets, restaurants, soda fountains, are headed: "Special Today" . . . and below this space is solid black area, taking up a large portion of the card. Then, below the black space, imprint: "Special at (theatre) today," and copy on theatre's attraction. Merchant, using chalk which is handed him along with the card, can write in his own specials in the black space. 

Variation is use of printed sheets, illustrated with picture of star of theatre's attraction. Blank space replaces black space and merchant uses ordinary pencil or paint in lettering in his "specials." • 101 •

These sheets can be gummed at top and bottom before distribution so that merchant might easily attach them to inside of windows. 

187. SWITCHBOARDS . . . In apartment houses, stores, large business places, hotels, the telephone switchboards are often very busy points. A few passes handed the operator, together with a request to mention the attraction wherever possible, will often achieve wonders in word-of-mouth advertising. Or, the operators of the boards can be invited to a special advance screening, or first showing of an attraction. Display panel might be placed near apartment house switchboards. 

188. CIRCULAR... Display for lobby might be made in shape of circular panel, protruding from an "envelope". . . lettered: "A gigantic Circular Letter' . . . to tell you about (attraction)."

Herald adaption would be imprinted on round sheets of paper, carrying copy: “A Real Circular Letter . . . calling your attention to (attraction).” 

189. BARKER... Some pictures especially suggest the use of a sidewalk barker . . . though one might be used on any outstanding attraction.

Good spiel is arranged, and memorized by uniformed barker . . . (preferably tall and talkative), stationed on sidewalk in front of theatre, attempting to sell the picture to those passing. Amplification might be used if city authorities permit.

Barker might be costumed as suggested by the attraction, as ring-master's outfit for circus story. Attractive girl, costumed, might qualify as barker.

Or, playing to capacity business,. some member of theatre staff should serve as a "barker," endeavoring to prevent walk-aways. 

190. PROJECTOR, PROJECTION... Portable projector 

(can be rented; or borrowed from a Y.M.C.A. or school), might be set up in a second-story window, shooting trailers and slides on a screen across the street (or against front of theatre). The "screen" would be attached to a light frame which is tied or wired securely to front of a building. Screen could be made up by having four or more sheets sewed together; or banner company or tent and awning company might make it up. Perhaps several trailers can be secured, so that film will not have to be rewound so frequently. While film is being rewound, slides are flashed. 

If projector carries sound equipment, speakers might possibly be placed behind the screen (wires carried across street, must not cross trolley or high tension wires). Or public address system might be 102

used, placing speakers behind the screen, and accompanying flashed pictures and slides with announcements. 

To add interest to slides, late news might be flashed, crediting cooperating newspaper. 

The stunt is, of course, a “natural” for election night, with returns flashed, together with theatre's announcements. Or, in football season, football scores from all over the country might be flashed. 

Adapted to a window, slides or trailers (from within) are flashed against the glass (which has been covered over with a sheet, or sign cloth, or with white paper). Opening in a display panel in the window should "frame" the screen .. opening being made part of panel design, as a wide-open, laughing mouth (through which the picture is projected). 191. A-BOARDS Two one-sheet boards, attached backto-back in the shape of an inverted V, can often be used for display on sidewalk in front of theatre, city authorities permitting. Also, the Navy Recruiting office generally has A-boards at post office, and in prominent locations; and if logical tieup copy can be worked out, they will permit use of their panels. 

Truck display might feature 24-sheet size panels similarly constructed, one poster facing one side of the street, the other poster in view on other side. Amplification could be added to the truck's equipment, making announcements, playing song hits. 

192. WRESTLING AND BOXING . . . Heralds can be distributed where athletic competitions draw crowds (heralds being • 103 ·

assured of better reception if distributed by pretty girls). Or bally of some kind might "make" the fights.

Announcements from the ring may be arranged. 

Trophy from star of attraction might be presented to winner of feature bout . . . good looking girl or local celeb making the presentation.

Tickets to wrestling or boxing matches are generally placed in a small envelopes when issued. Theatre can supply these envelopes, with ad on coming attraction (well in advance) imprinted. 

Local boxing arena might use "round cards," with title of attraction on reverse side. After showing round number, card is reversed and shown. 

In connection with attraction that features boxing, local athletic organization, Y.M.C.A., or gymnasium might sponsor a local amateur contest for “(star) Gloves," or a special trophy "from star."

Newspaper sports page might cooperate, or even sponsor the idea. 

Seconds at boxing matches might wear sweaters with attraction title lettered on back. Good looking girls, wearing lettered sweaters, could serve as "seconds" for a boxer or wrestler during a feature bout. 

Street flash on an attraction that features fighting might have boxing ring arranged on large flat-bed truck.. ropes, "fighters" in boxing trunks, referee and seconds Pretty girls in sport outfits or slacks act as "seconds." Lettered banners are attached at edge of the truck, extending down over the wheels. Truck stops at prominent corners, and boxers stage a brief sparring exhibition until gong stops them. The "seconds" can distribute heralds to crowds attracted while the "fight" is in progress. As gong sounds, fighters go to their corners, seconds fan them with towels, "referee" makes announcement about theatre's attraction. "Boxer" walking about streets in boxing outfit, gloves and all, will attract attention for a show that features boxing. Lettering on his back. (In summer, he might get away with just boxing trunks, with the copy lettered in water color directly on his back). 

Soda fountains might feature an "(Attraction) Punch," described as a "knock-out."

Photographs of famous fighters could be placed on display in the lobby. Local boxing or wrestling promoter might be able to supply them, or they might be available from newspaper morgue. 

Personal appearance of prominent fighter might be arranged, • 104 •

having him appear in lobby, meeting and greeting patrons; or introducing him from stage. 

A couple of girls, in fighting togs and gloves, might circulate around town, skipping ropes. Lettering on their backs, or they might be accompanied by an usher who carries sign, "A couple of knockouts from (attraction)."

Ad should be carried on sports page of newspaper. 

Maybe a couple of local dancing girls can do a "boxing" routine to dance rhythm, wearing shorts, sweaters, boxing gloves. Night spots and dance places featuring them, announce their routine as "inspired by (attraction)." Or dancers regularly appearing at a night club may be persuaded to present the boxing routine. 

Window display could feature a miniature "ring" . . . with miniature figures, or dolls, in the center. 

Local pugs might be invited to a screening, with their comment registered for sport page reproduction. 

193. DOOR-KNOB CARDS... Without which no collection of exploitation gags would be complete: Imprinted cards... with hole die-cut at top so that card may be hung over door-knobs in distribution. In addition to die-cut hole, top of card, to opening, may be cut to further facilitate hanging over door-knobs. 

Usually used house-to-house, or attached to door handles of parked automobiles, door-knob cards can also be distributed in tieup with dairies, attaching over tops of milk bottles left at homes. (See 339.) Or, places selling bottled beer can attach the cards over the bottles when serving. 

194. ORPHANS, AGED, HOSPITALS. . . Sponsored by newspaper, arrangements may be made to show an attraction for the inmates of a Home for the Aged; or an Orphanage; or hospital (for convalescents), showing it at the institution if necessary (as at hospital); or inmates can be transported to theatre. Stage show entertainers could be taken to the different institutions. 

If the inmates are to be brought to theatre (orphans would be), perhaps members of a civic club, or a bus or taxi company, will supply the necessary transportation. If bus is used, it might carry banners: "We're on our way to (theatre) to see (attraction)."

Entertainment provided must necessarily be of a type that the inmates would enjoy, and an attraction of which the authorities would definitely approve.

Perhaps some oldster in a group will have never seen a motion picture; and his reactions ought to be good for a newspaper yarn. 105 •

Value of the stunt to the theatre, aside from good will, depends largely on the publicity the newspapers give it, and newspaper cooperation should be arranged in advance. 

195. SLOGAN . . . All business places generally feature 

"slogans." With cooperation of newspaper advertising department, a double-run cooperating page of advertising could be arranged, carrying a number of merchants' ads, but omitting the names of the business places, merely carrying their slogans. Contestants are to identify the places by their slogans, submitting their answers to paper, with first so-many correct entries winning guest tickets. 

Later, the same page is repeated, but with the names of the business places added. Catch-line at top of page ties in theatre attraction, and space in center of page, at top, carries copy on the attraction, and describes the "contest."

Or tieup with radio station or program, or newspaper, can offer guest tickets for best submitted "slogan" suggested by attraction or star. This angle might be included in theatre space on newspaper cooperative page. 

196. NOISE... Card herald might be imprinted: "We don't need this (allow space for a small fire-cracker to be attached with glue) to make a big noise for (and into copy on attraction)." Especially effective around patriotic holidays, or if attraction suggests noise. 

Lad beating a drum might stroll about downtown sections . . drum being lettered: "I'm making a big noise for (attraction)." 

197. SWIM CONTEST ... Arranged with the cooperation of a swimming pool, Y.M.C.A., or beach, winners of a swimming or diving contest may be presented with tickets, bathing suits or trophies. Swimming meet might be arranged with sponsorship of

A.A.U. or local athletic association, or sponsored by newspaper. 

Perhaps pool will buy newspaper space, sport pages should carry stories. Display panels can be placed at pool in advance, and announcements made.

Made a feature of bathing girl contest at the pool might be featured in addition to the swimming contests. Or winners of swimming contests might be introduced as highlight of a bathing girl revue or contest at stage.

With an attraction that features swimming, or a swim star, an "aquatic queen" might be selected. 

198. CONFIDENTIAL... Reverse English on a campaign, pretending to be asking them to help keep a secret. 

Street ballys, the bigger and noisier and flashier the better (as sug- • 106 •

gested by the attraction), are bannered with "hush" copy, as: "Shhhh! (Name of attraction) is coming!" 

Or: "Don't tell a soul... but (attraction) is coming to (theatre)."

Etc. 

The same angle is also applied to window displays, heralds, trailers, and other advertising, including newspaper ads. 

Entire campaign could be built about the idea, or a single stunt might be used. 

199. FUNNY DIALOGUE, CAPTIONS. . . Newspaper contest offers prize for the best suggested dialogue submitted to accompany a scene from theatre's attraction which is shown. Extended over several days, a different scene would be carried each day. 

Lines would be placed under the illustrations, where the suggested dialogue is to be written in; or "balloons," such as comic strips use could be provided, where contestants might write in their suggested dialogue (if mats are used in reproducing the scene, the "balloons" would be routed out of the castings). First line of dialogue could be provided, with contestants to submit answers. Might be required that the submitted answer-line rhyme with the given first line. 

Might require answers to be "wise-cracks," or "gag-lines." Or, contest may be based on best jokes or stories submitted as suggested dialogue; or, the oldest gag, or the best gag of the week. Contest might be described as a search for a joke funny enough to submit to the star for possible radio use. 

Or caption above a scene from attraction could be omitted, with contestants invited to write a caption (for each of several scenes carried on successive days). If attraction title is brief, or single word, it might be required that title be included in submitted captions. 

Contest can be adapted to a lobby display, asking for dialogue or a caption for a displayed photograph enlargement. 

200. R.O.T.C.... Cooperation with military organizations in schools and colleges can prove of value. Tickets can be awarded winners in competitive drills, or inspection (with pretty girls presenting the tickets at inspection). Presentation will cause much discussion around the school. School may permit announcements in classes, or cards on bulletin boards; and cooperation might prove an investment, too, at a time when a band, or drill-squad, or military escort, is needed. 

201. AERIAL HERALDS... Arrangements made to have a plane drop a number of miniature parachutes over the city. Cooperating stores and business places buy newspaper space (possibly • 107 •

a cooperative page) publicizing the event. Guest tickets are attached to the miniature 'chutes, with the compliments of the cooperating stores. Or, a card can be attached, which is good for other major prize, in addition to the tickets, if brought to an indicated business place. Store's newspaper ads or radio announcements can be headed: "Watch the Skies . . . a Shower of tickets to see (attraction)."

Ready made miniature parachutes can be bought; or they may be made up from large handkerchiefs, attached at the corners (using short lengths of string) to a light metal washer. The 'chutes should be tried out before using, dropping them from a building, to make certain that the washer is the correct weight, and that the parachute will not descend too rapidly. 

Heralds can be similarly handled, in tieup with a store, dropping them from a plane over the city. Some of the heralds good for admission to see theatre's attraction, if stamped with store or theatre stamp . . . copy on herald, and in store's newspaper ads calling attention to this fact. 

202. LARGE POST CARD TO STAR... Gigantic over-size postcard... made after style of regular card . . . addressed to star of a coming attraction... copy lettered in "message" side (at top), to the effect that the signers are (star) fans, and intend witnessing the star's new picture when it comes to (theatre). "Card" could be made up in shape or design suggested by the attraction, as in the shape of a heart.

Card is taken about town, into stores and public places, where all are invited to sign it, . . . being carried about by costumed girls, or by messenger boys.

In evening, the card is placed on display in theatre lobby, in charge of attendant who invites patrons to add their signatures. Photograph of star might be presented those signing the "card."

Naturally, signers will first read the message, acquainting themselves with the fact that the picture will soon be shown. 

Card might even be sent to the studios. . . where the publicity department, if requested, might photograph the star of the picture together with the card... returning the photo for the local newspaper. 

And another newspaper photo, prior to this, may be secured by posing a pretty girl on the post office steps, "mailing" the card. If card is sent to the studio, stamps to carry it may be attached to the card directly. Or card might be made up by attaching paper to compoboard panel . . . the paper to be removed (after the signatures are • 108 •

secured), and sent in mailing tube . . . and asking studio to restretch it, cardlike, on another piece of board, before photographing. 

Stamp space on card could be covered with over-size outline of a stamp... possibly using star's likeness (press-sheet cover will often serve the purpose; or a still may be used). 

203. WAITING... Man, or girl, is stationed in front of theatre or in lobby, or atop canopy, in advance of coming attraction, appearing, perhaps, as center of a display on the show. Panel carries copy, "I'm waiting for (coming attraction). I want to be the first to see it when it comes to (theatre)."

Stooge used for the stunt should be seated in a comfortable chair. 

A miniature billboard or display panel can be constructed, with opening left in the panel, through which the "waiter" is visible, his chair being slightly elevated. Perhaps arrangements can be made to have meals served the "waiter" in front of the theatre. Newspapers might go for a story on the stunt. Columnists can use it for humorous copy in their columns. 

Another angle would have girls taking folding chairs about town, seating themselves for a few minutes on prominent corners the back of the chairs lettered: "I'm waiting for (star) in (attraction), coming to (theatre)."

Bench might be lettered: "Reserved for those waiting to see (attraction)," and placed in lobby or in front of theatre, in advance of showing. 

204. WHISTLES... As the "signal" that an attraction has officially opened at theatre, all manufacturing plants within "hearing distance" of city might agree to sound their whistles. Or, the arrival in city of star of theatre attraction might be the signal for the sounding of the whistle-blasts. Railroads, boats, might also cooperate. Chamber of Commerce can cooperate in arranging for the whistle-salute. 

205. SCHEDULES... Starting times of shows are important to patrons, and should be displayed out front. Cashiers, and others who are required to answer questions of patrons as to starting times of shows, must be supplied with correct schedules. Sound technician can connect a miniature speaker (from terminal of speaker panel backstage) into cashier's booth so that she can be constantly in touch with screen and consequently answering questions correctly. 

Typewritten, framed schedules should be placed in all rest rooms and lounges, in addition to box office, office, door. Next attraction should be listed too. 109.

Panels for display in front of theatre, headed "Next Show Starts," can feature a clock dial, with hands that can be moved to indicate the time next show is scheduled to begin. Space can be provided for card bearing attraction title. Clock "Schedule" might be attached to a panel; or placed directly in front of box office; or, larger, it might be displayed atop marquee. (See Photos.) 

Or two small clocks might be displayed in window of box office .. one of them set at correct time, the other set later to the number of minutes that the show requires. Above first clock is lettered, “Entering now..."; and above second clock is copy, "You'll be out at . . .”.

Thus, second clock always indicates exact time a patron entering theatre will be coming out.

Highlights of an attraction could be made the basis of a herald, or front display, that copies style of a time-table . . . listing events in the show that are especially notable or exciting, and the times that these events will appear. Adventure dramas, or travel stories, or story of jungle exploration might suggest an adaption. Or humorous highlights could be listed in their scheduled sequence in connection with a romantic comedy. Heading would read, "Time-table. . . of the most exciting trip you ever experienced (and into copy on attraction)"; or, "The funniest (or 'most amusing') events you ever witnessed ". Or time-table of songs in a musical might be featured. Predominate space is given attraction copy. 

Newspaper, as a service to their readers, should be sold on the idea of carrying daily a small box, always on the same page and in smallest type, that lists starting times of shows at all theatres. 

206. QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS... Contest based on previous attractions in which star, or stars, have appeared, would feature each day, for several days, a scene from the previous attractions, with an accompanying list of questions about the show. 

Scene from current attraction can be included; and copy on current attraction is carried in all stories. Newspaper might handle the contest after the manner of a high school "review," writing their stories in that style. "True and False" angle for a newspaper contest would feature an illustration from theatre's attraction, with a number of statements about stars and attraction accompanying it. Some of the statements are correct, others are not. Contestants are to determine which are right, which are wrong. Additionally, they might be required to "title" the scenes carried by newspaper, or to submit song-titles that the scenes suggest. • 110 ·

Or, questions and answers angle, can list a number of questions about the attraction, together with (but not in correct order) the answers. Contestants to correctly assemble questions and accompanying answers. 

Newspaper could feature a "Movie Query," listing ten questions about the attraction (accompanying story with illustration from attraction). Correct answers would be listed on another page, with no prizes offered, readers merely checking the questions for their own information and amusement. 

Contest (for newspaper, radio), may be based on answers to a question that an attraction may suggest. 

207. TELEPHONE CARDS... Small cards placed in tele phone booths can call attention to "hot number" (song or dance) in attraction.

Cards are attached to booth walls; or cards, having die-cut opening, can be attached over telephone mouthpiece. 

Or, larger cards, to be attached to telephones, can carry a list of often called numbers, with theatre's number prominently listed, and blanks for others. Ad for theatre at bottom of card, with space devoted to a coming attraction. Cards might be placed in homes, offices, stores, and in telephone booths. 

Cards can be made up with a detachable card attached, which is addressed to theatre on reverse side. Imprinted copy advises that theatre will call each week and notify of program changes, if person receiving the card will add name and telephone number, sending card to theatre. Ordinarily the number of takers will be limited, and cashier can make the calls. (Or program can be mailed.) 

Small stickers, distributed to homes, can carry copy: "Attach this sticker near your phone ... or to your telephone book." Lists emergency numbers, and carries space for numbers to be written in; and listing theatre's number, carries copy: "Call this number for 

Entertainment Information." 

208. ROAD SHOWS... Touring stage shows that feature advanced prices and advance ticket sales, may suggest methods for use in connection with a special screen attraction. 

Advance ticket sale, at box office, and perhaps at a special booth in a prominently located store, might be begun a week or several days before the attraction arrives. Agencies in drug stores, hotels, libraries, can sell the tickets. Agencies may be established in neighboring towns. "Road-show" type display for lobby should feature attraction • 111 •

billing, and photographs, framed and attached to a large easel panel. 

Or, made in several sections, the panels might be connected together with pin-hinges, standing upright without the necessity of an easel back. Additional to use at theatre, the panel can be placed in hotel lobby, or in a store.

Advance news breaks in papers are generally accorded a road-show attraction, using a good many illustrations. Road-show newspaper advertising, too, generally breaks well in advance with a sock ad, then graduating down to smaller space. 

Reserved seats might be sold, at least for opening night. 

209. EXPERIENCES... Person who has experienced adventures similar to those portrayed in theatre's attraction might be located, relating his experiences for newspaper interview and story, or for radio broadcast; or appearing on stage of theatre. Or, newspaper ad might carry his picture and quote him with reference to theatre's attraction.

Newspaper (or radio) contest could be based on experiences of contestants similar to those portrayed in, or suggested by, the attraction. Contest, as inspired by the attraction, might be based on most "thrilling," "horrifying," or, "embarrassing" experience; or "funniest adventure." Contestants should write brief essays (limited to 300 words or less) on their adventures. Art from attraction to be used in illustrating the contest for newspaper. 

210. COAT OF ARMS... Contest, for radio or newspaper, can be based on drawing of a coat of arms, the design to suggest or identify the star of theatre's attraction. A different player might be described each day-or newspaper would carry photographs of the stars, with contestants to create a coat-of-arms for each of them. 

For newspaper use, a drawing of a shield, in blank, might be reproduced, with contestants to draw in their suggested designs. 

Reverse angle for coat-of-arms contest would have newspaper reproducing a completed shield each day, which includes in its design sketches of items or activities that are identified with the star it is supposed to represent. Contestants to correctly identify the several stars. Photo of star of attraction could be carried, describing the shields as his designs for suggested coat-of-arms for other players in the coming show. Contestants would suggest a design for the star.

Occasionally a comedy "coat-of-arms" might be effectively adapted to front display.

Music stands, masking pieces, used in connection with a stage show, • 112.

might also be made up after the fashion of shields, with the design. suggested by the attraction. 

211. AMATEUR REVIEWERS . . . Guest tickets may be offered, for best amateur review of the attraction. Used as a newspaper contest, the paper's regular reviewer, or critic, might sponsor the contest and handle it under his by-line . . . illustrating with art from the attraction. Could be required that reviews be in rhyme. 

Or in the typical style that Variety Magazine employs in reviewing shows. School paper might sponsor the stunt, appealing to embryo critics among the students. Winning review should be reproduced in paper. Can be displayed in store window or lobby. 

212. PENCILS . . . Secured in quantity, from a manufacturer, pencils for distribution can be imprinted, "Make a Note 

Now . . . to See (attraction and cast)." Or, "Jot it Down (attraction) is coming to (theatre)." Or small dance program pencils could be used with attached tag carrying imprinted copy. 

Should be distributed well in advance to offices, schools, stores, business places. 

213. AD-WRITING CONTEST... Prize offered, in tieup with newspaper, for the best newspaper ad submitted on a coming attraction . . . using copy and illustrations which are carried in space allotted by the paper, or in regular theatre ads. Stores may cooperate, each carrying an illustration from the attraction in their ads (selecting a scene that appropriately illustrates their copy). 

Winning ad might be used in theatre's regular display space, or placed on display in newspaper office or theatre lobby. 

Or, contestants might prepare and submit suggested announcement for radio.

Contest could be conducted with school cooperation, supplying press-books for students to work from. "Gag-ads" might be basis of newspaper contest, with contestants invited to take any regular display ad appearing in the paper, and to reconstruct same as star of theatre's attraction (and most appropriately a comedian) might have written it. Angle appealing to newspapers, is that readers' interest is especially directed to all ads in the paper. 

214. RAIN... When rain begins, boys in raincoats might go about downtown section closing the windows of parked cars . . . and leaving cards on steering wheel, or in car, which carry the copy: "It started to Rain so we took the liberty of closing your car windows for you. Just another (theatre) service." Underline calls • 113 •

attention to coming theatre attraction. Boys carry umbrellas, on which attraction copy is lettered in oil. 

Through contacts in schools, arrangements could be made to letter (in oil) a permanent theatre ad on the back of slickers and capes worn by the school kids, possibly in exchange for several complimentary tickets to each kid. Enough of these and a rainy day causes the streets to be crowded with ads for the theatre. 

Umbrella service may be made a feature of the theatre service. 

Umbrellas loaned (with a deposit on same), in case of rain. 

Amateur weather prophets might be invited to attempt to forecast the weather, or to name the date of the next rain, in newspaper or radio contest, with tickets for those nearest correct. 

Display panel, featuring rain scene, could have speaker concealed behind it, with recordings of rain and wind sounds played through the amplification system, announcements cut in. 

With rain important to story or title, radio station might broadcast program of rain numbers, dedicated to attraction; or orchestra plays a series of numbers that deal with rain, as “Rain,” “April 

Showers," etc. 

215. HOT NEWS . . . Display panel in lobby is actually burned on edges (after it has been painted, so that charred edges show), and is lettered: "Here's Hot News ... So Hot it burned this panel!... Through this Opening ... Read!..." Arrow points to an opening in the panel . . . and looking through the opening, a panel carrying copy on the coming attraction is seen, together with an illustration or a full-length figure of a feminine star. Copy and illustration is flooded with red light, and small red gelatined spotlight might direct red rays (from behind the panel) toward opening in the panel.

Heralds, or cards for distribution, could be imprinted: "Red Hot 

News!" or "Here's Hot News!" And copy on the attraction.

Edges of the heralds are burned, with a blowtorch or using candles (and keeping a bucket of water handy during the process). 

216. WELCOME. . . Merchants can cooperate in "welcoming" a star or an attraction to town, carrying "welcome" copy in ads and perhaps a picture of the star. Similarly, stores can feature window displays which carry illustrations from the attraction, together with welcome copy. Imprinted "welcome" streamers can be attached to windows of all business places early in the morning (gummed paper attached at corners holds streamers). 

Personal appearance of a star, or arrival of stage show, should be • 114.

greeted with a band, and perhaps a "glee club," and an ROTC "guard of honor," and a special welcoming committee (perhaps arranged through cooperation of a luncheon club), and a parade to theatre. (See 434.) 

Newspaper or radio might offer guest tickets for best "greetings" submitted.

Cards possibly in shape of shields, imprinted with welcome copy, might be attached to light poles up and down main street. Street flags might be used in connection with them; or, at least, the use of the flags should be secured for the block in which the theatre is located. (See 593.)

Opening of a theatre might be made an occasion for a "welcome" campaign.

New arrivals in city might be "welcomed" to town, with a mailing card or letter being sent them. (See 314.) (and, in smaller type) for

217. GANGSTERS, OUTLAWS, CRIMINALS... Reward dodgers, printed after style of regular reward notification slips might be effectively used in connection with attraction where character portrayed is an elusive one, or hunted. 

Copy headed (large) "$5,000 reward (attraction title)." Then photo of star. picture and theatre and play dates. Copy makes it clear that it all refers to a drama, large top catch line serving to arrest attention. 

As a prelude to the trailer, several blank shots off-stage might be fired into a barrel, siren might be sounded. . . and trailer hits the screen. 

Newspapers carrying headlines that refer to actual activities of criminals might be used as background for display. 

Valueless auto might be secured for a few dollars from junk or old car dealer and adapted to front flash on gangster or outlaw story by shooting it full of bullet holes.

Comedy twist on gangster yarn might be stationing of booth in lobby where gangster might check their guns. 

Display of lethal weapons taken from gangsters might be secured from police for lobby or window (and attaching securely or placing in charge of an attendant). Pictures of gangsters might be secured (possibly from newspaper morgue). Used for display, perhaps asking patrons if they remember them; or attaching names instead.

Officer with tough looking customer handcuffed to him, ought to attract attention on sidewalks. Signs on their backs. If attraction shows and emphasizes the penalties of crime, as most of them do, • 115 ·

EN C Y C L O PEDIA OF EXPLOITATION 

a friendly judge might order certain prisoners to be taken to theatre to see it. Or it might be screened in jail. 

Police cooperation should be secured (See "Police"). 

218. NATIONAL TIEUPS... Arranged in advance, national tieups made by producers of motion pictures with leading manufacturing concerns, offer a ready-made opportunity for window displays, newspaper ads, and assuring whole-hearted cooperation ordinarily not so easy to obtain. 

Local stores handling the articles, in installing window displays, will also use display material on the attraction. And perhaps a local distributor can arrange for a number of local dealers to install full window displays. 

Illustrations are generally available, showing star with the article manufactured by the company with whom the tieup is made; and these stills might be used to illustrate newspaper ads that the store buys, or for display in windows. 

Perhaps manufacturer is carrying a national ad at about the time the attraction is to be shown locally, using scenes from the attraction or photograph of the star of the show, as illustration. Theatre might buy a small streamer ad underneath, or nearby, which makes it clear that the attraction will play the theatre; or the manufacturer's ad might be placed on theatre page or directly across from the page on which theatre's ad is run. 

If local distributor of the article has a radio program, they may include mention of the star and the attraction in his program. 

219. DEAD-PAN... Panel set up in prominently located window features an opening sufficiently large to frame the face of a man who stands or sits behind the panel. Copy on the panel, (most of which is devoted to theatre attraction, offers guest tickets to see attraction to anyone who can make the man laugh (he might be billed as "Sober Sam," or something similar). . . and obviously he must be able to control his inclinations to laugh. Used in connection with a comedy attraction, panel copy advises that this long-faced person actually laughed out loud when he witnessed the show. Window amplification could be used, with the microphone so placed that the man (or possibly a girl) would be able to speak to those whose attention is attracted, talking in a slow mournful voice. 

Or a "dead-pan" individual, with his face whitened to aid in drawing attention, and with very mournful countenance, walking through downtown section, perhaps handing heralds, carries sign on his back, "I'm all laughed out... after seeing (attraction)." • 116 •

220. BUMPER CARDS. . . With wording brief and title large, bumper cards should be imprinted or processed on good heavy grade of cardboard. Should be punched in at least three places, top and bottom so that they might be attached to automobile bumpers with string. Grommets can be used, but are not necessary, if the string inserted through the punched holes is also taken once competely over face of the card before being tied in rear of the bumper. Often bumper cards might be used to crash parades (other than theatre parades), placing the cards on bumpers of cars in the line of march.

Narrow imprinted or lettered (on both sides) cards can be attached in an upright position down the center of automobile hoods. 

221. WINTER, RADIATOR CARDS... Cards, imprinted with theatre ad, designed to cover over lower half of radiators, and to be inserted in edges of radiator coverings on automobiles, covering lower part of radiator and affording protection to car in cold weather. 

Can be made to fit certain more common kinds of cars, or of sufficient width that they might be cut to right width for any car. 

222. "NUTTYWOOD OPENING"... Travesty on the usual 

Hollywood opening. Especially adaptable to farce comedy with stars of "nut" type.

Use comedy radio announcer, comedy celebrities, arriving in broken down cars. Mugs in trick get ups, large shoes, etc. Cars with doors falling off and trick paint jobs. Reception committee (if used in selling stage act, the comedians themselves serve) rushing all arrivals to the "mike." Comedy band and clowning leader.

This stunt, as successful travesty, even more difficult than a straight Hollywood premier, but good for a lot of laughs and sure to create a lot of comment if the talent is available. 

223. PEEP-SHOW DISPLAY... Any idle store window or a lobby display panel might be utilized for this gag. 

Window is whitened (inside) with bon ami or window whitener, leaving openings, "peep-holes," at eye-level. Or beaver-board display might be made up to completely cover window, appropriately lettered, directing attention to the small openings. ... 

Curiosity-teasing catch-lines are used, as: “Warning! Don't Look in this Window! Remember What Curiosity Did!" or: "Revealing a 

New Thrill". . . or: "Not to be read by Inquisitive People;" or: "Men Only;" or any catch-line designed to whet curiosity.

Inside the window or behind the display panel is an attractive display on the attraction. Or a display of stills at eye-level, with the • 117.

stills animated so that they turn, or change. Or if the window is prominent enough to justify, a girl, attractively costumed, might be used in the window changing display cards which are placed on an easel.

The lettered catch-line might read: "For Good Looking Ladies 

Only." And inside window at eye-level is placed a mirror, lettered with attraction copy. Or a costume might be painted on the inside of the window, so that face of person peering in the window is reflected above the costume in a mirror within the window. Any lettering to be reflected in mirror to be in reverse so that it will read correctly. (See 672). 

224. MYSTERY LAMP... Light globe, placed atop small panel of glass, and not connected with light socket or (apparently) with any wires, continues, nevertheless to radiate light. Panel of glass should be slightly elevated. 

Used to draw attention to a display on an attraction, display card is lettered, "(star's) AMAZING MYSTERY LIGHT (following with attraction copy.)" Or, "Is it radio-controlled? The Amazing 

Mystery Globe... lighting your way to see (attraction and theatre).” 

Or similar copy.

Operation of globe is simple. Tiny enamel covered wires, the smallest made, are soldered to the base of the lamp and to the center connection, and extend off the glass panel, the wires being glued to the edge of the glass, and extending out of sight where they connect with wire extension. Adaptable only to window display, the light should be turned off before anyone is permitted in the window or to approach the light, since the wires, however fine, are still exposed, and might shock.

Similar is light globe suspended in a window by a shoe-string. 

Fine enameled wires merely run down the center of the shoe-string, and are attached with a drop of solder to the light globe center, and to the base where the shoe string is tied about it. 

Another method would show globe placed in a flower pot, with screw-in part of globe upended toward a light extension and socket that is suspended above the globe, though not connected. Though obviously separated from the connection the light globe is burning. 

Actually, wires leads through bottom of the flower pot, connecting with a socket into which the globe is screwed, the screw-in part in view above being merely glued on, a part from another globe neatly attached to the globe. Globe must be frosted and half buried in the flower pot. (See Diagrams.) • 118 ·

225. WORD BUILDING... Newspaper, radio or lobby con test based on construction of words, with tickets going to those making longest list of words, or to first so-many lists of over 50 words received, using the letters in the attraction title or star's name; any length words, just so the letters used are selected from those in title or star's name.

If used in lobby, a table with a good looking girl in charge, is made part of the display. Copy on panel offers tickets to those making up longest list of words in three minutes.

Contest could be included in store's newspaper ad or sponsored radio program. 

Another angle, would be requirement that contestants take part of title, or word in title, adding other letters to form words . . . as taking the letters "ove" from "Love" and building words which include the letters "ove." 

226. HAIR... Blonde, brunette, titian, whatever shade is suggested by the attraction title or theme, or featured by the star, might be made the basis of several stunts: 

In tieup with newspaper or radio station, admit free on opening day, the first 25 girls in line having hair of the proper shade. For a newspaper story or broadcast, a man might be placed in the line. costumed as woman and with proper colored wig... police to remove him from the line and pull off his wig just before girls waiting in line are admitted to theatre. 

Arrangements might be made to have reporter present. Also newspaper might go for a picture of the local girls. If tieup isn't set with newspaper or radio station, theatre ads can call attention to the stunt . . . or tieup with drug store or beauty shop might be set, with store or beauty shop using newspaper space to invite the girls. 

Beauty contest or bathing girl contest for girls with proper colored hair might be staged (in advance). Either in tieup with beauty shop, or in actual contest on stage of theatre, or in front of theatre on opening night. Held on stage, it should be immediately followed with a trailer on the attraction. Or a contest might be set with newspaper or radio station, basing it on photographs submitted by the girls.

Beauty shop featuring a permanent wave named after the attraction or its star, might use a window display on the attraction, as the center of which, good looking girls model hair dress during rush hours. Panel display features a circular opening in the center, where girls' heads appear as they model. Back of the girls (and back of • 119.

the opening) is a mirror. Modeling behind the opening, only girls' heads and shoulders will be visible. Or, beauty shop window panel might feature two openings instead of one, using two girls, and with copy along "Blond or Brunette” lines . . . using as models a blonde and a brunette. Beauty shop might buy newspaper space on a permanent wave named after the attraction. Using a photograph of star for illustration, beauty shop could advertise "We'll fix your hair like (star's)." Combined, might be an offer of guest tickets for girls most nearly resembling the star or stars of the attraction. 

An open car can serve as a street bally, with girl in rear seat (proper shade hair), neat cards or banner on sides of car. Opening day of attraction might be featured by parade of cars (in tieup with automobile dealer), all cars driven by, or carrying girls with hair of color suggested by the attraction. 

Girl ushers or cashiers could wear wigs of the proper shade the week in advance, and ribbons bearing the attraction title. 

Attractively costumed girls, having hair of other colors than that featured in attraction, might "picket" the theatre opening day, with placards claiming that the attraction is "Unfair to Brunettes (or whatever color hair is opposite to that publicized in the attraction).” 

Strands of hair (of proper shade) might be enclosed in letters sent the mailing list. . . letters being along "personal" lines, (but mentioning attraction).

Reactions of local celebs or athletes to blonde beauty (or whatever shade) might be made the basis of a newspaper story, using an attractive girl and an M.D., checking the resultant pulse count (to a hand-clasp or a kiss). A sphygmometer might be secured for this purpose. Local football or baseball players might be pressed into service for this "test," which should be staged on opening day in front of theatre. Possibly the "test" might be broadcast. Newspapers should go for a picture of the "test." Girls with other shades of hair could also be used for comparison (with girl with right colored hair naturally registering heaviest). 

227. HOUSE TO HOUSE CANVASS... Here is a campaign that will require several weeks and the services of an intelligent, personable woman . . . a campaign designed to win new patrons and please regulars.

Woman, as "theatre hostess," calls at home, visiting with housewives. Listing name and address, telephone number, on a card, she also records preferences, whether they attend the theatre or not • 120 ·

(and if not, why not). She presents the housewife with a couple of guest tickets to see a coming attraction at theatre.

An index of these cards offers a live mailing list of potential patrons, presenting also a guide as to preferences of theatre's patrons. Since attending the theatre, like going to a ball game, or anything else, is largely habit, the passes issued should prove an investment, tending to win new patrons (bringing them in once, with subsequent visits "on their own" made more probable). And the goodwill of those visited should be the natural reaction of this friendly and personal contact and acquaintance with a representative of the theatre. 

Working from a map of the city which is marked off, woman should systematically work street after street. She must necessarily be a person of personality, good breeding and education, who is able to talk and to sell.

Or, working several hours each day, some regular employee of the theatre might make the canvass. 

Using short wave, in tieup with radio station, the house-to-house canvass might be broadcast direct from the homes, making arrangements with persons to be interviewed in advance, however, by telephone. 

228. CLASSIFIED ADS... Effective use of classified news paper ads aside from contest and tieups, might be occasionally suggested by an attraction theme or title. Or, theatre might adver tise for items similar to those featured in attraction, for display purposes in advance of showing. Or for costumes similar to those used (as for costumes of a bygone day). Securing the costumes desired, classifieds later carry an ad for girls to wear the costumes. (Girls being used in window or on street, either on float or walking and carrying lettered parasols).

Occasionally effective ads can be scattered through all classifications on the classified page, such as ads selling Christmas "script" books.

Where an unusual item has already been secured for exploitation purposes, or an unusual person (as someone with qualifications rare in locality), an ad might be placed on classified page of paper for a single day, advertising for such article or person (with knowledge of newspaper), and "testimonial" letter sent paper on "results" of the ad might be reproduced by paper in their columns, or resulting in a story. (See "Newspaper Classified"). 

229. BASEBALL... Baseball games, attracting large crowds, might be invaded with many types of advertising. Ordinary bally stunts might include the ball park, and . . . • 121 •

Arrangements might be made to have a 24-sheet posted on one of the fences in view of the crowds, during, or just before the game. 

Announcements might be made at the game. Game could be dedicated to star of theatre attraction, with star (in person, if stage) personally throwing the first ball. Or a "proxy" for star (good looking girl, preferably), if in connection with screen attraction. 

Peanuts, sold at every ball game, offer an excellent means of reaching the fans . . . attaching small imprinted stickers to the sacks of peanuts, or rubber stamping the sacks. In tieup with radio station, arrangements might be made to broadcast the games, with frequent plugs for theatre's attraction cut in. A comedy "wind-up" contest for kids can be staged with tickets for the funniest wind-up. "Dynamite" stunt . . . arranging with ball park officials to have large box, labeled in large letters "Dynamite," carried on field just before game starts. Local celeb set to open box, or prominent and pretty girl. As box is opened, black oil-cloth on which word "dynamite" is lettered is removed . . . revealing copy, "Baseball Dynamite . . . compliments of (star's name and attraction copy)," and "Beat (opposition team)." And box contains flock of baseball bats, which are then distributed to home team. Photo of presentation, or opening of box ought to be good for sports page flash. 

Comedy baseball players, in comedy baseball get-ups, might entertain the crowds before the game starts on the side lines, after the Nick Altrock fashion. Much clowning (as pretending, seated on ground, to be driving an automobile), and comedy baseball playing (perhaps using basketball, painted to resemble baseball); and as a conclusion they unroll large attraction-lettered banner. And instead of baseball players they might be costumed as suggested by theatre attraction, or made up as clowns. However, their routine of comedy stunts should be set and rehearsed and planned in advance. 

Invite players to witness theatre's attraction as guests of theatre and newspaper, possibly introducing them from stage, with the newspaper going along for a sports page story on the event. Set if possible for opening night of feature. Especially effective if attraction deals with baseball. Bally man, on downtown streets, dressed as baseball player and with sign on his back, can draw added attention with a baseball which he throws against windows, after "winding up"... the "baseball" being made of cotton batting. Or a girl in baseball costume can carry a giant lettered papier mache baseball bat around town. Big league baseballs or bats will make great prizes for kids in any contest that might be conducted. • 122.

With cooperation of newspaper, or radio station broadcasting the games, a pair of guest tickets might be offered to any home town player hitting a home run; might be just for one game, or made a standing offer, if newspaper, sponsoring the stunt, or radio station, will mention theatre's attraction whenever a home run occurs. 

Might even be possible to put theatre's ad on the score board. 

230. DEBUTANTES... List of season's debs can be obtained from society editor of newspaper, and in connection with opening night of attraction, formal invitations might be sent them, special seats reserved, the event announced in society columns of paper. 

And maybe society editor will go for photo layout of debs attending. 

Where photographs of some stunt are made for newspaper reproduction, if a couple of debutantes can be prevailed upon to pose, the papers will be inclined to give the photographs better consideration. Might pose them with stage show star for a society page flash. 

231. TRAINED ANIMALS... Occasionally available at a time when attraction suggests use of same. Trained horse, with rider in costume, might be ridden about town, showing tricks in front of theatre. Or to City Hall, there to deliver an invitation to the 

Mayor (if permitted, the driver riding the horse up the steps and into City Hall).

Attractions occasionally suggest use of other animals . . . and tieup copy might be used to make appropriate the use of trained animals where they might be available and the attraction does not directly suggest. 

232. LETTERED HILLSIDE... Where some area, hillside or mountain, or river bank is especially visible to downtown section, or to large number of potential customers, name of attraction might be effectively "painted," using lime and water, and applying with a mop or broom. Letters should be high and wide enough to be effective, and carefully laid out. Electric lights might outline letters for a night flash. 

233. DUPLICATE ACTION... Story might portray action or incident that can be duplicated or reenacted locally, with newspaper cooperation, and consequent stories. 

234. ROLLER CHAIRS... Similar to those used at beaches • 123

on boardwalks, at fairs, wheel chairs might be pushed about town by husky lads . . . the chairs being placarded, "Hop in and Ride to (theatre), see (attraction)." Or, girls or couple, as suggested by the attraction, might ride in the chair, with banners carrying appropriate copy. Or girl, riding along in chair, could be busily engaged in reading a large book, on the cover of which the title of the attraction and theatre copy is inscribed. Or a cutout, lifesize figure of star of attraction cut from a poster, might "ride" in the chair. 

Similarly jinrikishas might be secured, or built up using bicycle wheels... pulled about town by lad wearing coolie hat, lettered banners or cards attached to the vehicle. 

If attraction features song hits, a portable phonograph can be carried along, and recordings of hit songs played. 

235. TOY TRAINS . . . The public never tires of watching toy trains in operation, consequently they might often be used to excellent advantage to attract attention to a window or lobby display. 

Miniature display, as a miniature airport and model planes set up in a window, could be encircled by track, with miniature train constantly circling about. Similarly, the toy train might be consistently added to many display panels, windows, lobbies. 

Lettered card, or miniature banner, should be attached to sides of cars drawn by train, carrying copy of theatre's attraction. 

And, if there is sufficient space behind display to line up as much track as there is out front of the panel, a novel touch might be given the display, by having train, at rear of the panel, curve into an opening which is made to resemble a tunnel . . . and then out of another opening at other side of display panel which is also made to resemble tunnel. Copy on panel, with arrow pointing to both tunnel openings, reads: "Watch the train change signs." In operation, the effect is that of train going into one "tunnel" opening, emerging immediately from other opening, with the sign on side of cars being changed (star's name might be shown before train enters tunnel, attraction title when it merges). Actually two trains are used: when train enters tunnel opening, instead of emerging immediately, it circles on extension track behind the display panel, and other train, running in same direction, bearing the other sign, emerges. Track behind the panel should be sufficiently long to detain the train behind the display until other train is out of vision of spectators. Entrance to tunnels should appear to curve, to offset any suspicion that track does not curve immediately to other opening. Trains will operate satisfactorily, running continuously and practically automatic, but • 124 •

an attendant should be stationed behind the display to make certain that both trains do not come into view out front simultaneously. 

Another tunnel angle, has track so arranged that, after entering "tunnel" (or going behind display panel, through opening in same which is made to resemble a tunnel), train in heading for the other opening is made to angle slightly (track layout) so that headlight on train strikes the rear of the panel (which from out front is the background of the display). The section of the panel which the headlight strikes is made of translucent glass, with lettering (copy on attraction) behind same... and as light strikes the panel, the lettering is silhouetted and made visible. Train runs to the right, so that words will be lighted in correct sequence (left to right). 

236. LIVING PICTURES... Oversize duplicate of picture frame constructed large enough for persons within it to stand upright, can be adapted to window or lobby display; or to float. Frame is shadow-boxed, with indirect lighting within the frame, and equipped with a curtain at front.

Within the frame, girls (attractively costumed), or characters the attraction suggests, (costumed), appear in a series of scenes (suggested by the show), concluding with girls holding cutout letters which spell out attraction title, or posed as part of a display on the attraction. Curtain to be closed in after each tableau, by girl in page costume in front of frame.

Card in front of frame announces presentation of scenes from (attraction).

Characters hold poses without moving for several "scenes;" but with some action introduced in the final "tableau," perhaps a girl stepping out and going through dance routine, if the attraction features or suggests dancing. "Scene" within the frame might be backed up by plush drop.

Or if available, a large mirror would be especially effective, with the back transparent, so that when lights are flashed on behind the mirror on concluding a scene, a display panel on the attraction is visible through the mirror. 

Another window display angle, would have life-like wax models posed in store window, showing display of gowns. Girl poses among the models, remaining motionless for several minutes, then changing poses. Display card invites those looking to see if they can pick out the star's "proxy" from among the models, and includes copy on the attraction. "Mechanical man," when available, might be adapted to this stunt. • 125 •

237. STENCILING . . . Where permitted by authorities, sidewalks can be stenciled in various designs, and with good results, (working at night to prevent tracking before paint dries). Design can be suggested by attraction. theatre, and with attraction title straight lettering might be used. large as a one-sheet. 

Large footprints can lead towards written across the footprints. Or 

Stencils can be small, or made as Stenciling should be done in watercolor or whitewash so that it won't stay forever; or oil paint would be used if it is put on well in advance and it is intended to remain for a time (using a "traffic" paint). 

Corners can be effectively stenciled, angled so that most of persons passing might read it. Curbings, fences, barns, vacant store windows might be stenciled, too. Stencils are cut from "stencil paper" (can be obtained from paper company or from firms who do a lot of shipping, using it for stenciling addresses). 

Where stenciling is not permitted, "water stencils" might prove effective. Costumed girls going about town with a linoleum mat in which the stencil has been cut, periodically stop and place stencil on the sidewalk, spraying it with water (slightly colored with milk) . . . using a spray-gun or sprinkling can. Then lifting stencil carefully, and on to another spot. Water, of course, dries away, but is visible for awhile. Or, flour might be sprinkled, instead of water. 

Stencilers should carry copy on their backs. Similar in effect, a group of kids, supplied with chalk, can write the title on sidewalks, walls, fences, all over town. 

238. SCHOOLS .. COLLEGES . . . School cooperation always pays dividends. Many ways of reaching students include: 

Small imprinted schedule cards (carrying program of football or baseball games school team is to play), with space devoted to theatre or coming theatre attraction, at bottom of card. 

Public address, or amplification equipment (or use of sound truck) might be supplied school for use at football games, if they do not have such equipment, with compliments of theatre . . . and with theatre's attraction announced repeatedly during the game.

Tire covers can be supplied during football season, carrying picture of football player, name of school, and theatre copy. 

Imprinted blotters are always an acceptable and a valuable method of getting advertising into schools. A ruler could be printed down one side of the blotter, with copy: "It's a good rule, etc." Real rulers, imprinted, might be distributed if they can be secured cheaply enough. • 126 •

If school is equipped with projector and occasionally screens pictures, maybe arrangements can be made to have them include a trailer on theatre's attraction.

In connection with picturization of a classic, the book on which the picture is based may be designated as required reading for book reports. Or students might compete in an essay contest based on, or suggested by, the attraction (with tickets for best). Film appreciation class may be featured by school, and they might base their studies on theatre's attraction.

Special rate might be given students. Possibly on certain shows, or certain evenings. Special tickets could be distributed to students which, when presented at theatre box office, give them right to special admission price. Might be a one-time affair, or made good for entire school term. 

Telegram sent sorority and fraternity houses with message about attraction, requesting that it be attached to bulletin board, will generally win space on the bulletin boards. 

Cards, or neatly lettered stills may be attached to bulletin boards in schools.

School library or bookstore is visited by nearly all students, and is consequently a great spot for any kind of display. 

Arrangements might be made with school to present tickets to several children in each class scoring highest in spelling competition. 

Will have children talking about attraction, as well as their parents. 

City-wide Spelling Bee might be arranged, with cooperation and sponsorship of newspaper or radio station. Finals may be broadcast over radio station; or even held on theatre stage. Trophies (from star of attraction) would be presented to the winners, and perhaps a trip or other promoted prize may be arranged.

Perhaps schools equipped with amplification hookup (so that voice can be carried to all classrooms), might permit announcement to be made, especially if the attraction is definitely commendable. 

On opening day of schools, blotters, rulers, scratch pads (all imprinted) will be unusually well received by students. Book store, or school book-shop may handle distribution.

Theatre might cooperate with schools in raising funds, for uniforms or other needs. Students selling benefit tickets, good on a certain night, with a percentage to go to their fund. School band might appear at theatre, out front or on stage, on the designated night and play; or a students' stage show might be presented. • 127 •

In appealing to school kids, cards or displays might be placed, with good results, in windows of stores and business places near schools.

Theatre might feature a "School Reunion Night," suggesting that all graduates of certain school or college attend on that night. Might arrange to show pictures on screen of graduating classes (still pictures being made into trailer form). With several important schools, different "reunion" nights might be assigned different schools. 

Schools plays or pageants might be presented on theatre stage. . . with students selling tickets on a percentage basis for some school fund. 

Support of school heads and Parents-Teachers organization can be secured if attraction merits such support. Letters should be sent educators, P.T.A. heads, if attraction can be construed as educational. 

Theatre might sponsor a "Facts about (town)" broadcast, with arrangements made for class rooms to tune in during the period and with authorities, librarians, editors, set to speak. 

See Nos. 39, 126, 200, 924, 994. 

239. EYES... For newspaper contest, or herald, drawing of star of attraction might be complete except that eyes have been omitted. Grouped around the drawing are several sets of eyes (drawing them to resemble those of other players, except for one set which are those that belong in the drawing). Invite contestants to see if they can pick out the right set of eyes and place them in the drawing. Guest tickets or other prizes for those correctly selecting the star's eyes, and identifying owners of other drawn eyes. 

Card-herald could be imprinted: "You'll be looking at the World through Rose Colored Glasses, when you see (attraction)." Two small openings are die-cut into the cards at top, and small strips of rose-colored gelatine or cellophane are pasted back of the openings. 

The openings might be connected with imprinted rules, between them and around them to resemble spectacles. And giant spectacles could be similarly made up for display in window of optometrist, with scene from attraction behind each opening.

Contest to select local girl with prettiest eyes could be based on photographs submitted to cooperating newspaper. 

First so-many girls with eyes of a designated color might be admitted free on opening day. Beauty shop or other business place might invite them as their guests, buying newspaper ads which devote space to attraction. • 128 •

Eyes, as near life-size as possible, might be cut from a photograph of star, and pasted to mirrors in lounges, rest rooms or in drug stores. 

Lettered copy asks, "Girls... Do you have Eyes like (star)? See her in (attraction)."

Star stills of featured player in attraction wearing glasses can be displayed in optometrist's window, and possibly used in his newspaper ads. Star of a stage show, or girls from the show, might appear in optometrist's store at designated time, demonstrating styles in glasses . . . with store buying newspaper space on the event. 

Herald can carry the copy, "She Pulled the Wool Over His Eyes," as a headline. Illustration from attraction is used, with small piece of wool pasted over eyes of man in the picture. In smaller type, offer guest tickets to those finding name of star (or theatre name) stamped under the wool. A small quantity of the cards are stamped before the wool is added, and placed among others for distribution. 

Devote most of space to attraction copy. after 240. REMINDERS... Small printed slips are made up the fashion of a slip from a memo-pad. 241. DOPE.. Capsules, obtained in quantity from a wholesale druggist, are filled with an imprinted, wound-up strip of paper... the paper being so wound that only the word "Dope" is visible (through the capsule), until the paper is taken out of the capsule and unwound, when it reads: "Dope... on (attraction copy).”

Distribute as heralds, or perhaps girls dressed as nurses (if attraction suggests) might distribute them on streets.

Anything of a size out of the ordinary will command more than usual attention, because of its size. Even an especially large or tall man used for street advertising will draw more than ordinary attention.

A giant replica of a radio can be used in lobby, or in store window, with recording of hit tunes coming from within (through amplification system).
