243. ASTROLOGY... Horoscopes might be printed, carry ing copy, "The stars indicate that this will be your Lucky Week...

244. NEWSBOYS, CARRIERS 

· · Arrangements can be made to have boys insert heralds in magazines or newspapers delivered to homes. Boys, in return, are invited to witness theatre's attraction.

245. BLACK ART... A display that is adaptable to a store window, or top theatre canopy, or theatre stage or boxes. A different sort of flash that commands attention.

As used in a window, a panel of lights is set up on both sides of the space which is to be used for the display. A full window might be more effectively used. Facing outward, illuminated panels are placed at extreme outer edge of display, against glass or window. 

Using narrow shadow box "trough" shadow-boxes, letters are cut out of the face of the panels, spelling out attraction title, permitting the light to shine through-the cutout letters being covered over (inside panel) with paper or sign cloth. These two panels, one either side, are only illumination in the window, and they should create a slight glare in the eyes of persons looking in the window, which is essential to the success of the black art "exhibition" within the window. Within the window there must be total darkness. 

Inside the window, a man dressed entirely in white is the center of attention and he works against an entirely black background, a non-gloss black back-drop. Floor of the window is covered with black cloth or paneling, too. Face of man working display is whitened, using flour or powder.

Man in white has an assistant who is dressed completely in black, • 131 •

ENCYCLOPEDIA OF EXPLOITA TI O N 

even his face being covered with a black hood; and against the black background he is entirely invisible to the onlooker. 

Used atop theatre marquee, or on theatre stage or in theatre box, the setup is identical. 

Action within the display can be suggested by the attraction being sold, most of the action being designed to be amusing. 

Suggested action: man takes off hat, places it on pedestal. . . it appears to leap back on his head (assistant in black supplying the motive power). Repeated several times, he throws hat to floor, with it flying back to pedestal. (Pedestal, or course, is also white). He might step out of shoes, with assistant walking them off. He can point with cane, with a red light seeming to come from end of it and traveling off-stage (red flashlight moved by assistant). 

At close of routine, man in white points to back drop, and letters comes into view, then he points again, and another letter, until title of attraction is spelled out, (assistant in black placing the white letters on display-the backs of the letters being painted black, and not visible until turned so that white face is toward audience). Or, stationary white letters can be brought into view by removing black covering from over them. And they can be made to disappear by reversing the process.

And, to conclude the routine, the performer can make himself disappear, by having assistant suddenly shield him with a black cloth. 

Used in theatre (stage or box), the stunt should be followed immediately with trailer on the attraction.

Black magic might be adapted to a display or announcement on stage, person dressed in black, against black, carrying a cutout figure, or display panel (suggested by attraction)—and with announcement followed by trailer. 

246. GIRL PAINTING PANEL Attractive girl, busily engaged in painting a poster will attract a great deal of attention. 

Prominently located panel should be used. 

In painting the poster, she can actually follow pencil lines which have been sketched by regular artist, with the colors marked, so that she is obliged to merely apply the paint in the designated places. 

Or, the panel might be previously painted, using oil paint, then covered over with powdered chalk (mixed with water), with girl using a bucket of water in "painting" the poster (she moistens brush in the bucket, uses it to brush away the concealing white. The painted display beneath the white comes into view as the white • 132 •

is removed, and apparently the girl has painted it). Several girls might be engaged in painting the poster. 

Instead of an outdoors billboard panel, a poster might be made up in the shape of a miniature billboard, which is used in a window. Or, a large panel might be placed on a truck (in an upright position) the truck traveling slowly about town, as the girls "paint" the poster. Banner on truck sides carries copy on attraction. 

Similarly, panel might be made center of a display for lobby; or used atop theatre marquee. Possibly the idea might be used at football or baseball games, or wherever crowds have gathered. 

247. MISSPELLED WORD CONTEST 

adaptable to theatre printed programs and coop. pages. Particularly

One misspelled word in each merchant's ad, and first so many persons submitting correct list of the misspelled words to receive guest tickets. Assures that every word of each ad will be read.

248. CLAIRVOYANT . . . A “seer," set up in theatre lobby, prophesies the future for patrons . . . including the information that an opportunity to witness (attraction) is about to come into their lives. 

Costumed man (or girl) serving as mind-reader, has a prepared "line," and "bases" prophecies on handwriting or palm-reading, or numerology, astrology, or birthdays. Or "prop" crystal ball, which might be an opalescent porch ball, with colored light underneath, can be used. Porch ball rests in pan of water in which dry ice floats, throwing off a mysterious vapor. Pan should be camouflaged.

Or a girl, dressed as a gypsy, might be stationed in the lobby. foretelling the "future" by "reading" tea leaves . . . and including the information about the coming opportunity to witness (attraction). 

Display panels of some sort should be built up around the seer, carrying copy on the attraction. An "assistant," also in costume, can talk to patrons (and advising them that there is no charge). 

Featuring a mind-reader or "mentalist" as a stage attraction, a "questions and answers" tieup might be arranged with newspaper or radio station . . . a certain number of questions being answered daily. (Additionally, see "mind-reader" classification.) ... 

249. FOOTBALL GAMES . . . An effective herald for dis tribution at football games (or at basket ball games, or at other games where large crowds are assembled) can be printed on light • 133 •

card, in bright colors . . . the imprint headed: "Come on (local team!)" And, then, in smaller type: "Throw this card in the air when (local team) makes their first Touchdown!" Then devoting larger part of card to copy on theatre's attraction. Distribute to crowds entering stands or fields. To be assured that maximum attention is received, attractive girls, dressed as cheer-leaders or in sports outfits, can distribute the heralds. ... 

Or, herald to be distributed after the game (any game) might carry the copy: "And now . . . what about tonight? How about a great movie? (Theatre) suggests (and into copy on theatre's attraction).” 

Perhaps arrangements can be made to have several footballs kicked out into crowds before game begins. footballs on which the attraction title has been lettered, and to which passes have been attached; and with catchers keepers. Banners might be carried on field between halves, by several attractive girls, displaying them first to one side of the field, then across field to other side. Perhaps arrangements can be made to have a float circle the field between halves . . . an attractively constructed truck, preferably decorated with pretty girls. Stooges made up as football players, and carrying copy on attraction on their backs might circulate among the crowds. 

If done cheaply enough, perhaps motion pictures of the game will prove worth while at the box office. Shots of crowds should be made between halves, and banner displayed telling them that they might see the pictures at (theatre) together with (attraction). 

Programs, carrying names of players and information concerning them might be distributed . . . with compliments of theatre, and with attraction given good space.

Arrangements might be made to present a football to home team at start of the game, with "compliments of star". . . and with appropriate announcements, and photographs for papers. 

Several persons might be given rolled-up, individual letters (on oilcloth), which together spell out attraction title; persons holding the letters to be seated in correct sequence across stadium (though widely separated) so that letters are in correct sequence to spell out title; and at a given cue they unroll the letters, stand and hold them up, making them visible across field, spelling out attraction title. 

If advertising isn't permitted on the field, it might be possible to hoist a banner on a nearby building, or above fence on a neighboring lot. However, it might even be possible to get an ad on the score board. • 134 •

Teams may be invited to attend theatre as guests in evening after game. Might be announced at game that they will attend.

During football season scores of all important games might be featured on a panel or bulletin board in the lobby. 

See other football classifications. 

250. SWEETHEARTS... Title of theatre attraction, or romantic theme, might suggest a "Sweethearts' Week." Cooperation of business places might be secured, displays in their windows offering special gift values as a feature of the special week . . . and mentioning theatre's attraction. Perhaps newspaper can sell a cooperative page, merchants' ads calling attention to gift-values. Combination boy and girl outfits can be featured by stores, as matched (colors) scarfs; or other accessories of identical color. Scenes from attraction used for ad illustration. 

Hearts might be used to sell the sweetheart theme in an attraction. 

They might be used as front decorations, panels being made in the shape of hearts, frames over stills being cut heart-shaped, and perhaps entrance to theatre being made to resemble a gigantic heart. "Sweethearts' Promenade" could be installed in lobby, or on mezzanine . . . constructing a huge heart, sufficiently large for couple to walk through opening in its center. Panel does not block lobby or mezzanine, and patrons are not obliged to walk through the heart . . . however a lettered panel attached to the heart, announces it as "Sweethearts' Promenade" and says that all sweethearts are to walk through it. Bench or settee can carry copy, "Reserved for 

Sweethearts" (and copy on attraction). "Sweethearts' Cruise Contest" may be arranged with cooperation of newspaper or radio station, offering prizes (perhaps a promoted trip, maybe a real cruise) to person outlining in most interesting manner, the cruise he, or she, would like to take with his (or her) sweetheart . . . the part of the globe that they would consider most romantic; and why. Stills from the attraction would be used for newspaper art in illustrating the contest. Broadcast station could feature the contest, building a "musical cruise" program about it. 

New words for "sweethearts" might be made basis of newspaper or radio contest. Or adapted to lobby flash, with pretty girl, in charge of the display, inviting patrons to register their suggestions, together with their names, in a notebook. 

Singer could be introduced over radio as "The Voice of Romance," singing love ballads and talking about attraction. Group of sweet- • 135

heart songs might be featured as a special program by a radio station and dedicated to theatre's attraction. Similarly a prominent orchestra might feature a group of sweetheart tunes.

Large jar of candy hearts, which most confectioners handle . . . together with display on attraction, may be placed in a window, offering guest tickets to person most nearly correctly estimating number of hearts in the jar. The small candy hearts can be inserted in imprinted envelopes, and distributed. Or pretty girls might hand them to patrons (in advance). Baker might feature heart-shaped cakes or cookies, naming them after attraction or its star. Heralds or programs can be die-cut in heart-shape. Couple of attractive girls in eye-arresting costumes might carry a gigantic cutout heart about town copy on attraction being lettered on the heart; or they might wear large hearts over their shoulders, "sandwich-man style." 

Cooperating florist might prepare a giant heart of roses. Photo of sweethearts of attraction placed in center. Heart be placed on display in theatre lobby, with credit card for florist; or it might be displayed in his window. "Sweethearts' Night" should feature a small promoted gift of each girl attending... perhaps a rose, from a cooperating florist; or candy, or cosmetics, secured from a manufacturer, and presented with the compliments of local representative. Special prizes could be presented (and announced in advance) to oldest sweethearts (married or single) attending, and to the youngest. "Sweethearts" Waltz might be featured by a cooperating ballroom and dedicated to attraction. Dancers might demonstrate it, and prizes can be offered couples stepping it off best. (See 259. 251. JIG-SAW PUZZLES ... Jig-saws might be used effectively as a contest for newspaper or heralds; or for window or street stunt.

Blank jig-saws on paper (with impressions pressed) can be secured in quantity and imprinted for distribution (using illustrations). 

A still, cut into small pieces (after style of jig-saw puzzle), and cut made up, might be used as a newspaper contest. Or a scene-cut might be used, newspaper cutting it into small pieces, with tickets for first so-many correctly assembled and submitted to newspaper. 

Or store might sponsor the stunt, devoting space to the jig-saw in their regular advertising space, with puzzles to be sent to store for • 136 •

competition. Or store might allot space on a herald that they print for the puzzle. 

A cooperative newspaper page might have a small piece of the jig-saw puzzle placed in each ad on the page, with readers to piece together (a scene from theatre's attraction). 

Jig-saw puzzle might be made from a 22x28 display card (attaching the paper to pressed wood, and applying the jig-saw). Girls repeatedly assemble the puzzle in a window, with whole duplicate of the card which they are piecing together on display. A jig-saw puzzle "marathon" might be staged, in lobby or window, with contestants supplied with duplicate puzzles made from small display cards or posters on the attraction. 

Giant jig-saw puzzle can be made up from one-sheet, or threesheet, with costumed girls spilling the puzzle pieces on prominent corners, and then assembling the "puzzle" on the sidewalk. In making the jumbo jig-saw, lithograph is pasted to compo-board and cut into large jig-saw style pieces, using cut-awl. Theatre and play dates first lettered on. 252. PICKETS . . Attraction might suggest travestied "picketing" by a phoney "society“ . . . as in connection with comedy gangster story, having tough-looking hombres "picketing" the theatre, carrying banners which proclaim the attraction as unfair to "Society for Fair Deal for Bank Robbers and Gangsters."

Ushers could "picket" theatre in connection with a comedy attraction, carrying large placards with copy to the effect that theatre isn't treating its ushers fairly in showing the attraction, that they can't be expected to look at it so continuously without laughing themselves sick... copy adding that everyone in town is rushing to see the attraction, making ushers' task harder. Copy might read: "Too many laughs make it too hard to work," and "Don't see (attraction) unless you're prepared to laugh as you've never laughed before." Ushers, in uniform, walk back and forth in front of theatre, picket-style, and about town, carrying banners. 

Certain color hair, featured in a show by star or girls might suggest picketing of theatre by several girls with hair of a different color. 

They walk in front of theatre and about town, copy on placards which they carry stating that (attraction) is not fair to (red heads, or whatever the hair color) and tieing in attraction title or star's name. "Pickets" are attractively costumed and picked for looks. Might be used opening night. 

253. BLOTTERS 

. . Always effective, imprinted blotters, ... • 137

when distributed to offices, schools, business places, are generally appreciated and kept. Blotters should be distributed well in advance of attraction.

Arrangements might be made to insert blotters in statements mailed by laundries, public utilities, department stores, etc. Small check book size blotters might be used.

Costumed girls might distribute the blotters to office buildings and business places, assuring better than usual reception. 

Straight ad can be carried as a blotter imprint, preferably using an illustration. Or a novel catch-line might be used, as: "Blot Away 

Your Troubles (or 'Blues') . . . Here's Good News!" And into copy on the show. ...

Message (in longhand) could be printed on blotter side, using reversed engraving, giving the effect of the written message having been blotted when it was written. Imprint at top (on blotter side) in straight unreversed type, "Hold Before Mirror." The "message" is copy on the attraction, "signed" by character in story, or by star of attraction. On other side of blotter, copy in straight type directs attention to the "blotted message." If idea is used, for instance, on mystery drama, imprint might read: "Take Warning! Lock

Or similar message, depending on the attraction. ...

Blotters are sprinkled with a cheap perfume or toilet water, or covered thoroughly with sachet powder.

Small, imprinted folder might be glued to the face of blotters, with good catch-line on front page, inner spread devoted to copy on the attraction. Blotters to which herald is attached might be imprinted: "Here's a Message that will blot away your Blues"... or something similar. 

254. "PLANTS" AND HOAXS... Occasionally a hoax of some kind will win a front page story, but it's best if newspaper can be "let in" on the stunt. If the stunt has news value, or is interesting or novel enough, newspapers might go for a phoney story anyhow, especially if the truth is subsequently to be disclosed. 

It's been a long time since Harry Reichenbach ballooned an ordinary appearing lithograph into a national institution by inciting a movement to have it suppressed and made September Morn a best seller and a by-word for a generation; or since he registered an ape at a • 138 •

fashionable hotel as Mr. T. Arzan; or had a star bring along her lion at another hotel-registering; or had a girl sit hypnotized in her chair after the crowds had left a theatre, still spellbound by the Svengali eyes of the star; all of which made as many headlines as a good-sized war. 

They can still be made in similar fashion. But the editors must be tipped off in advance. If preferred, the newspaper editor need not be told in so many words that it's a gag, or, on the other hand, that it isn't, giving it to him so that he can figure it out for himself and take it or leave it. If it makes good copy, he will generally take it. The newspaper man can then protect himself in the way he handles it, even though he spoofs the idea. However, where a gag makes a legitimate newspaper stunt anyway, it's a better idea to be frank about it and to let the paper in on it from the start. If they won't print it, there's no use fooling with the idea. However, it doesn't pay to attempt to bamboozle them or to trick them; they have a way of remembering such treatment, and cordial relations with the papers are sometimes endangered by hoaxing them without their knowledge. And, besides, most newspaper men are pretty smart fellows and will generally be able to add things up, anyhow. It's best to confide in them . . . not necessarily from an ethics angle, but just good business. In other words, don't make the paper a sucker along with the public. If a thing can be laughed off at the windup, its generally okay. ...

Many attractions suggest an idea—a rumor, that later ties into an announcement of theatre's attraction. Or incidents that are made to happen that will build into publicity on the attraction. Inquiries, apparently legitimately made, or requests for information (along lines suggested by coming attraction) might start the ball rolling. 

Report might be circulated that an event, similar to that about which coming attraction centers, is to occur locally. Rumor that the star of coming attraction is coming to town might be started. 

And then breaking theatre's ads in the papers on the coming attraction.

Objects, as suggested by theme or title of attraction, might be occasionally "planted" in the night, to be discovered next morning, with newspapers going along for a story (perhaps arranged in advance). 

And after a newspaper story, the first ad on the attraction breaks. 

Object "planted" must be striking, out of the ordinary and definitely news, and it might be planted (placed) either on a suburban street or a downtown location . . . in full view. On a horror shocker, a • • 139.

ENCYCLOPEDIA O OF EXPLOITATION 

coffin might be placed during the night in a downtown location... dummy in same, having a small lettered card attached; or a live "mechanical man" if available, might be placed in the box instead of a dummy, holding pose as long as possible when coffin is opened, then "coming to life" and delivering message about theatre's attraction, after sufficient attention has been attracted. 

Or, in connection with attraction in which "gold" is mentioned in title, men might begin "digging for gold" in prominently located spot, with newspapers going along for a story, and a subsequent story, when the men eventually find, not gold, but a panel bearing the title of the attraction. And with theatre's first newspaper ad on the attraction breaking immediately.

Or, an obvious hoax might be handled in a kidding way, as the introduction of a phoney wild man, “just arrived from Borneo" (or wherever the attraction would suggest). Clad in skins or “jungle" costume, he is introduced at luncheon clubs, night clubs, over radio stations and at the newspapers. And though he is quite apparently a fake "wild man," and his answers (in "jungle English" or even in Harvard English) to questions pertaining to the jungle are purposely designed to be ridiculous, it is never admitted that he isn't a legitimate "wild man;" in fact, theatre might insist (in a manner that can't possibly be interpreted as serious) that he's the real McCoy. 

Papers can kiddingly "interview" him, and record his "adventures" with civilization . . . getting several humorous easily-read yarns out of it. 

255. CRYING PHOTOGRAPH... A laughing photograph of a movie critic, or local celebrity, might be obtained, or especially posed; blown up to 1-sheet size, it is made the center of a display for lobby or window.

Varnished over, the photograph has small pipes or tubing connected with a water faucet and attached directly behind the eyes ... small openings in the photograph at the eyes permitting the water to flow through, running down face of photograph into a container at bottom, from which it is drained away. Very small amount of water is permitted to flow. 

Panel carries copy: "I laughed until I cried at (star and attraction)."

Tickets to be sold in advance for the special show.

Trailer carried the week in advance. 

Excellent contest, newspaper or radio, would be based on best New Year's Resolutions submitted. Newspaper would illustrate the contest with attraction scenes.

A trailer headed "A New Year in Entertainment," and listing coming attractions, might be carried first week in the new year. 

Playing stage shows, a photograph of one of the girls in the show, briefly costumed, standing before large cutout figures of year, and changing them into new ones, ought to be good for newspaper space. 

Or she might be posed holding a gigantic calendar page in front of her, revealing bare shoulders and legs. 

257. DIARY . . . Giant diary might be adapted to a lobby or window flash, having girl turn the "leaves."

263. TICKETS WITH PURCHASES... Occasionally a deal might be set with an enterprising merchant to sell him a block of tickets (perhaps at a special price), to be presented to customers making specified purchases, or purchases exceeding a certain amount. 

Store's ads can limit offer of tickets to first so-many customers, and mentioning theatre's attraction for which the tickets will be good. 

In appealing to children and confining the offer to kid tickets, store might require that children be accompanied by an adult. 

264. REFRESHMENTS . . . In tieup with bakery, bar or counter might be placed in lobby or on mezzanine floor, attractive girl serving either cake or small sandwiches, made with their bread; coffee distributor supplying coffee (demi-tasse). Affords distributor a means of making people familiar with products. Timely for 

Christmas Season, inviting shoppers to refresh themselves when they attend the matinee. Bakery might buy additional newspaper space on the tieup.

If attraction suggests, a small bar might be set up, perhaps serving (promoted) soft drinks or beer. Or, cooperating dairy might install a “milk bar." Or a large display panel "bar" may be built, with lifesize cutouts of stars standing behind the bar. 

265. RESTAURANTS ... Luncheon checks might be supplied prominent restaurants, with theatre's ad imprinted on the reverse side. Or, attraction copy can be rubber-stamped on luncheon checks used by restaurants. Placed face down when they are presented to patrons, most of checks are sure to be read.

Some restaurants will use imprinted paper napkins. Or places using paper napkins might permit them to be rubber-stamped. 

Restaurants might permit imprinted paper bands, or napkin rings, to be placed around the cloth napkins that they use. 

Prominent restaurant might "dedicate" special dinner to star, or "name" dinner after him, so imprinting it on their menus. 

Special dish could be "named" after attraction.

Tieup might be arranged between restaurant and theatre . . . with eatery making a combination offer of dinner and theatre ticket. . . . • 144 •

restaurant paying theatre for tickets used (perhaps at reduced price). 

For a specific attraction, or used regularly on certain day each week. 

In similar tieup, dine-dance place might mention in their ads that patrons might have dinner, leave to attend theatre to see (attraction), returning to dance without further charge. 

Cards displayed in restaurant might announce that patron selecting the "Lucky Chair" will receive guest tickets to see (attraction), eatery possibly buying newspaper space or radio time on the stunt. 

Different chair assigned each day. 

If attraction suggests the stunt, town's prettiest waitress might be selected, by photographs, votes or stage contest. (See "Restaurant" Classifications.) 

266. NEWSPAPER COLUMNISTS... Newspaper writers, carrying a daily column can include mention, which is very valuable since columnists generally have a wide following. Each attraction presents angles that should interest them, or some stunt in connection with the attraction might win their interest and a line or two of type.

Inviting them to witness an advance showing or screening might result in mention. If columnist refers favorably to an attraction, his comment might be reproduced in a newspaper ad. 

On sports attractions, sport page columnists would be especially interested. Supply information on attraction and players. Invite them to witness screening. They might invite, as their guests, local football or baseball team to witness the attraction. 

Perhaps theatre manager might serve as a "guest" columnist.

Or he might possibly conduct a daily column in the papers. Column might deal with, or include, things theatrical (including mention of coming attraction).

Newspaper columnist might assume for a day a role similar to that portrayed in an attraction, to obtain a good human interest story. 

267. DANCE ... Where a dance or dancing is important to story or title, the steps can be introduced or demonstrated by a dancer, or dancers, who are sent around to ballrooms, night clubs, parties, dances, banquets. Costumes suggested by the attraction. 

Steps can be demonstrated in lobby (if it is large enough), or even atop canopy (if safe enough), using phonograph or accordionist or pianist, playing numbers from the show. Or, dancers might perform in a large window, backed up by a display panel on the attraction. Dancers, or dance-team might be secured from a dance • 145.

school, appropriately costumed. Newspaper might use a photo of local dancers doing the dance step. 

Dancer might appear in a window, several times daily, as center of a display. Dance costumed, she also wears a half-mask, and perhaps a wig. Display panel invites those looking to try to identify her on a later day in the store (or at a "[star] Ball" at a night spot), when she appears in street clothes minus the wig (which changes the color of her hair and without the mask). Tickets for the first somany correctly identifying her. When she is in window, amplification carries musical accompaniment (which may be phonograph, or possibly an accordionist) to those outside window, together with announcements.

Perhaps pictures of the dance evolutions are available, successive pictures showing every move of the step. Or they might be especially posed, perhaps by local steppers. They might be planted, together, as a newspaper feature, with descriptive copy, or used as illustration for a herald to be distributed. Reproduced, the photos must, of course, be in correct routine. 

Perhaps stage show dancers or chorus can demonstrate a dance routine as a show feature. Or a routine "inspired" by an attraction. 

Or dance school steppers might serve, following at once with trailer on the attraction.

Dance contests on the stage might be arranged. Also, oldest and youngest tappers might compete; or highest kickers. Trophy or promoted prizes for winners. Newspaper might cooperate. 

Night club could feature the dance, or a dance suggested by the attraction, having their dancers or chorus present a routine, attraction announced in introducing the number. Programs mention the attraction as "inspiration" for number.

Radio broadcast might feature dance instruction idea, similar to broadcast morning exercises . . . announcer explaining the dance carefully, against a musical background (perhaps of tunes from the attraction). Then playing the number for listeners to step to.

Stores feature evening gowns, slippers to wear to dance, or to "do the (step) in." Both ads and windows.

Dancers could be featured on a float, which stops at important intersections, where girls go through a dance routine. In an automobile tieup, dancer might tap out a routine atop a new car (while car is stopped at intersections, not while car is moving). 

Dancer might perform on prominent corners. Small platform, • 146 •

which carries lettered copy, is taken along, on which she performs briefly to the accompaniment of a phonograph, or other music. 

Photographer from paper might snap dancers in various night spots (with their permission), reproducing as their interpretations of (the dance step). Newspaper feature might be based on interview of local dancers, or dancers in stage show at theatre . . . girls being asked questions about dancers in screen attraction. See 79 and 793. 

268. NUTS... Comedy of the "nut" type might suggest a display in the window of a store that handles nuts . . a container filled with nuts and containing small cutout figures of attraction stars, being made the center of a display on the attraction... and with guest tickets to witness the attraction offered to those estimating, most nearly correctly, the exact number of nuts in the bowl. Card asks: "Besides (stars), how many nuts in this bowl?" Sacks used by stores handling nuts might be imprinted, or heralds might be inserted in packages.

A novelty herald would be folded several times before distribution. 

First imprint reads: "Nuts to You!" Next imprint, visible on unfolding once, "Yes, Nuts to You!" Unfolded again, another imprint reads: "Yes, that's what we said . . . Nuts to You." Unfolded once more the full length of the herald is disclosed and the lead-off copy at the top of the herald, carries in large type: "They're Nuts to You ... (and into copy on attraction)."

Small envelopes (possibly glassine), might be imprinted: "They're 

Nuts to You... (and attraction copy)," a nut being placed in each envelope before distribution. Or, "I'm a Nut . . . and you'll be one too... if you don't see (attraction).” Or, “I'm a nut . . . over those two nuts (stars) in (attraction).”

Peanut vendors might have cards attached to their carts. 

Live (or taxidermist's) squirrels in a cage in window or lobby can carry copy on cage: "They're after those nuts (stars) in (attraction)." 

269. COLOR . . . Attraction title or theme, or intended appeal, will generally suggest the color for use in front panels and displays. Blazing action would suggest use of striking colors, fiery red, and bright orange; more subtle blends for emphasizing romance, whimsical or comedy moods. Patriotic colors might be suggested by attraction.

Different moods are represented by different colors. Red representing excitement, heat, fury, danger, action, passion, blood. Yellow: treachery, villainy, action, warmth, envy. Gold: power, glory, achievement, conquest, glamour, luxury. Green: peace, rest, hope, • 147 •

coolness, refreshing. Blue: serenity, coldness, dignity, romance. 

Rose: love, devotion, beauty. Black represents gloom or sadness or sorrow; blackish purple might be used. 

Season of year should also effect choice of color for displays; bright, hot hues being shunned in hot summer weather, with shades of green and blue and lighter shades of other colors being given the preference. Reversing this, warm colors should be used in cold weather. (This also applies to house lighting.) 

If attraction suggests a certain color, stores might feature it in their windows, calling the shade "(attraction title) (color)." 

270. CALENDAR . . . Calendar of month, imprinted on herald or blotter, carries dates of special attraction or special week in red (rest of printing in contrasting color), and includes this copy: "Red Letter Days for (town) (and into copy on attraction)." 

Can be adapted to lobby panel or top marquee flash. Or even to newspaper ads, underlining the dates, or setting them in bolder type.

Herald or card, in calendar sheet form can have the attractions for the month imprinted over the dates when they are to play. 

271. MANICURISTS. . . Through arrangements with a beauty shop, an attractive manicurist might be stationed, with table and full equipment, in theatre lobby... with willing patrons given. free manicures. Display panel carries copy: "Get your nails polished up... You've got to look your best . . . Because (star, or attraction title) is coming to town." Especially adaptable, of course, if attraction features manicurist or beauty shop. 

Manicurists invited to a special screening, are certain to discuss it with those coming into their shops. Lettered stills might be placed under glass covering on manicuring tables. 

272. PROGRAMS... House publication, handed to patrons is a proven method of directing attention to coming attractions. 

Distributed by staff, or by a spot-lighted usher or "page boy" (or girl) stationed in lobby, program might also be sent out to mailing list (folded and held together with a stamp and addressed). Or distributed house to house. They might be made available in hotels, restaurants, public places. 

Made up as a small printed folder, the program carries information in regular newspaper style, with headlines and stories and illustrations. 

Program on current show, listing players, is featured; but with most of space devoted to coming show. Program may be small, pocket-size; or tabloid size; or any size in between these two. (Check with printer • 148

so that program will "cut out" exactly, thereby eliminating wasted. paper and added unnecessary expense.) (Or program can be mimeographed.) Primarily devoted to stories concerning coming attractions, brief jokes, recipes, news items might be included. 

Program might be printed by theatre, or it might be supported by the advertisements of business places. Where town doesn't have a newspaper, the theatre's program (possibly just a mimeographed sheet distributed regularly) can include news items about town and surrounding countryside; patrons might be asked to phone items in; program can take the place of a local newspaper and become really important to the community. 

Frequently contests that do not require much space can be included (as 247).

Old programs might be occasionally adapted to display in connection with certain attractions. Modern stage revue might suggest display of old vaudeville programs as comparison, or old-time attraction background would suggest their use. Newspaper might aid in locating person who has collected old programs. 

273. MULES... Blanketed donkey, led about town, carries copy on the blanket: "I'm the only one in town that doesn't want to see (attraction and theatre) and you know what I am.”

Clown attempting to ride a small mule will attract much attention for a comedy attraction. He might appear with the animal on downtown streets, and at schools, playgrounds . . . Banner on the clown or on the mule carries copy: "Funny enough to make a mule laugh," with a grin painted on the mule's face with white greasepaint, outlining his mouth, extending it in a large "smile". 

274. LOBBY NEWS OFFICE... Newspaper story, or “hot news" emphasis on an attraction, might be basis for arrangements with newspaper to station a branch editorial office in theatre's lobby (in advance), assigning a reporter or columnist who will carry a daily column in the paper, referring to his appearance in lobby, interviewing different patrons. Might offer guest tickets for news stories or tips that newspaper uses. 

Star of stage show might act as "guest reporter" at designated intervals.. 

275. DARTS . . . Small stars (or hearts) of different sizes cover most of the surface of a display panel. Copy on the panel offers guest tickets to those striking one of the stars of a specified color with a dart which is supplied (darts being made up or purchased from a toy department, or part of a "game"). Lucky stars being 149.

"eliminated" when a dart hits one of them, thus limiting number of tickets.

Placed in restaurants, drug stores, taverns, at cashier's counter, customers are permitted several throws when paying checks. Or, made a feature of a lobby display, attendant allows each patron several throws. Distance from thrower to target should not be too great, experimenting for correct throw. Target panel carries copy on attraction. 

276. VENTRILOQUIST... Occasionally available, a ven triloquist might be used to good advantage in places where crowds go . . . in street cars, restaurants, department stores. Or used as a lobby flash, or a window (using amplification, and backed up by display panels). Or, man (or girl) might imitate a ventriloquist, keeping lips closed as nearly as possible, talking out of corner of mouth which is turned away from spectators when "throwing voice."

Seating himself (or herself), with dummy on knee, "ventriloquist" goes into a routine conversation with the dummy about attraction. 

Asks questions in usual voice; changes voice pitch for answers which are supposedly coming from the dummy.

Dummy might be made up to resemble the star of theatre's attraction. Head can be made from papier mache, and the lower jaw pivoted so that ventriloquist makes it move up and down. Art department of school might make up the head. Or a regular ventriloquist will have a dummy which might be clothed like star of attraction.

Conversation with dummy might be ended with the ventriloquist asking the dummy if he is going to see the attraction, and dummy replying: "I'm the only one in town that isn't going. That's why 

I'm a dummy.' 

277. GHOSTS... Men dressed as "spooks" (in long sheets) travel about town, carrying copy on their backs, "We're Ghosts. 

And we like it. We died laughing at (attraction)." Or, the copy is lettered on a small panel, which is cut up jig-saw puzzle style into a dozen pieces, which the "ghosts" (stationed in a prominent window) studiously assemble and reassemble. Or, they might be seriously operating an old "ouija-board," which is made to spell out name of the attraction, display panel carrying the copy. Contemplating use of “ghosts,” a newspaper ad might seek to hire a ghost. Running a classfied ad, paper might later carry a picture of one of the "spooks,' testifying to the fact that classifieds can even locate a ghost. 99 • 150 •

O F Radio or newspaper contest might be based on ghost stories, with the best ones reproduced or read over the air. Tickets for prizes. "Ghost message" herald might be made, by imprinting copy, and having a reversed cut made, so that paper must be held to light to be read (through the paper). Front carries copy: "Hold this 'Ghost 

Message' to the Light." Or, "Spirit Messages" might be made up by cashier in spare time, using invisible ink, and writing the "message" on slips of paper which carry printed directions for making the "ghost message" appear (the directions that accompany the invisible ink when purchased). Slips are handed to patrons with change.

Perhaps a "spiritualist" might be available, or someone who can perform some of the table lifting tricks of a spiritualist. Might work as center of a display in a window (which cannot be too well lighted), or on stage as a prologue to the trailer. 

Midnight showing of a "spooky" attraction can be billed as a "Midnight Thrill Show," publicly inviting all the ghosts in the

Great Beyond to attend. Might have man in sheet walk across stage just as feature begins, girl screaming. Skeleton (if one is available) touched with luminous paint carried down aisles as lights black out. Wind effect record played on non-sync or through amplification system. Balloons on which faces have been painted with luminous paint tossed out of the balcony.

Contest for newspaper or radio could be based on imaginary conversations with ghosts of famous departed persons. Cleverest submitted "conversations" winning guest tickets.

Tieup with photographer or snapshot developing place might set contest based on "ghost pictures" (double exposures, one picture being made over another). Photographer might buy ad and install window. Tickets for best "spook pictures."

Story based on ghosts or haunted houses might suggest a "search for a haunted house;" radio and newspaper inquiring for information leading to location of a house having the reputation of being haunted ... announcing that radio station, "inspired" by theatre's attraction, intends to broadcast direct from the haunted house at midnight, the night before opening of the attraction. Arrangements should be made to take along a group of wrestlers and boxers for "protection" (and their photograph, grouped, ought to be good for newspaper space). Given sufficient publicity, much attention can be focused on the ghost-baiting expedition, and numerous listeners at midnight can be assured. If a house, reputed to be haunted, is located, and written permission of owner secured, station could connect in a line • 151 •

for the broadcast. Some routine of activities for the broadcast must be planned, spooky business and surprises. Sound effect recordings can include howl of wind, hoot of owls, clank of chains, slamming of shutters. Flash lights might "go out" near midnight, with wrestlers "capturing" the ghost, only to find when a light is flashed on that it's one of their number; might clown the thing to a finish with footsteps coming down stairs slowly, and proving to be one of the station's announcers, or local celebrity, who claims he was upstairs playing a game of cards with the ghost, that's why he didn't appear. Police escort and ambulance might wait out front during the broadcast. 

If there proves to be no available "haunted house", no address would be announced, and the "visit" would be handled as a studio broadcast. 

278. PUNS... Lobby display, or newspaper contest might invite patrons to "pun the title" of attraction, or a word of title or star's name . . . including it as basis of a sentence (as, using "John:" "John the Navy and see the World.") Attendant in charge of a lobby display is equipped with a book in which patrons might inscribe puns they believe amusing.

Or newspaper classified page contest might invite readers to take any word from the page and include it as part of a pun-sentence. 

Space on classified page features attraction copy. Tickets for "best" puns. 

279. COMPOSITE PICTURES... Newspaper contest might be based on a series of composite photographs . . . face pictures of players cut into three sections each, the sections mixed up when reproduced by newspaper, with contestants invited to correctly reassemble the photos, identifying the players, adding a one-word description of each player. Extended over several days. Or, instead of face pictures, full-length photographs might be used, with figures separated into several sections. Or, contest (for newspaper or lobby) might be based on "perfect screen star" suggestions, a composite picture using face, legs, lips, hands (etc.) of different players; or, for most comical combination of features and physical characteristics. 

280. CHILDREN... Kiddie club might be promoted as a means of boosting kid attendance. Club could be "named" after star or subject appearing regularly at theatre, as after a cartoon character; club would be called the "(name) Club."

Membership cards supplied the members upon filling out application cards... the cards to carry corresponding numbers. Name, • 152.

address, age, birthday, school, grade, parents' names, secured on application card. Membership buttons could be supplied, carrying name of club and number.

Kiddie club meetings might be set for Saturday morning, before the beginning of the show, with a special program for the kids. 

Occasional meeting might be broadcast over radio station. Or a regular program might be put on the air. Included in meetings can be songs; entertainers from among the membership, with kiddie master of ceremonies introducing the numbers; occasional speaker on some educational subject or adult entertainer. Officers should be elected. Arrange club song. Entertainers from stage show might appear.

Newspaper might jointly sponsor the club. Paper would devote a column each week to the club's activities, including newsy items, which the "secretary" of the club supplies. Photographs of officers, upon election, should be carried in paper, printing also picture of club "president" presenting honorary membership card number one to Mayor, or to Editor of the paper. Star of coming show may be made an honorary member.

Maybe paper will editorialize on merits of the club. 

Ushers can take turns arranging and directing the weekly programs. 

Several numbers might be posted each week at box office, and children having corresponding numbers on membership badge or card, to be admitted free. Will make them wear their badges, bring their cards. Promoted prizes might be presented to owners of lucky membership cards (numbers).

Membership card can have a dozen or fifteen spaces, to be punched or stamped, one each week, and the holder entitled to a free admittance for the last space.

From record of birthdays on application cards, greetings and invitations may be mailed members on their birthdays: 

Occasional treats might be promoted for entire membership, as ice cream cones from an ice cream company. Promoted gifts might include (during school months) book-covers, name label stickers, imprinted scratch pads.

Timely events might be planned for the club . . . Hallowe'en parties (with appropriate contests), Christmas parties (with promoted or inexpensive gifts for all), pushmobile races, Easter egg hunts. (See 631.)

How about a kiddie newspaper? Making a bid for kid trade, or sponsoring a kiddie club, a small printed folder, made up after the • 153 •

style of tabloid newspaper, might be promoted. Kid members should be elected, or appointed reporters, honorary editors, etc. 

Business places might cooperate, sponsoring the sheet, and paying for same, or buying space. Activities and personals, birthdays, etc., that constitute news for the kids would be noted, together with plenty of show plugs and ads. Cooperating merchants assist in distribution, or schools may permit them to be distributed. 

Kid "beauty contest" or resemblance or impersonation contest might be promoted in connection with attraction featuring child star. Or a doll contest may be suggested.

Kid dance revue might prove an attraction, staged with cooperation of dance schools or various schools. 

In tieup with newspaper, readers might be urged to "adopt a child" for a day. . . responsible couples taking charge of a child from an orphanage, with the kid to be treated and entertained for the day including a visit to theatre to see attraction as theatre's guests. 

Cooperation with playground authorities can result in announcements for commendable attractions. Tickets might be presented to winners of playgrounds contests. ...

Junior interviews might be broadcast by a radio station, from theatre when kiddie matinees are featured. 

281. EDITORIAL... Newspapers are generally quick to lend their support, and possibly their endorsement, to anything definitely commendable.

Perhaps newspaper can be persuaded to comment editorially on an attraction that is outstanding as fine entertainment, or educational, or historical. 

Theatre sponsorship of a special "show season," or booking of a series of outstanding attractions, which are announced; or improvements which elevate standard of entertainment in the city; introduction of an outstanding stage attraction; any aid or sponsorship of a worthy cause, or effort that is of definite value to the community; any and all of these things might win a story on the editorial page might even be requested, if the justification is sufficient, and newspaper relations are as friendly as they should be. 

282. SKATERS... Figure skater might write out attraction title, on street or on ice, using a "magazine" of flour on one leg, which is arranged to spill a small stream continuously as he begins to skate, leaving a trail of flour. Skater could travel about town (roller skates), making different streets (or sidewalks), or (ice skates) ice- • 154 •

skating lagoons. And, of course, skating rinks. Girl skater might possibly be used.

Giant 24-sheet jig-saw puzzle (see 784) might be worked out on floor of a skating rink, by a couple of girl skaters, as a highlight of the evening. Display panels should be placed in skate-rinks if sufficient crowds are being attracted. 

Roller skating race might be promoted (through park), with trophy (from star of attraction) for winner. Age limit should be specified, and race might be set for girls only. Ice sports might suggest a trophy, or, "golden skates," named after star of coming attraction.

Couple of attractive girl skaters can travel about town, on sidewalks (with police permission), with copy on their backs: "Skate on down to (theatre) see (attraction), it's Great."

If skating is featured in an attraction, window displays in stores handling skates can be arranged, and perhaps skates can be promoted for winners of contests.

Group of girl skaters, in costumes or bathing suits, could skate to theatre on opening day (or evening) of attraction. Newspaper might carry ad for girl skaters, offering the first so-many arriving free admission, suggesting that they bring their own pillows. Skating rink might arrange for the girls, or girls from stage show might serve. 

They carry banner: "On our way to see (attraction).” 

283. NORTHERN Attraction with Far North background would naturally find "Eskimos," men or girls in heavy furs, distributing heralds. A dog-team might be available, pulling sled about town (in charge of their fur-costumed owner, and with the sled on small wheels if there is no snow-and equipped with brakes).

Or several dogs might be secured for lobby exhibition. 

Igloo can be constructed as a lobby display and "inhabited” by fur-costumed "Eskimos." Or a real ice igloo might possibly be constructed in winter near skating lagoon . . . panel carrying attraction copy being frozen into the ice or snow used in its construction. 

Explorers, or persons who have visited Far North might appear as honor guests opening night of attraction. Perhaps they can be interviewed over radio, including their comment on attraction. 

Books on exploration, or on North country should be featured by book stores in tieups. Robert W. Service poems could be featured; and additionally, a radio program might feature reading of one of the poems-"suggested" by the attraction playing theatre. • 155 •

Ice effect might be used in displays (especially if attraction is playing in summertime).

Fur dealers should go along for full window displays, and perhaps newspaper ads. Radio dealer might put in a window, or buy an ad, calling attention to the fact that through radio, even the Far North is no longer isolated. Refrigerator might be tied in for an ad. 

Perhaps a taxidermist or zoo or museum might have stuffed polar bear that might be secured for display. Perhaps museum has display of Eskimo articles, which they might permit to be placed on display in theatres; or at least a newspaper feature story might be based on the stuff. 

284. PATRIOTISM... Aid of patriotic organizations, and those interested in education, might be secured in connection with an attraction that appeals to patriotism.

Announcements at meetings, or letters sent members, will reach them. (Perhaps attraction can be screened for officials in advance, securing their sponsorship.) "Guard of Honor" might be arranged for opening night.

Various evenings might be dedicated to different organizations, urging them to attend on that night. Drum and bugle corps, or bands, supported by patriotic organizations might play. 

Patriotic colors and shields used in front displays. Bunting and drapings secured for front. Flag flying from marquee of theatre. 

Heralds use patriotic design or color. Miniature button-hole flags might be distributed, with small imprinted tags attached. 

If attraction carries patriotic appeal to those of foreign birth or nationality, an evening might be dedicated to those of that nationality. 

Veterans of some war which involved the country might be located for radio interview. If a Consul or representative of the government is in town, his support might be secured; he might be guest of honor. 

Medals or flags might be displayed. Support of local veteran or military organization might be secured as a tribute to other country represented. 

285. OPENERS Quantity of bottle openers, secured in tieup with bottler or brewer . . . are inserted in imprinted envelopes, or imprinted tags attached. Copy reads: "Get Ready for An 

Uproarious Opening . . . the opening of (attraction) in (town)." 

Copy for cooperating bottlers is included. Corkscrews might be used, instead of bottler openers.

Openers, in the shape of a girl's leg, might be secured with at- 156.

traction imprint stamped on, and distributed in connection with a girl show.

And, too, openers are especially adaptable to attractions dealing, in comedy style, with drinking. 

286. QUEEN FOR A DAY... Announced as having been suggested by the star of the attraction, and with the cooperation of newspaper and merchants, theatre undertakes to treat a local girl or woman to everything possible, for a day. 

Selected girl, or woman, is to become for a day a fine lady similar to character portrayed in the theatre's attraction, or suggested by the title; or to serve as a proxy for the star for a day, and to receive all attentions that star might receive. Title of attraction, or theme, might suggest the stunt, or be adapted to it. 

A girl might be selected in a contest conducted in cooperation with newspaper; or a deserving woman might be suggested by welfare organizations. 

With attendant newspaper stories, an elaborate program is laid out for the woman selected. Limousine, with liveried chauffeur, drives her about town; to stores, where a complete outfit is promoted for her, together with other gifts; to hotels where she is guest for dinner; to newspaper offices and broadcast stations for interviews, possibly to Mayor's office. She is given every attention possible to arrange, and as many gifts as possible to promote for her. Her evening ends with visit to theatre to witness attraction (which might precede visit to a night club as guest of honor).

Cooperating stores and business places carry copy on the stunt and the attraction which inspired it in their newspaper ads and radio announcements. 

287. PRISON. . . Story featuring convicts, or with prison background suggests use of front display panels painted to resemble stone of prison walls. Compo-board jail could be constructed in lobby, with stripe-clad "convicts" inside. Openings in display panels might feature bars, prison window style, with illustrations displayed behind the opening, and through the bars. "Guard," might pace top of marquee, carrying rifle. Sidewalk "barker," in front of theatre, can be costumed in striped convict garb (which can be secured from a costumer). Cashier's window might feature "bars," through which tickets are sold.

Heralds distributed through business section by man in convict costume, title of attraction plainly lettered on both front and back of his costume. He might wear lettered card that carries copy: • 157 •

"I broke out of jail to see (attraction)." Several men in convict costumes, with signs on their backs, might be handcuffed together, marched along street, man dressed as a warden, or guard, following behind with a rifle. 

Display for lobby, or front, might feature articles from prison, or duplicates. especially those featured in the story. Reproduce scene from attraction. Police might lend crime apparatus for display. 

If a couple of bloodhounds are available, a man dressed as a prison guard might pilot them about town, copy on his back proclaiming that he is looking for (character or star in attraction). 

Illustrations from other prison-stories, or actual life pictures of notorious criminals might possibly be used for display. Screening might be arranged for officials (perhaps in prison). Newspaper may be interested in carrying story or editorial dealing with prison reforms. 

Sirens, such as prisons use, might be occasionally sounded out front. 

In advance, siren can be placed in front of screen, sounded as trailer hits the screen. 

For a street flash, two men, one dressed to appear "tough," the other dressed to resemble police or detective, and handcuffed together, might attract attention. Ad on their backs. 

Interviews for radio or newspapers might be arranged for judges, ministers, or prison reformers or for warden of some institution (depending on attraction).

Radio thrill-sketches might be immediately followed by announcements on attraction.

Radio station might do a broadcast from jail or penitentiary in connection with theatre's attraction. . . running a line into jail, or using a mobile transmitter. Announcer tells what happens in jail, talks to prisoners, includes plenty of mention of attraction. His photograph, in stripes, as he prepares to make his prison investigation, might be carried for newspaper space . . . story crediting his trip to jail as "inspired" by theatre's attraction. ... 

288. MASKS... Title of attraction is lettered on half-masks 

(covering the eyes), which are worn by ushers in advance. Especially adaptable for a coming mystery story. They might be worn to "tease" a title, or to arouse curiosity in connection with a coming show . . . lettering title, adding a question mark. Lettered masks might also be worn by persons distributing heralds, in offices, stores. 

Full-face paper "masks" might be printed up, using a likeness of star of a coming attraction. The masks might be made round, and • 158 •

sufficiently large to cover the face completely. Small holes are die-cut at the eyes, and small slit is die-cut at the nose, to permit breathing. The "mask" might be folded slightly to more closely fit face (at the same time forcing a slight opening at the nose). Copy on attraction is printed on reverse side of the mask. 

Full-face masks can be distributed to children, carrying picture of a star that will especially appeal to them. Or, they can be handed to girls at bathing beaches and swim pools, where they can be used to protect girls' faces from the sun (shielding their faces, while achieving a sun-tan). 

289. HANGERS... Cards, imprinted on both sides, and with perforation at top where length of string is used to suspend them, might be hung in stores, and in any public places, and in front of theatre and in theatre lobby; smaller cards might be attached inside street cars or buses or ferryboats or trains. 

Cards might be die-cut to outline an imprinted illustration (as the figure of a girl; or an airplane). Photograph of the star or a girl, can completely fill in one side of the card;-no copy. attraction imprint being carried on other side. . . both sides coming into view as the card revolves (as it will do, if suspended, by a length of string, at the top).

Cards might be made up square, or they might be made up long and narrow. Ordinary window cards can be used for hangers, in theatre lobby or under marquee... three cards folded and stapled together back to back to make up a single hanger. 

290. INVENTIONS... New inventions, or devices that hold public interest, can generally be adapted to a window or lobby. 

Tiein copy might describe attraction as "just as marvelous;" or describe device and attraction as "two modern miracles." The device made center of a display on attraction. 

Displays that depict progress might feature television, sewing machines, airbrakes, telegraph, cotton gin or cotton picker, airplane transportation, photography, wireless, electric lighting, printing, steamships; with patrons invited to name the inventors. Anything new that intrigues interest might be adapted. Queer gadgets, mechanical and electrical, will draw much interested attention. 

Similarly, scientific devices which will arrest attention, might possibly be secured and demonstrated in connection with a display on an attraction.

Crazy inventions might be made the basis of a newspaper contest ... preferably in connection with a comedy... contestants to submit • 159 •

drawings of “crazy inventions" of method of bringing into view panel carrying title of theatre attraction. "Convention of Inventions" might invite local inventors to display their brain-children on mezzanine floor on designated evening. Distributors of various electrical devices might install displays and stores could show latest developments. 

291. MAGIC . . . Any mystifying illusion or display of legerdemain is certain to command interest. 

An amateur magician or card manipulator might appear, as the center of a window or lobby display, presenting several tricks that conclude with introduction of attraction title. Title might be lettered on backs of cards, which, together, spell out title; or on a length of lettered ribbon which is "produced." If local prestidigitator will not himself serve, perhaps he will agree to teach several simple tricks to someone else, perhaps a girl.

Illusions can occasionally be simply constructed, or they might be rented from a magic supply house, and are always effective. 

Illusion of a display floating in air might be simply achieved by holding it from behind, by use of an arm which extends through the background display panel. Attendant, a pretty girl preferably, can pass a large hoop twice over the display "to show that there is nothing holding the display in the air." Actually, when hoop is passed over the display the first time, it is then around arm behind display... and in passing over the display the second time, the hoop is brought back to starting point (passing it behind the display). 

Second "pass" (reversing sides) removing the hoop from over the horizontal arm. Done quickly and easily. Live girl, seated on the end of the "arm," legs or skirt concealing any upward view of the "arm," might be used instead of a display . . . the hoop being sufficiently large to be passed over her. Ends of display are masked in, so that "back-stage" view of operation of the illusion is not visible. 

Copy on panel might carry the copy: "You can defy the laws of gravitation... but you can't defy the laws of Laughter, when you see (attraction)" . . . or other copy as suggested by the attraction. 

Books on magic, describing many tricks and illusions are available at book stores and libraries. Amateur magic sets might be purchased cheaply, and tricks from these sets might be used. The sets also make very acceptable prizes for children. 

292. LETTER TO STAR . . . Tickets might be offered for cleverest "fan letters". . . letters to be addressed to star of theatre attraction. Additionally, arrangements might be made to have • 160 •
