News- star answer personally the letter which is selected as winner. paper or radio sponsors the contest; or store can incorporate it in their newspaper ads.

Giant "fan letter" can be made up, using a giant "sheet" of paper, or panel. Message about coming attraction inscribed and on display in lobby, patrons are invited to add their signatures. "Letter" in giant envelope can be sent star. . . with newspapers perhaps using photograph of it being mailed by pretty girl. 

293. COMPASS. . . Featured in lobby or window display, as people will generally stop and observe a compass. Display carries copy: "You won't need this to lead you to (theatre) when (attraction) comes to town. . . you'll be able to follow the applause (or 'the laughter')."

Where a direction is indicated in an attraction title, a compass can, of course, be effectively adapted to a display. Might carry copy: "This compass will point the way to (and into attraction copy)." 

294. TIRE COVERS . . . Tire covers will prove especially effective on taxicabs as they are continuously on the streets. Also, private cars can carry the covers. 

Tire covers might be lettered with theatre name only, with space allotted for attaching imprinted cards, which are changed as program changes. 

295. WRONG... Contest for newspaper might be based on pictured scenes from current or previous attractions . . . with information carried under illustration, most of which is wrong, some of which is right. Contestants locate "what's wrong here."

Or another character (from an illustration on another attraction) is included in the picture (second illustration being cut out and pasted over illustration used, before having engraving made, making a composite picture). Contestants to locate errors in illustrations, as well as in the accompanying "information." 

Novel herald can be based on out-of-date laws, that are still on the records in many places . . . heading the herald: "Is It Wrong? . . . 

Perhaps Yes, Perhaps No..." Following with copy: "Do you know it's wrong, and against the law, to (quoting then a number of the antiquated laws), but its okay, anytime, to see (attraction).” "Laws" listed can include those out-moded statutes to be found locally still remaining on the statute books, which might be secured from an attorney. Or, some of these obsolete old "regulations" might be used: "In Boston, it is against the law to hiss an actor. 

In Virginia, to miss church three times. In Maryland, for a wife to • 161 •

rifle her husband's pockets while he sleeps. In Texas, to carry a cane. 

In Nevada, to listen in on a party line. In Pennsylvania, to sing in a bath tub. In West Virginia, to sneeze on Sunday. In New York, to eavesdrop. In Louisiana, to wear a hat-pin which projects over half an inch from the crown of the hat. In Zion, Ill., to make faces at anyone. In Buffalo, for a girl to wear a college boy's fraternity pin. In North Carolina, it is considered legally a nuisance for a person to swear publicly for two hours. In Georgia, it is illegal to slap a man on the back. In Portland, Maine, to tickle a girl under the chin with a feather duster. In Newark, N. J., to sell ice on Sunday without a doctor's prescription. In Kentucky, those operating a still must blow a whistle; and it is against the law to sleep on the floor of the state house. In Kansas, there is a law limiting the length of shirt-tails. In Pennsylvania, all restaurants are obliged to be equipped with wheel chairs. In Connecticut, all couples in public places must remain at least six inches apart. In Portsmouth, Ohio, ball players are included with vagrants, beggars, thieves and suspicious characters, in being subject to imprisonment if unable to give a reasonable account of themselves. In Ohio, a young girl must not be hired to dance on a tight rope on Sunday—except in a church. 

In Virginia, no man may beat his wife with a stick thicker than his thumb. In Los Angeles, wearing false whiskers on the street is prohibited." (All of these old laws being subject to error or repeal. 

Check those applying locally.) ... 

296. ADMISSIONS. . . Card, carrying admission prices should be plainly visible in front of theatre box office. When theatre is closed prices should also be carried on a card which is placed over box office opening and which is lettered: "Good Morning! (Or 'Good

Evening,' if theatre closes for supper hour) Theatre Opens at (time), and (prices)."

A two-for-one tieup with newspaper would have the paper devoting large space to theatre's attraction and carrying copy: "Your Guest is Our Guest... You are invited to bring a guest free to see (attraction and date). This ad clipped out will admit one person if accompanied by one paid admission." Offer might be limited to include ladies only, or kids only, and confined to a single specified matinee performance. Merchant might cooperate instead of newspaper, buying large newspaper space for the offer. . . which also devotes space to theatre's attraction. 

Prices should be carried in ads and displayed especially prominently out front if they are definitely an attraction. • 162

EN C Y C L O P E DIA OF EXPLOITATION 

Special early admission price might be made to prevail for a brief period as theatre first opens doors-perhaps fifteen minutes. . . billing the special prices as "Early Bird Prices." Might be used as a daily feature; or only on opening matinee of attraction. All those in line at box office by the time fifteen minutes (or specified time) expires admitted at a special and lower admission price (an usher can be placed in line of waiting patrons as the time expires, with the prices changing as the usher arrives at box office). Or, of course, the special prices could be extended for several hours. Advertising special "Early Bird Prices," a sidewalk man can wear a "bird" costume, with placard bearing price copy about his neck. 

Schools and colleges might be favored with a special "student's price," if this business justifies. A special "identification card" might be issued.

Organizations might be made a special group price. Fraternities, sororities, civic and church organizations might be interested. 

Consider all contemplated price changes thoroughly and from all angles first. 

297. SAFE... Panel for lobby or window constructed to resemble a safe, with door (an opening in the panel) "open," revealing an ordinary wastebasket placed within the "safe." Panel carries copy: "The boss accidentally threw a picture of (star) in the wastebasket... so we're putting the wastebasket in the safe." Actual photograph might be placed in the wastebasket, raised from bottom so that a portion of it is revealed. Photo of girl or girls in a musical show might be used. Actual safe might be used.

Heralds, in the form of small envelopes, can carry the copy: "If you throw this in the wastebasket . . . Put the wastebasket in the safe!" Inside the envelope is an imprinted card, which carries brief copy on the attraction, devoting most of the space to a photograph preferably of a pretty girl in the show.

Patrons might be invited to try to open a real safe which is used as center of a display . . . with a reward of tickets if they succeed. 

Stop numbers might be given, though in jumbled form and without number of turns, and perhaps without final number. Safe is spotlighted, and display on attraction is placed inside it, in case it is opened. Starting from last number, one additional number can be given each day, until all numbers but one are given. Or "clues" to the combination might be carried among the classified ads, in a newspaper tieup. Display copy advises that "burglars" and locksmiths are barred. • 163

ENCYCLOPEDIA OF EXP L O I T A T I O N 

298. SUN DIAL... Large white circle is painted on the sidewalk, in front of theatre, or in prominently located downtown corner. 

It is noted at what point a shadow of a person standing in the center of the circle will fall at a certain time . . . and a clock face is painted in (the figures) accordingly. Thus, a person stepping to the center of the circle, can tell by the direction of his shadow, the time of the day (approximately).

Copy lettered at top, or across the circle, should suggest, "Stand in the center of the sun dial to learn the correct time." Then follow with copy: "It's time to see (attraction copy)." 

299. MEGAPHONES... Lettered megaphones might be effectively used for announcements at football games, or other competitions which attract crowds. 

Printed paper megaphones can be made up by imprinting fold-over sheet of paper of proper pattern, the two edges being stapled together to assume shape of megaphone when rounded out. Distributed at games, megaphones carry copy: "After the game; see (attraction)." 

300. CONCEALED TICKETS... Cooperating store adver tises, in newspaper ads, or on display cards in store and in store windows, that some "lucky" packages of a certain commodity will have theatre guest tickets attached (to bottom of packages) or inserted inside same, devoting much space to attraction. 

Local distributor of some commodity might work the tieup out with a number of stores, arranging large group of windows and assigning several concealed guest tickets to each store. ...

Hidden ticket idea might be adapted to theatre, attaching tickets to bottoms of certain seats . . . making an announcement or flashing a trailer which calls attention to the stunt, emphasizing the attraction for which the tickets will be good, suggesting that patrons look under their seats. Lights might go up for a moment so that patrons can check and double check.

Similarly certain restaurant seats might be "lucky," and tickets to go to those selecting the lucky chair (changed each day that tieup continues). . . and restaurant cooperating with advertising and displays. 

301. WINDOW CONTEST . . . Might be set with a chain of stores; or in a tieup with distributor of a commodity sold by all stores; or all stores of a certain type, as grocery stores; with prizes offered (cash most effective) for most attractive windows. Stores to submit snapshots of their windows, photos being placed on display • 164 •

in theatre lobby, with patrons to pick the winner by casting their votes in a receptacle which is provided. 

Store patrons can secure vote blanks at stores, but they should be deposited at theatre.

Windows to combine a display of merchandise and theatre display material. Tieing up with a distributor, who aids in securing the windows, the merchandise used in the window must be that sold by the distributor (as breakfast food, or soap).

Contest will assure a multitude of attractive window-displays all over the city.

In connection with an outstanding attraction, or inaugurating a "special (attraction title) week," merchants' association or chamber of commerce might cooperate in working out a display window contest, with all downtown stores competing. Cash prize or trophy to go to window adjudged best, and all to in some way tie in with theatre's attraction. Trailer in theatre should direct attention to the contest, and a scheduled "unveiling" of all windows at a designated time on the day attraction opens, with public urged to come downtown and go window shopping before attending show. Newspaper should cooperate, selling stores special ads on the items they will feature, and according the stunt news stories. 

302. SULTAN . . . Dressed in Oriental costume, turban, robes, man travels about downtown section, carrying copy on his back: "I left my Harem to see those gorgeous dames (or name of feminine star) in (attraction).” Or, carrying no banners, he might hand out small imprinted cards that carry the copy. Or a couple of girls in Oriental get-up might accompany the "Sultan," handing out the cards (in this event, cards imprinted: "He left his harem, etc.)" Or, he might ride about town in a bannered limousine.

Adapted to lobby, "Sultan" might pose as the center of a built-up display on the attraction, spotlighted and imperturbably smoking an Oriental pipe . . . copy on panel proclaiming: "He left his Harem to see (star or girls) and he's waiting until (attraction) comes to (theatre) on (day).” 

303. COSTUMES AND PROPS... With cooperation of studios, actual costumes or articles used in an attraction might possibly be secured and placed on display in a prominently located window. Style store featuring dresses like those worn in attraction, might place the original in a window together with a copy. Similarly, various articles. 

Duplication of articles identified with an attraction might be made • 165.

the basis of a window display. Replica of jewel or jewels might be displayed in a jeweler's window. Or a duplication of a costume, together with photos from attraction showing the original. Various articles might be duplicated. 

304. TEAMS... Where an attraction features a well-known team of players, a contest for newspaper or radio might be based on famous teams of history, radio, comics, stage, etc. One name of the teams announced, with contestants to supply the accompanying name. Star team, from attraction, should head the list, and illustrations (for newspaper) should show scenes from attraction. 

Currently popular teams might be used in combination with those of history or fiction. In addition to contemporary teams, those listed might include Adam and Eve, Leander and Hero, Jack and 

Jill, Punch and Judy, Tristram and Isolde, Antony and Cleopatra,

Othello and Desdemona, Sampson and Delilah. 

Pals portrayed in an attraction might suggest a contest based on famous pals of history. 

305. SHOCKING... Penny arcade "shock machine" might be secured, or electrician might construct one, with shock delivered from small batteries when two handles to machine are grasped. 

Made the center of a display, a panel carries the copy: "Do You Want a Shock? Hold the handles (etc.) And if you want a REAL Shock, see (attraction)." 

306. WISHING WELL 

Novel display for lobby is designed after the style of an old-fashioned well, possibly even including the bucket, or a reproduction of one, hanging above the well. Copy suggests that patrons look in "The Wishing Well,” and make a wish, and that they'll learn how to win happiness. Looking into well, they see a mirror, on top of which cutout letters have been placed (appearing to be floating on surface of water), carrying: "Message," "see (attraction)." Pretty girl, costumed, at the well might invite patrons to take a look and make a wish. 

307. NEWS-STANDS... Newspaper or magazine tieup would suggest use of large cards directing attention to both the magazine and attraction. Cards displayed at news-stands and whereever magazines or papers are handled. 

Heralds might be inserted in papers, particularly Sunday papers, on stands. 

Bricks with attraction title lettered on (in oil) might be supplied news-stands, being used to hold down stacks of newspapers. Both sides of bricks should be lettered. • 166 •

Papers and magazines might be rubber-stamped. Or small stickers might be attached. (See "News-stands.") 

308. SOAP BOX ORATOR. . . Adaptable to most at tractions, a man (or a girl) makes a “stump speech" which refers convincingly to action and incidents that theatre's attraction pictures . . . the speech being concluded with: "If you don't think 

I'm right, go see (attraction) at (theatre).”

The speech must be prepared along briefly interesting lines, and must be delivered convincingly. "Speaker" should take a soap box along with him, and arriving at prominent corners or parks, he places the box on the sidewalk, mounts it, and goes into his oration. 

Hecklers might be arranged, to mingle with the crowds, ask questions which the speaker answers. Concluding his "pitch," the orator moves along to another prominent location, where stunt is repeated. 

And if he's pinched for disturbing the peace, it ought to make a good news story before he's bailed out. 

309. TRAVEL 

Transportation systems-railroads, airlines, bus lines, should all be willing and glad to cooperate if attraction features or suggests travel. . . arranging window displays, placing displays in their waiting rooms, including copy in any ads. 

Travel agencies and bureaus will install window displays if travel or foreign locale is featured. And perhaps including mention in travel letters they mail out . . . or attaching imprinted stickers to their correspondence, or rubber-stamping travel literature. Maybe travel agency will buy newspaper space.

Large globe of world might be used as center of a window display, perhaps revolving. Copy: "In all the World . . . No Thrills (or 'Laughs,' or 'Excitement') such as you will enjoy in (attraction)." (A window tieup that might be used in connection with any attraction, regardless of travel angle.)

Giant map of area attraction refers to could be effectively used, perhaps especially blown-up or enlarged, for window or lobby. Stills attached directly to the map. 

Theatre front, or canopy top might feature a giant globe of the world... which might be made to mechanically revolve (with attraction title attached, using cutout letters). 

Heralds might be made up to resemble a passport, or a railroad or boat ticket.

Luggage store should be a "natural" for a window display. Other stores can feature travel outfits (clothes) installing windows. 

310. NEWS COMMENTATOR... In tieup with newspaper, 

• 167 •

well-known columnist from the paper, or the editor, appears at theatre (on stage) several times each day with late news flashes which he announces, using house amplification system. Or, more conveniently, he might phone the late news flashes to the theatre, where they are read off (in dramatic news-flash style) while a silent film is run on the screen- -a film which has been especially photographed in the newspaper editor's office, and which shows him busily engaged in his usual activities. Newspaper stories should mention the stunt.

Radio news commentator might mention theatre's attraction and offer guest tickets for the first ten persons phoning him if he makes a mistake in pronunciation in his news announcements. 

311. PROCLAMATION. . . Mayor might be persuaded to issue a "proclamation" honoring the star of the attraction; or designating a certain specified week as “Laugh Week,” or “(name of star) Week;" or after some angle suggested by the attraction. Proclamation could welcome a star or stage show. 

Cut made of the proclamation should be carried in the newspapers and papers might carry it as a news item. 

Original proclamation, or blowup of same, might be used as a lobby display.

Or, if Mayor won't issue a proclamation, an advertisement could be headed (perhaps with approval of Mayor): "If I were Mayor of (city), I'd issue this Proclamation: (then following with copy on attraction in proclamation style)." 

312. COURT, LEGISLATURE OR ASSEMBLY... When an attraction carries a definite moral lesson, or sets a splendid example, it might be possible to have a friendly judge sentence some juvenile culprit to witness the attraction . . . arranging with newspaper to carry story, perhaps with photos. Attraction should be screened in advance for the judge, so that he can be certain that his actions will be justified.

Star of stage show might be introduced in court, perhaps sitting with the judge through a session. 

Or, perhaps arrangements might be made to have stage star appear before a legislative body.

Or, a picture could be screened in assembly room, for legislature or other law-making body, using portable projection equipment. 

Or, for Governor.

Newspaper should go along for stories and pictures. 

313. VACANT STORES . . . and even vacant lots 

· 168.

sometimes offer ideal spots for cutout displays, and for lithographs. 

Check business section and prominent locations. 

314. GREETINGS . . . New arrivals in city might be greeted with a special card of welcome, and invited to see a show as guests of theatre (on presentation of card at box office). 

A tieup with several merchants or manufacturers might make it possible to present new arrivals with samples of the commodities sold by the cooperating business places, together with tickets. 

Names of new-comers can be secured from Chamber of Commerce or from Power & Light Company. 

Similarly, cards of congratulation could be sent to newlywed couples, to couples celebrating wedding anniversaries, birthdays, graduates, new babies.

Drug store or confectionery can offer new arrivals a get-acquainted soda on presentation of card (which is then stamped, and to be then used for admission at theatre). Store shares cost of printing and mailing the cards. 

315. GIRL FRIEND... Small envelopes, imprinted: "We dare you to give this to your Girl Friend!" are handed to mẹn as they leave theatre (and when accompanied by a lady). Inside the envelope a small card carries copy: "Please let me take you to see (attraction) when it comes to (theatre)." Or, folder type herald might be used with the "dare” copy on front page, and the request copy on inner page; attraction copy on reverse side. 

Reverse angle would have herald handed to ladies (to be handed by them to their escorts), using copy: "Please take me to see (attraction)."

Or, a small folder, to be handed ladies leaving theatre with their escorts, carries copy: "Dear Lady . . . Here's the way to see one of the year's outstanding shows . . ." Page two then lists attraction title and cast, and carries copy: "I'd like to see this show" and dotted lines where lady's name may be signed. Page three says: "Tear off opposite page and hand it to your boy friend, telling him you want to see (attraction)."

Envelope handed men accompanied by girl friends is imprinted: "Don't show this to your girl friend!" Small card inside the envelope, reads, in script: "Be sure and see me at (theatre) on (day,)" the "message" being signed with name of feminine star of attraction.

Attraction imprint on reverse side removes any danger of misunderstanding. Also adaptable to a folder. Might be handed out by attractive girls, as patrons leave theatre. • 169 •

316. ICE... Printed cards, paraffined, might be frozen in cakes of ice through special arrangements with ice company. Iceenclosed cards being placed in prominent locations (where there is no danger of anyone falling over them.)

Objects can be frozen into ice, including waxed display card on attraction, and items suggested by the show. Cutout letters might be connected by wire and frozen. Roses could be included in a block of ice. Also, perhaps a few guest tickets, which will attract attention, crowds waiting until the ice melts down to them. Tickets might be offered for best estimates as to time it takes for the ice to melt.

Ice cakes might be adapted to "cool" advertising, freezing cards carrying "cool" copy into the cakes. Used in window or lobby, icecake must be placed in receptacle that is large enough to hold water when it melts.

Girls from stage show might be pictured (for summertime) at a swim pool, in bathing suits, seated on blocks of ice. Newspaper photograph (arranged in advance) points out easy method to beat the heat. 

317. COURT OF BEAUTY... A campaign can be built about the selection of a "Court of Beauty," who are to "sponsor" or welcome arrival in city of theatre's attraction.

Selected in advance, in contests conducted by night clubs or swimming pools or on theatre stage, this group of pretty girls will meet the arriving star, or "receive the film" (at theatre, opening day, or at railroad station or airport. See 140).

Week in advance of attraction, the girls, after their selection, are introduced as the "(attraction) Court of Beauty)" at night-spots, restaurants, swimming pool, luncheon clubs, where they are guests of honor. Newspaper should carry picture of the winning girls (who can be two red heads, two blondes, two brunettes). Other activities can be planned for them. Swim pool or dance spot sponsoring the selection will naturally make announcements. Girls should be on hand on opening night, in evening gowns, acting as hostesses. 

318. SIDEWALK CAMERAMAN... Copying manner of sidewalk cameramen who snap pictures of persons passing, handing them a card which makes it possible to secure a print of the picture, man carrying a camera, apparently takes pictures of those approaching. He actually takes no pictures, but hands person towards whom the camera was aimed, a card which is imprinted: "The Greatest • 170 •

Picture Ever Made . . . (and into copy on attraction);" or: "We didn't really take your picture . . . we just want to call your attention to a real picture (and into attraction copy)." 

Man (or girl) snapping the pictures might be costumed as suggested by attraction. 

319. GYPSY... Traveling about downtown section, girls dressed as gypsies could carry copy on their backs: "Even the Gypsies are coming to town to see (attraction)." Or, they might hand out imprinted cards which carry the copy. 

If gypsy theme or musical number is featured in an attraction, a "gypsy" violinist, and a dancer (both in costume), may appear in lobby, in advance, as center of a display panel on the attraction; or, with copy on violinist's back, they might travel about city. 

Perhaps a hurdy-gurdy can be secured, and with man and girl in costume, sent about city.

Gypsy fortune telling booth in lobby, or store, has pretty girl "telling their future," and handing out a card that carries the prophecy that they're going to see (attraction). 

320. SIMILES AND HYPERBOLES ... Contest, for radio newspaper or lobby, might be based on construction of most amusing hyperbole (an exaggerated comparison . . . as: "Such a good salesman he could sell nighties to nudists," or "Fans to Eskimos.") 

Tickets for best ones submitted. 

Commonly used similes might be made the basis of a contest, with prize for the longest list of commonly used and generally known similes (as "busy as a bee"); and including a new and original simile suggested by the attraction. 

For newspaper, illustrate with scenes from attraction, and if attraction does not actually suggest the contest, it might be described as the star's pet contest. 

321. RETURN TO LIFE... Portrayal in an attraction of walking dead, or bringing of dead back to life, or other angle dealing with life and death, might suggest a display which features scientific apparatus. Or "scientific" setup, including test tubes, neon lights that periodically flash on, simultaneously with a buzzer... and with man, or girl, dressed as character in the attraction, and as center of the display, perhaps on an operating table, periodically slowly “coming to life."

Perhaps someone might be located who may have been very near to death, or apparently dead and then revived. His story ought • 171.

to be interesting for newspaper or radio, including comment on the attraction.

Pallid persons, in sheets, can patrol top of canopy. 

322. LOVE ADVICE ... Girl seated at table, is center of display in lobby or store window. Display panels invite patrons to bring their love problems to her. Used in connection with attraction that deals romantic angle heavy. Those stopping to speak to girl are advised to see the attraction for a perfect example of romantic happiness. Used in a window, amplification makes it possible for her to speak to those passing; or her conversation with those tallking with her might be broadcast to the street... using several "stooges" who ask for her "advice," bringing humorous love problems. Girls should be pretty, attractively costumed. 

Letter, outlining problem similar to that portrayed in attraction, might be reproduced in newspaper's "Lonely Hearts" column.

Letter might even mention attraction title. Arranging with reporter who conducts the column in advance, he might even mention attraction in his comment. 

323. MAKE-UP TABLE... Small table, in lobby as center of a display, faces a large mirror, which has light sockets (and lights) surrounding it, top and sides, after the fashion of dressing room make-up mirrors backstage. "Props" on the table include photograph of stars of coming attraction, and cosmetics which cooperating druggist might wish displayed. ...

Copy on the mirror, or on small easel card invites women patrons to use "(star's) Make-up Table” . . . and additionally, they might be invited to compare their lips with those of the star, whose photograph is on display. 

Especially adaptable to attraction that deals with backstage story. 

Or, in connection with stage show, one of the girls in the show (or a local, as "proxy" for her) might actually “make up" at the table on opening night (clad in brief dance costume, and applying the cosmetics). Or a local girl might be stationed at the mirror, apparently applying makeup. . . turning and handing heralds to those whose attention is attracted; or, the mirror might be unopaqued, and she can occasionally press button which illuminates display behind the mirror (mirror becoming transparent, and the display coming into view). 

If attractive blonde (or red hair) wigs can be obtained, they might be made available, and women patrons invited to try them on. • 172.

Especially adaptable if star of attraction is vivid blonde, or famous for color of hair.

Or couple of attractive girls can carry small tables and folding camp stools about town, which they place on prominent corners, proceeding to make themselves up rouge, lipstick, etc. Panels on front of tables carry copy: "We want to look our best we're going to see (attraction) at (theatre).” ... ... 

324. LECTURERS, SPEAKERS 

Occasionally an authority on some subject suggested by an attraction will be found available... and in connection with certain attractions the services of such person can prove very valuable. He might make appearances at clubs, or schools, organization meetings, meetings of department store employees, before women's organizations, Little Theatre Groups and Drama Clubs; at factories, and over radio, making talks which are designed to sell the attraction.

He might make a brief talk from theatre stage as a prologue to the trailer on the attraction.

Theatre manager can occasionally place special emphasis on a coming attraction, by briefly addressing audiences from stage about it. 

325. LUCKY . . . Newspaper or program contest can list lucky telephone numbers, selected at random from telephone book, including them in ads. Those discovering their telephone numbers, and identifying themselves at newspaper office, to get guest tickets. 

Might be used to add interest to a cooperative page. Or classified page might carry the numbers throughout classified ads . . . with space on page devoted to attraction.

Similarly automobile numbers might be used. Or names, instead of numbers. 

Stores could list lucky numbers or names in their window or newspaper ad. Lucky ones to receive tickets... and the store giving the attraction space in their newspaper ads, windows. 

Lucky names or numbers might be used as a radio feature, calling out the lucky ones selected. Merchant may cooperate, adding the stunt to a sponsored program, announcing theatre's attraction. 

Emphasing "lucky" angle, newspaper contest might be based on "my luckiest day," or "experience.' 

326. SOCIETY REPORTERS... In tieup with newspaper, tickets (mentioning attraction) are offered for social items phoned and used on society page. Or, most interesting society item of each day.

Especially effective in connection with society drama. • 173 •

327. PIRATES... "Pirate Ball," at cooperating ballroom or night club, invites public to attend in costume, with tickets for best costumes. 

Pretty girls in brief pirate outfits distribute heralds, which suggest that an attached key be tried in the lock on a pirate chest in theatre lobby... those opening the lock to win tickets.

Ushers and cashiers, barker on sidewalk, might wear pirate getups. 

Candy store window can feature a "treasure chest" of butterscotch wafers (which resemble "pieces-of-eight"), with cutout pirate figure. 

Tickets offered for best estimate of number of wafers in the window. 

Display in lobby, featuring a chest of the butterscotch "goldpieces," is in charge of a pretty girl "pirate," who hands out the wafers to patrons.

Ship models, flying pirate flags (skull and cross-bones), can be used for window displays. Ship model in a bottle might be secured. 

Selections from "Pirates of Penzance" might be featured over radio station, dedicated to the attraction. 

Kids can be invited to draw pictures or color pictures of pirate ships, with tickets or other prize for the best. Or they might be asked to write a letter about pirates, with best letter to win. Kid pirate matinee could be staged, with prizes offered for kids in best pirate get-ups.

Book stores might feature Robt. Lewis Stevenson stories and other yarns about pirates; also libraries. Perhaps pirate relics might be available for display. 

Pirate galleon might be constructed atop canopy, with pirates "walking the decks."

Float could be constructed over a truck or flat street car to resemble a pirate galleon, with group of "pirates" (mostly attractive girls) aboard. A boat, in seaport town, might be disguised to resemble pirate vessel, flying black flag and properly bannered. 

328. LANGUAGE, FOREIGN . . . An attraction that features a foreign star, or has a foreign setting suggests, naturally, an appeal to those who speak the language, nationals of that country or language students. 

Language newspapers might be used for advertisements and stories. Heralds, printed in the language, should be distributed to those who speak the language. Patriotic societies and nationality organizations might be contacted, having announcements made at meetings. Certain night may be dedicated to the nationality, members urged to attend. • 174 •

Telephone calls could use a person speaking both the foreign language, and English. Swift and brief message in the foreign language, is followed in English with, "In other words, don't miss seeing (attraction) at (theatre).”

In appealing to foreigners, someone of their own race can gain best results (he can address them in their own language, contact the officials of their organizations, arrange to sell tickets in advance). 

With a heavy foreign population, perhaps an occasional attraction in their language might be shown at a late show. With the support of their organizations, it should prove successful. 

329. SKIS... Novel street stunt can be arranged by con structing oversize "skis" over back wheels of automobile. Wheels are concealed, and car appears to be traveling around on the skis . . . while actually, wheels fit through an opening in the skis, to reach the ground. Car will attract more attention when there is no snow. 

Driver should be costumed in furs, banners carrying copy: "I skied all the way from Alaska, just to see (attraction)."

If ski-jumping is featured in a screen attraction, local ski-jumpers (if any) should be contacted. Local champ jumper might be persuaded to appear in person, perhaps interviewed over radio from theatre lobby on opening night. Stores might feature displays of skis, ski clothes and displays on attraction. 

With heavy snow, couple of girls in ski-pants, traveling along on skis, could wear signs, "We're skiing along to the (theatre) to see (attraction)." 

330. JINGLES, PERSONALTIES IN RHYTHM... Con test, for program, radio, newspaper or lobby flash, asks patrons to describe the players in a coming show in rhyme. Best jingles receiving tickets 

331. SMALL TOWNS. . . within drawing radius, might be visited, arrangements made with leading store to keep a poster or window card on display in the store. Possibly cards can be mailed each week, together with guest tickets, for merchant to place on display.

Newspapers in the smaller towns, perhaps weekly papers, will often run prepared stories or cuts sent them. Preferably scene cuts, or mats, carrying attractive girl illustrations. The type might be previously set, mats or type-high cuts made up and supplied the Letter accompanying the mats, or cuts, asks them to run same if at all possible, and invites editor to make use of the enclosed · 175 •

guest tickets. Arrangements might be made to supply a cut or story each week on the same basis. 

Operating in very small towns, exploitation of attractions naturally has definite limitations. At the same time, every potential patron in the community can be reached with much less effort and expense. 

A monthly calendar, listing the attractions on the dates they are to play, will aid in letting them know what's playing. A few window cards, strategically and regularly placed. Telephone calls. Rural routes can be reached by cards or heralds, addressed to "box holder" (if names are not available). Theatre can be made the center of the community, around which everything else revolves, with a minimum amount of effort, but with proper spirit of cooperation, in a small town.

Personal contact is of major importance in a small town . . . meeting and greeting patrons, membership in organizations, clubs. Theatre operation can, and should, be on a high standard, with a clean, neat theatre and good projection. Purchases should be made locally if prices permit. Intelligent bookings are most important. Highpowered stuff may be of little use in a small town, but the theatre operator must be a showman. 

332. IDENTIFY THE BODY . . . Photos of well-known feminine stars have head of comedian (featured in theatre's attraction) superimposed (the composite picture, giving the effect of comedian's head on the girl's body). Or if several comedians are featured, several figures might be used each day. Reproducing the composite pictures, accompanying newspaper stories say that comedian invites readers to see if they can "identify the body" (of feminine stars pictured). 

Correct answers might be carried an another page to which readers are referred; or tickets might be offered for first correct answers. 

333. MUSEUM . . . Cooperation of a museum will often make available for display purposes in lobby or window, items which might be suggested by the attraction, or which may be used for comparison in a display. Or a display panel might be placed in the museum. Or photographic reproductions of items or documents within the museum might be used to illustrate a newspaper feature. 

334. FAMOUS MEN AND WOMEN... Newspaper contest in connection with attraction that portrays a renowned character, would have contestants submit a list of five, or ten, famous (and departed) men (or women) that they would call back to life were they so empowered. And why. Art from attraction as illustration. 

An attraction dealing with life and death, or with supernatural or • 176.

reincarnation or spiritualism, is, of course, a "natural" for this contest. 

335. ENDORSEMENTS Attractions often merit and suggest the endorsement of certain groups or organizations. Endorsement could be used in publicity, or called to the attention of membership of the organization. The endorsement might be used in lobby and newspaper. Heads of organizations, or a committee might see a screening in advance of regular showing. 

Organization (women's club, possibly) might permit a letter to be sent out on their stationery and signed by them, endorsing the attraction. Sent to their mailing list, and to others who would be interested. Theatres handle printing, mailing.

Personal endorsement of manager of theatre can be used to add importance to an occasional attraction. Should definitely be a first-rate attraction that audiences are certain to like; though possibly one that also needs a little lift. Endorsement might be worded: "If I had but one more picture to see this year, it would be (name of attraction) (and sign name of manager)." Underline theatre play dates. Endorsement might be used in newspaper ads, and on lobby panels, window cards and imprinted stickers. 

336. BROADWAY... With a Times Square background, 

Broadway songs might be featured over radio and by leading orchestra, dedicated to theatre's attraction.

Perhaps, with newspaper cooperation, the main street might, for a single day, be officially renamed "Broadway," with merchants cooperating to make it a special sales day, advertising "Broadway values at Main Street prices." Mayor's official proclamation and 

Chamber of Commerce support might mark the renaming. Crossstreets might be "numbered" similar to those that cross Broadway near Times Square. 

Grand opening ceremonies in front of theatre (See 11) can be billed as "Broadway Night," and "Broadway comes to (town)." 

337. CLIMAX . . . Giving brief synopsis of an attraction, except the ending (and not giving away too much of the plot), patrons are invited, through newspaper or radio tieup, to complete the story. 

Cleverest suggestion for an ending wins. 

Illustrate for newspaper use with art from the attraction. 

Highlight or climax of an attraction, usually the ending, might be made the focal point of attention by announcing that patrons. will not be seated during that period (as, "the last five minutes"). 

Patrons might be asked, in trailer which precedes, or follows the • 177 •

feature attraction, to refrain from telling their friends about the ending of the attraction (that they might not spoil their friend's pleasure in witnessing it for himself) . . . with similar copy carried in newspaper ads. 

338. POST CARDS... Imprinted post cards often provide an economical way to get a message to the mailing list . . . or to a list of persons to which the attraction would particularly appeal. 

Post cards (provided by hotels for the use of guests) might be secured from a hotel in a distant and important city. Addressing the cards to local mailing list, and imprinting a message (writing the message, or using reproduction of handwriting), stamps are attached and cards are returned to the hotel, or to someone in the distant city, to be mailed . . . so that when they arrive locally they will bear the postmark of the other town. Message should go something like this: "Hello! Having a wonderful time! This is a swell hotel!

Just saw (attraction) and think it is marvelous. Don't miss it when it comes to (city). Regards to the gang." Sign girl's name, or, to avoid any domestic consequences, sign man's name and girl's name, as "Mary and Charles." If possible have same person writing "message" address the cards so that handwriting is identical. 

Locally made post cards could carry message (in longhand, written or imprinted), "Dear . . . Am in (town) and want you to be sure and 

Will be here until (day). See me at (theatre) (sign name of girl star; or attraction title, if it is girl's name)." Ad on attraction carried on reverse side. see me. 

339. DAIRIES... Cooperation of Dairies, or Dairy Council 

(organization of local dairies) could result in their using photograph of star of coming attraction in their newspaper ads, emphasizing that motion picture stars must be hardy, healthy . . . and that the healthiest of foods is milk, etc.

Caps placed atop milk bottles might be imprinted, using attraction copy, or cut of star of an attraction. Those of a certain color (posted at theatre) would win guest tickets (the number of the lucky color being limited). Or numbered, they might check a list of numbers.

Cards, placed about the necks of bottles of milk by dairies, can carry copy on theatre's attraction, with dairy tiein line at top. 

Milk or dairy angle in a story will receive support of local dairies, with banners being placed on their trucks and wagons, and perhaps a parade of bannered wagons. Perhaps a "cow milking contest" might be staged, in a public place, or on stage. . . with pretty • 178 •

milk-maids performing. Milk drinks could be featured by fountains. 

Milk wagon, bannered, with a group of pretty girls as "milk-men" could tour business section, handing out heralds on the attraction. 

Tieup with dairy might be worked out where local sculptor (check with art school) models figures or scenes as suggested by a coming attraction from butter. He works in a refrigerated room, and the figures are displayed in advance in theatre's lobby in refrigerated show cases. Dairy pays the "sculptor" since it's a great ad for them, but it's also an excellent ad for the coming attraction. 

340. PENNIES... Cards for distribution, printed with two die-cut slits at top, so that pennies can be attached to the cards (or pennies might be pasted to the cards), carry copy: "May we offer you this penny for a moment of your time, to call your attention to (attraction)." Or, "Here's your start toward your first million and for a million laughs see (attraction).” 

341. BRIDGE, CARDS, GAMBLING 

If cards or gambling is prominent in theme or title, cards (actual playing cards or enlarged replicas of same) might be used prominently in lobby and front displays.

Novel herald is printed in shape and size of a playing card, with ace, diamond, club, heart, in correct colors, printed in the four corners. Copy imprinted in center: "Aces in Entertainment (and into copy on attraction).” Or, cards made up to resemble ace of hearts, might feature a drawing of star of attraction, with attraction title carried. 

Good looking girl stationed at certain (specified) times in front of box office, invites patrons to draw a card. If they draw an ace (or card suggested by attraction), they also draw a gratis admission. 

Or card manipulator might be secured; and after running through several manipulations, he invites those whose attention has been attracted to draw a card, or distributes them. Substituting "decks," each card distributed carries an imprint on theatre's attraction. 

Letters can be sent bridge clubs, if playing of bridge is featured in the attraction. Guest tickets supplied as prizes will assure mention.

A Bridge Tournament might be arranged for mezzanine floor or lobby, if space permits, and if local enthusiasm is sufficiently high. 

Small table, equipped with a deck of cards, might be made part of a lobby display . . . with patrons invited to play a game of solitaire, with guest tickets as a prize if they "win."

Gambling equipment might be possibly borrowed for display from police department. · • 179.

Cardboard could be die-cut in shape of poker chips, and imprinted, for distribution. 

342. CURVES. . . Highway curves are generally strategic spots for display panels, or cards, affording "head-on" location for the display.

In connection with girl show or musical, cards might be imprinted: "Curves Ahead," or "Dangerous Curves Ahead". . . and then, in smaller type, carrying copy on the attraction. Cards, larger size, are tacked along highways, along streets (following street car and bus routes and main traffic arteries). 

343. INTELLIGENCE TEST... Using scenes from attrac tion, newspaper reproduces one each day, asking readers to gaze intently at the illustration for two minutes, then to turn to another specified page, where a list of ten or more questions is based on the illustration... asking questions about the illustration, and position of persons and articles. Checks powers of observation. 

No prizes are required as the stunt is purely an interesting newspaper feature. Accompanying stories point out that the scenes are from theatre's attraction.

Idea might be adapted to heralds, printing scene, together with attraction copy on one side of the herald, then printing list of questions on the reverse side. 

344. CIRCUS GROUNDS... where thousands are attracted, should be bannered, or heralds distributed. Contact circus publicity representative with the show. Frequently they will permit banners to be placed in the menagerie (perhaps theatre might screen a picture for the circus people, if time permits). 

Banners on elephants for parade and showing in big top can generally be purchased. ... 

345. TRAILERS PREMIER Patrons might be invited to come early on a designated matinee (through screen announcements, or ads), and "to witness a special preview of scenes from coming attractions." With coffee (or tea), and cakes (promoted) being served, while the patrons witness the scenes from coming shows.

Following the showing of a series of trailers on coming attraction, connected one after the other, and minus date strips, the regular matinee showing of the regular program is begun. 

346. STILL POST CARD... Using a still from attraction, artist draws in a conversation "balloon" (as used in comic strips), and in tieup with store or business place, character in the illustration • 180 •

is made to mention the values or special items at the cooperating store. 

Engraving is made of the still, post card size, and printed on cards, which the store sends out to the mailing list. Side panels, also the work of the artist, carry copy on theatre's attraction. Merchant shares cost of card and mailing, since it gives him a novel ad. 

347. COMMITTEE . . . A group of club members, or members of women's clubs, might be organized to "sponsor" the showing of an outstanding attraction. Invited to a "tea," or luncheon, the attraction is discussed, and their support solicited. 

Or, a luncheon club might be asked to lend their names to the committee "sponsoring" the appearance of the attraction in (town). 

Aside from actual talk about the attraction that formation of a "committee" will create, society page and other newspaper mention. should naturally follow. Names of the members of the committee could be used on special letterhead on which a letter is sent to the mailing list calling attention to the attraction.

Perhaps the attraction will appeal to certain people, or to certain groups, who would be glad to have their names used in connection with it. Names of "sponsors" would be carried on letters in connection with an important motion picture, or an opera, or an outstanding stage attraction. 

348. TOPSY-TURVY... Comedy attraction might suggest novel window or lobby display that features table attached, sideways, by the legs to an upright panel, with dishes, usual table equipment, and perhaps some "prop" "food" attached in correct place "on" the table. Since table is at angle, everything must be attached tightly, so that it doesn't fall off. Panel carries copy: "This table is reserved for (star). It ought to please him, as everything is topsyturvy and crazy in (attraction)." Other crazy touches might be added if used for window display. . . as false teeth in a gold-fish bowl, "flowers" "growing" out of an upside-down and opened umbrella, 

... man appear- "Upside down Man" can be used for street bally . . ing to be walking on his hands. He merely reverses costume, painting shoes to resemble hands, placing his feet through the sleeves of a coat, with an attached dummy head held in place, and with trousers on over his head; wood braces (held on man's shoulders) hold the trouser "legs" upright, with shoes attached to upper end of each extension. Copy on his "back" might read: "Everything's Topsy 

Turvy in (attraction)."

Block of type, set upside-down at top of a newspaper ad could • 181 •

carry copy, "The Whole Town's Topsy-turvy . . . just like this type. over this hit!" 

349. SUMMONS... Foldover herald printed up after style of a regular court summons, carries copy: "Summons (in script type)." Inside imprint: "You are hereby summoned to attend (theatre) to witness (attraction and cast)." Star's name can be "signed." Sticker "seals" might be secured cheaply in quantity from a stationer, and attached to the front page of the herald. 

Traffic Violations type "summons" might be made up after style of a regular summons, and attached to windshields of parked cars. 

Okay of police department should be secured, and copy in support of police safety-drive can be included. 

350. $500 A SEAT ... Novel stunt that will create much talk and break newspapers for stories. First move is ad in newspapers headed: "$500.00 a Seat". . . and, then, in smaller type, asking if there is anyone in town willing to spend five hundred dollars for an evening's entertainment . . . with the money to go to a very commendable charity (which is specified). 

Ad further advises that, for the specified amount, the theatre will present a private preview of the attraction, for the exclusive delectation of any individual who would be humored by an advance showing in solitude . . . adding that only one person (who might bring one guest) would be thus accommodated, and for but a single performance. 

Conclude with copy: "$500.00 for one seat... and (picture) is yours .. (and copy on picture)."

Amount might be changed to $100.00 if $500.00 is out of the question, or $1000.00 if there is possibility that someone might go for a donation of that amount to community fund or to some charity. 

If some drive for funds, community fund, etc., is current, the ad might be tied in to the drive, with the private showing to go to first person making a donation of the required amount. 

If a taker is found, newspaper should use picture of him sitting in the theatre looking at picture, surrounded by empty seats. 

Newspaper could sponsor the stunt in connection with one of their pet funds, in which event it would be assured plenty of newspaper space. 

351. PROBLEM... Contest for newspaper or radio might ask contestants to tell what they would do if confronted by problem which character in story faces. Featuring "What would you do” angle, contest for newspaper use would be illustrated with scenes from the attraction. • 182 •

352. FORESTRY .. Attraction with forest or backwoods background might suggest newspaper contest based on identification of leaves of trees and plants; or of tracks of wild animals. 

Window or lobby display might be arranged with boys scout or forestry department aid . . . and including display material on attraction. Authority on forestry, or boy scouts with forestry training, could appear in theatre lobby opening evening, being interviewed over radio and for benefit of patrons. 

353. CHAIN LETTERS . Periodically popular, the 

"chain letter" might be made the basis of a herald, listing names of stars of attraction in chain letter style, and carrying the message: "Take (amount) to (theatre) box office . . . ask for a ticket to see (attraction). You'll be so delighted you'll want to Tell Ten of your friends... and when they see it, they won't break the Chain"

Devote rest of space (most of it) to attraction. 

354. MODEL AIRPLANES AND BOATS... In connection with aviation attraction, model plane building contest might be sponsored in newspaper tieup. (Or perhaps newspaper or Y.M.C.A. already sponsors a model airplane club.) Club might be called "Junior Flyers" or similar title. Prizes (including tickets) for best model constructed. 

Arrange model flying contest in park, or auditorium, offering trophy (named after attraction or star) for model that remains in the air the longest or the one that flies furtherest. Models constructed might be used further for window display, building miniature airport using grass-mat, sanding off "runways," building miniature hangar . . . probably circling entire display with miniature electric train. Name of attraction in cutout letters, placed in foreground on the grass-mat or suspended in the background. Miniature banners on sides of the electric train. Model planes suspended in air (using black thread). . . some of them on the "ground." Concealed electric fan can turn the propellers on the planes. Perhaps model dirigible and mooring post can be secured and added to the display. Miniature revolving light can be arranged, after style of airport beacon.

Models or photos of famous planes might be secured for window display. 

Paper airplane models might be secured and imprinted to give away to kids.

Boat model contest may be similarly arranged in connection with an aquatic story. • 183.

355. LETTERED SUITCASE... Affording an opportunity to get attraction title into a street stunt, a lettered suitcase can be advantageously used in connection with many street ballys. 

Girls promenading in costume suggested by the attraction might carry a small suitcase on which the attraction title has been lettered ... or tieup copy that includes the title. 

A couple might be dressed as "rubes" and wandering about town, carrying battered suitcase which has been lettered: "We're on Our 

Way to See (attraction) at (theatre).” 

Suitcase can have translucent sides (paper or glass) with attraction copy lettered on inside, and in reverse. Lights inside suitcase arranged to flash on when person carrying the suitcase presses button making the lettering visible, then, through the panels in the sides. 

Or the suitcase might periodically open (on prominent corners), spilling clothing (including lingerie), and revealing the attraction title lettered on inside of cover. Repacking suitcase, on to another spot where the stunt is repeated. 

356. LAUGHING GAS.. Lobby or window features, as center of a display, an oxygen tank. Panel carries the copy: "If you want to laugh steadily for an hour and a half. . . you can take this Laughing Gas... or see (attraction)." ... 

357. MR. GLOOM .. A tall thin man is dressed in funereal style . . . and traveling about downtown section, he carries copy on his back: "I Refuse to Laugh . . . So I'm not going to see (attraction).” Or, “I don't want to be Happy, so I won't see (attraction)." Copy might be lettered on a suitcase, or umbrella, which he carries. If it is sure that he will not laugh too often, guest tickets might be offered to those who make him laugh.

Man, made up as the personification of Old Man Gloom (long whitened face, high silk hat, frock coat, unbrella, tight, high pants), might "picket" the theatre... carrying a sign that says: (“Attraction) is Unfair to Gloom. Go in and see for yourself. It'll make you laugh right out loud." Sign can be signed "Society for Prevention of Laughter and Banishment of Happiness." 

Old Man Gloom's appearance can be built into a big affair, with the cooperation of a newspaper and a friendly luncheon club. "Old 

Man Gloom" appears around town, in old open car, until on day of opening of theatre's attraction (which should be a comedy) when Old Man Gloom's funeral is celebrated . . . with brass band leading the procession. Dummy, dressed as Mr. Gloom, might be dumped into the river as feature of the "ceremony." • 184 •

358. TICKET STUB PAYMENT . . . Affording a graceful method for a merchant to make a temporary reduction in price on some article, the store can accept theatre ticket stubs as part payment on a specified article. Can be limited to a certain attraction and should be given ad space. Can be the amount of theatre admission, indicating that patrons can thus see show as store's guests. 

359. ESCAPE... Occasionally the services of a stunt man are available an "escape artist" who specializes in escaping from a strait-jacket, or other "escape." Making an "escape" (at an announced time and in a public and prominent location), he displays banner: "I had to escape. . . I want to see (attraction) at (theatre) tonight." If strait-jacket artist is suspended in air (and not too high) for his escape (and the stunt should be covered by insurance), fire department might permit use of one of their hook and ladder wagons, with the ladder raised . . . (and stationed near theatre). ...

Magic shows often feature escape artists. And perhaps some local talent might specialize, as a hobby, in (safe) escapes. 

Handcuffs could be featured as center of a lobby display, in connection with an appropriate attraction, with tickets offered anyone who can escape from the handcuffs. 

360. TOWN CRIER . . . Man costumed after fashion of oldtime "town crier" might travel about downtown streets. Stopping on corners, he rings bell, then delivers spiel about attraction beginning with: "Hear Ye, Hear Ye." Small portable amplification outfit could be secured or made up, working from batteries (and which might be built into a cheap suitcase), which he carries about with him, for his announcements. Or he might be sufficiently loud voiced, or use a megaphone. 

361. AGITATION... Well in advance of the first announcement of an attraction, perhaps some "movement," or agitation can be promoted, along lines suggested by attraction. A "committee” might be formed (with theatre in no way connected) which agitates for safe driving . . . with theatre following with ads on an attraction which deals with the subject in title or theme. Or agitation for suppression of unnecessary noise (honking of horns, etc.), might be promoted in advance of an attraction that features noise in title or importantly in theme. 

362. FEATHERS 

Imprinted cards for distribution have feathers attached and carry copy: "If you think this feather can tickle you, wait till you see (attraction).” • 185.

Large feathers might be distributed to those leaving theatre.. tag attached to feathers carrying copy: "It's a Feather in Our Hat ... and we're proud to announce that we're bringing you (attraction).” 

Or imprinting might be placed directly on the feathers. Staff might wear them, also newsboys, cab drivers, others. 

363. AMBULANCE . . . In connection with a comedy attraction, ambulance can be parked in front of theatre, bannered: "Just in case a (theatre) patron laughs himself sick at (picture)." 

Or, ambulance arrives at theatre, with screaming siren, and backs up to entrance. Uniformed attendants take stretcher into theatre. 

Presently they come out, carrying man on stretcher who is laughing hysterically and sheet partly covering him carries lettering on both sides: "He laughed himself sick at (attraction)." Or copy can be lettered on shades in ambulance (on both sides) which are pulled down as ambulance pulls away. Stunt repeated at intervals. ... 

364. BLOW ON THE SPOT. . . Card for distribution, carries copy, imprinted in blue: "Blow on the Spot." Then, imprinted in red, is a circular imprint (or in some shape suggested by the attraction). Then, copy in blue: "If the spot stays red, you are in perfect enough physical condition to withstand the terrific laughs (or thrills) in (attraction)." Most of card space is devoted to the attraction. 365. FISHING Where crowds are attracted to river front, or dock, or pier . . . man (or girl), in costume, with fish-pole and line, is apparently fishing. At regular intervals the pole is lifted, pulling into view a three-cornered display at the end of the line, on which copy (on attraction) is lettered (in oil). Bottom of display is open, so that water will spill out; and weighted, so that it will remain upright and sink readily. Use strong line, or rope, and short stout pole.

Adapting to a laugh-attraction, as a window stunt, a boy, or attractively costumed girl, wearing a dunce-cap, is seated on a high stool, "fishing" in a pail, or barrel, of water (not necessarily filled with water, if water is not visible). Display card in window carries copy: "Silly as Simple Simon, and nine times as funny as he ever was .. Three-sided panel attached to end of line is pulled into view when the pole is lifted. Carries name of star and attraction. 

Pole is lifted periodically whenever attention is attracted. 99 When fishing is featured in an attraction, displays should be arranged in windows of stores selling fishing equipment. Members of Isaac Walton Society and others interested in fishing should be • 186.

contacted. Mounted fish might be borrowed for display in lobby or window. An authority on fishing might make a radio talk including mention of theatre's attraction (perhaps speaking just after witnessing the show). 

366. PRESIDENTS . . . Attraction with historical back ground might feature use of newspaper cooperative page which carries a cut of a President in each merchant's ad (ads might be small, double-truck might be used, and all the Presidents might be carried). 

Guest tickets to see attraction are offered to first so-many lists of correctly identified Presidents received. A second printing of the cooperative page on the opening day of the attraction carries the names under the photographs of the President. Present President featured center, and larger than the others. 

Or a contest might be based on the question: "What would you do if you were President?" 

367. PROPHECY . . . Harry Reichenbach, on the occasion of a championship match, distributed a herald which stated that one of the boxers would surely win (this in large type), because the other boxer had seen a certain comedy, and laughed himself weak. 

The idea might be adapted to any kind of combat or competition, armies or individuals, or teams, playing along with public sympathy in selection of the "winner." 

368. TWO FACED GUY... For a comedy attraction, a tall fellow walks about downtown section, laughing and smiling . . . with card on his front carrying the copy: "I'm laughing because I just saw (attraction)." Mask (can be made from papier mache) on the back of his head shows a frowning face, and card on back carries the words: "I Didn't," "Or I'm frowning because I didn't see (attraction)." 

369. SNAKE CHARMER... Dressed as a burlesque Hindu, street bally man stops on prominent corners, squats on sidewalk before a wicker basket, and proceeds to blow in snake-charmer fashion, off-key, on a flute. Inside the basket he has a ten cent store "snake" (imitation, toy)... attached to one of his fingers is a black thread, the other end being attached to the "snake;" and passing his hand over the basket, he slowly lifts his hand, lifting the "snake" too-making it appear at first glance to be rising out of the basket. Small easel panel, which the "charmer" carries along and which he places beside him on the sidewalk, carries copy: "For Sale . . . One Snake. This 

Charming Gentleman is going out of the Snake Charming Business . . . and Wishes to sell his Snake to obtain money to buy a ticket to ... • 187 •

see (attraction) at (theatre)." Or copy can be lettered on a small banner which a stooge holds, as the "charmer" performs. 

Or an attractive girl "charmer" might be seated as the center of lobby display, weaving her spell over the "snake". . . incense burning nearby . . . panel carrying copy: "This little charmer really doesn't belong in this display... but she wants to call your attention to the hundred lovely charmers in (musical attraction that features a bevy of girls)." Or other copy. If the panel behind the "charmer" is black plush, the thread will not show.

And, the stunt might be used, minus clowning, for lobby or window, in connection with a story with India setting. 

370. BUTTONS... In connection with a comedy attraction, arrangements might be made to station a tailor or seamstress in the lobby... "to sew on buttons laughed off." Ads advise that tailor will be on hand. Tailor, or girl, appears in lobby, sewing prop buttons on garments . . . display panels carrying explanatory copy. 

Gag might be adapted to a herald, attaching buttons to imprinted cards. Card carrying copy that button is to replace any that might be laughed off while witnessing (attraction). 

Jar or basket of buttons might be made the center of a window display, with copy representing them as having been laughed off by those witnessing the show. Guest tickets could be offered to those estimating most nearly correctly the number of buttons in the jar. 

371. STREET... Where "street" appears in title or is important to story, arrangements might be made to have the Main Street or square of town officially renamed (as suggested by attraction) for a day. Mayor's proclamation might be secured, and perhaps newspapers will carry stories on the stunt. Photo of girls putting up new name sign on the street ought to be good for newspaper art.

Or, lettered arrows might be placed about town, with the "street" copy predominating. Arrows, die-cut from cardboard and imprinted, should "aim" in direction of theatre.

Theatre aisles could be "named" (in advance) after the most important or famous streets in the section indicated. (Where an attraction is set in New York City, the aisles might be placarded as "42nd Street, Broadway, Seventh Avenue, Fifth Avenue," etc. . . . with line on attraction under the street name.) Cooperating department store might similarly name the aisles in the store, with cards carrying attraction title and theatre copy. • 188.

372. POLES... Light poles or other poles (trolley supports, etc.) can occasionally be used for a good card flash, authorities permitting. Using two cards to a pole, fastened together at edges with spreader-type paper clip, the cards are made to encircle pole; or string or wire might be used to attach them against the pole. 

Or printed or lettered "shields" might be used. Or cloth pennants.

Or small cards might be attached to the poles by means of gummed paper.

Rarely permissible, but sometimes possible, a four-sided panel might be built about prominently located lamp posts, closing in base of posts. Theatre advertising is then posted or lettered on the panels. Paneling might be so constructed that cards could be slipped into constructed frames. 

Replica of lamp post (six or seven feet high) might be constructed, with man (who can clown the stunt, imitating a drunk) carrying the "lamp post" about town at night, placing it on corner, apparently leaning against it. Comedy cop might "chase him," working with him for laughs. Illumination within the "lamp" is arranged by means of batteries, and man switches lights on, which light up the "lamp," also illuminating (from within) cutout letters (covered over with colored paper) which spell out name of attraction. Doorbell might be attached, which he rings. 

373. CLASSIFIED PAGE... Classified 

Classified pages of newspapers are widely read . . . and classified page contests react to the advantage of both the newspaper and the theatre. . . building reader interest for the newspaper, winning valuable space for theatre attraction. 

Generally space for the contest is allotted at the top of the classified page . . . part of the space advising just how tickets might be won, but most of the space devoted to display on theatre attraction. 

Details and explanation can be listed under some certain classified page classification, referred to in display space. 

Prizes (generally tickets) go to first so-many correct entries received at newspaper office, or to entries adjudged best. 

If contest carries over a number of days, yesterday's winners might be listed each day on the classified page, so that they might call for tickets at newspaper office.

Some classified page contest angles include .. “Questions". . . Ten questions, asked about and referring to ten different classified ads which are carried the same day (as, "Who has a horse for sale?") . . and readers being invited to locate correct • 189 ·

answers. It is obviously necessary for contestant to read through the classified ads. "Most Valuable Ad" or "Best Ad" . . . with offer of tickets for best letters explaining why certain ad of same day is most valuable. 

Limit letters to 50 words. Contestants naturally required to read all ads (important to paper). "Name in Classified". . . adapting No. 325 to a classified page contest. "Laugh ad" (or "Scrambled ads," or "Chuckle ads," or "Jumbled ads") . . . Contestants to attempt to make up most amusing 4-line jumbled ad-taking one complete line from each of any four ads on the page, combining the lines for humorous results. "Ad Romances" . . . Contestants to make up story, combining complete lines found in classified ads of same day. "Synopsis Gag"... Brief synopsis of story (not giving away the plot) is prepared and lines planted throughout the classified page. Contestants to assemble the lines in proper sequence. Added requirement might be that contestants, after assembling the lines, copy them in their own handwriting . . . offering additional prize for most interesting handwriting. "Limerick Contest". . . Four (or two) lines of a limerick made up and included in contest copy on classified page . . contestants to add another line taken from one of the ads on the page, or concealed among them. "List Productions"... Scattering titles of pictures in which star has appeared throughout the ads on the page. Contestants to assemble them in correct sequence, perhaps state names of other actors appearing in each. "What a Classified ad did for Me" . . . "Success story" based on results obtained from classified ads, winning letters reproduced daily. 

Or ad selected by judges and reproduced. "Missing Words" . . . Dialogue from attraction, or sentence pertaining to attraction, carried in space allotted theatre ... with some words left out and dashes inserted for each word omitted . . . and the words scattered through the classified ads. Contestants to locate the words and place them in their proper place in the ad. "Telegram"... Contestants to take lines from ads, make them up in telegram style for humorous effect. Tickets for funniest. Might call 'em "Laughograms." "Treasure Hunt" . . . "Hiding" words of a brief sentence about the attraction by scattering the words through the classified ads. • 190 ·

ENCYCLOPEDIA EXPLOITATION 

O F "dig out" the words, Prizes to first correct

Copy in space allotted at top of page ties in line, "Dig for Treasure among the Classified Ads." Contestants to reconstruct them into their correct sequence. entries each day. "Dialogue Lines" scene at top of page probably with "balloons," or space for copy or "dialogue" cut into the picture. . with contestants invited to select dialogue, or conversation for each person in picture, from among the lines in the classified ads, trying to achieve an humorous effect. "Facts About Stars"... scattering items about stars throughout classified ads. With contestants to correctly assemble them, identify stars.

Guest tickets might be presented to every person placing a “houseto-rent" ad on certain day. Or a "swap" ad. Or other classification that paper might be interested in building up. Paper allotting enough space to theatre attraction to justify, on other page then classified page. Paper might offer theatre tickets to finders of lost articles advertised in the classifieds . . . according theatre a news story occasionally, and space on the classified page. 

Or guest tickets might go to persons placing classified ads to run three consecutive days. With paper assigning theatre display space to equal value of ticket cooperation. 

374. SECRET THOUGHTS... Newspaper contest carries scene from attraction; and copy: "He says (and then a dialogue line from the attraction." Next line reads: "What he really thinks:" (and leave space for contestants to write in their ideas of "what he really thinks"). The same for her reply, reproducing the actual reply, leaving space for contestants' suggestions for her actual thoughts. 

375. ARM IN SLING... Several boys (or attractively costumed girls), walking abreast through downtown sections, all have arm in sling (each the same arm). Copy on their backs, or on the sling, reads: "We fell out of our seats laughing at (attraction) at (theatre)." 

Sling should be over-sized and very obvious. Instead of wearing signs, they might hand out cards that carry the copy. 

376. VISITING CARDS... Small cards, imprinted after style of regular visiting cards, with name of star of theatre's attraction, are used for distribution house-to-house. Corner of cards are imprinted, in script: "Called while you were out . . . see me tonight at (theatre)." Similar card might be placed on parked automobiles, • 191 •
