imprinting: "Recognized your car while passing. See me tonight at (theatre)." 

377. SUPERSTITIONS ... Novel broadcast from front of theatre (especially effective on a Friday, 13th), might have announcer asking those who stop, to break mirrors (small mirrors purchased in quantity), to walk under a step-ladder, and to break other well known superstitions (and including attraction mention). Newspaper might use art of pretty girl (perhaps from stage show) breaking one of the rules, or holding black cat. 

Newspaper might picture stars of coming attraction, listing their "pet superstitions," and asking newspaper readers to submit theirs, with guest tickets for most interesting ones. 

378. RAFFLES STUNT . . . In tieup with newspaper the public is invited to attempt to identify a person on streets of city, who is to represent star of the attraction, or character in the story, or the attraction title. Prizes, or guest tickets are offered, with compliments of newspaper and theatre, to first person identifying him. 

No makeup or costuming of any kind is used by person impersonating the character. Those attempting to identify "Raffles" (substitute name of attraction character) must have a copy of newspaper in their hand and tapping him on the shoulder with newspaper say: "You are (name)." (Or girl might be used, instead of a man, as suggested by the attraction.)

Newspaper carries daily photos of "Raffles," with the eyes masked. 

Making it clear, however, that on the street he will not be masked he might even be someone that they know, their neighbor or their best friend. He might even be the newsboy on the corner who sells them the newspapers with which to tag Raffles (a good selection). 

To make identification more difficult, have "Raffles" character also carrying a newspaper, as though he too were looking for the elusive Mr. "Raffles."

Stores might buy cooperating newspaper ads, announcing that he will appear in their stores at specified times, or between certain hours. "Raffles" could be one of their clerks. Store might sponsor the stunt. "Raffles" could be paraded thru streets, masked, (if a girl, wearing a wig, too), in a bannered automobile. "Raffles" might not actually put in an appearance for identification until final day. 

If "Raffles" is not identified by opening day of attraction, announce that he will stand in front of theatre (opening day) at (opening time) · • 192.

until identified (the crowd attracted making it difficult to identify him). Might increase prize each day, until identified. 

"Raffles" search might be adapted to a telephone or direct mail campaign . . . suggesting (in tieup with paper, or radio station) that they phone any friends whom they suspect might be the mysterious person (emphasizing that the "Raffles" is well known, that he may be one of their friends), or send a postcard, delivering message: "You are (name), who is being sought in connection with (attraction) and (theatre)." Assures much telephone and postcard mention. 

379 VENDORS. . . Who sell ice cream or candy or other items along the line of march of a parade, or at a ball park, or where crowds have gathered and vendors are working . . . might carry imprinted cards attached to containers in which they carry their merchandise. 

380. FALSE TEETH... In connection with comedy attrac tion, false teeth placed on display under glass, in lobby. . . or in store window... with card saying that the teeth were "laughed out" and lost while the owner was witnessing (attraction). 

Large classified newspaper ad carrying similar copy might be placed in papers, and newspaper might go for a story. ... 

381. NIGHT GAMES Baseball or football at night . . . 

where such games are inevitable . . . might be capitalized on to some extent, by arranging for special bannered bus or street car transportation to theatre after game, for last show, or midnight performance. 

Imprinted cards placed in all parked cars whose owners are watching the game. Announcements made at the game. ... 

382. TOY BALLOONS . . . Inflated small balloons might be used as center of lobby or window display with space enclosed by ribbons. Cutout life-size figures could be placed in the enclosed space or window with them. Electric fans (concealed) keep the balloons moving about, attracting attention. Tickets can be offered those guessing nearest correct number of balloons.

Appealing to kids, a shower of balloons can be dropped from theatre roof at a specified time, on opening day, perhaps with cooperation of newspaper or of business place. Street should be kept clear of traffic for the several minutes that it requires to drop the balloons. Tickets attached to a number of the balloons.

As highlight of a grand opening, girl might clip string releasing dozens of imprinted gas-filled balloons, to some of which tickets have been attached. Prize offered for balloon found longest distance from theatre. 193.

Small balloons, imprinted, make excellent gifts for kids, and an excellent ad in appealing to them. Can be distributed at carnivals, fairs, and wherever crowds are gathered. 

Gas-filled balloons might carry a light banner over football game, or place where crowds are gathered. Light piece of wire holds banner straight. Direction of wind must be noted. 

Gas-filled balloons, attached in bunches to top of marquee add a festive appearance to front of theatre. Comic faces might be painted on balloons. Perhaps made to resemble a comedy star. 

383. RECORDINGS . . . Exploitation records, that carry song hits or a brief enacted highlight, and announcements, can be used to good advantage for radio broadcasting, for sound trucks, for lobby, front displays. 

Labels typed with song title, name of theatre's attraction which features it, and play dates of attraction should be pasted over titles on recordings sent radio stations, and assuring a better chance for announcements 

Recordings can be played for intermission music, or "break" music at end of show. Arrange to have the record played at a luncheon club; or over a cooperating broadcasting station, with playing dedicated to luncheon club (radio at luncheon tuned in). 

Special sound effect records can occasionally be used in connection with a front or a lobby display, as an airplane effect record; or a tap-dance; or a laugh record. Effect records can generally be secured from a radio broadcasting station. . . where they might also be used to back up special announcements. They can be used through amplification to front of theatre. 

Special recordings of song hits or announcements in connection with a coming attraction, might be delivered to newspaper critics; carefully and attractively wrapped, with title on the record covered over with a special sticker on which critic's name has been lettered. 

Miniature recordings, specially prepared, can carry brief message about attraction. They are attached to imprinted card, or inserted in envelope. Music store includes them with all record purchases. 

Where star of a coming attraction has made a number of recordings, radio station might feature a complete program of his recordings, with announcement of attraction. 

384. BENEFIT TICKET SELLING ANGLES .. Arrange ments might be worked out with organization to sell script books (books of tickets), or tickets for a specified attraction, and with a percentage of the gross sales to go to the organization. (Organiza- • 194 •

tions' percentage is based on the number of tickets that they sell, and scaling from 20% to 33%.)

Organization is to sell tickets in advance, and to settle in full before the opening of the attraction, so that their selling campaign will not conflict with box office sales.

Benefit tieups should never be set in connection with an outstanding attraction; arranged, instead, on good pictures that need a little help at the box office.

Benefits might be set with Fraternal organizations, Church organizations, Veterans' organizations; Luncheon clubs and Women's clubs (for benefit of charities); Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts; Patriotic organizations; Junior League; Sororities and Fraternities; Old 

Folks' Home (with the sponsoring organization selling the tickets); 

Fire and Police Fraternal organizations; Newspaper Milk Fund (or other sponsored charity); Stores (employee organizations);

Union organizations. 

Cooperating organizations can have members canvass house-tohouse and store-to-store. Popularity contest would have girl selling most tickets as the winner. Punch boards may be used by organizations. Or they can assess each member a certain amount for the tickets. Organization might set up ticket box on street corner. 

Schools could sell them for band or football uniforms. Aiding "committee" might be rewarded later with a special screening and a dinner. 

385. LIP READER . . . Attractive girl, in prominently located window, panel carrying copy to the effect that she is repeating wisecracks from the attraction (or names of featured players), and inviting those watching to see if they can read her lips. 

386. MERRY-GO-ROUND... "Horse" (from an amuse ment park carousel) might be used for lobby or window, carrying copy: "I'm tired of going round and round on the merry-go-round ... I'm going straight... to (theatre) to see (attraction) when it comes to town."

Amusement park might let one of the carousel horses in use carry the copy. ... 

387. GUMMED WRAPPING TAPE . . . Many stores use gummed paper tape in wrapping packages. Working far enough in advance the gummed paper can be secured from manufacturer with imprint on theatre's coming attraction carried... and business places using it in wrapping packages (definitely set before tape is ordered). • 195.

388. THRILLERS 

stories, might include: 

Shock stunts for shockers and thrill "Warning," in newspaper ads and panels out front of theatre, to those with weak hearts, as: "Warning. Not for the young, the scarey, the nervous. . . but if you enjoy thrills, chills, and spinetingling sensation, while your hair stands on end, see (attraction).” 

Radio or newspaper contest can be based on question: "What was your greatest thrill?" Or: "What was your most shocking (or surprising) experience?"

Newspaper ad might announce "Nurses in Attendance." From hospital (uniformed); or, couple of girls in nurse outfits. 

First aid equipment ("for those who can't stand the shock”) can be placed on display in a spotlighted showcase in lobby week in advance. 

Local ambulance company might station an ambulance in front of theatre. It can be bannered, calling attention to fact that it is stationed there for benefit of those unable to withstand the thrills in (attraction).

Or ambulance, without banners, can pull up in front of theatre several times daily, siren screaming. Attendants alight hurriedly, enter theatre with stretcher, carrying out and into ambulance a woman who has "fainted," upon witnessing thrill highlight of attraction.

Scream, at thrill highlight, might be effective without the ambulance follow-up, girl "planted" in audience producing the scream. 

Arrangements might be made to take out "Fright Insurance," insurance company issuing blanket policy (for the publicity), insuring the theatre (with consequent newspaper stories) against any patron being frightened or shocked to death.

Ushers might wear skeleton costumes, if attraction suggests. 

Actual skeletons and skulls may be used if adaptable to attraction (guarded or attached so that they will not be lifted). 

A display in lobby (or in window) in advance of showing, might feature candles, "for those who will be afraid to go home in the dark after witnessing (attraction)." Miniature candles might be distributed as heralds, with small attached tags carrying "afraid to go home" copy. Large candles can be sent newspaper critics, with attached card carrying "afraid to go home" message. 

Cash prize might be offered first woman to apply who is willing to • 196 •

watch screening of coming thrill picture alone at midnight, with no one else in the theatre, all lights out. 

A "guard," a big, tough-looking fellow, can be stationed in lobby, in advance of showing, armed with a rifle, pistols, a sword and a baseball bat. Panel carries copy offering him as an escort for timid patrons who are afraid to go home after witnessing the show. 

Hair dye, for "those whose hair turns white," smelling salts and nerve tonic might be used in lobby and windows.

Green floodlights, illuminating theatre front with ghastly glow will aid in lending the correct weird atmosphere. "Thrill-chart" might be used as front display . . . with chart background divided into squares, and graph running in jagged lines upward, through words "Thrills," "Chills," "Panic," "Shock," "Fear," "Amazement," "Terror." Stills added. 

Series of "warning" teaser ads might be used in newspaper, or over radio, when attraction title suggests same as: "Warning! (Title) is coming to (city)". . . following with announcements. Heralds could be made up as "Faint Checks," entitling holder "to return again to see the attraction in event he or she faints when witnessing it." (See No. 55.) 

389. INVISIBLE GOLDFISH... Goldfish bowl is filled with water (and no fish). Oscillating electric fan is arranged behind display panel back of the bowl and out of sight, so that it will periodically cause a slight ripple on the surface of the water, creating an illusion of movement in the water. (See photos.) 

Panel carries copy: "(Star's) Invisible Goldfish," and copy on attraction, and asks on-lookers to guess how many fish in the bowl. 

At "Feeding Time," announced on small card, small amount of granulated sugar or salt is sprinkled into the water. 

Or, with a goldfish in bowl, card can carry copy: "This poor fish isn't going to see (attraction)." 

390. SEASON PASS... Cards same size as season passes, are imprinted (in very small type). "Don't let the (and then in large type) SEASON PASS (then back to smaller type) without seeing (attraction) at (large type) (theatre).” 

Sign with name of the star of attraction, using script style type, or with name of manager of theatre. Only words that will stand out will be "Season Pass" and name of theatre . . . rest of type being smallest possible. 

391. WARNING... Small cards for distribution (in offices, stores, and downtown business places) carry copy (in large type): • 197 •

"Warning!... (and then in slightly small type), "Don't go home tonight!"... (and then in very small upper and lower type), "Until you've seen (attraction copy).”

Small folder might be imprinted: "Warning! Your turn is coming!" Inside fold of herald carries copy: "Your turn is coming to see (attraction)." 

392. COAT HANGER... Small envelopes are imprinted: 

"International one-piece coat and hat hanger. . . with compliments of (star)." Word or name, suggested by attraction can be substituted for "International." Most of space is devoted to attraction. 

Ordinary nails are placed inside envelopes before distribution. 

393. PAPER NAPKINS... Imprinted in corner with ad on theatre's attraction, and distributed in advance to restaurants, soda fountains, and all eating places that will use them. Or, paper napkins in use in eating places, might be rubber-stamped. Or, small imprinted stickers attached. 

Imprinted paper serviettes (or "doilies") might be supplied restaurants. 

394. OVERPRINT NEWSPAPERS... Quantity of news papers are secured, and rushed to printer, who already has type set up, and who overprints the papers, usually using red ink or other bright contrasting color. Or old copies might be used. Variation is imprinting of edge of papers. "Extra" copy might be used, and the papers distributed by boys who shout "Extra" in best newsboy style.

Or, instead of print-job, a rubber-stamp might be prepared, and the papers stamped. Similarly, gummed stickers might be printed, just big enough to cover the headlines on the papers. The copy, large and brief, is headed “Extra." Only the top edge of the stickers is attached to papers. Regular newsstand and newsboys might permit stickers to be attached to papers. 

Color ink might be suggested by attraction; as, green ink for an Irish story. 

Newspaper had best be advised of intention of overprinting papers. 

Secure their permission. 

395. SIDEWALK “PITCH”. . . Man stops at important downtown locations, in alley entrances and on corners, places a small suitcase on a small tripod or table which he carries along, proceeding then to deliver a "spiel," or "pitch," in regular sidewalk spieler style.

He tells his "audience" that he has a gift for them, that he is selling nothing, but that just for the advertising he is prepared to give them, • 198 •

absolutely free, an item which will solve problems for them, steer them nearer to happiness, make life more sublime. When a small crowd has stopped, he swiftly distributes sealed envelopes, saying "I thank you, and you'll thank me;" then on to another location.

The envelopes contain an attractively printed card that carries a photo and copy on theatre's attraction. 

396. PULLING HAIR ... Man drags a "woman” about the streets by her hair. . . "woman" being, of course, a dummy (with the "wig" securely attached, and perhaps small rollers attached under the dummy). Copy on man's back says: "She didn't want to go with me to see (attraction)." 

397. SPECIAL ISSUE... In connection with an outstanding attraction, occasionally a newspaper can be persuaded to run off a "special edition," with front page given over, in news style, to theatre's attraction, illustrations and stories on same. After regular edition of paper has been run, the revised "special edition" copies might then be printed.

Theatre will probably pay for expense involved in resetting page one (headlines and several lead stories, in addition to illustrations). 

Copies can be distributed about town by boys in newsboy "Extra" style. Or girls or boys in costume suggested by attraction might distribute them. Or, if only few copies are available, they might be used for lobby, front or window display. 

398. DISAPPEARING BALLYHOO... Where picture title suggests use of some article or animal . . . and same is secured and placed on display in theatre... might arrange to have it "disappear" ... and through newspaper and radio offering reward for return ... playing for novel newspaper story. . . arranging to have the article "returned" in time for another story. 

Classified ad might be carried when arranging to borrow the article (even if already secured), another classified ad when it is "lost." 

Paper might go for story on effectiveness of classified ads in first. locating the article then, when it is lost, securing its return. 

Emphasizing humorous angle, the lost "article" could be a tractor, or something equally ponderous. Ads might ask the "light-fingered" individual who took it to return it, with no questions asked. 

399. MAKE HER SAY "YES"... Telephone is center of a display in the lobby... panel carries copy: "If you can make the 'No Girl' use the word 'Yes,' you win guest tickets. Ask her about (and into attraction copy)."

Telephone is connected with another phone in office, where con- • 199 •

cealed operator answers the phone, "plugging" the coming attraction, carrying on conversations with those that try phone, studiously avoiding use of the word "Yes," in all conversations, except for an occasional exception. Conversation can be amplified so that others in lobby can hear. 

400. A MILLION... "If I had a Million" might be made basis of essay contest for newspaper in connection with an attraction that refers to a million, or to money. Or contest might be based on suggestions for spending it. (Or an amount indicated in the story.) 

Window marathon might have a girl or man attempting to count to a million before the attraction opens . . . using window amplification so that the counting and occasional humorous comment mentioning the attraction can be carried outside. 

401. SCOTCH . . . Scottish background to a story would suggest window displays of plaids and information about the clans they represent. Special "clan" nights would have descendants of various clans urged to attend . . . dividing all of them over several nights and listing them (in small type) in ads. Bag-pipers in kilts might play.

Dancers who can do a Highland Fling could be sent around to night spots, in Scotch kiltie costume; and a Highland Fling contest might be staged, at night spot, or on stage. Heralds might be distributed by girls wearing kilties. Bag piper, in kilt costume would draw attention on streets, sign on his back. Newspaper contest could be based on best Scotch jokes. Tieups can include tweed, tam o'shanters, golf.

Comedy Scotch herald, a small envelope, carries the copy: "Enclosed is a penny . . . for a moment of your time to call your attention to a most unusual attraction." The envelopes are sealed; inside there are no pennies, just an imprinted card which carries the copy: "The envelope was already sealed, so we couldn't include the penny . . . but the attraction is (and into space on attraction)." Man or girl in Scotch kilts distributes envelopes. Comedy Scotch stunt can have stage announcement made by man clad in Scotch kilties, prefacing his announcement with denial of fabled Scotch thrift proving it by throwing a coin away (to one side of stage). Looking about for the coin throughout his announcement, as he finishes, exits, trailer on the coming attraction hits the screen and the Scotsman comes back with a flashlight looking for the coin. He can appear briefly and silently throughout the show between the different subjects, looking for the coin. ... • 200 •

402. RULES Newspaper feature might be based on star's ten rules for success; or for smart dress (or for achievement as suggested by the attraction). Or, a newspaper contest might ask contestants to submit suggestions for ten rules. Contest might be handled in a comedy vein (depending on attraction), asking for comedy rules. 

Comedy "rules" for winning women (or "attracting women") could be requested; or attributed to stars of attraction.

Funny rules might be used in herald or newspaper ad. A comedy football feature, might suggest use of these "rules:" "New Football 

Rules for (year)" . . . "1. When a player slaps a member of another team on the shoulder, this shall be declared a 'touchback.' 2. When the ball is declared dead, the players of both teams shall perform an autopsy. 3. If any player should kick off, all cheering sections must attend the funeral in a body. 4. In the event of any player getting a punt, he shall immediately take the referee and go duck hunting. 

5. If the quarterback does not say 'please,' the center does not have to pass the ball to him. 6. All teams playing (strongest team) shall be permitted to equip their players with hatchets, swords and sawed-off shotguns. Bombs are barred. 7. All football players shall attend school for at least one hour each semester. 8. Any game ending in a tie shall be decided by a pinochle game to be played by the captains of the opposing teams. 9. If there should be more than one buck in the center, the game shall be halted while the players shoot craps for them. 10. There must be a college for each and every football team." (Following these "Rules" with attraction copy.)

Comedy Bridge Rules might be used for novel herald. Headed: 

"Sixteen New Rules for Bridge," and following with this copy: "1.

Always pick up the cards as they are dealt. You will be ready to bid ahead of the others. 2. If your hand is rotten, mention it. It will guide your partner in his bid and play. 3. If your partner bids first, don't hesitate to raise. He has to play it. 4. Never hurry.

Try several cards on a trick until you are sure just which one you prefer. 5. Occasionally ask what is trumps. It will show you are interested in the game. 6. Walk around the table when you are the dummy, and look at the other hands. Tell them what cards are good, and how many tricks they can take if they play right. 7.

Don't show lack of interest when you are dummy. Help your partner out with suggestions. 8. Talk about other subjects during the game. 

It makes for good fellowship. 9. Feel free to criticize your partner. 

He will do much better as a result. 10. Always trump your partner's · 201 •

tricks. Never take a chance. 11. Never try to remember rules.

It's too confusing. 12. If its a money game, always stop when you are ahead. 13. Always explain your plays, particularly, when set. 

It shows your card knowledge. 14. Disagree with established rules and conventions. People will know you are a person of independent mind. 15. Eat chocolate caramels or other adhesive candy while playing. It keeps the cards from skidding. 16. Instead of playing bridge, give a REAL party. Take your friends to see (and into attraction copy)." 

403. WAR, SOLDIERS . . . War photos, trophies and souvenirs might be placed on display in window or lobby (and safely under lock and key). Machine gun, helmets, bayonets, gas-masks, and other wartime equipment might be borrowed (perhaps from Veterans' organization). Display of medals may be arranged for a jeweler's window.

Sand-bag "trench" might be arranged in front of theatre, or on top of canopy, with "soldiers" in uniform "on guard."

Military organizations, or drum and bugle corps or band might march to theatre on opening night, possibly playing in front of theatre... perhaps as part of grand opening ceremonies.

Certain evenings could be dedicated to different veterans' organizations.

Local military organization and their equipment (trucks, searchlights, big guns, etc.) might be secured for a night parade. 

Searchlights might be secured from an artilllery or anti-aircraft unit for "grand opening," flashing the lights through the skies, and up and down sidewalk.

Soldiers or sailors might fire a salute as part of grand opening ceremonies. Local soldiers or sailors or veterans, can serve as a guard of honor.

For street flash, a caterpillar tractor or a truck might be transformed into a wartime tank. And if there is an army tank corps stationed nearby, perhaps the services of a real tank, or several of them, can be secured.

War heroes may be invited as special guests on opening night, especially decorated heroes. Decorated box seats should be reserved. 

Photo of veterans in front of theatre might be planted for newspaper space (arrange in advance). 

Former prisoners of war might be sought out for a newspaper interview, including their comment on attraction. • 202 •

Special program of war songs over radio station, can be "dedicated” to the attraction.

Buglers' contest could be arranged, opening night, in front of theatre. Toy soldiers might be used for lobby or window display. 

404. "TEASER" ANGLES... Ads in newspapers, or cards, or posting, or heralds, designed to arouse curiosity, with announcement of attraction to follow, after interest has been secured. 

Adapting to newspaper advertising, a provocative title might be carried in separate space in newspaper, with no descriptive copy, for several days in advance of first direct ad on attraction. 

Or "arriving" angle might be used... with part of a title, perhaps one letter, carried the first day, with an additional letter added each subsequent day, until title is completely spelled out. 

Or, part of a cut might be carried in first "teaser" ad, with subsequent ads showing more and more of the illustration, until entire illustration is used in an ad, with attraction announced. 

Sometimes, characteristic parts of star's make-up can be used in a teaser ad; as a hat, or shoes, appearing alone in first ad, another familiar item of star's costume added each day until, lastly, his face is added, together with announcement of the attraction. 

Stickers can carry curiosity-arousing illustration or catch-line. 

The stickers attached to mirrors, windshields, windows, correspondence, newspapers on newsstands. 

If title either asks a question or makes a definite statement, it might be especially adaptable to teaser use in newspaper and billposting. Imprinted paper streamers might attract attention if posted around town in advance of regular billing . . . covered over, when attraction arrives, with streamers carrying full information on the attraction. 

405. SHERLOCK . Comedy detective, dressed in two way cap, smoking a pipe, and equipped with a large “magnifying glass" (the glass made up of large round panel of glass), carries copy on his back (or it might be lettered directly on the glass), "I'm on the trail of the best show of the year. Its (attraction) at (theatre).”

Magnifying glass in a window or adapted to lobby display might be focused on a finely-written message on an attached piece of paper. 

Copy on panel carries copy: "Sherlock Holmes would have been delighted if he had discovered this clue." "Message" is copy to effect that “Happiness is just around the corner. . . that (attraction) is coming." 203.

406. APOLOGY. . . A heading for a newspaper ad, or herald: "We owe everyone in (town) an apology . . . for not having told you in every way possible about (attraction)." Or similar copy. 

And into ad on attraction. 

Or, playing to turn-away crowds, next day ad might “apologize to the hundreds turned away," urging them, however, to return and see (attraction). 

407. STEAMING KETTLE... Placed on top of a cake of ice will win attention for a window display. "Steam" is produced by use of dry-ice within the kettle, upon which water drips continuously (from smaller container inside the kettle and above the dry ice). Cake of ice is placed in a container sufficiently large to contain water when it melts. Display panels carry copy: "Amazing! 

Water Boiling atop a Cake of Ice! But More Amazing . . . (and into attraction copy)." ... 

408. COMEDY HORSE ... Two men, wearing a comedy horse costume (from costumers), travel about downtown section. 

Banners on the "horse" carry the copy: "If you think this is funny, wait until you see (attraction);" or, "Here's a good bet (and into attraction copy)."

Type of costume used might have man visible, through costume, from waist up . . . horse's "blanket" concealing his feet . . . and miniature legs being made up and attached at sides. Man wears gay shirt and jocky cap. Or, costume might completely hide two men who wear it. 

409. LENT... Programs need bolstering, selling, since many people are inclined to include theatres among the things denied themselves. Additionally, theatre patrons generally are in a frame of mind where they would prefer entertainment that is definitely of a higher type, during Lent. 

Give-aways might aid in bolstering business. Perhaps cooperating with merchants, a car, or several cars, might be given away. 

With Easter approaching, a fashion show could be arranged with a cooperating business place, and with talent added. 

Cooperation with a church might permit use of theatre for noontime or morning daily services (before matinee starting time). Perhaps an attraction may be booked that a minister might like and recommend. 

410. TIMELY... Perhaps an attraction, through coincidence or perfect timing, is booked while, or shortly after, a story along the same lines has been breaking in newspapers. In this event, clipped • 204 •

stories from the papers make a marvelous addition to lobby panels featuring illustrations and copy on theatre's attraction. 

Perhaps attraction ties in naturally with some local (or national) activity. Check. 

411. DYE... Distributor of popular brand of dye might place a demonstrator in theatre lobby, as center of display on attraction which carries copy: "Change your Blues to Rosier Hues ... (attraction)." And with paneled displays on the dye. Interest in dyes and colors will draw attention to displays on the attraction. 

Idea might be adapted to a window display. 

The tieup will prove especially valuable in focusing attention on color in an attraction, perhaps a motion picture in a new color process; or a number in a stage show that features vivid contrast of colors. 

412. FINGERPRINTS ... Where attraction suggests it, a display of finger-printing equipment and records might be set up in lobby, arranging same through the cooperation of the local bureau of identification or police department. 

Patrons, or those who desire it, might be finger-printed, and their prints filed for their protection and identification with the National bureau. Children's prints might be registered at a special matinee performance. Newspaper may sponsor the idea, or at least accord it stories.

Enlargement of fingerprint "of star" might be displayed, with patrons invited to compare theirs. 413. BARRELS . . Placed prominently about town, or hauled about town on a bannered truck, barrels might be lettered: "A Barrel of Fun (and copy on attraction)." 

Or, barrels, placed on corners, could carry copy: "Don't Look 

Inside! Remember what Curiosity did to a cat!" As they'll sure look inside, display is placed inside the barrel. 

Or, one barrel, on a wheelbarrow, might be lettered: "It's a Barrel of Fun (and into attraction copy)." Wheelbarrow pushed by men or girls in costume.

For a beach bally, a man promenades the beach in a barrel (costumed under the barrel in bathing trunks), the barrel lettered: "I hocked my clothes for money to see (attraction)." Or, stunt might even be adapted to Main Street. 

414. MANY LANGUAGES... Catchline for an ad or herald is printed in several languages . . . following with copy, in English, "In other words, don't miss seeing (attraction)," and into attraction copy. • 205 •

415. HOW FAR CAN CAR RUN?... On prominent down town corner a rear wheel of a car is lifted from the ground. Motor started. Banner atop car offers tickets to see attraction to those guessing nearest correct mileage that car will register on a gallon of gas. Or, the bannered car can travel about town, having a pretty girl give the starting signal (for photos, which the auto dealer might plant for newspaper space). 

416. RAILROADS... Railway stations might permit dis play panel in railroad station. Ticket offices might install special windows, tieing in "Travel by Train" idea, if the angle can be adapted to theatre's attraction.

Miniature electric train can be used in window displays effectively. 

Or, a toy train can be used as a prize for kids. Placed on display in lobby well in advance, perhaps store will contribute the train for mention they will receive. 

In connection with a railroad story, railroads will generally cooperate willingly, supplying signals, semaphores, lights, safety devices, switches, etc., for front display.

Attention of railroad employees should be directed to an attraction with railroad theme. Railroad Brotherhoods should be contacted. 

Doorman might be costumed as a railroad conductor, or an engineer. Sidewalk barker, costumed as a conductor, might periodically signal with a lantern (flashlight type) and shout "all aboard," following with spiel, in train-caller style, about attraction.

Train effect record might be played in connection with front or lobby display using amplification if out front. Radio station could use effect record as background for an announcement. 

Railroad songs can be made the basis of a contest for newspaper or a program for radio. 

Perhaps an automobile that is designed to resemble a locomotive might be available, and might be secured for street use. 

Herald for distribution could be made up after fashion of a railroad excursion herald, or imitating a ticket in design. Time-tables of local trains might be featured on a card which devotes most of space to attraction.

Broadcast "suggested" by the attraction might be arranged from depot . . . with radio interviewer meeting trains, interviewing people he meets in the depot, mentioning the attraction, perhaps asking a question suggested by the attraction. (See No. 418.) 

417. CRYING TOWELS... Paper napkins, or paper towels, to be distributed as heralds, are imprinted: "Crying Towels.

418. EXCURSIONS (RAILROAD OR BUS)... Transportation company might place special "excursion" cards on attraction in all towns within drawing radius of town. 

Card, though devoting most of space to theatre's attraction, directs attention to rates (per mile) to city, or round-trip cost, suggesting travel by (transportation company) to (town) to see (and into attraction copy).

Local passenger agent delivers cards to station agent in each town, who is instructed to place the cards in depots and in prominent windows about the towns. Cards must be packaged into correctly counted groups for each town.

Excursions should be met on their arrival with banners Excursion boats might be similarly met. Or any arrival of large groups. 

419. SIMILARITY, DOUBLES... Contest in cooperation with newspaper offers prize to girl most nearly resembling star of coming attraction. Contestants submitting photos. Photo of a daily winner, together with a photo of the star of attraction, carried by paper, asking for local doubles.

Beauty shop, or other business place could sponsor contest, buying newspaper space, part of which is devoted to theatre's attraction. 

Store might have winner make "personal appearance" in store, modeling garments or hats.

Contest might be based on the appearance of girls themselves, staging a contest at theatre or in the cooperating store. 

If person resembling star of attraction can be located, his experiences in being mistaken for star might make a good newspaper feature, together with photographs comparing him with star. ... 

420. MATS . . . Lettered, in oil, with name of attraction and theatre name, linoleum mats can be placed on sidewalks about town and in prominent places where they will be seen . . . used where local ordinances will not permit stenciling or lettering of sidewalks (which is better, safer, if possible).

Mats must be definitely made to lay flat against sidewalk. Water glass might be used to hold them down. Or, in hot weather, roofing • 207 •

paper might be used instead of linoleum mats, the heat making the mats adhere to the sidewalk.

Rubber mats used in theatre lobby may be similarly stenciled or lettered with the title of a coming show. 

421. HOMING PIGEONS... Most cities boast of associa tions of carrier pigeon fanciers. Might arrange with them to sponsor release of birds from front of theatre on opening of attraction. 

Identical messages about opening of attraction to be carried by each bird.

Traffic in front of theatre must be held (through police cooperation) for the minute or so that it requires to release the birds. 

Some prominent local person, or attractive girl might "officially' release the pigeons (for newspaper photograph). 

Carrier pigeons on display in lobby in advance carry copy: "These 

Swift Messengers will be released (day) to carry the message that (attraction) has arrived in (town)." 

422. MILLINERY 

Hat Shop buys newspaper space, which offers guest tickets to theatre's attraction for best hat design drawn over an illustration of star. Or contestants might be required to submit a drawing of a hat design suggested by title of theatre's attraction.

Shop might name a specially designed bonnet after theatre attraction or star . . . or dedicating hat to star, putting in a full window display. 

423. KISSING CONTEST Kiss or heavy love interest in a film, may be the inspiration for a "Kissing Contest," announced for theatre lobby at a designated time. Actual "contest” is a solo affair, contestants making kissing noise before a microphone, which is connected through amplification . . . with the speaker also in lobby. Microphone and the "contestants" are placed on a slight elevation... and several "stooges" had better be arranged, so that there will definitely be several entries; a couple of girls might be included. Newspaper stories might develop on announcement of the "contest," and on its finally proving to be a solo affair. 

Or microphone can be placed in charge of a pretty girl . . . copy on the panel advising that "Miss (attraction)" is staging a kissing contest. Any "entries," instead of kissing the girl, are invited to present a solo kiss over the microphone.

425. STENOGRAPHERS' CUFFS... Paper strips, designed to fold around the wrists as cuffs to protect clothing of office workers, can be distributed to offices, stores and business places. 

Paper clip is attached to each strip before distribution in pairs to office girls, stenographers, clerks . . . the "cuff" to be attached about the wrist by means of the paper clips. 

Imprint the "cuffs:" "Make a note on your cuff to see (attraction).” 

Or, perhaps attraction might suggest copy. 

426. THEATRE OF THE AIR . . . Broadcasting part of theatre's program direct from auditorium or from booth. A five minute highlight of current show might be featured, a short musical, and possibly a newsreel; with trailer on the current attraction given the feature spot. Or, the trailer that is currently being shown at theatre might be broadcast much as a brief enacted sketch might be handled. ... 

427. DYNAMITE Two men carry box, painted red and lettered: "Dynamite" and "Danger" about town . . . and arriving at prominent corner, they toss it roughly to the sidewalk. Dynamite!'. . . see (attraction and theatre)."

Display for lobby might feature several panels made to resemble gigantic sticks of dynamite (painted red and fused), panel carrying "dramatic dynamite" copy. Electrician would arrange wires running through one of the "fuses" to tip (where wires are parted 8") and connecting with house current through a Ford spark coil and a toy transformer, which produces a spark, and makes the fuse appear to be sputtering.

429. SHELL GAME. . . Small spotlighted table has three half cocoanut shells placed on it . . . and panel carrying copy: "Can you beat the Shell Game? Find the Nuts under the Shells." On table, under each shell, is attached a picture of one of players in coming comedy attraction. 

430. LOBBY TRAILER... Using portable projector, trailers on coming attractions might be screened in the lobby for waiting patrons, or for incoming patrons. Projector is focused (perhaps from behind) on a small screen or panel of translucent glass which is part of a display on coming attraction, and placed high enough so that all might see. 

16 mm. projectors are available and might be rented, running a continuous trailer, and showing a specially prepared 16 mm. trailer. 

Or, instead of film, specially prepared slides might be flashed. Also newspaper or radio station might supply latest news flashes . making up slides as news comes in. Stunt might be adapted to theatre front on a current show (recessing screen). 

Live entertainers might serve as a lobby "trailer" on an attraction singing and playing numbers from the show, or a coming show. 

Entertainers elevated so that they are in view, as center of a paneled display on the attraction.

Another "date" angle would have telephone connected into lobby, as center of a lobby display panel. Copy urges boys and girls to “use our phone. . . to make a date now... to see (attraction) when it comes to town."

432. POPULARITY CONTESTS. . . As suggested by at traction, a contest might feature the selection of town's "most popular" fireman, or policeman, or bathing girl, or shop girl, or stenographer, or school girl . . . anyone of any group. . . Arranged in cooperation with newspaper, inviting readers to send in their "votes" (a coupon carried in the paper). 

Telegram from star of coming attraction could introduce the contest. The wire, to editor of paper, states that star would like to present an autographed photo, or trophy (or some item suggested by the attraction) to most popular local person (of group suggested by attraction).

Newspaper could reproduce the telegram with their first story on the contest. Later stories accompanied with art on the attraction. 

Studios will send wire, or autographed photo if requested. They should be contacted well in advance.

Popularity contest stunt might be adapted to radio, basing it on letters sent the station.

Another popularity contest idea, would be selection of most popular girl employees in stores, factories. Letter to business places, stores, factories, offices, might ask them to permit their employees to conduct a contest to determine most popular girl employee, who is to receive guest tickets (which are enclosed). 

433. SAME NAME. . . Where title of attraction, or star's name is unusual, through newspaper or radio cooperation, guest tickets might be offered local residents of same name. 

Newspaper would find material for novel story on the aggregation of persons of same name. Required to attend a certain performance, a group photo can be made in front of theatre. They might be "organized" as the "(Name) Club." 

434. STAGE SHOWS... Personal appearances, vaudeville, stage shows of any kind present many opportunities for tieups and promotion.

Star, on arrival, could be met at station or airport by band, and committee wearing imprinted ribbons bearing "welcome (star)" copy. Luncheon club members might agree to act as the official greeters (with celebrity appearing at their luncheon-which might be broadcast). Reporters, newspaper photographers should be on hand. Local official should greet the star, and extend welcome to city. 

Ceremonies can be broadcast. • 211 •

Star, or entire show, might be escorted to city hall by band and motorcycle police, or large group of motorcycles (See 950), with arrangements made to have Mayor greet them and extend “key to city" (for photograph for newspapers).

Automobile dealer supplies a group of cars company through main streets to theatre. taken on a "sight-seeing tour" of the city bannered). Car, with uniformed chauffeur can be placed at disposal of star while in city, parked near front of theatre, with neat card in windshield lettered, "(star's) special (name of car)." (bannered), carrying 

Company might be (with cars properly Aviation welcome could be extended, flying local planes out to meet train, flying over it on its way to city. One of them might tow a lettered banner. Or, planes might meet airliner in air over port. Air show might be staged previous to arrival of airliner (the show will aid in drawing crowds to port) as part of the "ceremonies." "Welcome" streamers can be attached to the windows of all stores on Main Street. Similarly, stickers might be attached to automobile windshields. Valances on hotel, department store canopies might carry welcome copy, mentioning star's appearance at theatre. 

Valances can be made up locally, using lettered oilcloth. Only ends of canopies would be used, if covering front, additionally, is too expensive.

Arrangements might be worked out with hotel or restaurants to have company as dinner guests, together with newspaper critics, local celebs. Should be good for newspaper photographs and radio mention if orchestra is broadcasting from dining room. Company should dress for dinner, if so prepared.

Star arriving with large company might be met at station or airport by theatre attendant with several cats. Explained that star wired requesting that manager have five cats at station. Star explains that she wired for "five cabs." Newspapers picking up the gag for stories, might use pictures. Actual wire might be sent, to show. Or star might be met with thirty-two revolvers . . . with the explanation following that star wired for a .32 revolver to use in his act.

Arrangements might be made to have newspaper critic meet star, who is coming to city, at nearby town, boarding plane or train and interviewing him en route.

Interviews by newspaper writers must be arranged; for stars or entire company.

Radio broadcast might include interviews, guest appearances on 212.

other programs, special program (using material, songs, etc., not used in show); broadcast from back-stage on opening day with announcer roving around from one dressing room to another with microphone, introducing talent for gags or brief numbers. Radio announcer might "watch" a show from back-stage, in this event broadcasting but part of the show. If star of show is famous for several songs, or has made recordings, these might be featured over the air. Special broadcasts can be "dedicated" to the star.

Arrangements might be made to have stars made honorary members of luncheon clubs or police or fire department... with photographs for the newspapers. "Guest Nights," on evenings after opening would have other entertainers (band leaders, soloists with bands appearing in the town, night club entertainers), making "guest appearances" during the show.

Contests suggested by some type of entertainment in the show might help to build up business on an off-night. For instance, with a banjoist featured, a contest for local string pluckers might be sponsored; similarly singers if the star of the stage show sings. 

Star can shower lucky heralds from the skies . . . store buying newspaper space calling attention to fact that star of stage show will fly over city at specified time, dropping heralds (which can be dropped by "proxy"). See No. 201.

Star might "write" a newspaper ad, possibly in his hand-writing and signed by him—either for theatre or a store . . . and using photos. 

Feminine star might serve for a day as guest editor of women's page of newspaper, or as guest columnist. "Back-stage at (name of show)" can be title of a newspaper feature, with newspaper staff cameraman shooting frequent candid camera photographs back-stage before and during the performance .. action shots, obviously not posed. Feature story accompanying group layout of the pictures tells reporter's experiences while watching the show from back-stage. 

Morning dance "school" might be presented (one morning) for ambitious would-be dancers, with members of chorus, or featured dancers as instructors.

Girls and performers in show might appear as guests of night club after the show . . . introduced to patrons, and over radio. Escorts should be arranged for the girls. Dance spot could name a certain evening in honor of the star, newspaper ads and announcements calling it "(Star) Night." Star and company to definitely be present. • 213

"Cabaret Night" might be made a feature on one evening of the stage show... with "after-show" following last regular performance, and all performers seated at tables on stage and, working from tables, introducing specialties not done in their acts. Or "afterpiece" can be routined revue-style, presenting song and dance specialties, comedy "bits," and full-stage scenes, or "black-outs." 

Candid Cameras Matinee can have owners of small cameras invited to try for photos of stage show scenes. Camera shop cooperates in contacting camera enthusiasts. Prize for best snaps, displayed in window, and in lobby. 

If star has appeared in pictures, scenes from one of them may be made part of advance trailer, or used as an introductory trailer. 

Or a short could be booked on the same program. 

Arrival of performers at theatre (first matinee or opening night) might be broadcast. One performer or girl in each car (automobile dealer supplying cars and drivers), and as each one arrives at theatre, announcer interviews performer until arrival of next car. 

Affiliations of stars or performers should be checked. If they belong to lodges, organizations, orders, local members of same organization might be contacted, their attention called to fact that performer is a member.

For a novel, different story, newspaper reviewer might be seated in stage band, perhaps holding an instrument as though playing it, getting his review of the show from this angle. Perhaps photograph, made from wings, showing him sitting in with band, might be used in connection with his review. 

Dancers might "test" stockings . . . hosiery shop supplying them with hose, and using a leg photograph of the girls for an ad. 

Star or dancer, or a chorus girl might make a talk before a luncheon club on some subject other than show business, a smart talk that will impress club members.

Perhaps newspaper sports page would "sponsor" a long distance golf match between the star of theatre's stage show, and the star of the screen attraction . . . with the screen star wiring his or her score to the sports editor for comparison with that of stage star. Chorus girls might serve as caddies for the stage star, and photographs should make the sport page. Golf photo of screen star might be sent telephoto to run with that of stage star. 

Insurance company might, for the advertising, insure dancer's knees, or chorus girl's toes, in connection with and to direct special attention to a spectacular number in the show. • 214 •

Stage star can be identified with any commendable activity; can be best man at a wedding or on a white horse at the head of a parade; might be present wherever public attention is focused. 

Many activities are possible that will win newspaper stories with accompanying photographs picturing the stars, or girls in the show. 

Local events offer many angles to tie to; and players might be posed with many local scenes or identified with popular local events or 

Should new buses be introduced into town, a photograph of girls in the show "taking over" a car, ought to be good for newspaper space, for instance.

Drives or civic activities should have star identified pictured buying first Red Cross Seals. 

as star Company might be photographed "taking over" a railroad train, posed about front of the engine (and railroad should place copies of the photo on display in ticket office windows and in stations). · • Or company could be taken to inspect the telephone exchange. 

Or girls from show might be pictured (in bathing suits) "starting theatre cooling plant." Or exercising in a gymnasium. Or "demonstrating" (for a photograph) a jiu jitsu hold. Or engaging in a summertime snowball fight (in bathing suits, and with a cooperating ice company supplying the "snow"). Or posing for a portrait. Girls might stage a "hiking race," from city hall to theatre. wearing shorts, and "started" by some local celebrity, "paced" by a bannered automobile and police escort. Chorus numbers could be rehearsed in some unusual spot . . . running through a routine or two (with phonograph accompaniment if other accompaniment isn't available) in park, or at a swimming pool, or atop an important building (but far from edge), or on a boat-any unusual setting. Sport page might use pictures of girls or players at baseball park "working out" before the game; or posed with local sports star.

Entire company might be taken to a swimming pool, to swim as guests of the pool and for photographs in bathing suits (for newspapers as well as for display at pool). 

At newspaper office, they may be pictured around a linotype machine, in press room, or a group of the girls surrounding the editor and star. Grouped, and a cut made, a very interesting and novel newspaper feature can be worked out. Entertainers might visit hospital, entertaining the convalescent patients, under sponsorship of the paper. Similarly, orphanages, old folks' homes, etc. Star might act as a "newspaper reporter," interviewing some local notable •215.

who is in the news, or a football or baseball team just before a big game. If Mayor is agreeable, a group of girls from show might visit city hall, going through a group routine (in costume or in sports outfits) in front of city hall or on steps . . . with music supplied by accordion or a portable piano which is brought along. Games, baseball or football, might be "officially" started by star. . . throwing first baseball, or tossing football on the field; or, visiting with home town players before the game, wishing them luck; and similarly any other game or competition. Star might present trophy at a race.

Using a selected group of chorus girls, arrangements might possibly be made with some school or college to submit girls to an "intelligence test" (test generally given freshmen), in competition with a group of the college girls. Whatever the result, the test should be good for newspaper, besides showing off the girls and getting a lot of mention around the school. Or girls might "challenge" girl athletes of school or college to a foot race.

Perhaps two stars of stage show might engage in a paper selling competition, taking opposite corners at busiest intersection at rush hour. Returns should go to newsboys who ordinarily occupy the corner and who stick around to help out. One of the girls in the show might challenge a male star to a "fast dressing" contest... to be staged in a downtown store window. (They enter window wearing bathing suits, over which they dress.) Store might buy ads on the stunt.

Title of show, or act, should offer additional angles for tieups or newspaper stories. Photos taken for publicity purposes can be placed on display in windows about town. 

Newspaper cooperative page, or individual merchants' ads might welcome star or show. Newspaper cooperative page of ads might be sold on basis that star will make a "shopping tour," visiting cooperating business places at an agreed time. 

Star can appear in a clothing store for photographs, which store uses in a newspaper ad. Actors may act as demonstrators, salesmen, or merely autograph articles on sale in the store. 

Music stores can feature song hits featured or introduced by star, or show. If star plays a musical instrument, a window of instruments might be installed, including photographs of star, who could appear in store and autograph sheet music copies or recordings, or demonstrate instruments.

Radio dealer might buy newspaper space using photograph of star • 216 •

posed with one of their radios (which is installed in star's dressing room at theatre, and photograph made there). 

Automobile dealers might go for newspaper space, using photograph of star or girls in show, posed with one of the new models. Possibly newspaper will carry the picture on automobile page. 

Store might illustrate an ad with a photograph of star inspecting an article that is named after or dedicated to him. 

Girls in show can model hats, or hose, bathing suits or lingerie in a ladies' store, with store's ads largely devoted to theatre's attraction. A fashion show might be set for a matinee performance, with the girls modeling gowns, lingerie, furs, etc., store publicizing the event. . . which might be worked as a separate unit, or included in the regular stage routine. 

Drug store would feature cosmetics with photograph of star or girls as center of the display. Hair dressers could name a permanent wave after the star, or dedicate a hair dress to star (and using photograph of the star in their ads). Hair dresser might agree to fix the hair of girls in the show (without charge, as an advertisement), calling attention in their ads to the fact. Autographed stills (to owner or manager of prominent business place) will generally be assured of a prominent place in front windows. 

435. COMMENT . . . In connection with screening of a notable attraction, those witnessing it might be invited to inscribe their comment and their names in a large ledger which is placed on a table in the lobby. Book might be later used as feature of a display for lobby, or in other prominent place, spotlighted, with panel copy inviting patrons to read the comment, the opinion of others who have seen (attraction).

Or, "comment cards" can be handed those witnessing a screening, requesting that they inscribe their comment and signatures, asking permission to use same in lobby and ads. Comment may be reproduced, above signatures, in newspaper ads, or on lobby panels. 

Radio station might arrange to broadcast comment of patrons leaving theatre after showing of a notable production. Or, during a special screening or following a regular showing, carrying microphone, on a long extension up and down aisles, asking patrons how they enjoyed the attraction. 

436. COUPLE MEETING... Two men, or man and woman, visit hotel lobbies, restaurants, and other places where crowds gather, and entering separately, they "meet," shake hands, and greeting each other loudly, they mention that they are in town to see • 217 •

(theatre's attraction); or they loudly make a date to see the attraction, as they have both heard it is outstanding. Then on to another spot and another "meeting." 

437. SKETCHES, PICTURE PUZZLES ... Drawings, as basis of a newspaper contest, depict scenes in which things pictured (together with dialogue "clues" in comic-strip "balloons") can be connected together to suggest star's name (as man, standing near a wall, holding an ace and an overflowing stein of beer, with a "balloon" carrying word "Eh," or including it prominently in a sentence... representing Wallace Beery. Titles of star's previous pictures, or title of a coming show, can be represented. Optional list of names is carried, one of which is the correct one. Contestants must identify star or title represented.

Local sketch artist, working from stills, can make up a series of illustrations, 8x10, that can be used instead of stills, as a change, for front display, or newspaper. 

438. CYLINDER... Made up a foot or more in diameter, a cylinder or drum, might be made to revolve back of an opening in a display panel . . . perhaps over (horizontally), the box office . . . as it revolves, bringing several lines of copy consecutively into view through the opening.

Or, for window or lobby display, a horizontally revolving cylinder might have a series of 8x10 stills loosely attached at top of stills . . . so that on reaching a certain point, as the cylinder revolves, moving downward, the stills fall over. Copy on reverse sides of stills. 

439. MASKED AUTOMOBILE... Automobile driven about the city has all windows and windshield completely covered over with black cloth. Apparently the car is completely masked, since no one can see in the car. However, those within the car have clear vision through all windows of the car. Black glazed muslin is used to "mask" the car, being attached inside the windows, with the glazed surface facing outward. Copy lettered across the windows and the windshields (using water color): "The (name of attraction) Mystery (name of car)."

Or, instead of masking the car, the driver may be masked. Preferably a girl, banners on car ask: "Who is the Mysterious masked driver of the (attraction) (car)?" Driver is unmasked in front of theatre opening day. 

440. WOMEN'S PAGE .. Society Page in newspaper shouldn't be overlooked in appealing to women. Special ads can be • 218 •

occasionally effectively placed on the page. Scene cuts, or illustrations from the attraction, might be carried. 

Editors will generally accept good fashion illustrations of stars for use on women's page. 

A "Designers' Contest" might be arranged for the Fashion page carrying full-length illustration of star . . . and suggesting that readers draw their design for a dress over the illustration (or a hat; or a scarf). Tickets to best so-many. Costume "designs" might be required to be made of actual cloth pasted over the figure. "Beauty Hints" under star's name and illustrated with star's photograph (from coming attraction) might be available or possible to secure. Series of chapters might feature care of skin, hands, eyebrows, eyes, hair. 

441. GROWING OLD . . . Card, or herald is imprinted: 

"How to keep from Growing Old". . . following with smaller type, "Always Race with Locomotives to Crossings; Engineers Like it; 

It breaks the Monotony of their Jobs. Always Pass the Car Ahead on Curves or Turns; Don't use your Horn. it may Unnerve the fellow, and cause him to turn out too far. Demand Half the Road ... the Middle Half; Insist on your Rights. Always Speed; it shows you are a Man of Pep, even though an Amateur Driver. Never 

Stop, Look or Listen at Railroad Crossings. . . it Consumes Time; 

Anyway, let the Train stop for a Change. Always Lock Your Brakes when Skidding... it makes the job more Artistic. In Sloppy Weather, drive Close to Pedestrians . . . Dry Cleaners appreciate this Consideration. Never Look Around when Backing Up... there's never anything Behind You. Drive Confidently, just as though there were not millions of other cars in service. But . . . in all Seriousness. 

here's a Sure Way to 'Keep from Growing Old'... Laugh the Years 

Away... see (and into attraction copy)." 

442. CRAZES PUZZLES ... Freak stunts which are oc casionally the rage, can always be tied in for publicity, or used as an attraction. Endurance runners or dancers, champion "tree-sitters,' jig-saw puzzle champs, endurance piano-players, etc., might make appearance in theatre lobby, or be introduced from stage. 

Newspaper ad might carry copy that champ had to suspend activities to see (attraction). Appearance of stunters at theatre might be handled in comedy style or seriously, depending on the "champ." 

Stunters might cooperate in advertising attraction during the stunt they are performing. Perhaps they might be placed in lobby 219.

or store window, surrounded by theatre advertising; or broadcast may be arranged, with attraction mentioned. 

Puzzle crazes that sweep over the country periodically might be capitalized on similarly. Marathons or contests might be set for lobby or window, with theatre advertising incorporated in the display. 

Games that come into popularity, including card games, might be played in theatre lobby or lounges; prizes offered in outstanding games; perhaps a tournament for theatre lobby can be promoted. 

Imprinted "games" might be supplied patrons if not too expensive. 

Printed puzzles (as cross-word puzzles), can often be adapted to newspaper reproduction, or used for heralds or programs. Blank "cross-word" may have contestants invited to pencil in star's name in any arrangement, then to fill in spaces both up and down with words which can be found in the encyclopedia, or dictionary. 

443. MYSTIC RADIO ... Radio made part of display for lobby or front of store with copy on display calling it the "Mystic (name of attraction) Radio" adding that it will answer all questions. Copy included: "Is there something you wish to know? 

Ask the Mystic (attraction) Radio . . . It will Answer!" Two-way amplification, carrying voices both ways, enables hidden operator to hear questions asked and to answer them (microphone out front being concealed behind a panel or within the radio, carries voice to operator he speaks into a microphone that is connected through the radio).

Attendant (costumed) prevents persons from tampering with the radio... and repeats questions if necessary for microphone to pick them up.

Several "plants" might be arranged, who ask comedy questions, and get funny answers. 

If cashier has a view of the display, perhaps she can telephone names of persons in front of the radio to the "operator". . . who can amaze them by calling them by name.

Operator must use good judgment, and confine answers and "advice" to straight comedy. And mentioning attraction continuously. 

Also, instead of using a radio as center of display, a papier mache figure, or a dummy, or a display modeled after the star or suggested by the attraction, can be used . . . with mike and speaker concealed in same. Might have dummy stationed at a microphone in lobby as though announcing. (See Diagrams, Papier Mache.) ... 

444. BACKSEAT DRIVERS... Foldover herald is imprinted
