Certifying that the holder of this Certificate has passed all tests for Hysteria, and is licensed to Operate, Dominate, Irritate and Criticize the Chauffeur either from the rear or from the front Seat." Copy on attraction at bottom of card (as "But why worry about who's driving, go see..."). 

Attraction copy is imprinted on reverse side of the card. 

445. CHALLENGE... In tieup with leading store, or stores, a challenge is issued to studio that town can select six girls (or any number, perhaps one from each of several stores), as beautiful as those shown in coming attraction.

Resolving into a beauty contest, each store (or other business place) sponsors and selects a girl . . . with final selection from among these girls to be made when they appear on opening night at theatre ... with prize or trophy, or perhaps a trip, for the winner. In connection with a stage show, girls in the show might act as the judges in picking out the prettiest local girls (there being no actual contest between show girls and local girls).

Newspapers should carry daily stories in advance, as each girl is selected by a different business place to represent it. . . illustrating stories with photographs of local girls and the girls in the coming attraction.

Arrangements might be made with luncheon club to clown the idea, with club claiming (for newspaper stories) that they can pick more handsome man from their members than star (of coming attraction). "Challenge" trailer or ad can carry copy: "No matter how many pictures you've seen, we challenge you to compare a single one of them with (attraction)." Or similar wording. 

446. FRIGHT WIG... Wig, to be worn by bally man on streets, is especially prepared by hair dresser or costumer, so that hair stands on end. His back carries copy: "My hair stood on end when I saw (attraction)." (Attraction must be appropriate, of course). 

447. DEPOTS, TERMINALS, SUBWAYS 

Display panels, cards or banners might be placed in depots and terminals for • 221 •

buses and trains, or planes. Distribution of heralds might be permitted. Stunt men might meet crowds arriving at rush hours. 

Displays may be effectively placed about subway exits, arranging windows, placing cards on newsstands or other locations. 

448. LAUGH HURRICANE ... Three outstanding words, in big type, on a herald or in newspaper space, are: "Warning!" "Hurricane," and "Tornado." Smaller in-between type makes the copy read, however: "Warning! (town) can be prepared for a Hurricane of Laughter . . . when (attraction) comes to town." (Then following with copy on the attraction and concluding with: "It's a veritable Tornado of Titillation, a Hurricane of Hilarity!" Might be adapted to radio spot announcements, starting them: "Storm 

Warning! (Town) can get set for a Hurricane . . . a Hurricane of laughter, etc." 

449. MOTH BALLS... Camphor balls, placed in a sealed bottle of charged water, will keep continuously diving to the bottom and then returning to the top. 

In window or lobby, copy on display cards says that thrills (or laughs) in the picture are as endless as the motion of the amazing mystic spheres. 

450. SIT DOWN STRIKER ... Girl seats herself during rush hours in front of theatre, in comfortable chair, and attaches herself by means of handcuffs and long chain to some front fixture. 

Panel beside her carries copy: "I'm on a Sit Down Strike. And I won't leave until my sweetheart takes me to see (attraction)." 

451. SIGN THE BOOK... Ruled cards ... with spaces for a hundred signatures and addresses, are imprinted at top: "The bearer is trying to earn a ticket to (theatre) to see (attraction) . . . and in order to get this ticket, he must have this card completely filled out. Your signature attached certifies that he has called to your attention the showing of (attraction) at the (theatre), and does in no way obligate you."

As one of these cards will reach attention of a hundred people, a large number of cards is not necessary and they can be limited. Boys (possibly Scouts) might get the signatures for tickets or prize.

Names, checked for duplication, can be used for mailing list. 

452. GIRL MEASUREMENTS... Using measurements of feminine star, newspaper might cooperate in search for a local girl of nearly identical measurements. Photograph of star is carried, together with her measurements, marked on the photograph ankle, calf, thigh, hips, waist, bust, neck, arm, together with weight • 222 •

and height. Girls might be invited to submit their measurements. 

Prize (from star), perhaps a bathing suit, and tickets, for the winner.

Idea might be adapted to a store's ad. 

In connection with stories, newspaper could use a photograph of local girl, in bathing suit, being measured for the contest. Perhaps some local celeb can be applying the tape measure. 

Lobby display might feature life-size cutout figure of a girl, on slight elevation, several feet forward from back panel of display. Card attached to back panel describes the figure as feminine perfection (as seen in attraction) and inviting girls to compare measurements. 

Measurements are then listed on the card-bust (which might be 34″), waist (25″ or 26″), hips (34″), thigh (18″), calf (13″ or 14″), ankle (7″) . . . or approximately these measurements . . . with white ribbons extending from the listed measurement on the card to the cutout figure, attaching at part of figure to which measurements refer. 

Small tape measures might be distributed, with attached tag carrying copy: "Have you a figure like (star)?”, and listing measurements, carrying copy on attraction. Tapes handed to girls in stores, offices. Or, tags can be imprinted: "Here's a full measure of fun (and copy)." 

453. DAYS UNTIL Series of small advance newspaper ads are modeled after usual "Days till Christmas" announcements that break in newspaper around Christmas time . . . ads carrying copy: "(Number) Days until (attraction copy)." Illustrated with photo of Santa Claus (and more effective if out of season), ads might carry copy: "(Number) of Days . . . Until Mr. Santa Claus makes his first Out-of-Season Appearance . . . to bring you (attraction).”

Might be adapted to a front or lobby panel, changing the number of days each day. 

Near Christmas time, use of a series of advance ads might tie in with Christmas attraction very effectively. . . billing the attraction as: "(Theatre's) Christmas Treat for (town)." 

454. LOCAL EVENTS... Current events or topics of con versation, often offer angles for copy on attraction, tieing in the local event with attraction title. Check local headlines. 

455. STOP-GO... Display for lobby or window made up after style of traffic signals, alternately flashes red and green the red, when lighted, reading: "Stop! . . . and see (attraction)" and then the green, when lighted: “Go . . . see (attraction)." The red and green lights in the painted semaphore might be spotted behind the letter "O" in "Stop" and "Go." • 223 •

E N C Y C L O PEDIA OF EXPLOITAT I O N 

Cards imprinted, "Stop! Go see (attraction)" might be attached to poles at arterials or through streets where cross-traffic is required to stop. Word "Stop" is large, and stands out at first glance. 

456. PAINT. . . Paint store, might have man (or pretty girl), "demonstrating" their paint in their window, by continually lettering the name of theatre's attraction on a small panel. 

Man might travel about town, setting up panel on curb, and proceeding to paint it. After finishing, he attaches a panel lettered: "I'm painting the town. My wife's gone to the country, and I just saw (attraction)." 

457. LOBBY BROADCASTING STATION... Duplication of a broadcasting studio set up in lobby, microphone being made the center of attraction display. Slight elevation provided for announcer, entertainers, so they are easily in view. At certain times each day, programs are broadcast, attraction announcements included. 

Night clubs might supply entertainers, band leaders might act as guest announcers. Piano or musical accompaniment is necessary. 

If radio hookup is not possible, amplification equipment might be used instead, with programs and announcements carried outside the theatre. Song hits from the attraction may be featured. 

458. NEWSREEL... Tieup might be made with newspaper or radio station . . . having a special introductory trailer made up for regular use in connection with newsreels. The trailer carries the copy: "The (theatre) (Newspaper or Radio Station) News." Or: 

"The (theatre) (name of newsreel) News... Presented in cooperation with (radio station or newspaper)." The trailer takes the place of regular newsreel leads in daily use. 

Newspaper should accord special publicity in exchange. Radio 

Station would mention the newsreel and theatre's attraction after each newscast. . . as, “For illustrated news, see the (station) Newsreel at (theatre) where (attraction) is now showing." The tieup might, in addition, pave the way for future close cooperation. 

Newsreels often carry subjects that are of sufficient interest to merit ad and front billing. Additionally, occasional flashes might appeal to certain groups, or individuals . . . whom cashier might telephone. 

Occasionally a newsreel will show a subject with which a coming attraction will deal. In which case, a trailer might be effectively cut into the newsreel immediately following the scene (regular trailer or a specially made up single flash trailer). 

459. SUNDAY BUILDUP... Effective especially in smaller towns, an ordinary penny post-card might be sent the rural mailing • 224 •

with copy imprinted: list, or to smaller surrounding towns "Come to (town) Sunday (then listing Sunday attractions)."

Several merchants ads are included on the card. . . a couple of small spaces on either side (perhaps a restaurant, hotel, drug store, garage) ...with business places cooperating in paying for cards and printing. 

460. PUSHMOBILE... An old automobile . . . with shafts placed behind it . . . and a horse or mule hitched behind so that the animal is pushing, instead of pulling the car. 

Banner with copy tieing in attraction. Probably especially adaptable to comedy or story dealing in comedy manner with automobiles. 

461. NO BULL... A costumed man leading a belled cow about town... the cow bannered: "This is no bull . . . (attraction) is funniest picture yet produced" (or copy suggested by attraction). 

The cow can be even placed on a truck, banners on the truck carrying the copy. 

462. DIXIE... Southern story background suggests use of bales of cotton (real or imitation) and banjo-playing darkies. 

Display panels can depict southern scene-hanging moss, magnolias, girls in crinoline costumes, steamboats on the river (shadowboxed river scene can picture a steamboat which has a practical paddle-wheel on the back, which turns in a concealed trough of water). 

Patriotic organizations may lend their support, perhaps attending on a special night which is dedicated to them. Band or orchestra can play "Dixie" before showing of attraction.

Southern songs featured over radio stations; and singer with leading orchestra might sing "Dixie," dedicating it to the attraction. 

Southern flag might be displayed. Relics and souvenirs of the 

South might be used for window display. 

Book stores and libraries can feature books which have a Southern locale. Essay contest based on southern history might be arranged in schools. 

463. WHISPERING CAMPAIGN... Theatre staff whisper ing a word about a coming attraction to each patron entering the theatre. First the cashier as she sells the tickets, then the doorman, then the usher as he seats the patron. 

Trailer on the attraction can begin with "s-h-h-" copy, and request "Keep it a secret, but (attraction) is coming." Or voice over sound system, or recorded with trailer, might whisper copy on attraction at beginning of trailer. 

464. TREADMILL... A treadmill unit might be available and adaptable to window or lobby flash; or one might be constructed • 225 •

In use, display panels would extend from the bottom to slightly above (several inches) the tread. "Mill" (continuous belt of slats, on rollers), horizontal, is motor-driven . . . or constructed at a slant, weight of person walking on it drives it. Made the center of a display on the attraction, and featuring action suggested by the story, couple might appear walking together, or soldiers marching, or sprinter running, or man following or chasing a girl . . . or whatever story suggests. In a window and featuring a costumed girl, panels can carry copy: "She's on her way to (theatre) to see (attraction)” ... or a small sign made up after style of roadside direction arrows might point straight ahead, carrying copy: "To (theatre) and (attraction)." 

465. POWDER . . . Small envelopes, for distribution, are imprinted: "Vanishing Powder," with copy to the effect that troubles will vanish "if you sprinkle the powder about. . . then go see (attraction) at (theatre)." Or, imprint: "A Breath of Sweetest Romance (and into copy on attraction)” . . . placing scented powder (ordinary talcum) inside the envelopes. Similarly, "magic herbs" envelopes would contain green tea. 

466. BANNER FROM BUILDING Banner might be unrolled for an eye-catching stunt, from the top (or an upper window) of a prominently located building... preferably after some action or music suggested by the attraction. . . as, a man in uniform appearing and blowing a bugle (or a group of buglers), then another uniformed man permitting the lettered banner to swiftly unroll (banner being rolled from bottom, held securely at top . . . nothing at bottom of banner to tear loose, though cross-strip of wood might be used at top to aid in holding it straight). After banner remains in view for several minutes, it is drawn up, rewound, and the stunt repeated. ...

Or, instead of bugles, two men dressed as sailors might signal with flags to each other from tops of building . . . one of them permitting banner to unroll after sufficient attention has been attracted. 

Man with trumpet might play chorus of hit tune from attraction, after which the banner is unrolled. Etc. 

Variation would have several persons stationed at prominent corner staring and pointing to an upper window; others will stop and stare too; sufficient attention attracted, banner is unrolled. 

467. MEN'S STORES. . . Photograph of male star of theatre's attraction might be used by men's store to illustrate a newspaper ad or mailing piece... with mention of attraction included. 

Window displays might feature articles named after star, or • 226 •

dedicated to star of theatre's attraction: gloves, hats, neckties, shirts, shoes... with display stuff on attraction included in the display. 

Picture of girl in attraction might be adapted for ad or window use by using copy: "If (name) were buying a gift for her sweetheart, she would certainly include (article)." 

468. WASHING . . . Company selling washing machines might feature a machine in their windows, together with copy: "You'll save enough time with a (name) machine to see (attraction and theatre)." Copy on attraction completes the display. Washing machine distributor might buy newspaper ads, using scene from attraction for illustration. Copy might call the attraction a "cleanup in laughs."

Novelty herald could have a clothes-pin attached, herald carrying copy: "Wash Day is Abolished! Girls Leave Home! Boys too. . .

They're all going to (theatre) to see (attraction)." Company selling washing machines might cooperate on the cost of the heralds, including copy to the effect that their machine has abolished washday, made it possible to enjoy leisure by witnessing (attraction copy). 

469. FAN CLUBS... Many stars have fan clubs (organized groups of admirers), dedicated to them throughout the country. 

Members are enthusiastic supporters of any attraction in which star appears, and should be contacted. Or, a local club might be "organized" (perhaps with cooperation of newspaper or radio station). They should be asked to tell their friends about the attraction. 

470. ISMS... When a star is known for his bright remarks or witty sayings, illustrations might be used by newspaper as feature, carrying a "saying," or home-spun philosophy attributed to star under the illustration. 

Newspaper contest might be featured under heading: "I wish I'd said that," with contestants to submit their favorite quotations and their authors, and reasons for selection. "Sayings," or well known expressions of famous screen and radio stars could be scattered through the ads in a classified page tieup . . . with space on page devoted to attraction and offering tickets to first so-many persons locating all the quotations, naming the person identified with each. 

471. WHAT'S WRONG HERE... Scenes from attraction, in which items that are definitely out of line are shown, might be made the basis of a newspaper contest . . . as scene showing ancient Romans, one of whom is pictured smoking a pipe; or otherwise introducing • 227 •

some modern device into a scene where it would be out of place or historically incorrect. Artist can adapt stills on the attraction, adding the articles as inconspicuously as possible . . . with contestants to attempt to pick out the mistake and to describe it in rhyme. 

Or newspaper feature might use drawings made up from stills on theatre's attraction, but with as many errors included as is possible. 

Drawings could be carried as a series of daily contests in paper, with tickets for first so-many correct lists of errors. 

472. HARVEST... September or October could be desig nated as "Harvest Month," calling attention to the "Harvest of Hits" to be shown by theatre during that period. 

Displays might feature actual farm produce, pumpkins, shocks of corn, etc. Giant papier mache cornucopia, or horn of plenty, can be made the center of a display, with the produce pouring from the horn, together with panels carrying titles of coming attractions. 

Merchant cooperation might be arranged, perhaps with cooperation of local Chamber of Commerce, inaugurating a city-wide "Harvest Month," with stores carrying "harvest" idea in their ads and window displays. Selection of a "Harvest Queen," with aid of merchants, might be a feature (see No. 50, No. 533). 

473. SCRAP BOOK... Prepared "scrap book;" can be placed on a spotlighted pedestal or small table (to which it is attached) in drug store and other business place. Panel which completes the display invites patrons to look through star's "(Name of attraction) Scrap Book."

The "scrap book," any type of book which is attractive in appearance and sufficiently large, carries name of attraction lettered on front cover, and inner pages are given over to clippings of stories on attraction (from fan magazines, newspapers, press-books), and stills of scenes from the attraction. 

474. GIRL AND AUTO... Adaptable to almost any attraction with title that in any way refers to a girl or uses a girl's name a flashy open automobile being secured, top back, and neat sign carried on each side. Uniformed chauffeur drives the car; and attractive girl (of type suggested by attraction) rides in back seat. 

475. DOGS. . . Attraction featuring a dog, or start of a serial, or a show especially appealing to kids, might suggest a "pet matinee," or a "dog matinee," for the kids perhaps with cooperation of newspaper. ...

Some promoted prize (perhaps an ice cream cone, or candy) might be offered to every kid bringing a dog to the theatre at a specified • 228 •

time, before theatre opens, and sufficiently early for them to take their dogs or pets home again. Prizes should be offered for best looking dog, homeliest dog, smartest dog, funniest dog.

A dog show might be promoted locally; or cooperation with a dog show might be possible; with special "blue ribbon," from the canine star of attraction, for the winner. Dog, led about streets by an attractive girl, could be wearing a lettered dog blanket. Basis of a contest with pup as a prize could be submitted letters telling "why 

I want (name of dog)." Or, naming of the dog; with reasons for name selection. Dog being awarded "with compliments of (star)." "Me and My Dog" snapshots may be made basis of contest with best snaps of kids and their dogs winning tickets. 

476. COLOR SPOTLIGHT. . . Securing use of a powerful searchlight first, a series of teaser ads break in the papers . . as, "If the light is Blue, SHE will be at City Hall," or, "If the light is Red, SHE will be at (streets)" finishing the series with, "If the light is White, SHE will be at (theatre).” 

On opening night of attraction, a white searchlight sweeps through the skies from top of a downtown building . . . periodically illuminating a large banner which is unfurled from top of another building, the banner carrying copy: "SHE'S at the (theatre). . . (star) of (attraction)." Or, light might be placed atop theatre marquee, with ads announcing that if light picks out a person on the sidewalk that person will receive guest tickets. 

477. AIR CIRCUS... In connection with an aviation show possibly presenting trophy, named after attraction or star in some contest. Tieup might be made with newspaper and radio station for their sponsorship, and for publicity . . . and possibly with charitable organization, which will receive the returns of a collection to be taken up at the airport (charity organization might be newspaper's sponsored charity). Pilots at airport should supply the show on the strength of the large numbers of people attracted to the airport, many of whom will spend money there. "Air Show" should be staged in advance of opening of theatre attraction, and preferably on a holiday or on Sunday, and in the forenoon, so that it does not interfere with regular matinee attendance at theatre. Flyers should present various stunts and aerial acrobatics. Added interest might be drawn to newspaper stories, by asking for a local girl to make a parachute jump (not permitting her, in case she volunteers, to jump; sheriff or her parents might stop her). Amplification equipment might be used, announcements made during the air show, plugging · 229 •

theatre attraction. Sky-writer might perform. Though especially adaptable to air story, an air show might be staged in connection with any sort of attraction; or in connection with welcome ceremonies greeting arrival of star by plane at airport. Flying organizations may cooperate in arranging the air show. 

478. VALENTINE... If attraction plays near St. Valentine's 

Day (or, if story suggests), display panels might be made up Valentine style. Window displays can be arranged, with still from attraction featured as the center of a large valentine. 

Newspaper could feature photos of stars as center of drawn valentine designs, with contest based on best submitted valentine inscriptions in rhyme to accompany the photograph. Comic valentine idea might be followed out for comedy stars. 

Patrons might be invited to sign giant valentine, on display in lobby, to be sent star of Valentine Day attraction. Carries photo of star, and copy. 

479. BETTER FILMS... Support of Better Films Council and other organizations can prove invaluable in connection with a high-type film attraction. Their membership might be contacted; they might make announcements at a meeting of their members; and their membership might actively sponsor the local showing, perhaps selling tickets on a percentage basis. They can aid in securing school support on an educational feature, and securing support of women's clubs. They might supply a mailing list of members, to whom letters can be directed. 

480. MR. SHAKESPEARE ... Appeal should be made to 

Shakespearean societies, schools, colleges, in connection with an attraction based on a Shakespearean play. All educational organizations will gladly lend their support. Better films organizations and women's clubs will be glad to help. 

Sponsorship committee might be organized well in advance, with members meeting at a tea, discussing plans for showing of the attraction. In addition to lending their support, they, or some socially important local club might sponsor the sale of tickets on the opening night, on a percentage basis, assuring the attendance of the town's socially elect in formal attire. A socially prominent group might act as "ushers" (Junior League or debutantes), on opening night. 

Broadcast from lobby should be featured, with prominents being introduced. Society editor should be present to jot down names of those attending, noting the costumes of the ladies. Roto page layout in papers and editorial comment is a possibility. • 230 •

Schools might base a study period on the particular play that has been filmed; or they might allow credits for those students who witness it. They could further cooperate in advising their students to see the attraction. An authority on Shakespeare could appear before school assemblies and clubs, especially women's clubs, speaking about Shakespeare and about the attraction. Schools might sponsor an essay contest on the influence of Shakespeare on every day English. 

Schools may even permit students a half holiday that they might see the attraction. Superintendent of schools should lend his endorsement, and if he does, it should pave the way toward wholehearted cooperation from all school heads. 

481. VOTES, ELECTION 

.. Around election time, or if story concerns an election, small envelope heralds might be imprinted: "A Reward for Your Vote!" Inside envelope is printed slip, reading: "For greater entertainment as your reward, vote for (and into attraction copy)." Or, heralds may be made up to resemble ballots and election cards. 

Campaign cards, similar to those circulated by candidates might be printed, carrying photo of star, and copy: ("Star) is content with his status as king of comedians (or whatever 'title' is suitable), and is not running for the office of (office for which election is being held)." 

See (star) in (attraction). Only words set in large type are "(Star's name) for (office)". . . balance of copy being set in smallest available up-and-lower, so that at first glance only the large type is read. 

Added election angle could be use of "electioneer" going through a "campaign" speech, after the manner of regular political speaker, possibly from back seat of open car which is stopped at busy intersections. "Speech" should be brief, humorous, and calling attention to theatre's attraction. Attractive girls pass out "campaign cards" or heralds. Car appropriately bannered. "Electioneer" might be used as barker out front. 

482. "CLOSED" CARDS. . . Printed cards, large enough to be read at a glance, carry copy: "Closed. Gone to see (attraction) at (theatre), and are attached to the doors of business places on holidays or Sundays, or late on the evening preceeding. 

Cards imprinted at an angle, with perforation in top corner so that they can be attached with string to the door. 

483. HOTEL CLERKS, BELL BOYS, TAXI DRIVERS... 

Can be of much value if they are boosting for the theatre. An occasional complimentary ticket might prove a valuable investment. 

484. OUT OF FRAME Specially made up trailer has 

... • 231 •

first "flash" (which merely shows reproduction of a still from a coming attraction) out of frame. Running out of frame for about ten seconds the next flash appears in frame and carries copy: "Please pardon us... We're all excited . . . we just heard about a great show that's been booked for this theatre." Next flash carries copy: "You can see for yourself... Look at these scenes...' Follow immediately with regular trailer. 99 

485. LOVE BIRDS AND CANARIES... Cage containing two love birds and two, or more, canaries, can be used as center of an effective window display, possibly in pet store, or store handling birds.

A letter is attached on the front of each bird (a small tag, placed over their heads), spelling out (together) attraction title or star's name (which must be brief).

Tickets are offered those witnessing the birds in line in correct order to spell out the specified word.

Birds are lettered, however, so that for correct spelling, the love birds would have to be placed on either end. Love birds will not permit the canaries to come between them, and consequently they never get in correct order. 

486. HANDKERCHIEFS... If they can be secured cheaply enough, handkerchiefs can be imprinted (with either "move you to tears," or "laugh 'til you cry" copy), and distributed to ladies in advance. Or, instead of imprinting, small stickers might be attached. Or, paper handkerchiefs or napkins might be imprinted and used instead of actual handkerchiefs. 

487. MOTHER-IN-LAW... Jovial looking man walks down street between pretty girl and grim looking woman. He hands out cards that carry imprint: "I just saw (attraction), and even with my mother-in-law along, I enjoyed it." And he can carry the same copy on his back. 

488. WEDDING INVITATION... Herald imprinted after the style of a regular wedding invitation, copy calls attention to "Wedding of Mirth and Romance;" or, in connection with attraction that features a wedding in title or story, calling attention to the screen wedding.

Herald might be modeled after a marriage license; or a marriage license reproduced, using names of characters in story. . . overprinting, "Warning! See (attraction) first." 

489. LADDER . . . Couple of girls, carrying a not-too-long ladder about town will attract attention. . . stopping on important • 232

corners, and placing ladder against building, one of them climbing the ladder, permits a banner to unroll (other girl seizing and holding other end of banner) . . . the "banner" carrying copy: "We've got to get 

UP Early Tomorrow... (star) is coming to town. . . in (attraction)." 

490. SELECTING BEST... Sports page readers might be invited to select eleven best football players, or best baseball players, with their reason for each selection. Or, in connection with showing of musical, ten best song hits, either of the year, or of all time, might be selected. Or best radio entertainers or stage stars. 

Whatever the angle in the attraction some "best" is suggested and can be made the basis of a tieup, newspaper mentioning theatre's attraction in all stories, with tickets for winning selections. 

491. STREET PAGEANT... Ambitious plans might in clude promotion of a street pageant which is designed to promote business of stores as well as theatre's attractions, with different gaily decorated floats entered in a parade, and other celebration. 

Products of the section might be used as a theme in the parade (as peaches, or cotton, or flowers). Pretty girls ride on the floats, or march or skate along line of march in costumes. 

Block in which theatre is located might be roped off for an hour, for street dancing, and ceremonies in front of theatre, which are broadcast, including speech by officials. Prizes might be presented for most attractive costumes, prettiest girls. 

Previously selected "queen" of the festivities might "arrive," to start the festivities... coming via boat, plane or automobile. Several dances might be arranged, at which she presides. She could be crowned on theatre stage, her princesses introduced (from various clubs, who select the girls to represent them). 

Parade and street action should terminate early, with program at theatre scheduled to follow immediately. 

492. HOLLYWOOD... Studio background might suggest selection of a proxy for the star (No. 887); selection of "(town's) 

Own Movie Queen," who will serve as movie queen for a day (No. 

286); Impersonation contest (No. 172); "Hollywood premier” (No. 11). Main street renamed "Hollywood Boulevard" for a day (No. 371). Float, traveling about downtown section, might feature movie studio setup, with cameras focused on a couple of pretty girls. 

Hollywood Ball (See 79), and Beauty Contests (50). 

493. RUBBER BANDS... Even rubber bands (wider type), might be bought in quantity and imprinted. Distributed in offices, stores, brokerage offices, banks and business places. • 233 •

494. NEWSPAPER SERIAL... Can often be planted for newspaper space, and are available on many pictures (story of attrac tion written in a series of chapters, or episodes). 

If serial isn't available, a very acceptable serial can be arranged by selecting stills which carry the story along in correct sequence, having the paper carry one or several each day (in advance) with brief synopsis of that part of the story under each illustration. 

Final episode should not tell too much of the finish of the story. 

Using weekly papers, several chapters might be combined. Serial can even be added to heralds which are regularly distributed, perhaps imprinting on reverse side. 

495. CHECKING THROUGH THE STILLS 

Radio program featuring boy and girl, who look through a set of photographs on a coming attraction, describing the pictured scenes in their enthusiastic comment. Music, songs, announcements complete the program. ... 

496. ACTION . . . Attraction might suggest or portray a stunt that might be safely duplicated locally . . . with assurance of newspaper stories. Check story details. 

497. NERO... Dressed in flowing Roman robes and sandals, and wearing a wreath, a big tough-looking fellow sits as center of a lobby or window display, and plays a fiddle. Display panel carries copy: "The Hottest Event Since the Burning of Rome"... and copy on attraction.

In window, amplification might carry the "music" and occasional remarks of "Nero" to outside window. He should be able to clown the stunt for laughs. 

498. SCALES 

...

Wherever scales are placed, theatre or store, an attached display on attraction might offer tickets, or star photographs, to those whose weight is exactly the same as star's (whose weight is given). Using a scale that prints the weight on a small ticket, certain tickets might be stamped, and these winning. 

Novel adaption might offer tickets for boy or girl weighing, together, a specified amount... boy to pick up girl, weighing together. 

Novel adaption of "weigh yourself" scale stunt for lobby, has different face made up for pointer-type scale, with divided spaces (all over 85 pound mark on scales) lettered with catchy lines, or lines suggested by the attraction . . . as, "Good to her Mother," "Sweet and Simple," "Beautiful and not so Dumb," "Movies, and then Straight Back Home." Tickets for certain spaces. 

499. PLAY. . . Attraction based on famous play, or story 

• 234 •

that features writing of a play, might be used as basis for a contest, via newspaper or radio, for best locally written play . . . which might later be enacted by Little Theatre players, or other group, on stage, or over radio station. "Playwright" might "set up" in a store window, with his typewriter, display panels in window announcing that, "inspired" by attraction, he intends to write a play in a specified number of hours, to enter in the contest. Window amplification can be used. 

Letters can be sent literary clubs; educational groups might be interested. Copies of old plays, and old programs from presentations of famous old plays might be secured and used for window display. 

500. FEATURE PAGES. . . Newspapers regularly use prepared feature stories . . . which consume several columns; or in 

Sunday papers and magazine sections, occasionally a full page. 

If the stories are prepared in advance, they should be newsy, interesting. Most papers will prefer to prepare features themselves, using material submitted. Rotogravure pages, if featured by Sunday edition, might use photographs of stars, or girls in show. Perhaps paper will carry a large photograph, "suitable for framing," of star. 

Amusement pages will, of course, regularly use scene stills if they are interesting; newspaper will generally bring out an art layout page on one day, at least, of the week, which features illustrations and stories on week's attractions at theatre. 

501. BROADCAST WINDOW Layout and style of regular broadcast station is duplicated in a store window. Microphone is connected through amplification equipment with speakers placed outside window. "Announcers" to introduce talent, make announcements. Song hits from picture are presented. Stage show talent can be introduced. Announcer continuously tells about attraction, attracting the attention of those passing the window. 

With cooperation of radio station, actual broadcast from the window might be arranged.

Using amplification equipment, and with telephone company cooperation (small towns), or by running lines, a "broadcast" from a window “studio" (or from "studio” in theatre building), might be carried into prominent restaurants, stores, or other locations. 

502. 1089 ... Write down three figures, then reverse same and subtract the smaller figures from the larger three figures, leaving a three-figured remainder... then reverse the remainder, and add these new figures to the remainder and the total will be 1089, never varying. 

Based on this mathematical trick, tickets might be offered to those • • 235 •

A O following instructions and working out the problem to a different total. Adaptable to lobby or window; or used on a radio program. 

Or carried on heralds or programs. 

503. REACTIONS... Tickets, through radio or newspaper, are offered for best submitted "reactions" to an attraction. Naturally those wishing to send in their opinion of the show will first prefer to see it. Might ask contestants to submit reasons "why they like (star of attraction)," or to tell what they like best in the show. 

504. WRECK . Theme of attraction, or title, might suggest use of a wrecked automobile. Could be secured from a garage, and placed on display in front of theatre. Or, in prominent spot about town. Or, mounted aboard a truck, which tours town. 

Banners carry copy: "The driver was in a hurry (or going too fast) to see (attraction) at (theatre)." Or, "Drive Carefully to (theatre), to see (attraction)."

Cooperation of newspaper, automobile dealers, boy scouts, might be secured in a "Drive Safely" week, tieing in attraction. Parade may be arranged, with band, a wrecked car on a bannered truck, and theatre advertising. (See No. 964.) 

505. TRADE PAPER ADS. . . Attractive display ads on attractions, in the trade papers, often offer effective angles and copy for newspaper ads. Occasionally, too, they are excellent for lobby panels or for "blow-ups." The best advertising brains in the business prepare these ads, and they are generally very effective. 

506. AUTOMOBILE DEALERS... Local distributors of automobiles will generally cooperate in any reasonable publicity effort, participating gladly in parades, street stunts. 

Introducing new models, dealer could place an automobile on display in theatre lobby. . . buying large newspaper space which sells theatre's attraction (repaying theatre for the display), as well as calling attention to car. Elaborating on lobby display, and if space permits, a lobby "Auto Show" might be presented . . . perhaps competing with a regular automobile show (at some other local point), placing several models in lobby, automobile dealer or dealers buying newspaper space, radio announcements, and supplying several entertainers (who could also broadcast from the lobby). 

Midget car, or automobile of unusual design, would attract attention on the street, bannered with theatre copy. Pretty girls as passengers. 

507. ICE ON RIVER... Near much traveled bridge, might 

• 236

offer a great spot to stretch a weighted and tied-down banner, or to arrange display of large cutout letters. 

Or, twenty-four sheets are actually posted on the ice, using a number of them, blanketing a strategic point. 

508. NEIGHBORHOODS... Sound trucks, floats and other travelling displays should include neighborhood centers . . . small groups of stores, isolated "business districts." Heralds and other advertising should also be distributed in these residence sections. 

Neighborhood theatres can cooperate closely with community organizations to their advantage. Community paper might prove of value, and small program listing should be carried in city daily papers. Manager should visit with owners of individual business places in the neighborhood, discussing mutual problems. 

Important that neighborhood operator know personally as many of his patrons as possible. He might even call on a certain number of residents each day, visiting, leaving a pass. Small amplification set might be arranged on automobile which travels neighboring streets daily announcing programs. Heralds, distributed throughout drawing radius, are important. 

509. SIDE SHOW For "side show" story, or circus attraction, real "side show banners" with the usual painted figures and eloquent copy might be secured or duplicated. Perhaps real freaks or entertainers (magicians, dancers, contortionists, barker, singers) may be enlisted for a brief periodic sidewalk ballyhoo. 

510. SCOOP . . . Herald idea for use in connection with a competition of some sort in which there is much interest . as a championship prizefight: Two sets of tabloid-style heralds being prepared in advance . . . with one set carrying bold headlines, photograph, and story on victory of one of the fighters, the other set announcing the other fighter as the winner. Rest of copy devoted to attraction. When fight ends, a group of boys are turned loose, running the papers about town shouting "Extra" and handing the papers to everyone they see (the correct set; the others are destroyed). 

They might even be distributed at scene of the fight, if it is local, where out-going crowds will be amazed by the appearance of a paper so soon. 

511. MERMAID . . . Using a large circular goldfish bowl, a girl or a display might be made to appear within it. Display placed back of the bowl (upside down, unless close, as the bowl reverses it). 

A person placed back of the bowl, as part of a display, might be made to appear within the bowl, and right-side-up, by using three large • 237 ·

EN CY C L O P E DIA OF EXPLOIT A TI O N 

mirrors: lower mirror (below bowl), being placed at 45° angle, facing girl. . . . reflecting into horizontal top mirror . . . from which third mirror (angled, and between the two, reflects into bowl, which is filled with water). Much experimentation is required in focusing and placing mirrors. Person would be concealed within an enclosure, brightly lighted. Electric fan blowing hair will add to underwater illusion. Place goldfish in bowl, water to be changed frequently. 

Window shade might be added inside enclosure so that girl (who may be briefly costumed) can conceal view until posed. 

512. OPEN LETTERS... Newspaper ads might be headed: 

"Open Letter to Mayor (or other prominent person or official)." (And preferably with his consent.) "Letter" calls special attention to reasons why Mayor should see or endorse the attraction.

Or "letter" merely urges Mayor to take time out to see the show, even though he is busily engaged in managing city's affairs. 

513. CHARITY BALL 

In tieup with newspaper, a ball named after theatre's attraction, as “(star, or attraction title) Ball" may be arranged... with profits to go to newspaper's selected charity. 

Cooperation of ballroom is essential. 

Committee of local prominents might aid in arranging details. 

Ball might be made a costume affair (with the dancers invited to wear costumes suggested by the attraction). Prizes for the best costumes; and photos of winners should make newspaper columns. 

514. CHARITY SHOW... Periodically newspapers engage in drives for their milk funds, and Christmas funds; or for the relief of some distress or disaster. Aid of theatre in arranging a show for the benefit of the fund will result in added goodwill as well as generous mention of theatre and attraction. 

Special midnight show might be arranged, perhaps showing screen attraction which is set to open soon at theatre with percentage to go to fund (attraction must definitely be pleasing, so that the audience which attends the special showing will praise it, urge their friends to see it). Or, outstanding screen attraction which has already played secured gratis from exchange. Employees donate services. 

Night clubs, hotel ballrooms, radio stations, orchestras-all might be combed for talent for the benefit show. Even wrestlers and boxers could be used (in an "exhibition"). An orchestra or several orchestras may volunteer.

Morning benefit show, aimed to appeal to kids and their parents, might be presented at theatre. Exchanges should contribute old cartoons, comedies, perhaps an old feature. Small admission is 238

charged, receipts to go to newspaper's fund. Trailer on theatre's regular attraction should be included on benefit shows. 

515. OLD TIMES... With attraction dated in years gone by, and if it is advantageous to call attention to the time of the story, perhaps relics of that day might be secured for display. Classified ad may bring to light a few souvenirs of days gone by, either cos tumes or articles. (See No. 228.) 

Costumes of the period might be worn by heavily moustached men and buxom women. "Old Time Dance," or "Bowery Ball" could be staged with public invited to wear costumes of that day, with prize for best.

Old tin-types, clothes, bathing suits, family albums, old fashioned stereoscope (with patrons invited to take a look, with scenes from attraction to focus on), could be made part of a display; mementos of another day, old jewelry, photographs of old landmarks, old pictures of downtown streets might be used for window or lobby (locked show cases, or watched). Old hansom cab, or a hurdy-gurdy, might be secured for street use, properly bannered. Perhaps old files of local newspaper carry back to date of attraction story . . . and newspaper might reproduce a picture of one of these as a feature, or permit them to be placed on display in their windows or a store window. 

Radio station should feature a medley of old tunes, dedicated to attraction. 

516. YELLING, WHISTLING... Where star of attraction has a peculiar "yell" or a saying, a contest might be based on best rendition of a similar yell or expression, or whistle. Staged for kids at playgrounds; or at theatre kid club or Saturday matinee, on stage or out front. Or, contest can be similarly staged, at night clubs or dance spots, with adults competing. Radio might broadcast the "contest."

Kids yelling to each other across the street will attract attention with the topic of their conversation being theatre's attraction. 

517. FRONTS. . . The theatre's show window, the front, requires special consideration, constant attention. If the theatre is centrally located the front displays are very important. 

Display frames should be neat, painted, attractive. (See 170.) 

Stills should be carefully considered. (See 85.)

Where constructed fronts (made of paneled compo-board, painted, lettered), are used, many novel and attractive designs might be employed-including cutout letters, cutout figures, boxed panels; the only limitations being the artist's inventiveness, ability, imagi- 239 •

nation-and the budget. Usually, the attraction will suggest an idea or design for a front.

Panels are built of compo-board backed up with one by two frames. 

Must be tailored to fit front of theatre, sidewalk slant, and variations in the design of building front. Where panels angle together they can be attached with nails, or more quickly, by use of pin-hinges. 

Ordinary screen door hook can be used to anchor display panels against wall or building (from behind). Molding will add a finished effect to a front. Theatre should have several sets of panels, so that while one is in use, others are being washed and painted. Beaverboard panels painted with water colors will stand numerous washings. 

One of the most important pieces of equipment in the art shop is a cut-awl, using it to make cutout letters, cutout figures, and to cut wood, compo-board, or pressed wood in desired designs. Attraction sign "stencils" can be made up effectively, using a cut-awl-(panels to replace glass letters ordinarily used in attraction sign, copy being cut into compo-board panels, openings backed up with cloth or paper). 

If locally permissible an overhead panel suspended under marquee (perhaps about four by ten), constructed as light as possible, using one by two frames, faced with beaver-board, will draw attention from either direction.

Separate cutout letters used for front displays, cut from compoboard or two-inch insulite, if regularly made the same size and design, can be kept and repainted and used again. Insulite letters, cut with a band-saw at the mill, from design tracings are always effective. 

Third-dimensional constructed letters, built of compo-board over a constructed frame-work, can be effectively used for brief titles. 

Cutout figures painted on compo-board, or lithographs mounted on compo-board and cutout, can be attached against front panels, effectiveness being increased if they are raised on blocks instead of being attached flat against display panels. Lights might be placed behind cutouts. Blow-ups or enlargements of photographs, can be mounted on beaver-board, cut out and used. Enlargements might be used to face large cutout letters that spell out attraction title. 

Or, letters might be faced with mirrors, which are attached with LePage's glue. Small spotlight, using color-wheel could be focused on mirror-covered letters. 

Animation, any kind of movement, can add tremendously to the effectiveness of a front display. Cutout figures can be made to move as suggested by attraction (see No. 48). Most attractions will suggest some sort of mechanical movement. Live animation can • 240

occasionally be used effectively. As, a dancer, or musicians; or, in connection with a jungle attraction "live savages," marked up with war-paint, clothed in skins, beating tom-toms. Girls might swing on a trapeze under canopy in connection with a circus attraction. (See Designs.)

Some miscellaneous suggestions can include: 

Neon used to outline title letters, or a figure, or a design. Tinted shades of cellophane occasionally used to cover stills. Frames for stills wrapped in tin-foil. Compo-board frames for stills, made up in designs suggested by the attraction. Stills might be mounted on beaver-board, with edges beveled and painted for good effect. 

Stills can be compo-board mounted and cut out, beveled, with edges painted, and attached to posters or panels. Display heads and panels using flitter entirely—“painting" the displays by applying desired colors of metallics (no paint at all); color-wheel might be used. (See Photos.)

Display panel, or section of same, might be made of translucent glass, lighted from behind. Copy can be lettered directly on the glass, or, cutout letters, covered over with black flitter, are attached directly to the glass, using glue. Or, glass can be used to silhouette a figure . . . as a figure of a dancing girl cut from a display panel, opening backed up with glass, illuminated from behind the panel. 

Oilcloth can be used to cover a paneled front display instead of paint, either for a single front display—or for permanently covering over panels, and attaching cutout letters and figures and stills each time attraction changes.

Title might be spelled out on a display panel in stills. Actual newspaper headlines used as background for panel displays if appropriate. Blinking eyes on marquee or lobby panel (in some instances, effective)—the eyes in the display being cut out and replaced with sign cloth, upon which the eyes are painted, lights on flashers being placed behind the "eyes;" or, using mounted lithographs the compoboard might be removed from behind the eyes. Or, eyes animated, made to roll or to move from side to side. Display panels for small frames can be painted on glass, using water-color, afterwards washing the glass (saving cost of cardboard). 

A panel, or an enlarged illustration, might be effectively encircled with lights . . . sockets wired into the panel, and connected into marquee flashers, so that they appear to travel around the display. 

A series of lights (sockets wired into display) might be arranged to light up, one globe after another, in succession until all are lighted. • 241 •

ENCYCLOPEDIA EXPLOITATION 

O F Each socket is connected with a terminal which is in sequence with other contact terminals; across these contact terminals a copper slide is driven by a small motor, making contact as it traverses the contacts, then being drawn back and repeated. Or a revolving drum might make and break the contacts with "fingers" (the contacts) playing against it. (See photo section for design.)

With illuminated front display, lights under marquee might be connected on dimmers, mechanically driven, dimming down so that only lighted displays are illuminated, then dimming up again. 

Figures on an endless belt, motor-driven, can bring into view a series of appropriate figures. Only top part of belt is visible, of course, showing figures attached to the belt in upright position. Or, background (painted on a motor-driven endless belt) can be made to race past a cutout display, making the stationary cutout figure appear to be traveling.

Endless belt can be made to bring stills into view behind an opening. (See Designs.) Or revolving wheel, or circular panel, to the edges of which stills are attached (behind the display), brings stills into view through an opening. 

518. MARATHON 

With automobiles featured, a "marathon driver," sponsored by automobile dealer and theatre, and perhaps also by newspaper, would win attention. Announced as "inspired" by theatre's attraction, marathon driver is "officially" started by some visiting or local celebrity, newspaper according the stunt daily stories. Prize is offered anyone finding the driver stopped for more than half a minute (he can rock the car back and forth when stopped by traffic or stop light). Banners should be attached to the car. Arrangements should be made with a restaurant to feed the driver (in the car, in front of restaurant, as he "rocks" the car). (Arrangements must be made, too, for some secret place where car and driver can be concealed at night, so that the driver might get some sleep. Perhaps a garage). Other business places might cooperate, mentioning stunt in their ads, with the "endurance driver" stopping regularly in front of their business places. 

Might be possible to secure a girl driver instead of a man. She might wear a mask, and her identity kept a secret until she is unmasked on stage or at ballroom or in show window, or in front of theatre, on opening day.

Should arrange to have a nurse "in attendance" during the drive, or at theatre where the driver regularly "stops." And furniture • 242 •

store can have bed prepared in window (and announced in advance), where driver rests after completion of the "ordeal." 

Driver might be dressed picturesquely, perhaps suggested by the attraction. Newspaper could sell a page of cooperative ads, with enduranceer stopping at business places that buy ads. Newspaper stories are, of course, essential to the success of the stunt; or radio broadcasts which might be arranged at regular intervals from front of theatre. And attraction must be mentioned each time.

Driver might be given a name suggested by the stunt, or applying especially to the attraction. Might be called "Enduro." Or, (city's) Mysterious Masked (name suggested by attraction).”

Instead of a straight endurance drive, public might be merely invited to estimate number of miles the car will travel in a designated number of days.

Same marathon idea might be adapted to a bike-rider. Or other means of locomotion. Bike-rider could cruise the streets, or he might be set up in a store window or atop canopy, pedaling-or even atop an automobile, with the bicycle securely attached, using guy-wires, so that "rider" can pedal.

Bike-rider can terminate the stunt with a challenge to all comers to race him on opening day of attraction, with cash prize to winner should he lose, and tickets to any others. Motorcycle escort for the race might be arranged.

Marathon of any kind should, of course, terminate before opening or on opening day of attraction. 

Window or lobby "marathon" used several days in advance of opening, could feature several bikes set up as center of a display ... the bikes being placed on slight elevation and attached securely. 

Pretty girls in brief costumes (sweaters and shorts) ride the bikes, one resting at all times (on lounge, or settee) while others ride. 

Attraction might suggest some sort of "marathon" exhibition. 

519. AERIAL ADVERTISING... Aerial advertising, writing the name of theatre's attraction across the sky, could include a plane towing a banner on which title of attraction is lettered. Banner should be 80 to 100 feet in length, and of light weight material; it is lettered (using lampblack) with large letters and brief wording. Or letters might be attached to a specially made net. Kite nose is used in flying banners, most airports being so equipped. Siren might be added to plane's equipment, to attract added attention. 

Autogyro, or new type plane, would draw more than ordinary attention. Use of glider might be adapted. • 243

Neon letters can be placed on the under wings of a plane for an effective night-time flash. Two sets of letters may be used, arranged to flash intermittently . . . showing attraction title in one flash, and theatre name in another . . . switch controlling the lights being operated by the pilot. (See Photos.)

Sky-writing (writing attraction title in smoke), is very effective if not too expensive. (Newspaper ads or radio broadcast announces: "Watch the skies tomorrow!") Someone at airport might have equipment. Or an amplification equipped plane, can make announcements over city and surrounding towns. Under side of wing might be lettered with attraction title, using water color. 

520. CHAIN TELEPHONING... Chain telephone calls, with the aid of theatre's employees, each of whom call five acquaintances, with brief message about theatre's attraction, asking each person called, to, in turn, call five more persons, with the request passed along. Or, instead of telephoning, the idea might be adapted to persons encountered on the street. With a women's club sponsoring or endorsing an attraction it might be requested that they put the chain telephone stunt into effect. Their membership, if sold on the idea, will keep the telephone company busy. 

521. DISTORTION MIRRORS... Distortion mirrors, the sort used in amusement parks, making reflected images appear thin or fat. Used in connection with a comedy attraction, in lobby or prominent location, attached panel might carry copy: "You'll have a smile this wide, when you see (attraction);" or perhaps the title of the attraction will suggest tieup copy for mirror. Mirrors may be obtained from an amusement park, or perhaps a glass company will have one of them.

Cards might be attached to the distortion mirrors in an amusement park... the card carrying copy: "After you've laughed at this, laugh at (attraction copy)."

Small pocket-size distortion mirrors are occasionally available at small cost in quantity. Imprinted sticker is attached in corner of each mirror, and mirrors are distributed in advance. "You'll have a smile this wide" copy can be used. 

522. SLEEPING GIRL... Attractive girl in bed in a furniture store or department store window, can have display cards carrying copy: "She's Resting . . . so that she might secure sufficient rest to withstand the terrific laughs (or thrills) in (attraction)." Or bed might be mounted on a truck . . . girl in bed, and banners on truck • 244 •

carrying the copy. Or card (for window use), can say: "Call me when (attraction) comes to town, I don't want to miss it." 

523. LIVE BABY ... Oldest of gags is announcing of the awarding on a certain night of a live baby, with the actual presentation of a squealing white baby pig, with the porker all dressed up in baby clothes.

Stunt for smaller town that might create talk would be advertising in classified columns of newspaper, or in display ads, for several "live babies," to use in a display . . . with actual display featuring live baby chicks... and with newspaper picking up the gag for a story. Panel could carry copy: "We heard that (attraction) is a show to crow about. . . and we want to begin early." 

524. VERSE ... Newspaper features a daily scene from attraction . . . with contestants asked to describe the scene in verse, or to submit a poem, or poetic quotation that best describes the scene. Or poems might be "inspired" by a certain attraction, or a season of the year (as Christmas verses), with theatre guest tickets for prizes. 

525. SNOW BANKS... And dirt banks alongside excavations in the street, offer "natural" spots for placing of cards attached to pieces of lathing, driven into the banks. Ordinary window cards can be used, perhaps back-to-back and visible in both directions. 

Large strategically located snow banks might be “lettered" with attraction title, using a flit-gun and water color. Might even be possible to attach banners to snow-plows. 

526. HAIRPIN HERALD Has hairpin attached, inserted in die-cut openings or glued, and is imprinted: "Pin Down your Hair! A great thrill (is coming into your life! (and attraction).” 

527. NEWSPAPER CIRCULATION . . . In a tieup with newspaper, and in return for an allotment of space on current attraction, guest tickets might be offered for each new subscription (for a limited time). Gratis space should more than repay theatre for guest tickets. Or, theatre party might be given those newsboys who bring in a couple of new subscriptions, with paper allotting space. 

528. EARLY NEW YEAR... A novel way to sell a series of coming attractions, at other season than the first of the year. 

Especially effective in summer or fall-trailers, newspaper ads, radio announcements, lobby displays carry copy modeled after regular New Year ads, (using illustrations that are ordinarily used at the first of the year and which newspapers can supply from their mat service). The "Happy New Year" angle is played up, but following • 245.

with copy that explains that it is a "New Show Year," beginning a year of great hits, etc., and following with listing of attractions. 

Cooperative advertising in newspapers could be based on the "New 

Year" angle. 

529. RADIO AMATEURS... Together with a business place or local manufacturer, which shares the expense and credits, theatre might sponsor an amateur program over local radio station . . . broadcasting weekly programs in which amateur entertainers compete for prizes. Tickets presented all contestants, mentioning attraction.

Announcements might be secured on a regularly established radio amateur hour, by entering an "amateur," who "imitates" star of theatre's coming attraction (and who mentions both star and the attraction). (Perhaps arranged in advance with program sponsor.) 

530. GOOD MORNING CARDS . . . Cards attached to section of stiff wire or laths, and (early in the morning) placed on the lawns of residences facing towards the house. 

Copy: "Good Morning! May we call your attention to (attraction)." 

531. TABLOID... Heralds might be effectively made up after style of regular tabloid, as to size and layout, featuring photographs and flashy headlines. Tab-herald might be distributed by boys crying "Extra!" Might be inserted in newspapers or magazines. 

532. GOLD DIGGERS. . . Attractions featuring girls of the type called "gold diggers" (good time girls who are after the $'s), would suggest emphasis on the "Gold" in displays, using gold flitter, gold paper and cloth, and gold neon. ...

Attractive float might be adorned with shapely girls . . . who hand out printed stage money, which carries copy on attraction, whenever truck stops. Truck could be designed as a studio set, placing moving picture camera on truck, perhaps atop cab, focusing on girls. 

Other items can include: Beauty contest (see No. 50), for proxy (see No. 887). Girl contest, based on measurements (see No. 452). 

Candy store window display of butterscotch wafers, with tickets. offered to those most nearly correctly estimating the correct numbers of wafers in the window. Or candy made up to resemble gold or coins (wrapped in foil paper and stamped with name of attraction). 

Store windows featuring gold cloth, or models, or articles named after attraction or stars.

Gold Digger "tools" made center of display for lobby or window .. including cosmetics-powder, rouge, lip-sticks . . . and perhaps • 246 •

a cook book, and other items which a modern girl would use. Diploma might be included. And a typewriter. Should flatter modern girls and simultaneously hand men a laugh.

Girls distributing heralds could be dressed in stage money.. hundreds of "bills" being sewn to costumes which they wear. 

Couples celebrating golden wedding anniversaries, invited as guests of newspaper and theatre; with photograph for paper. "Gold diggers theatre party" might be set (with sororities, girl organizations), girls inviting boys. Society editor might aid. 

Songs and sayings that include the word "gold" might be made basis of radio contest, listeners being asked to submit them. 

533. NEWSPAPER COOPERATIVE ADS . . . Stores or business places might find it advantageous to include illustrations from theatre's attraction in their ads, or to use the attraction title as a sales catch-line. And where attraction directs attention toward a certain article or business, similar local business places will often find cooperative newspaper ads of much mutual benefit. 

Individual ads, one or several, might be used. Or they may be grouped together, forming a full page of ads; theatre's ad being included; space devoted to a contest. A double-truck (or two-page spread) might be sold. Or a special section (several pages) including stories, ads.

Tieup ads can be more easily "sold" if suggested copy is prepared in advance and shown the merchant in finished form. 

Business place or dealer might display an article in theatre lobby (an electric refrigerator, a radio, an automobile); in return, dealer would buy large newspaper space, devoted mainly to theatre's attraction, using photographs. Smaller illustrations might possibly show star of attraction posed with the article. Store's ad should definitely devote enough space and copy to theatre's attraction to justify use of lobby space.

Occasionally a full page devotes almost all space to theatre's attraction (perhaps in connection with opening, or new policy), with merchants who wish to aid and who bear expense of page, receiving credits at bottom of page. 

Often cooperative pages include contests to add interest, generally allotting space in center of page to explain. Page might be printed in two colors (at an extra charge). 

Some ideas can include: "Congratulatory page.' 99 Numbers or correct names cooperative page...

each ad containing • 247 •

blank space in which a number (or the name of a star) is to be written ... the correct number, or a star photograph being placed in windows of cooperating stores. Readers to visit the windows, to get correct number or name. Tickets for first so-many correct pages. "Why I Trade There" angle . selection of one business place. with prizes for best reasons for "Telephone Numbers" Cooperative page. . . or, rather, two pages in succession. Store names are left out, only the telephone numbers and copy carried. Tickets to go to first so-many persons submitting pages with correct names written in. Second page carries names of stores and winners. "Trip or Vacation Days” . . . tickets for best suggested trip, and list of supplies (from cooperating stores) that would be carried. "Stars"... headed "We've consulted the stars". . . smaller type, of (attraction title)... for the newest in Fall Styles." Or, "Let's go shopping with (star)."

Large drawing, representing downtown section of city, might carry the ads on cartooned billboards, buses, banners, dirigibles and airplanes... theatre and attraction billing being very prominent. 

Many other contests can be adapted. 

534. SCRIM. . . Adaptable to front, lobby, window use, displays placed behind scrim (thin cloth) become visible through the scrim when light is flashed on (behind scrim); unlighted, only lettering or design on the cloth is seen. Star's head might be painted on scrim, character he portrays appearing on panel behind scrim. 

Empty store window might be covered over (inside) with scrim, on which copy is air-brushed. is air-brushed. Title of attraction is set up in electric letters (spare marquee letters), or neon outlined letters . . . and placed behind the scrim, within the window, and arranged to flash on and off, appearing through the scrim when they are on. ... 

535. FLOATING GLASS . . . For lobby or window, a still or other object might be made to appear to float without visible support, by attaching it to a pane of glass which is made to move. 

Another pane of glass in front of pane to which object is attached, fills in an opening in display panel through which the second (moving) pane (and the attached object) is visible. Glass is made to revolve by cutting it round and having it ride on rollers (only square section of it would show, edges being out of sight behind display panel, together with motor-driven rollers which keep it moving). Object attached to glass (by drilling hole in glass, or by using suction cups), • 248 •

should be pivoted, bottom weighted, so that it maintains the same upright position while the glass to which it is attached revolves. 

536. WHEELS .. Imprinted (on both sides) cards, circular or square, might be attached to the wheels of bicycles ridden by delivery boys and messenger boys. Hole is diecut in center for hub, and card is slit or diecut from the hole to outside edge of the card.

Hoops, with photo of star of attraction centered inside same (attraction title on other side), might be rolled down the street by kids or girls. 

537. COMMUNITY SING 

With well-known song featured or suggested in an attraction, a singer might be introduced (perhaps accompanied by guitar, or accordion), appearing in aisles, asking patrons to join together in song. Radio station broadcasts from the theatre, taking microphone into audience, and announcer aiding singer in getting patrons to sing. In addition to radio station microphone (portable), on long extension, a microphone attached to house amplification system might also be used, so that individual singers in house, when microphone is handed them, might be heard above all others (adding to amusement of audience). Song hits of coming show could be introduced. Following song feature, trailer on the coming attraction hits the screen. 

Where regular community singing programs are featured, over radio stations or at other public gatherings, song-hits from the attraction may be introduced. Luncheon club might attempt the songs, particularly if broadcast. 

538. TOYS... Often toys can be used for miniature displays for windows or lobby or front . . . (as, toy automobiles, in a display that features automobiles, perhaps attached to an endless belt). 

And occasional visits to department store toy departments (especially just after Christmas) might reveal bargains that might be used later to advantage. 

539. WHO'S WHO... Contest, for lobby, newspaper, or windows, might be based on identification of drawings or photographs of stars.

If used in lobby, photos might be attached to a display panel, numbered, patrons being invited to correctly identify the photos, leaving their identifications at box office. Photos of characters similar to those portrayed in the attraction might be used; or historical figures; or famous beauties, or radio favorites. 

Perhaps baby photos of the stars of coming attraction might be 249.

secured; with patrons asked to correctly name them, including a ten-word-or-less description of each star (or local) identified. 

540. ONE WORD... Here's a stunt for imprinted cards or heralds, on an attraction having more than one word in title (or star's name might be used). In small box in corner of herald, print one word from title of attraction, then in smaller type, offer free tickets for complete set of cards spelling out name of attraction . . . suggesting that they match cards with their friends until a complete set is secured. Control number of admissions thus made available by having cards bearing one of the words printed in the desired limited quantity. 

541. LINGERIE... Illustration showing girl clad in lingerie might be used for a newspaper ad, or for front display, in emphasizing cool comfort of theatre (for summer) . . . carrying copy: "You'll feel this cool . . . in (theatre)." Newspapers mat service can supply an illustration. "Lingerie show" could be arranged as an attraction, or as a prologue to a trailer on a girl show, with cooperation of local department store or lingerie shop. Shapely girls, serving as models, show latest fashions in feminine underthings, lingerie, pajamas, etc. For musical accompaniment, perhaps the services of a girl accordionist (clad in pajamas) might be secured. Store should buy ads, install windows. 

542. SMILES... Effort might be made to find the city's "loveliest smile," or "prettiest smile," or "happiest smile," in connection with a comedy attraction, or a breezy romantic story. Or, the smile sought may be one most like that of star of attraction. 

Contest could be based on snapshots submitted, sponsored by newspaper or radio station. Daily newspaper stories on the contest carry smiling photos of stars of the attraction. Photo of a group of good-looking smiling local girls might be used. 

Cameraman might ride about town on an elaborate float, or in an open car, with panels and banners calling attention to offer of prize for winning smiles . . . and inviting girls to pose. Photographer, standing on the truck with a camera, snaps photos. 

Smile songs could be featured by orchestras or radio station (as, "When Irish Eyes are Smiling"), and dedicated to theatre's attraction. "Smile Marathon" might be staged, with a couple of attractive girls comfortably seated in store window, and smiling... display copy stating that they are out to set a new endurance smile record, in preparation for a date they have to see (attraction). • 250 •

543. TELESCOPE... Where available, real telescope might be used, setting it up on a prominent corner (with attendant in charge-perhaps a girl in short costume, but wearing star-covered cape and high-peaked hat). Telescope is trained on display. 

Placard on telescope tripod invites them to take a look at a “new star,' ," or "The most important star." Attendant invites those passing to have a look, emphasizing that there's no charge. 

Duplicate of a telescope might be made up by a tinner, using several different size sections of tin tubing, or it could be made up from several different sized mailing tubes. Phoney telescope should be mounted on a photographer's tripod, and aimed towards sky. A look into telescope reveals name of star or attraction, and theatre name . . . cardboard, with lettering cut out, tinted paper placed back of cut-outs, being placed in big end of "telescope," and a small light placed back of that (operated off a small dry-cell battery, arranged so that attendant might flash the light on when "telescope" is in use). 

544. ICE CARNIVAL . With winter sports winning attention, a "(name of attraction, or star) Ice Carnival" might be staged with cooperation of newspaper (publicizing the affair), and radio station broadcasting it. 

Ice Queen might be selected, in girl contest at theatre, or by "votes." She could be featured in a parade, receive gifts from merchants. Ice skating races and other winter sports might be featured, with trophies presented winners "from star of (attraction)."

Hockey games might permit announcements, heralds could be distributed. (Check No. 249, some items might be adapted.) 

545. GET ACQUAINTED... In larger cities, a certain night might be set aside as "Get Acquainted" Night, aiming directly at people who formerly lived in smaller towns, or other states, inviting them to attend, and get acquainted. Informal tea might be served in lounge or on mezzanine, where they are introduced; or a dance might be arranged after the last evening show. Those "registering" should be handed a paper badge to wear, which carries copy: "Howdy!

My Name is (space for name); I formerly lived in (space for town)." 

Different evenings, appeal might be made to different groups. 

Different states can be divided over the several nights. 

Perhaps group will arrange to meet again, or regularly, at theatre. 

Newspaper might use a photo of the group, and manager, or performer from theatre stage show, welcoming them. • 251 •

If attraction is set in or refers to some certain state, appeal might be made to those locals who hail from the state referred to. 

546. STATEMENT... Herald is made up after fashion of bill with name of theatre at top. And copy: "To Mr. and Mrs. 

Theatregoer (and name of town)". . . then, in statement style: "To two solid hours of amazing enjoyment (list attraction, with admission prices listed in price column)." 

547. CHANGE CARDS... That carry a running story about the attraction might be placed on an easel with a girl periodically showing them, removing one card at a time (placing it at back of the pack) until all have been shown. Window, possibly that of a furniture store, should be furnished as a boudoir, and between changing cards, girl lounges about in negligee in window. 

548. BREAKFAST PREVIEW... Early morning showing of an attraction might win special attention for an attraction and perhaps a newspaper story. Could be called a "Stenographer's Matinee." 

Ads announce opening of attraction with 6:30 or 7:00 (a.m.) "Breakfast Matinee" with breakfast to be served before show starts. (Bread company will supply bread for toast and sandwiches, perhaps also a girl to prepare it; similarly, coffee distributor will supply coffee.)

Radio station might broadcast a special program during time breakfast is being served, dedicated to those attending breakfast matinee, and with radio in theatre tuned in. Newspaper carries photographs of girls attending.
