And what's more, there are dozens more just as pretty in (attraction)." And copy on attraction on back page. Where 

550. ORGANIZATIONS AND CONTESTS 

number of returns on a contest are especially desired, letters might be sent all organizations suggesting that all their members compete and pool their entries in the contest, any winnings to go to the organization. For instance: on a cartoon coloring contest, all members would submit an entry to the club, the organization to then submit them to theatre. 

551. STAGE WEDDING 

Especially valuable where • 252 •

attraction suggests same; however, a stage wedding can be made a good box office bet at any time.

Arrangements should be made well in advance for a couple (or two couples, making it a double wedding) to be married. In tieup with newspaper or radio station, couples are invited to register their names, and screen trailer can invite them to be married on stage. 

Several couples may be lined up in event first couple changes minds. 

Identity of bride and bridegroom can be kept secret, having them masked until wedding, unmasking them after the ceremony. 

Arrange well in advance for the services of a justice of the peace or minister.

Newspaper cooperative ads have cooperating merchants each buying newspaper space, perhaps on a cooperative page, and contributing wedding presents (which are placed on display) for the couple. 

Stage should be set as attractively as possible for the wedding.. flowers, plants, palms, borrowed from a cooperating florist orchestra on stage to play a special "theme song" (which might be written for the occasion by some local composer). . 

Organist (or orchestra) playing Lohengrin's wedding march for wedding party to march down aisle (from mezzanine floor or lobby where they have assembled, and up specially built steps and over orchestra pit onto stage). Wedding party should wear customary costumes... bridesmaids, ushers, flower girls, ring bearer. Groom enters from wings; also minister or justice of peace who is to perform the ceremony.

Before procession down aisle, soloist can sing "I Love You Truly," or "O, Promise Me." At conclusion of ceremony, Mendelssohn's wedding march is played.

Florist should supply bouquets of roses for maids to carry as they march down aisle, and bride's bouquet. 

If staged in connection with a coming attraction, trailer might immediately follow the ceremony. 

Wedding march might be used as background music for radio announcements. 

552. MYSTIC FOUNTAIN An arresting window flash an illusion, where a stream of water appears to be running out of a faucet which is suspended in the air by a wire. (No pipe connections.)

Display panels carry copy: "Two Miracles of Modern Ingenuity 

... the 'Mystic Fountain of Bombay' and (attraction).”

Stream of water appears to flow into a funnel . . . and in front of • 253.

funnel is card lettered: "An Endless Stream of Water from Nowhere."

Operation of the stunt is by means of glass tube... the tube extending from faucet, down into the funnel. Below the funnel a small rubber tube is attached to the end of the glass tube . . . the rubber tubing carrying to a faucet where water supply is obtained. (Water flows up tube, overflows where tube-top is covered by faucet.) Also connected over concealed end of funnel is section of garden hose which runs to a sewer or drain . . . the rubber hose being within the hose, at end of funnel, a V-shaped opening being cut in the hose, some distance from the funnel, where the tubing comes out, the place where tube and hose divide being taped tightly and coated over with putty so that it will not leak. 

False floor can be built to the display to permit sufficient room for the hose arrangement beneath the false floor at bottom of catchfunnel.

Obviously window selected must have water supply near, and consequently confectioneries, soda fountains, etc., are preferable. Or a centrifugal pump might be used to return the water. (See photographs.) 

553. "ALL MY LIFE"... Heading for folder herald, im printed in large type; and then following, inside herald, and in smaller type: "I've been bawled out, called up, held up, held down, bulldozed, blackjacked, walked on, cheated, squeezed, mooched, panhandled, stuck for sales tax, dog tax, and syntax, baby bonds, and matrimonial bonds; red cross, green cross, and double cross; I've worked like heck; lost all I had and part of my furniture, and because I won't spend or lend the little I earn and go beg, borrow, or steal, I have been cussed and discussed, boycotted, talked to, talked about, lied to, lied about, held up, robbed and darn near ruined. And the only reason I'm sticking around at all, is to see (attraction).” 554. DOODLES Most persons have a habit of idly scribbling while telephoning . . . drawing odd designs of some sort. 

Calling this "doodling," newspaper might feature a contest which extends over several days, which offers guest tickets for oddest designs submitted. 

Telephone-scribbling of stars might be secured and used to illustrate the contest, together with photographs. Or, Mayor, or local celebs might permit scraps of paper from their desk pads to be used.

556. TURTLES... Lettered turtles (the smaller ones) might be used for novel window display on attraction having brief title. 

Enough small turtles are used, each with a letter painted on his back, to spell out the name of attraction if placed in proper sequence in a line (or, the name of the star of the attraction) . . . and guest tickets are offered to those who see the turtles lines up so that they spell out the title. Adaptable to puppies or to birds (see No. 485). 

Turtle race might be staged in front of theatre, or on beach or playground, or public square, naming the different turtles after different stars in the show. Each turtle might be "started" (from the center of a circle) by a good looking girl. Newspaper might go along for a picture, and humorous story. 

557. THE KING... With a king as a character in a story, or referred to in title, merchandise tieups, for windows, newspaper ads, might have articles referred to as "fit for a king," or, emphasizing "regal comfort," and including copy on attraction.

"King's" proxy might "arrive" in city . . . in uniform, and attended by great formality. (See 887.) ... 

558. CRAZY . . . Comedy Golfer, in an exaggerated golf outfit, might bat a peanut down the sidewalk with a golf club . . . with an attractive costumed girl caddying for him. Or: "If you think this is crazy (or 'funny'). . . just wait 'til you see attraction).”

Or, a fellow wearing a big fur coat in the hot summer time. 

559. LUCKY BILLS... Cooperating business place might announce in newspaper ads that on a certain day that they will put into circulation in change handed patrons in their store, a number of • 255 •

560. CHRISTMAS... Arrival of Santa Claus in town might be made a civic event, with Claus being met at railway station or airport, parading to city hall in bannered cars (perhaps behind a band), where Mayor can present him with "key to city," thence to theatre. 

Mayor can officially proclaim him town's official Santa Claus. Selling cooperative pages, newspapers arrange to have him appear in various stores at designated times or on certain days, in theatre at certain times each day.

Star of theatre's attraction might be pictured on cards which carry the copy: "(star) says, 'Help the Mailman.' Shop and Mail Early. 

And see (attraction)." Cards will find a welcome in most windows; and postmaster might permit them to be attached to mail boxes. 

Postmaster might permit mailmen to distribute (well in advance of 

Christmas rush) heralds which urge those receiving them to shop early and mail early... the heralds also, of course, carrying copy on attraction (perhaps "quoting" star of attraction). 

Theatre might offer to wrap Christmas packages for patrons, securing the services of an experienced package-wrapper. Postoffice might establish a sub-station for mailing of packages in theatre lobby, announcing this service. Theatre might check parcels for shoppers, special check-table or counter carrying copy: "Check your Christmas 

Parcels Here . . . and for a Very Merry Christmas, see (Christmas attraction)." Coffee (supplied by local distributor) might be served shoppers attending matinees.

Wreaths, garlands and holly, and Yuletide decorations add to attractiveness of the theatre at Christmas time. However, they shouldn't go up too early. . as advance notice of the coming of 

Christmas might incline patrons to watch pennies. ...

Newspaper ads for the several weeks immediately preceding 

Christmas should carry an excess of white space, so that they will stand out against the heavy mercantile ads of the period. Christmas attractions should be announced in papers well in advance, as newspaper efficiency diminishes in December. 

Toy matinee might be featured (see No. 514). Or, an autographed star still of Christmas attraction star is offered to every kid bringing a toy to any performance the week before Christmas. Arrangements • 256 •

made with boy scouts or fire department to repair the toys, and they are turned over to charity organization. "Toy Mountain" might be featured, in lobby, with patrons invited to bring along a new or old toy. Or, display in lobby might be set up as "Santa's Workshop," with man dressed as Santa Claus repairing old toys which are brought in. Requests of kids that theatre Santa Claus receives might be written down on a postcard and mailed to their parents. 

Displays in lobby can feature Christmas attraction as "(theatre's)

Gift to (town)." Seasonable lobby display might be constructed in the shape of a fireplace, with stockings hanging; or a miniature "snow covered" landscape (on a slight elevation), with toy train constantly circling the display (miniature banners attached to sides of toy train).

Prize (from star of attraction) might be offered, with newspaper's cooperation, for best lighted lawn Christmas trees. Light and Power 

Company should lend their support, too. 

Free morning show for poor kids and orphans might be arranged for Christmas Eve morning (charity organizations selecting the children who are to attend, and supplying gifts). 

Amplification units, placed about business section, playing carols, might have a recording of an attraction song hit introduced, and announcements. 

Department stores should, in banner headings across the tops of their ads, suggest that readers come downtown, do their shopping, attend a movie . . . calling attention to downtown entertainments, since this information will help draw shoppers downtown.

Street bally downtown will prove especially effective, because of the shopper-jammed streets. "Employees' cards" might be distributed to clerks in stores, entitling them to matinee prices until 6:30 (or time after closing of stores), the week before Christmas.

Benefit show might be arranged for newspaper's Christmas charity fund, or Goodfellows (see No. 514).

Electric train will make a fine give-away for kids; and might be promoted and placed on display in lobby. Presented at a matinee the week before Christmas, other gifts might be arranged for kids, with Santa Claus making a personal appearance and distributing small inexpensive novelties to all kids present. Gifts for adults, too, might be promoted and presented to ladies attending matinee performances. Christmas turkeys might be given away (see No. 634). "Merry Christmas Revue" might be arranged as a stage pre- • 257 •

sentation the week in advance of Christmas, with cooperation of dancing school.

Man dressed as Santa Claus might deliver cards to homes Christmas morning which are imprinted: "I had to come back to tell you about (attraction)." Signed, "S. Claus." 

561. INITIALS... Contest, for newspaper or radio, might be based on drawings which use star's initials as basic foundation for the drawing . . . with tickets for cleverest drawings. (The initials are to be incorporated into the drawing-any design might be chosen.) Accompanying illustration, for newspaper use: photo of star whose initials are used. 

562. TWINS... Emphasizing the angle, “Twice the Fun" (or "entertainment value of most shows"), twins might be invited to attend opening matinee or evening as guests of theatre and newspaper. Photo of the twins in front of theatre ought to be good for a newspaper photograph and story. Or dual role, or twins in story would suggest use of the stunt.

Identical twins, preferably pretty girls, identically costumed, might be used in connection with two lobby panels on a coming attraction... using "magician" (who might also introduce several manipulations), who "disappears" one of the girls (girl stepping through a swinging panel to behind display and out of sight, with panel swinging back into place, while "magician" holds black cloth in front of her) . . . and immediately crossing lobby to another display on same attraction, having the other girl "appear" by same process. Appears to be same girl. 

563. STRAW HATS... With coming of spring, straw hat season might be introduced with photograph of star of stage or screen show shown wearing a straw hat... newspaper using the photograph as a feature, or stores using it to illustrate an ad. 

Old straw hats, secured in exchange for a few tickets from hat stores might have lettered or imprinted paper bands attached, having newsboys wear them on important corners. 

564. LOCAL NEWSREEL... Arrangements might be made with local business place to sponsor (and pay for) a local newsreel. 

Might be promoted under sponsorship of newspaper or business place as a regular feature. Newspaper could have their regular photographer "shoot" news events that occur locally. Reel would be titled "(paper) Local News Extra," (or store).

Small portable camera is necessary equipment, or perhaps ar- • 258 •

rangements can be made with local photographer who is equipped to make the pictures.

Local newsreel especially valuable in football season, when football pictures are worth something, especially shots of those games that are played away from home.

Moving pictures of opening night crowds or crowds at beaches, other places attracting crowds, might prove valuable. When filming, banner should be displayed which tells where the pictures may be seen.

Shots might be made of employees of various stores or factories (perhaps at an outing or other gathering) and shown on a special night dedicated to the factory or store (when their employees are urged to attend).

Several stooges should trail along carrying extra camera cases when shooting pictures of football games or places where crowds will be gathered... theatre name and attraction title being lettered on them. 

565. MINSTREL . . . Regular “minstrel-style" parade and concert might be arranged, with band (in some sort of uniform), parading streets, stopping on important corners where they play a number, at the conclusion of which an announcement is made, or a banner, carried by costumed girls, is unfurled. 

Small portable platform, possibly in shape of and resembling a drum, might be carried along, on which girl might present a dance number (if in keeping with attraction). Number from show might be played.

In connection with stage show, the entire personnel of show, in costumes, might "march" in the street parade. Spread people out, four, or even two, abreast, plenty of space between lines. Two of the girls in the parade can carry a lettered banner. 

Window display might feature a couple of costumed blackface entertainers, made up ministrel-style, and an "interlocutor." Using amplification system for benefit of those outside windows, they crack a few jokes, include much mention of attraction, present a few songs or musical numbers. Couple of girls in costume might be introduced for dance numbers. Routine is swift, short . . . and repeated at frequent intervals.

(Any lettering surrounding the girl to be in reverse so that it will reflect correctly in the mirror.) And, in smaller size, a cutout figure can be used. Copy on outside of the "case."

572. REVERSE LETTERS . . . Lobby panel (translucent glass or white paper), lighted from behind, has title of attraction lettered in regular manner on back side of the panel. panel, the lettering consequently appears in reverse. of panel (in straight lettering) invites patrons, "just for fun,” to try and read the title of one of the year's outstanding shows, adding that if they can't read it to walk around to back of panel. 

Perhaps the services of someone who can write in reverse might be available... possibly someone with engraving experience. Placed in a window as center of a display on theatre's attraction, the man writes and rewrites copy about theatre's attraction (in reverse) on a pane of glass, using a soap pencil (glass between man and those looking in window, and writing consequently is readable to them). 

573. HARD OF HEARING... If theatre is equipped with a number of wired seats and earphones for the benefit of the hard of hearing, the attention of those who are hard of hearing should be directed to this equipment. The deaf have an organization, the officials of which should be contacted, and who will be glad to supply a mailing list of members; and stores selling amplification equipment for the aid of the deaf will have a list of names of their customers. 

Earphones are generally made available at box office or check room, with patron making a deposit for the earphone which is returned when the unit is brought back. Wired seats should be distributed over house, with several near front. Handle of arm rests of seats which are wired, might be painted white to facilitate locating them. 

574. ALPHABETICAL... Contest for newspaper might be based on a still from theatre's attraction, or a drawing from a photograph which shows a large amount of detail, or action. Paper offers • 261 •

tickets or other prize to person who makes up longest list of articles seen in the illustration which begin, in spelling, with a certain specified letter. Name of star might be used, and one letter used each day, with a different illustration, until all the letters in his name are used. 

575. FIRST... The first of anything is always news. First attraction of its kind. First time a new innovation is introduced. 

A first appearance in city of a noted entertainer. 

Additionally, newspaper feature or contest might be based on other famous "firsts" (as the first person to fly the Atlantic). . . tieing in with theatre's "first."

First use of new and novel device is always assured of extra attention-winning value. Display on an attraction can be harnessed to any new invention or device that will win attention, for window or lobby flash. 

576. CASHIER'S NOTES... Cashier might, in spare time, write up number of neat, brief notes, calling attention to coming attraction, handing them out with tickets sold.

Notes might be signed with title of coming attraction; or written as "personal note from your cashier" (which might be printed on the slips of paper). 

577. PAY ENVELOPES. . . Small envelopes of size and type generally used by business places and manufacturing plants in making up pay rolls, can be printed up, allowing spaces for names and amounts and days, but with most of space on envelope devoted to coming theatre attraction. Arrangements made with places having big pay rolls to use the envelopes. 

Small envelopes of the pay-envelope type can be used where some small object is to be distributed (samples, candy, small photographs), with copy on the attraction being imprinted on the envelopes). 

Imprinted envelopes might be supplied for reserve seat sales for opera engagements, wrestling, boxing. . or other attraction that might call for reserved seats. 

578. COUGH DROPS... Confection cough drops samples, promoted in quantity from the manufacturer, are inserted for distribution in small envelopes, imprinted: "Bring this (brand) Cough 

Drop along. . . You'll Laugh yourself Hoarse when you see (and into attraction copy)." 

579. FACTS. . . Interesting and unusual facts or features about a show might be combined to make up an interesting feature for newspaper or radio use. 

Illustrating the "facts," and combining them in a several-columns • 262 •

wide drawing, newspaper might carry the drawing as a feature. 

Unusual hobbies or experiences of stars might be included, as well as incidents pertaining to the show or its production . . . and, most important, title of attraction should be given good space. Feature might be carried under a descriptive title, as "Film Flashes," or "Screen Scenes." 

580. PERPETUAL MOTION. . . The effect of perpetual motion might be realistically produced, using a wheel (about 30" in diameter) in which openings (triangular with rounded corners) are cut. . . using golf balls seemingly to drive the wheel-the balls rolling, as the wheel turns, in groove formed by attaching two wheels, exactly alike, together, with a one-inch space between them. Actually, shaft of wheel penetrates through panel and behind it, and is turned by a worm-geared motor (which is out of sight behind the panel), using a loose, slipping belt. (See Photos.)

Golf balls might be painted varied colors. Lettering around edge of wheel might ask: “Can this be Perpetual Motion?" and carry copy on attraction. Wheel might be incorporated in front or lobby or window panel to draw attention to a display. 

581. COOKING SCHOOL . . . As a morning affair, or as a more brief matinee feature. Joint sponsorship of newspaper may be secured, and cooperating business places should buy newspaper ads which sell the stunt and attraction as well as commodity or item which they are featuring. Cooking expert supplied by utility company, or secured from school. National manufacturers should cooperate, through local distributors and representatives, supplying ingredients featured and necessary supplies. Dishes prepared might be awarded to some lady present; and in addition samples (supplied by manufacturers) might be distributed, and perhaps cooperating merchants will give away important prizes. Utility company, interested in selling cooking equipment, might join in sponsoring the affair and sharing expense. Used as a matinee feature, the stunt should be staged before beginning of afternoon's performances (with demonstrator using two ranges, in one of which duplicate dishes have been previously cooked, so that finished product might be shown at once), or presented in two interludes, before attraction, when food is prepared and set to cook (on range at one side of stage and out of way), and after showing of attraction, when cooked food is shown.

With newspaper sponsorship of a cooking school, in theatre or an • 263 •

E N C Y C L O PEDIA OF EXPLOITATION 

auditorium, the cooking expert might be persuaded to name a recipe after star of theatre's attraction, announcing it. 

582. BABIES... Special prize (cup, or cash bank account), might be presented first baby born after opening of attraction (perhaps also requiring that it be named after star). Cooperation of newspaper should also be assured. Merchants might go along for additional prizes. Bank might contribute a bank account. 

Department stores and shops selling baby clothes and equipment for children should cooperate with window displays and newspaper ads. 

Baby contest for lobby or mezzanine, can be based on photographs, with ballots provided so that patrons may vote. 

583. GREETING CARD TICKETS. . . Adaptable to any sort of greeting cards, but apt to prove of especial value around Christmas time when great quantities of greeting cards are exchanged. persons sending cards might be invited to add pleasure to the cards they send by making them good for admission to the theatre, with person receiving the card invited to attend as guest of the sender.

Handled by making available at the box office special printed stickers, which are numbered and handled exactly as tickets are handled. Printed (using specially drawn cut) on gummed paper, after the fashion of postage stamps, the sticker-tickets are several times larger than an ordinary postage stamp, and are bound, in easily detachable style, in small booklets of 20 to 25 tickets.

Patrons can buy one sticker or a book-full. In booklet form, the stickers might be separated by small pieces of waxed paper (exactly as the stamps in the booklets of stamps sold by the post office).

Money is collected in advance, as the stickers are sold; and the greeting cards with attached stickers are accepted as tickets at the door. 

Special price might, or might not, be made on complete booklets of stickers. Deal might be made with places and agents selling greeting cards to also sell "stickers." Can be made available for both adults and children. They can be made available in doubles, too, so that person receiving the card can take along a companion. 

A number of stickers might be attached to a single card. 

Copy on the "sticker" will say that the card, with a "sticker" attached, will be good for an admission on presentation at (theatre) as the guest of the sender of the card. 

Attention is directed to the sale of the stickers by trailers which • 264 •

describe their use, inviting patrons to treat their friends to the most pleasant gift of all, to add to the pleasure their remembrance will bring. Display cards, too, in lobby, reproducing an enlargement of one of the "stickers," might be used. Display cards might be placed on counters in stores selling greeting cards. 

And, too, actual greeting cards might be sold by theatre, instead of the stickers to be attached. 

In cases where card is not quite enough, this service solves for patrons the problem of an inexpensive gift. 

584. MARQUEE TITLES... Newspaper contest repro duces photograph of front of theatre, with attraction title appearing on one line, other line or lines blanked out. Contestants are to pencil in on blank lines the titles of other attractions, which will combine in a humorous manner. 

585. FARM... Attraction with a farm background would suggest rural atmosphere for lobby. Actual farm produce, sidewalk barker in overalls and straw hat. 

Miniature display for window or lobby might feature a farm-yard, house, barn, etc., using toys. A real husking bee might be arranged for the lobby, bringing in several bushels of corn and some real huskers maybe broadcasting the "championship match" from the lobby. Barn dance might be staged in lobby after show, or an "Old Fiddlers' Contest." Arrangements might be made to have announcements made at meeting of 4-H clubs and Granges. Display of blue ribbons and stock prizes might be arranged for store window.

Blue ribbons might be distributed, with copy imprinted: “The 

PRIZE hit of the year (and into attraction copy)." Or, large lettered "first-prize" blue ribbon might be attached to a display panel on the attraction. (See No. 57 and No. 91.) 

586. TEST DRIVERS... With cooperation of automobile dealer, or automobile association, arrangements might be made to secure use of equipment which tests drivers' reactions, sight, hearing. 

Installed in lobby (in charge of an attendant), it will attract much interested attention. Especially adaptable to an attraction which features driving, emphasizing safety; however, display panels on any attraction might be built around it, and ad might be imprinted on the "results" cards which are handed persons taking the test. Copy might say: "Drive carefully to the (theatre) next week to see (attraction)." • 265 •

587. LAUGH WEEK... A special week, featuring a comedy attraction, or several comedy features, might suggest inauguration of a special "Laugh Week;" or "Happiness Week.'

Possibly Mayor might designate the week in a proclamation as "Laugh Week," the proclamation being reproduced for newspaper. 

Special "Laugh Week" trailer, cards, and other accessories can be used. Border composed of laughing faces might be used on newspaper ads during week.

Masks for display frames might be made up as a face with wideopen mouth, as in a laugh, with billing lettered in mouth. Stills may be similarly masked. Laugh record may be used. 

Man, in window, "attended" by pretty girl "nurse," laughs hysterically, continuously (window amplification used) panel carrying copy, "He just saw (attraction), and he can't stop laughing!"

Radio station might stage a "Laugh Contest" from sidewalk in front of theatre. "Laugh thermometer" may be made up with a ribbon, painted partly red, partly white, animated to run up and down "thermometer". . . the thermometer being lettered, "Uproarious," "Comical," "Laughable," "Shrieks," "Howls," "Such Fun."

Clown serves as barker in front of theatre. For laughs, he can hand persons passing theatre a rose, and as person takes the "stem" of the rose, clown lifts rose, leaving person holding “stem." (Quantity of straws being used, the rose stem inserted in the straws.) 

588. LOCK. . . Herald, or hanger card might be die-cut in the shape of a lock (to be attached over door knobs of homes in distribution), or feature an illustration of a lock, and imprinted: "Lock up everything . . . and go see (attraction and theatre)."

Hardware store showing a display of locks in a window might carry similar copy on display panel. 

589. TRAVEL RACE... Especially adaptable for use in connection with attraction that features or suggests travel, or has a foreign setting-tieup between theatre, newspaper and leading stores being worked out, with stores and theatre distributing "mileage slips" with every purchase (where they are requested). Newspaper sponsors a "race" to point indicated in the story, based on the "mileage slips." Contestants to deposit their votes regularly, with newspaper carrying daily "distance covered" by contestants; first one "arriving" at designated "destination" winning a (promoted) trip, or complete outfit from the stores and tickets from theatre; or other prizes.

Each "mileage slip" might represent a certain number of miles; • 266 •

each cooperating business place would pay for mileage slips which they use. Newspaper might carry a daily clip coupon, good for a certain number of "miles." And newspaper might sell a cooperative page of advertising to the merchants who are "in" on the stunt, all of the ads mentioning the attraction. The "race" should be begun sufficiently far in advance. 

590. ACCORDIONIST 

Where available, accordionist, preferably an attractive girl, might play numbers from a musical attraction, making tour at busy hours of restaurants, dining rooms, luncheon clubs, tea shops, playing numbers, making attraction announcements. Accordionist costumed as suggested by attraction. 

Girls distribute imprinted cards to diners. 

Accordionist might also play in theatre lobby, as center of a display, and over radio. Or wherever musical accompaniment is required.

An accordion school, if there is one in town, might supply a half dozen players for lobby or front flash, or for a float, playing hit tunes from attraction. 

591. BUSINESS SECTION BROADCAST... With a special theatre broadcast arranged (preferably for Saturday or other busy day, and at busiest time of day), arrangements are made to place radio receivers up and down the main street, in every block, all of which are tuned in on the program. Program might feature hit tunes from attraction, together with announcements, and should be made as elaborate as possible.

The radio receiving sets, placed on sidewalks about town, should each be in charge of an attendant. Display panels with the radios, carry copy on the attraction, devoting space to cooperating dealer who supplies the radios. (Dealer should also receive announcements on the broadcast program.) Talent from stage show might be featured. 

Stunt would prove especially effective around Christmas time when armies of shoppers are on the streets. 

592. MERIT. . . Tieup with large department stores and factories might have guest tickets offered to employees who are selected as meriting the tickets by their records for the week . . . for sales, efficiency, best sales or promotion idea of the week. Announced at meetings of employees, with attraction mentioned. 

593. DECORATIONS... Welcome accorded an attraction, or featuring an opening, might include street decorations, perhaps • 267

the entire length of the main business street; or at least the block in which theatre is situated. 

Special flags and banners are generally available (used on special occasions to decorate street), and arrangements might be made, through proper contacts, to have these flags put into use, perhaps with addition of small banners which carry copy: "Welcome (star or attraction)." Specially printed cardboard "shields" might be attached to poles, as the center of flags or bunting. 

Strings of lights might be put into use for night-time flash. Perhaps the light company can supply them, lights that are extended across main street at Christmas time. Theatre block at least, should be brightly illuminated. 

Theatre front decorations can feature large banners, pennants, flags and bunting. Special valance might be used (see No. 28). 

594. DINNER, LUNCHEON... With personal appearance of a star, or important personality, special dinner for press might have newspaper critics invited as guests of the star. Or possibly a cocktail party might find better favor with the newspaper lads. 

Or, dinner might be arranged with cooperation of luncheon club or prominent business men, or Chamber of Commerce, with star as guest, newspaper critics invited . . . and with tribute paid star in speeches. Program could be broadcast. Newspapers should go for pictures and story. 

A dinner might well serve as the springboard for a special campaign in connection with the showing of an important and worthwhile attraction. Group selected as guests including club officials, educational heads, city officials, newspaper critics. . . their support being solicited in bringing the attraction to town, asking them to serve as a "sponsoring committee." (See No. 347.) 

595. JIG-SAW ENVELOPE . . Imprinted: "A jig-saw

Puzzle for Impatient People." And in smaller type: "Directions: 

Mix pieces very thoroughly. . . then piece them together until picture is complete. Then turn to reverse side for an important message." Inside the envelope is small printed picture of star or scene from picture, which is cut in jagged, jig-saw style, in just two pieces. Imprint copy on reverse side (before card is cut). 

596. SONG TITLES... With newspaper contest illustrated with scenes from attraction, readers are asked to title the scenes, using appropriate song titles. 

597. ADD THESE UP... Accompanied by mathematical

plus signs, illustrations representing the entertainment elements pictured in the story, might be adapted for display or ad use. 

For instance, scene picturing romantic team might carry the word: "Romance," then the "plus sign" and a comedy scene which carries the word: "Comedy," etc. Might be finished off with an "equals" sign which is followed with the words: "Two Hours of Grand Entertainment," or something similar. Stars might be named similarly, instead of entertainment elements. ...

599. LIARS... Card, for distribution, might be made up after style of a membership card or license, and carrying the copy: "Liar's License . . . The Bearer (space for name) having, by reputation and long practice, coupled with a vivid imagination, exhibited all the necessary requirements, is hereby empowered to lie, prevaricate, and to show every other recklessness with the truth considered expedient by him, and in connection with all matters, subject to conditions, and provided he goes to see (attraction copy)." Might add: "Lies might be told at any time or place . . . with the single provision that the truth must be told about (attraction)—that it is great entertainment." Conclude: "In witness wherefore, is attached the Seal of Ananias.”

If attraction features a prevaricating character, newspaper or radio contest might be based on tall stories . . . with daily guest tickets for most outlandish lies submitted. Adaptable similarly to alibis, excuses, reasons for action. 

600. SCRIPT... With the cooperation of the studio, perhaps a page, or several pages, of the original working script of an attraction can be secured.

With cooperation of the newspaper, the script might be reproduced as illustration of a Sunday magazine feature, or a daily feature. 

Might be placed on display in a prominent window. Or, in a locked showcase, in lobby. Still photographs illustrating the scene represented by the script might be connected by ribbons. 

Reproduction of a page of the script of an especially hilarious. ⚫ 269

sequence might be adapted to a herald (could be taken down from screening of the attraction), headed: "Here's part of the script from (attraction). Audiences are roaring so loudly, we're afraid you'll miss some of the laugh-lines." 

601. VOX POP . . . Voice of People columns conducted by newspapers might print a letter which refers to theatre's attraction, or a letter on a subject which is suggested by theatre's attraction. 

Submitted under name of some local person, the letter should be definitely interesting, mention of attraction should not be too broad; and, preferably, editor should know that the letter is going to be submitted. 

602. MESSAGE TO GOVERNOR... In connection with an outstanding attraction, arrangements might be made well in advance with newspaper to aid in selecting a local girl who is to act as messenger in carrying personally an invitation from the theatre, the newspaper, and possibly local Mayor, and civic organization, to the Governor, inviting him to attend showing of attraction as guest of honor.

Transportation companies, airlines, railroads, or bus lines should supply transportation for the girl in return for newspaper mention which they will receive. 

Girl might visit Governors of several nearby states; with photographs being made of presentation of invitations, which are used for newspaper reproduction. Several girls might be selected, if transportation can be arranged, and sent along instead of one. They should be attractively costumed . . . perhaps attraction will suggest special costumes.

Similarly, invitations might be carried to Mayors of nearby towns and cities.

With the cooperation and joint sponsorship of a luncheon club, arrangements might be made with similar luncheon clubs in cities visited to sponsor the girls' visits and to have them attend club luncheons as guests.

If Governor attends, he would be honor guest at luncheon, attending showing of attraction as special guest. 

603. LIBRARIES, BOOK STORES. . . Almost every at traction will suggest some certain type of book, either because of background or theme or author. (Or a definite author or authors might be indicated.) Generally book stores and libraries will install displays of the suggested book or books, and including display • 270 •

panels on theatre's attraction. Or they will distribute book-marks (see 21). 

604. BRITISH... With English background important to a story, cooperation and sponsorship of local patriotic organizations should be obtained. Drum corps or band from local military organization might appear and play in front of theatre on opening night. British consul should be invited to attend. 

Lists of nationals in city or drawing radius might be obtained from British consulate, and these might be contacted, directing their attention to the attraction.

English speaking society will cooperate. Newspaper feature might endorse the attraction, paying respects to Britain. English flag might be displayed, together with American flag. Perhaps some person now located in city will have originally come from section shown in the attraction; might be interviewed over radio. 

Giant map of world, or a slowly turning globe of the world, with English possessions all the same color, might attract window attention and might be appropriate.

Special local radio program might be dedicated to an English city, perhaps one portrayed in story. Local prominents might appear on the program, greeting citizens of the English city. Entire program is recorded, and the transcriptions are sent to wireless station in the English city, where arrangements might be made (should be made in advance) to have the recorded program featured. Attendant newspaper stories can be arranged on the stunt. (A stunt that might be worked out with any foreign city suggested by the attraction. Perhaps they will return a similar recorded greeting, which mentions attraction, and which local radio station will use.)

Products of different parts of British Empire might make an interesting exhibit. Travel bureaus might cooperate with window displays and a travel campaign directing attention to part of Britain featured in the attraction. English tweed, china, pipes, and other items typically British might be featured in merchandise tieups. (See 603.) 

605. ACTORS... Ballyhoo people made up and costumed to resemble those in theatre's attraction, mingle with crowds on sidewalk . . . with an open, bannered automobile, with cameras set up and focused on them, following as though taking pictures of them. "Cameraman," "Director," and a couple of attractive girls might ride the camera-car. 

Banner copy calls attention to theatre's attraction. Car might • 271 •

also stop at prominent locations, focusing cameras on upper windows of buildings . . . and when sufficient attention attracted, banners carrying copy on attraction being unrolled out a window. 

606. SHOPPING FOR A GIFT... Newspaper contest might be based on suggestions for an appropriate gift for star or player. (Series of photographs of girls or stars carried daily.) Contestants to submit reasons for their selections. 

Store might sponsor the stunt in their advertising space, requiring that gift suggestions be items featured by the store. 

607. CHURCH... Ministers might be invited to screening of an attraction that will merit their support. Perhaps they would comment on it from their pulpits. Perhaps the theme or title might be such that it might suggest or be adapted to a sermon; and maybe a friendly pastor or rabbi or priest can be persuaded to preach it. 

608. TELEPHONE NUMBERS BOOKLET . . . A novelty herald, for use in connection with a girl show or stage show . . . imprinted in large type on front cover: "Telephone Numbers;" and, then, in smallest possible type, "This Booklet presented with the compliments;" then in large type, "Of the Lovely Ladies in (attraction).”

At first glance only the words in large type stand out. 

Booklet comprises four pages. . . two small sheets of paper stapled together, and folded in center; or, it can be just a folder. 

Inner pages feature blank lines (where names and telephone numbers might be written in), and are headed: "Blondes," "Brunettes," "Redheads." Remaining spaces carry copy on attraction, or photographs of girls in attraction.

Attractive girls might distribute the booklets, handing them to men. 

609. CARTOONIST 

Or sketch artist, in a window as center of a display, sketching quick drawings or caricatures of stars of theatre's attraction. Miniature cards on an easel might be changed with different sketches; or using amplification he talks as he sketches, announcing attraction. Drawings, upon completion, might be handed to those watching. Paper on which drawings are sketched would carry imprint on attraction. Attraction might suggest sketches other than just stars of the show. Or those watching might be sketched in "attempting" to find (star's) perfect romantic type. Stunt might be adapted to lobby. 

610. NOVELTIES... Many unusual novelties are generally available from novelty printing companies, and adaptable to any attraction... unusual heralds; novelty printed matter; attention- • 272.

winning items, as the "magic slate" (which permits person to write on a small sheet of composition, the writing disappearing immediately when the sheet is lifted, when another message might be writtentheatre's ad being imprinted on front cover). Cigarette holders, ash-trays, pen-knives or similar novelties might be bought in quantity economically enough for distribution (imprinted), or with imprinted tags attached, or inserted in imprinted envelopes. Tieup copy may be suggested by attraction, or imprint may be headed, "With the 

Compliments of (star)."

Novelty printing houses will be glad to send samples and prices. 

Addresses of novelty printing places can be secured from Showmen's 

Trade Review or other trade papers. 

611. FIREWORKS. . . Fireworks might be used to call attention to a gala opening or other theatre event. However, all possible hazards must be considered, and all precautions taken. 

Fire Department should be consulted. 

Noise-makers might be safely exploded atop canopy or atop theatre. Red fire can be used for unusual illumination (signal flares used by railroads).

Where pyrotechincal display is announced as part of some municipal celebration, and certain to be witnessed by crowds, arrangements might be made to have title of theatre's attraction displayed, by illuminating a banner with flares. 

612. TENNIS . . . Where tennis courts are prominently located and visible to passing traffic, possibly arrangements might be made to attach a cloth sign to the nets which are used . . . or cutout cloth letters which spell out the attraction title. ...

With the friendly assistance of the sports editors, contest might be arranged for local tennis courts, with winner to receive a racket "from star."

If there are tennis scenes in an attraction, members of tennis clubs will be interested and should be notified.

616. PLANT A TREE ... With cooperation of local civic club and newspaper, a tree might be planted in local park and dedicated to star of attraction. Forestry organizations might cooperate. Boy Scouts might aid.

Great deal of ceremony might be arranged in connection with planting of the tree. Mayor or local celebrity might turn the first spade of earth. Drill corps or band might perform. Photographs should be carried for newspaper space. And later, photo of star receiving the photographs might be carried in newspapers. 

617. PRESS-SHEETS, MAGAZINE CLIPS . . . Repro duction in the press-books of the various accessories (6-sheets, 24sheets, etc.), can be used on paper streamers for window tieups (as sundaes, sandwiches), the illustration being clipped and pasted on the window-streamers. • 277 •

Miniature 24-sheet "billboards" (using press-sheet illustration of the poster) can be used for placing on hotel desks, counters in cigar stores, etc.

Photo stuff from magazines (film magazines and others) can occasionally be adapted to use. 

618. SELLING DOLLARS... Especially adaptable to at traction featuring money in title or theme, is stunt of man attempting to sell dollars for 90c, or even half-price. With newspaper to play the stunt ... and the refusals that he will get from most persons . . for novel story, tieing in attraction. 

In relating difficulty in selling them, story might say that it was necessary for him to buy the last dollar himself. Stunt might be used as a radio tieup and broadcast. 

619. ANKLES, LEGS . . . If legs or ankles are important to story or title, or where star is known for her shapely limbs, a "perfect legs" contest might be arranged either as a window stunt, or as a stage contest. Girls would appear in bathing suits, and for competition would stand behind a curtain which conceals them except for their legs. (Numbers might be attached to the curtain, in front of them.) Hosiery shop might join in sponsoring the contest. (No. 816 might be adapted to legs.) 

620. MAPS... (Adventure, Travel, Foreign). 

Prizes might be offered to those who identify "high spots" of world by latitude and longitude. Different spots are indicated each day, together with illustration from attraction. 

Contestants might be also required to state what particular place on the globe that they would pick as their idea of the world's high spot of adventure and why. 

621. TAKE A CHANCE... With neither attraction title or star's names announced, the public might be invited to "Take a 

Chance," and see the show. . . with the assurance that they will call it one of the most entertaining shows of the year (billed as “Take a 

Chance Week").

Photographs of players have masks drawn over the eyes. Gambling theme, with "It's fixed so you can't lose" copy, can be used for lobby and ads. 

622. LOBBY SKETCHES Newspaper contest might 

"introduce" house artist, explaining that he is stuck for an idea for lobby, or front display panels for coming attraction, and asking for suggestions. Guest tickets for the cleverest submitted (which paper reproduces). • 278

623. MINIATURE PHOTOS... Photographer might make up a quantity of miniature photos of star, with photographers' credit-line prominent on photograph, together with autograph of star. 

Or, cut might be made from photograph (perhaps autographed) of star, and quantity of "photos" printed on glazed paper (for distribution). 

624. CODE MESSAGES... Morse code message might be made basis for newspaper or radio contest, or adapted to window or lobby flash. "Can-you-translate-this-message" angle might be used in newspaper contest, with "message" about attraction to be translated from dots and dashes; or, reversing this, a caption under an illustration (on the attraction) might be translated into dots and dashes. 

As radio contest, listeners might be asked to try to pick up and read a dot-dash message; with first so-many to win tickets. 

625. ALLITERATION, TONGUE TWISTERS... Contest angle for newspaper or radio . . . contestants being invited to submit sentences about attraction with every word of submitted sentence to begin with same letter. Requirement might be added that star's name or name of the attraction be included in the alliterations submitted. 

626. BLOTTO... Contest might be based on best "reflected signatures," contestants to write their signatures on a piece of paper, then folding it quickly before the ink is permitted to dry . . . the blotted names creating all sorts of odd designs, and most unusual get tickets. ... 

627. WOMEN'S CLUB DISCUSSION . . . In connection with showing of an unusual or class attraction, it might be possible to arrange to have some prominent local clubwoman discuss the attraction before her club and other women's clubs. Or the discussion might be arranged for a department store, the store mailing out invitations to hear her, possibly buying newspaper space. 

Woman selected for the discussion should be an authority on the subject, or at least well-informed. She might be a member of the staff of a library or theatre guild. 

628. NO LAUGHS. . . In connection with a comedy attraction, offer might be made, through newspaper story, of a prize to first ten persons to apply who can watch the attraction from beginning to end without smiling. Several "plants" should be included among the ten, who laugh, and are disqualified, for newspaper story purposes. • 279 •

629. TOO BUSY... Folder, for distribution, imprinted with the catch-line on cover: "Are You Too Busy?"

And inside the folder, this copy: "Too busy to Live (for persons afflicted with Hurryitis)” . . . (and then in smaller type): "He hadn't time to greet the day, he hadn't time to laugh or play, he hadn't time to wait a while, he hadn't time to give a smile, he hadn't time to read the news, he hadn't time to dream or muse, he hadn't time to just be kind, he hadn't time to see a joke, he hadn't time to write his folks, he hadn't time to eat a meal, he hadn't time to deeply feel, he hadn't time to take a rest, he hadn't time to act his best, he hadn't time to help a cause, he hadn't time to take a pause, he hadn't time to pen a note, he hadn't time to cast a vote, he hadn't time to sing a song, he hadn't time to right a wrong, he hadn't time to send a gift, he hadn't time to practice thrift, he hadn't time to exercise, he hadn't time to scan the skies, he hadn't time to heed a cry, he hadn't time to say good-bye, he hadn't time to lend or give, he hadn't time to really live, he hadn't time to read this verse, he hadn't time... He's in his hearse. STOP (large caps), (and then in smaller type): "Your hurryin' and worryin'. . . Take time out and enjoy yourself. . . and see (attraction copy)." 

630. ANNIVERSARY . . . Celebrating theatre's birthday suggests many angles . . . including:

Special Newspaper Page. (See No. 533.) A parade 

No. 64). Birthday cake . . . (see No. 261). (see Merchants might cooperate as a group, placing cards in their store windows, also calling attention to their years of service. Perhaps other business place might also be celebrating an anniversary of their own... and they might be tied in to theatre's celebration. Coupons handed out by cooperating business places with purchases might entitle those receiving them to chance on gifts to be given away at theatre on opening night of week, or anniversary of opening night.

All couples married same week theatre opened, might be invited to attend as guests. 

631. HALLOWE'EN

Ads and heralds might bill a special Hallowe'en show as an "Old Fashioned Hallowe'en Party" . . using usual illustrations of witches and black cats and pumpkins. 

House staff might be costumed in clown suits, or skeleton costumes, for the occasion. Favors might be secured together with quantity of serpentine and paper hats. Orange and black for the lobby; perhaps adapting ordinary crepe paper, and using cutout witches, cats, etc. • 280 •

Hallowe'en contests can include: costume contests, prizes for the cleverest, prettiest, funniest costumes, prizes for kids and adults. 

Balloon contest. . . half dozen boys supplied with large balloons to be blown up, first one bursting the balloon is the winner. Stringchewing contest... a pass being tied in middle of string and kids taking ends of string in their mouths and chewing towards the pass, first one arriving at the pass to get it; hands not to be used; several sets of kids used at the same time. Shoe contest. . . number of boys taking their shoes off, then being grouped at opposite side of stage; shoes are thoroughly mixed then dumped in a pile; at a signal, the boys rush for their shoes; first one finding his shoes and putting them on and tieing them is the winner. Flour contest . . . pans of flour with several dimes in pan; kids at given signal, to place hands behind them and take the dimes out with their teeth. Apple-ducking contest. . . tubs and hard apples, and kids to get the apples with their teeth. Cracker-eating contest... kids being handed a small box of crackers; first one to eat them and whistle a tune is the winner.

Pie-eating contest . . . pies being placed on tables, contestants to eat them without aid of the hands. Milk-bottle contest... boys supplied with bottles of milk to which nipples have been attached. . . ... at a given signal, to start to drink the milk. Threading Contest placing boxing gloves on boys, giving them a needle and a long thread. 

632. RETURNS, ELECTIONS, BALL GAMES, PRIZE- 

FIGHTS... In connection with elections, championship fights, world series baseball games, and other events that draw widespread interest in immediate returns, the results can be announced in theatre. Those interested might thus attend the theatre, and at the same time be assured of hearing the final results immediately. 

Returns might be announced "through cooperation of (local newspaper)," with the paper supplying the information immediately to theatre. Tag-line might be included in all announcements: "Read the (paper) for full details" (or radio station).

Small projector (or using artist's baloptican) might be set up in house, and focused on small screen at side of stage, slides prepared as information comes in, and flashed immediately (show not being interrupted in any way).

If continuous returns are not announced, the winners, at least, might be announced, by preparing, in advance, two flash trailers (or an individual trailer for each person in competition), each trailer • 281 •

announcing "the winner." When final returns are received, the correct trailer is selected and immediately run. 

633. ONE WORD DESCRIPTION... Contest for radio or newspaper or lobby might be based on best single word description of the star of attraction. Or, best five-word description (no more, no less). 

634. TURKEYS, CHICKENS... Before Thanksgiving and 

Christmas (several days before), turkeys are excellent "give-away" prizes. Tieup might be made with a merchant, securing a number of turkeys in return for credits or announcements.

Turkeys might be placed in a cage in the lobby in advance, cage gilded and lettered: "Birds in a Gilded Cage (and into copy announcing evening of give-away)." And instead of presenting turkeys to lucky winners, patrons might be invited to register their estimate for the weight of the birds (together); those nearest correct winning. 

Or chickens might be similarly awarded. 

Rooster might be used as center of a display on an attraction, which carries copy: "Something to Crow About!" Hen hidden nearby prompts Mr. Rooster to crow. Or amplification might be used, playing a recording of fowl crowing with speaker concealed behind cage. 

635. DANCING SCHOOL... Where dancing is featured in an attraction, dance schools might make announcements to their pupils, or permit them to be made. Tickets to see the coming attraction might be presented to pupils who win school dance contests. 

Dance schools can supply girls for dance contests, amateur nights, and for general advertising purposes where services of attractive personable girls are required. 

Dance school might present, as a feature for several evenings, a dance revue in which all their pupils are featured. Might arrange with them to sell tickets on a percentage basis. The revue shouldn't be limited entirely to kids; some older dancers should be included (perhaps "graduates" of the school).

Perhaps arrangements can be made to have a dance school or dancing instructor teach a class in dancing on theatre stage each Saturday morning, in connection with theatre's kiddie club. School can be scheduled to immediately precede the regular opening of the house. Box office would open early. School receives in return for their services a lobby announcement or announcement at kiddie club; and best argument is fact that theatre class presents an excellent medium for enlisting students in regular classes at the school. • 282 •

636. POSTER ON THE FLOOR... Where sufficient space is available, a poster (any size) can be placed on the floor or sidewalk, using “water-glass" to attach it. Display in background can possibly tie in with floor poster. In removing poster, use alcohol to dissolve the water-glass.

Used on sidewalks (and with okey of authorities), should be placed in early hours of morning, so that they are dry by time heavy traffic hits them. Should face the flow of early traffic, placed at an angle, on corners. 

637. CLOCKS 

.. Imprinted stickers attached to clocks about town carry copy: "Time to see (attraction)."

Tickets might be offered those guessing nearest to correct time a clock, on display in a window, will stop (using eight-day clock). Or, as a gag, an electric clock might be used, with the answer, obviously: "When the juice is turned off."

Window display of alarm clocks carries copy: "Set your clock. 

You'll want to be on time to see (attraction)."

Display panel might be made up to resemble a clock, with a still placed at each hour position. Lettered copy: "A Thrill a Minute.”

Large clock "hands" might be made to move; and stills might be placed in chronological order.

639. BULLETIN BOARDS... All factories, schools, plants, large offices, corporations, gymnasiums, department stores, hotels, and other places employing a number of people, generally have bulletin boards where messages are attached. Arrangements might be made to have neatly imprinted or lettered cards attached to these boards. 

Specially printed card or herald (prepared for mailing or distribution) might be used for bulletin boards.

Lobby bulletin board might be featured as a place to attach interesting clippings from press material received on an attraction. 

Might be clipped from press-books or trade papers. Can be headed: "Things to Know about Pictures," or "Star Gazing," or similar title.

tion, the character pictured in story of theatre's attraction. If this is so, he ought to be good for newspaper interviews in which he is asked questions about attraction. He should see the show as theatre's guest, with his reactions perhaps good for another story. 

Entertainers similar to those pictured in an attraction might be located, too, and used in front of theatre, or on a float; or on stage. 

641. START SHOW. . . As a part of the formality of beginning the showing of an important attraction, perhaps arrangements can be made to have the Mayor or some important dignitary to officially "star" the show (for the benefit of radio broadcast, and newspaper photographers).

His Honor might be pictured in theatre projection booth, starting the machines; or, he might be photographed, backstage, pulling the rope which will raise the curtain on an important stage attraction. 

Or, Mayor might "start" the show by throwing a switch which is wired into a panel in the lobby (and which sounds a buzzer as a cue). 

Show might be officially "started" from an airplane circling overhead (for story purposes) through radio signal from the plane. 

642. BATH... Can be made the center of a display for lobby or window, if attraction suggests. Shower bath set-up might be featured with cutout life-size figure of feminine star within the bath, head and shoulders extending through the curtain. Rain effect recording might be secured from radio station and played through house amplification system back of the display to lend realism. 

It's been a long time since Anna Held's famous milk bath, still, a "milk bath" might be staged as a sensational stunt that should win newspaper space and much comment. . . to be used, however, with discretion and full consideration of town and attraction. 

If attraction suggests either beauty or bath, it might be announced that a girl will take a beauty bath, in milk, in theatre lobby at a specified time. . . or, in window of a cooperating store or beauty shop. 

Classified ads are carried in newspaper in advance, reading: "Wanted. Attractive and shapely girl to take a milk bath in (theatre) lobby (or window of cooperating store), as part of advertising campaign in connection with showing of (attraction).” 

Newspapers might pick up the gag as a novel story. 

Actually, girl wears low-cut swim suit (without shoulder straps). 

She is screened until she is in the tub (which is elevated slightly, and made part of a display, with copy tieing in attraction. Plumbing supply place might supply an elaborate tub for a credit mention). 

Quantity of milk has been added to water in the tub, making it • 284 •

impossible to see the girl, or that portion of her which is submerged. 

Newspaper men witness the first "bath." 

643. LIFE... With all other subjects naturally of secondary importance, it is also only natural that many stories will deal with life, or life and death.

And, in connection, displays of scientific life-saving apparatus might be arranged (pulmotors, oxygen tents, etc.), and demonstrations of life-saving methods (by life-guards or boy scouts or coast guard).

Cooperative ads of business places might urge readers to make life pleasant, or safe, calling attention to their products and to theatre's attraction.

Essay contests, for newspaper or radio might be based on "life after death" experiences, or "near to death" experiences. 

Scientific magazines and spook magazines on newsstands might be rubber-stamped with copy on attraction, or imprinted adhesive labels attached to the covers. 

644. GLASS TANK . . . Small glass aquarium, preferably a square tank, might be effectively used (especially if ocean or river is important to story), placing it behind lobby display panel, the tank being visible to patrons through an opening in the panel (except top, bottom, sides). Tank is illuminated from behind panel. 

Display copy on coming attraction might be lettered (in oil) on metal or glass, and submerged within the tank. Or, cutout figures from still might be pasted to panel of glass and varnished over, and placed in the tank.

Or, still might be placed behind the bowl, so that it is visible through the water (which might be slightly tinted with bluing), giving it a weird effect. Cutout figures from stills might be attached to edge of an electrically driven phonograph turn-table, revolving behind the bowl and visible through it. 

Added angle is placing of a great many goldfish in the tank, offering guest tickets to patron estimating exact number. 

645. FISH SWIM THROUGH DISPLAY 

A small aquarium made part of a window display . . . with a small ring suspended within the bowl, a ring large enough, however, for goldfish, which are also within the bowl, to swim through. Display cards call fish "(star's) Trained Goldfish," and offer tickets to anyone witnessing one of the fish swim through the ring. 

Or, instead of ring, cutout letters spelling out star's name, or title of picture might be used, provided there is a letter "o" in the words • 285

that might be used instead of the ring. The letter "o" might be made larger than other letters. 

There is no chance of fish swimming through, as center of the ring is glass, not visible when in the water. Curtain ring might be used, with glass cut to fit inside ring tightly; or ring might be made of plastic wood molded around circular glass. Might be adapted to goldfish bowl or aquarium already in use in store window.

647. RAMBLING CHECK . . . Aid of luncheon club is en listed by theatre in starting several dollars in circulation about town. 

In tieup with bank, several over-size checks, for a dollar each, are covered by a deposit. Checks, with newspaper following the stunt, are presented to several club members . . . who are to immediately place the check in circulation. Imprint on the check carries star's name and copy on attraction . . . and urges those receiving the check to endorse it and put it into circulation immediately . asking that it be cashed at bank on a specified date. Check presented as “with compliments of star of theatre's attraction." Newspaper follows the checks as well as possible, asking readers to phone and notify them if they get the check. ... 

648 BILLIARDS If featured in an attraction, and if billiards can be capitalized upon without detracting from appeal of the picture, billiard table might be set up in lobby, with guest tickets offered to patrons making a certain difficult shot, which is explained by attendant. Cue ball might be spotted behind the eight ball, with display panel carrying copy: "Get out from behind the 8-ball. You're in for good luck... you're going to see (attraction)." Billiard expert might make exhibition shots.

And, of course, pool halls and billiard parlors should be circularized, or display cards placed. 

649. MONEY . . . Old coins, or money of different nations might make an interesting window display, or (under lock and key), for the lobby. Panel might carry copy: "All the money in the world couldn't buy a better show." Confederate money might be used for display.

Heralds might be made up after style of stage money, with attraction copy imprinted. Drawings suggested by attraction, as bevy • 286

of girls, might be featured on the "money." Copy might say: "$1,000 worth of Laughs . . . For Regular (theatre) Prices." Stage money might be attached in large quantity to front panels. 

Displays of counterfeit money might be arranged, if attraction suggests. A legitimate bill might be placed with bogus ones, and those whose attention is attracted asked to pick out the good one. 

Man (or girl) might be placed in a prominent window, busily engaged in flipping a coin. Panel carries copy: "I'm trying to see which wins most often-heads or tails. But heads or tails, I'm going to see (attraction)." Two blackboards are placed in the window, one on either side, one lettered at top "Heads," the other "Tails"... the "flipper" in the window marking up each flip of the coin.

Contest might be based on number of words meaning money, or slang expressions, colloquial terms. Tickets for longest lists. 

Toy banks might be bought cheaply in quantity and distributed to patrons in advance, with imprinted sticker attached; or cooperating store might hand them out with purchases. Electrical appliance tieups might be based on the money-saving angle. 

650. SPORTS PARADE... Attraction dealing with sports, or with any one particular sport, might suggest a "sports week," with various evenings dedicated to various games. Worked out with cooperation of sports editor, those interested in various sports might be urged to attend on designated nights. Local champs in various athletic activities might be invited as guests of the paper. 

Sports tieups made with athletic stores, places specializing in sports goods, bikes, clothing, books, automobiles. 

A "Junior Olympics" might even be worked out for a Saturday morning before the opening of show, with sports page offering trophies or medals (named after star of theatre's attraction), for winners of various events which are planned (running, jumping, swimming. 

Or regular track meet might be worked up, perhaps with playgrounds or school cooperation. Boy scouts might aid).

A stage or lobby "Sports Parade of Fashions" might be staged, handling much after the manner of a style show . . . with girls modeling all sorts of sports costumes, from bathing suits and tennis costumes to skiing outfits. Worked out in tieup with a store. Can even be staged in the windows of the store (with display cards on the attraction tieing in). 

651. MANUFACTURERS... Of many articles will occasion ally be interested in placing samples of their products in the hands of • 287 ·

potential customers. Many of them, manufacturers of cosmetics or candy or harmonicas, will be willing and interested in having theatre handle the local distribution for them. 

Local distributors, or the manufacturer direct, might be contacted.

Theatre audiences are good potential customers for most products, and distribution in theatre is very desirable. 

In distribution, the article is placed in an imprinted pay envelope, which carries imprinted ad on the coming attraction. . . with catchline tieing in with the distributed sample. 

652. HAWAIIAN... Attraction with Hawaiian locale sug gests front and lobby display panels carrying out the Hawaiian atmosphere; palms, sea scenes, Hawaiian music.

Hawaiian entertainers and perhaps a hula dancer might be used, in lobby or out front of theatre.

Papier mache volcano might be constructed, using paper streamers (blown by an electric fan within the "volcano"), flashing red floodlights, burning incense. 

Couple of "Hawaiians" might be used in connection with an attraction that doesn't deal with Hawaii . . . having them carry banners, "Even the Hawaiians are coming to town. . . to see (attraction)." 

653. FILM CLIP . . . Trailer company might make up a quantity of duplicate clips, from a film clip... the clips attached to cards, which are imprinted: "Just a peek at (attraction)," or, "See for yourself the Breathless Beauty of (attraction)." Cards distributed as heralds. 

The film clips (several frames each), might be stapled to a card, over an opening which is die-cut into the card; or two slots might be die-cut into the card and film inserted at either end in the openings • 288 •

... with opening between the slots, the size of a film frame, die-cut cut.

654. LIE DETECTOR... For novel lobby or window flash 

(using amplification) a "machine" might be made up to resemble a lie-detector... wires attaching to forearm of person being questioned, and leading to a panel behind the person, which features two globes which might represent "Truth" and "Lie" (one representing a deviation from the truth might be red). Switches which control lights can be placed under carpet and contact made by pressing foot on them. 

Pretty girl might be used as the "subject," questioner asking her a routine series of questions, and with the "lie-detector" reacting each time she answers . . . sometimes with humorous results (as, to query: "Have you ever been kissed?" girl answers, "No," and lie-detector flashes "lie" light repeatedly). "Demonstration" ends with series of questions about attraction, with answers and machine's indications reacting to boost attraction. Wind-up questions might include the dialogue: "You saw a preview (or special screening) of (attraction), didn't you?" Girl answers, "Yes," and machine points "truth." "Did you like it?" "No," and machine points "lie." "Really, what did you think of it?" "I thought it was swell," with machine pointing "truth," etc.

Perhaps a real scientific lie-detecting apparatus might be available, and might be secured for a special demonstration . . . having a "subject" witness an attraction that is really outstanding, then attempting to give the wrong answers to questions about the attraction when tested by the machine. Newspaper might cover the demonstration with a story and photograph. Patrons might be asked to try to outwit the machine, asking questions to which the answers are obvious. Well-known local young lady might serve as the subject. Questions should be carefully arranged so that all reactions would be of credit to the attraction.

sleeve, carries copy on his back: "I just met those gorgeous dames in (attraction) at (theatre)... You'll want to see 'em, but don't say

656. "MOVIE VISION" . . . Lettered on lobby display, featuring a mirror panel. Copy invites patrons to press buttons for a view of (attraction). Pressing button turns on lights behind special mirror which is not opaqued and immediately becomes transparent when lights are flashed on behind it. Panel behind mirror, which is illuminated when button is pressed, features a small opening, back of which a drum is made to revolve when the button is pressed, displaying a series of stills which are attached to the revolving drum. 

Lights might be arranged on flashers. 

657. PROMOTION, GIVE-AWAYS... If give-aways are considered, a trip or an automobile, the cost can be divided among cooperating merchants, who share the cost of the car, or a large part of the cost. Merchants distribute coupons with purchases or payments on account, and receive mention in advertising, on lobby panels or trailers. Also, if article, or articles, to be awarded, are placed on display in theatre lobby, the cooperating merchants will receive credit there.

On smaller items, individual merchants might give the items in exchange for advertising.

Samples of various kinds (as gum, candy, cigarettes), might be promoted from the distributor, or the manufacturer. Samples are distributed by theatre, inserted in imprinted envelopes. 

In using heralds, store might share the expense, if they are numbered, with certain numbers good for guest tickets to see theatre's attraction, if brought to store to secure the winning tickets. Winning numbers posted in store where they might be checked by those receiving heralds.
