659. BATHING GIRLS. . . Suggested by an attraction that features swim scenes or bathing girls, or a star who is noted for • 290 ·

curvatious charms, a bathing girl revue might be arranged. Or, it might be presented as an added attraction. 

Bathing girl contest can be staged at a cooperating swim pool. 

Or on theatre stage. Or in front of theatre on opening night, or opening day of attraction. Or, as a feature at cooperating night club or dance spot (with announcements given attraction). Contest might be made a feature of a stage revue, using beach setting (beach umbrellas, and possibly sea background) and building up to promenade finale. 

Manufacturer of swim suits might supply the swim suits, with local distributor cooperating. Different merchants might each supply a swim suit and a girl . . . with the suit on display in their windows in advance. 

Winner of contest gets prize, and perhaps a loving cup (“from the star of attraction"). Perhaps a trip might be promoted for the winner, or she might be entered in a national beauty contest. She also receives the title of "Miss (city)." 

Where contest is a one-time stunt, three or five judges might select the winner. Or applause might decide. If contest is presented as part of a stage revue, and it is necessary to present it for more than one performance, different judges might be arranged for each performance, votes of all of them being tabulated at conclusion of last contest . . . girls being held on stage after last showing (with other entertainment introduced) until all votes are counted, so that winners might be introduced. In event of tie, applause might determine the winner, or duplicate prizes and twin "titles" might be awarded. Photo of the contest, or of the winners, should be good for newspaper space. 

Staged at pool, or at night club, away from theatre, trophy should be presented with "compliments of (star of attraction)." Newspaper might sponsor the contest. 

Cooperating photographer might make bathing suit photographs of the girls who have entered the contest, for newspaper reproduction or lobby display. 

Bathing girls might also be used to effectively adorn parades or floats, or canopy or lobby displays; or to dress up a street stunt, as good looking, shapely girls in bathing suits can be relied upon to draw attention. Where their use might be suggested by an attraction, and an elaborate float cannot be used, an open automobile might be secured, banners placed on both sides, and bathing girls seated all over it. • 291 •

Bathing girl "contest" might be made part of a stage show, using girls from stage attraction, staging the "contest" as a unit in the show.

Grand opening of an attraction might feature arrival of bathing girls . . . the girls arriving at theatre in individual cars, mounting platform in front of theatre, and modeling swim suits before entering theatre. Publicized in advance as "Search for town's perfect showgirl type," or (in connection with a musical or girl show), "showing the latest in bathing styles and pretty girls," or, "the newest hit of the year, and the newest thing in swim suits." Appearance of the girls will assure a crowd of spectators for opening ceremonies. 

A group of girls (or men) wearing swim suits on which the title of attraction has been lettered, will attract attention at beaches or at swim pool.

Photographs of stars in bathing suits might be used in window tieup display of bathing suits. 

660. NUDIST COLONY A teaser gag . . . starting with small ads in newspapers, preferably not on theatre pages (possibly on page opposite theatre page), running each day for week or more in advance of opening of attraction... each ad headed: "Nudist Colony" (in large caps); copy varying each day. as "Those interested in joining this new colony in (city) are requested to watch this space for complete information" . . . "Complete information in (day's) (paper)" . . . "Watch tomorrow's paper for complete information and instructions". . . and then on final day, the "instructions" advising those interested to meet certain type of car, license number (from another state if possible) at specified place (some distance from theatre), suggesting that readers fall in behind the car. When the curious who fall in behind the car follow it by a winding route, to the theatre, where in front is displayed a cage of monkeys or baboons, labeled "Monkey Nudist Colony," or "(star's) Baboon Nudist Colony."

If picture is to receive a "formal" opening, with broadcast and all the trimmings, time the "parade" to the theatre to arrive during the ceremonies, when the announcer might comment on the stunt. 

Be sure to plant follow-up story in newspaper to satisfy curiosity of those who have been following the ad series but missed the parade to theatre. 

661. POINTS OF CHARM... Contest for newspaper might be based on contestants' analysis of attractiveness of star of attraction . . . the selection of points of beauty, of qualities that attract. • 292 ·

Beauty page editor of newspaper might point out points of charm of star, using photo for illustration. 

662. CHECKERS... Expert checker or chess player might be stationed in lobby, as center of a display, inviting patrons to try and beat him, with guest tickets to see coming attraction for those who can beat him.

Panels carry copy on attraction. Catch-line might be carried: "It'll be your move (day) . . . You'll want to hop down to (theatre) and see (attraction)."

Giant checker board might be made up for window use, with costumed girls playing, walking across the "board" to move the "checkers." Periodically, the girls turn the “checkers" over, with letters on reverse side spelling out attraction copy. 

Couple of costumed girls, or bally men can seat themselves (on folding chairs) at important corners, engaging in a checker game. 

They play until sufficient attention has been attracted, then they turn the board over, revealing an ad on the attraction; and on to another spot. ... 

663. SCREEN TESTS. Occasionally screen tests can be satisfactorily worked out, if tieup with newspaper can be arranged and tests made on theatre stage. 

Tests, of course, hinge on ability to have pictures made satisfactorily and economically enough on theatre stage; and photography should definitely be good.

Girls who are entered, compete on evening tests are to be made, with several winners to be made up on stage, and photographed, reciting prepared lines. In connection with stage show, the star of stage show can advise in regard to make up; if not, some local beauty shop can provide an expert.

Arrangements might be made, well in advance, to have some studio look at the films if sent them. The tests are also run the week following at theatre. 

664. TALENT TESTS. . . In tieup with radio station, radio talent try-outs might include all sorts of potential radio talent (as suggested by attraction); or if attraction features singing star, the contest can be limited to singers. 

Newspaper, radio station and theatre might cooperate on the proposition, with entries received in advance. Elimination contest might be held if there are a large number of entries. And the final contest to be held on stage of theatre, or in radio station. 

Arrangements might be made to have star wire newspaper or radio • 293 •

EN C Y C L O PEDIA OF EXPLOITATION 

station, suggesting the contest . . . with prize being announced at same time. If trip can be promoted, it can be announced as “with (star's) compliments."

Engagement over local radio station, or in theatre stage show, might be offered to winner as a prize. . . the winner to be paid for the appearance. 

665. SPORTS ANNOUNCERS... Broadcasting important football or baseball games, with a tremendous air audience assured, perhaps arrangements can be made to have the announcer mention theatre's attraction.

Perhaps some deal might be necessary with sponsor of the broadcast, repaying him in some way for the announcements. 

666. BARBERS, BEAUTY SHOPS . . . Reverse lettered cards might be placed behind chairs in barber shops or beauty shops so that the cards are correctly reflected in mirrors . . . and customers looking into mirrors will read the message. (See 674.)

Barbers and beauty shop attendants might be invited as special guests to witness the screening of an attraction that is definitely entertaining . . . on the theory that they are inclined to talk, and that they daily come into contact with many people to whom they will mention the attraction.

Shop might feature a special hairdress which is named after attraction or its star.

Distributor of a permanent waving machine might arrange to place cards in all beauty shops in town tieing in attraction... this in return for exhibition of a machine in theatre lobby, with panel carrying tieup copy. Cards would carry cut of star. Firm might go for direct mail mention to beauty shops, too. 

667. POLICE . . . In connection with attraction dealing with police work, or crime, or a murder-mystery, police and detectives might be invited to see an advance screening. Police might escort film to theatre on opening day, for newspaper photographs. Police department might issue police card or police pass to star of attraction. 

Chief might permit himself to be quoted in ads. Officers might be radio-interviewed as they leave theatre after witnessing the attraction. 

Might set two screenings, one for early morning, one late at night, so that both shifts might see the picture. 

Police equipment, and seized guns, blackjacks, handcuffs, billies, and gas guns and machine guns, and crime detecting apparatus and displays, might be borrowed for a lobby or window flash, for attraction that deals with crime or gangsters or police methods. (Articles • 294 ·

E NC Y C LOPEDIA OF EXPLOITATION 

might be tagged with explanations.) Equipment and articles should be placed under glass; or wired to panel, and in charge of attendant at all times.

If the police cars are radio equipped, the police dispatcher might be persuaded to say something about theatre's attraction. especially if theme of attraction is one that glorifies activities of the law enforcers. This announcement not only for the benefit of the police tuned in, but also for the large number of persons who habitually listen to police broadcasts. Police might permit a spare police car to be parked in front of theatre on opening day with radio tuned in on police calls.

Perhaps police band will parade to theatre on opening day. Or squad of police might parade, might go through a drill. A benefit proposition might be worked out with the police which would justify and assure their support. They might sell tickets, with a percentage to go to their fund; or they might distribute cards which urge those receiving them to attend on a certain night and to present the card at that time. . . a certain percentage of that sale to go to police fund if card is presented at box office (thus there is no selling of tickets outside the theatre). 

Trophy might be presented in police shooting competition, the trophy named after star of attraction. ... 

668. FIREMEN . . . If activities of fire department or firemen are shown, a special screening for firemen might be arranged, with their comment used over a broadcast after it is over. Chief might permit his endorsement to be added to a newspaper ad. 

Film might be delivered to theatre on opening day by a fire truck; or by an escort of firemen. Fire department drill squad might perform in front of theatre on opening day; or a giant extension ladder might be "demonstrated" in front of theatre. Playing stage shows, the star might be made an honorary chief or assistant chief. 

Fire effect for display can be made up, using strips of silk blown by a concealed electric fan, red floodlights, burning incense, or (if outside), steam exhaust. 

669. MARRIAGE... Wedding gown and suggestions for brides' wardrobes might be displayed by women's shops. Cooperative newspaper ads, illustrated with scenes from the attraction, might make appeal to "brides." Newspaper classified page contest might be based on question: "Where can a Bride buy (listing articles daily that are advertised on classified page). 

Pretty girl dressed as a bride, together with a "groom," might ride • 295 ·

about town in an open car, to which tin cans and "just married" cards are attached, with display copy on theatre attraction also included. Car might stop at busy intersections where "bride" hands heralds. Visiting newspaper office, "bride" might deliver an invitation to movie critic or well-known columnist. 

Cooking department of store or newspaper, or store selling cooking appliances should cooperate with newspaper space or windows. 

Wedding on the stage might possibly be arranged for opening night of attraction (see 551). Rice, in small imprinted envelopes might be distributed as heralds. Those couples securing marriage licenses on opening day might be invited to see the show as guests of theatre and newspaper.

Woman's Page of newspaper will perhaps use a still of "bride" in trousseau. If imitation wedding rings can be secured in quantity cheaply enough, they might be attached to heralds, or with imprinted tag attached, used for distribution. Jeweler might install window display of rings. 

First girl married after opening of attraction might be interviewed over radio, or for papers. 

Contest angles, for newspaper and radio, based on or suggested by marriage, might include best written proposal submitted, without use of usual phrase, "I Love You." Newspaper illustrates with scene from attraction. Or, "Best Marrying Age." Or, “Best

Description of How Husbands Proposed." Or, "Most Romantic 

Place to Spend Honeymoon." Or, "Requirements for a Perfect 

Sweetheart." Or, "The Honeymoon is Over When . . ." for a humorous contest.

Couples celebrating silver wedding during showing of attraction might be invited. Couples who have celebrated their golden anniversaries might be invited as guests of honor (with newspaper interview). Longest married couple might be sought. "Bride" might appear in the lobby, in full regalia, handing patrons imprinted cards (see No. 488). 

Stores might cooperate in arranging a "hope chest" (gifts) for first couple married after opening of attraction, cooperating merchants buying newspaper space. 

Comedy rules on "How to be Happy though Married" might be basis of radio or newspaper contest . . . with suggested answers similar to "Live in (town), send your wife to Hong Kong."

Real estate company tieup ad uses illustration from attraction showing romantic team, and carrying at top of illustration a listing • 296 •

of marriage license applications (from newspaper), and beneath the illustration a listing of apartments. Copy on attraction completes the ad. 

670. ANALYZE CHARACTER . . . Newspaper can invite readers to analyze the characters of stars from photographs which they publish (one each day for several days), (to attempt to figure out just what sort of person star is, his likes and dislikes and natural inclinations). Or, contest copy can be imprinted on the back of small photograph reproductions for distribution. "Character analyst" might appear in theatre lobby in advance, telling patrons about themselves. . . including information that they're just the type that would enjoy the coming attraction. 

671. JUMPING BEANS... Mexican jumping beans will attract attention to a window display, calling them: “(Star's) amusing 

Mexican Jumping Beans." Or, catch-line: "The romance and thrills will keep you jumping, too, when you see (and into attraction copy)." 

A lighted globe under the beans will keep them hopping. The beans can generally be obtained from a novelty store. 

672. THRILL TEST . . . Arrangements made to have a psychologist, or authority from a local school or college (for newspaper photographs), test reactions of patrons to a thrill-attraction.

Perhaps equipment from school might be used, or the "test" may be based on variation in pulse beat or blood pressure. Reactions of a person watching a "thriller" might be measured and comparative tests (for newspaper stories) based on a "who's thrilled most" angle. 

Test a girl and a man; or a redhead and a blonde. 

673. THRILLOMETER... Panel in which peep hole is cut (with display of stills behind same), carries copy: "Can you stand the thrill test?" and "Test your reactions." A large thermometer (made up by cutting glass tubing into compo-board paneling), is connected by rubber tubing with a hot water bag concealed under small elevation or platform on which person stands to look in the "peep hole." Glass tube is filled with a colored liquid, which rises in tubing when a person's weight is placed on the platform. "Degrees" of excitement might be registered alongside the "thermometer." 

674. TABLES . . . Stills or printed cards can be placed effectively on tables in restaurants, beauty shops, barber shops (manicuring tables), drug stores, lunch rooms, grills and bars. If tables are glass-covered, the photos or cards should be placed under the glass. If stills are used, attraction title should be lettered on each still. 297 •

Or, two stills or imprinted cards can be placed back to back and placed on tables. Printed cards might be made up folder-style (as an inverted "V"), imprinted upright on each side, and placed on tables. 

675. TITLES... Tieups of many kinds can often be based on the titles of attractions. Titles should be weighed and considered from every point. Things or persons that would be suggested by, or connected with, the title might be adapted to advertising. 

Many articles can be "named after," or "named in honor of," the attraction in tieups, as perfumes, dresses, colors (of materials), pearls, sandals, shoes, shirts, ties, hats, fashions, ice cream, sodas, etc. 

Actual endorsement of star need not be used. 

Title might suggest teaser campaign, especially if it is a single word, a name, a statement; or if it is brief-title alone being posted in advance . . . following up with regular ads. Similarly newspaper ads and imprinted stickers. 

Title of attraction might be shouted, via amplification, from theatre marquee top, or from roof of building. 

676. STAGE CARD ... Often vaudeville acts have been introduced by a costumed girl, who carries a lettered card across stage. Similarly, a girl can carry a card on stage which announces the coming of an attraction. 

677. MICROSCOPE... Display in lobby directs attention to "The World's Smallest Billboard . . . Calling Your Attention to the Year's Biggest Production." Microscope, as the center of the display, is focused on the smallest possible replica of a billboard, with title of coming attraction lettered on it in microscopic lettering. 

Jeweler or engraver can prepare the "billboard," working it up under a microscope. Should be placed in charge of an attendant, or "billboard" end of microscope protected by a glass enclosure. 

678. TOUCH WINDOW... Those looking in at a window display are invited to touch a designated spot on the window . . . with animation within the window or illumination of a scene or display resulting.

Point to be touched is indicated by circular card attached direct to glass. . . but behind the card a copper wire is connected which carries body capacity to grid-glow bulb which is concealed (a photoelectric cell arrangement which makes animation possible on merely placing the hand near the grid-glow). 

679. POCKET BOOKS. . . Newspaper classified ad can carry this copy: "Lost . . .

If cheap pocket-books can be bought in some quantity, a card is inserted in each pocketbook, carrying the copy: "Tell your friends of your Good Luck in finding a (name of attraction) pocketbook... then bring it to (theatre) and receive guest tickets to see (attraction)."

Copy is imprinted on pieces of white silk cut the size of paper money, giving a money "feel" to the purse before it is opened. The purses are dropped in stores and business places throughout city the day before opening of attraction. 

680. VANISH LETTERING... Color wheel in front of a spotlight, focused on a display, causes lettering to "vanish" as beam of light of identical color as lettering is thrown on it, then changing light. Adapted to a window display, the window would be dark, other than the spotlight illumination. 

681. STATE... With locale of attraction in a certain state, and if it is of box office value to feature the locale, items identified with state can be used for display, or for newspaper features. State song can be introduced by orchestras, over radio, dedicated to attraction. State flags, if state has been represented by several in its history, can be reproduced by newspaper, with kids invited to color same. Program of popular songs which have featured or mentioned the state can be introduced over radio and properly dedicated. 

School essay on the state might be arranged. Giant map can serve as background for a display. Travel and transportation agencies will cooperate with window displays. Stores selling items produced in the state, or identified with it, will cooperate. Outlines of state (from map) can be covered over, for lobby or front with a composite display of stills. (See 545.) 

682. MOTHERS... Newspaper can cooperate in locating oldest living mother in city. If possible she is to be guest of theatre on opening of attraction (or on Mothers' Day). Newspaper might make portrait which they will carry in their columns, together with an interview. Attraction can be dedicated to her, and her photo might be placed in dignified display in lobby. Florist should present her with beautiful bouquet of flowers. Auto dealer to supply transportation for oldest mother and her family to theatre. Presentation of copy of the photo and the flowers made at theatre, with Mayor or important official making the presentation, paying tribute • 299 ·

to all mothers. Prize might be offered to youngest mother, too; and she ought to be good for a newspaper story. 

Gold Star Mothers should be specially invited guests on Mothers' Day. 

683. CALL SLIPS . Personal letters sent to all doctors, advising them that if they will fill out one of theatre's "call slips" when attending the theatre, they will be enabled to receive calls at the theatre without confusion or delay. They are advised that "call slips" (one of which is enclosed in each letter), are to be secured from the cashier. And the letter might be underlined with a P.S. about a coming attraction. "Call slips" carry spaces for listing name, date, seat location, time, usher's name.

When the list of doctors has been covered, other listings might be similarly used nurses, railroad men, dentists. 

684. BOWLING... Trophy (from star of coming attraction) might be offered with sports page sponsorship of team turning in best score of week. Sports page pictures of winners and trophy, and mention of attraction follow.

Long distance contest between local team and team in some other city, perhaps a foreign city, can be arranged, with the trophy to go to the winner. . . and consequent newspaper stories. 

685. TROPICS... Palms and beach background would be featured in displays. South sea spears, grass mats and grass skirts, paddles and native leis, might be used. To add effectiveness to a large lobby display, a wave-effect machine can be rented (from a theatre supply house, or projector company), and used against a sea background, giving the effect of rolling waves. Illumination would necessarily be reduced, and perhaps confined to blue lighting for best effect. seas.

Merchant tieups are numerous. Stores can feature a tropic weave, or cloth; or clothes; or bathing suits of a tropic design. Perfumes could be compared to the romantic breeze of the languorous south 

Jewelers might feature pearls. Pet stores, with monkeys and tropic fish. An aquarium of tropic fish might be placed in lobby in advance, as center of a display, with an attendant to tell patrons about the fish (as many persons are interested in tropical fish). 

Florists can feature orchids as the loveliest flower of the tropics. 

Music stores, broadcasting stations, orchestras, can feature south sea island music. Lingerie shop display can carry copy to the effect • 300 •

that if the tropic maidens in (attraction) wore 'em at all, they'd find "these" to be the best.

686. MONTH'S TOP SHOW... Outstanding attraction being designated as "The Month's Top Picture". . . or other similar distinction suggested by the attraction. . . and campaign being built about this angle. 

Window tieups can feature the "top" angle, possibly referring to merchant's line as "top buy" of the month. Merchandise tieups can also emphasize "The Tops" in their advertising copy. "Top" copy should be carried in all advertising on the attraction, newspaper ads, trailers, stories, radio announcements, etc. 

Orchestras can dedicate the month's "top tune" to theatre's "top attraction." 

687. CONGRATULATIONS. . . For use in connection with an outstanding attraction, or production in which star's performance is especially notable, a dignified poster can be made up, perhaps after manner of a scroll, carrying copy to effect that signers wish to congratulate the star on his (or her) performance. Those who have witnessed attraction might be invited to add their signatures. 

The display might be set up in prominent downtown location, perhaps in prominently located store, where attendant secures signatures. Or in theatre lobby.

Newspaper might use a photograph of a celebrity adding his signature to the scroll.

Or telegraph company can have an attendant to take the names of those who would like (for several cents) to have their names added to a special telegram of congratulation. The telegram being placed on display in window or lobby, made up in all length possible, before being sent. 

688. MOURNFUL AND HAPPY . . . Street stunt for a comedy attraction can feature two men, who circulate about town during rush hours.

One of the men is pleasant-appearing, perhaps stout, and keeps laughing or smiling. He carries banner: "I'm Happy. I just saw (attraction)." • 301 •

Other man must be sad, melancholy type, perhaps smaller, thinner, than his partner. He appears sorrowful, displeased. The sign he carries bears the words, "I Didn't." Men walk side by side, and must keep "in character." 

689. REVIEWS... Theatre might capitalize on a newspaper critic's favorable review, by reproducing it, or most favorable part of it, as part of a newspaper ad. Or the review, with most favorable phrases underlined, can be photographically enlarged for front display. Dealing out an especially favorable phrase in praising attraction, the critic can be quoted in attraction sign, or marquee letters. 

With an important screen attraction that is assured of favorable comment, perhaps a special screening of the attraction can be arranged for the reviewers, so that reviews might break in the newspapers before the opening of the attraction. 

690. FIRE DEPARTMENT DELIVERING FILM 

With a friendly fire department, arrangements might be made to have the film delivered to the theatre by a firetruck, with firemen handling the lettered can of film over to theatre. ... 99 Copy on film can, or on small banner which might be attached to truck, might feature "hot" copy. as: "Hot from the Studios. . .,' "Entertainment News so Hot that Only the Fire Department could 

Handle It."

Perhaps newspaper will use photo of the film being handed to theatre manager. 

691. SUMMERTIME SANTA CLAUS . . . Santa Claus, in the person of a man wearing complete Santa Claus costume, "arrives" in town in the middle of the summertime. Riding about town, Santa's car carries banners that say that he couldn't wait 'til December to bring (town) the greatest entertainment present in history. 

Or, after Christmas he can carry banner: "I'm sticking around to see (attraction)." "Santa Claus in Summer" angle can be adapted to newspaper ads ... using illustration of Santa Claus... and copy to the effect that the attraction is a Christmas present for (town) delivered in the middle of Summer. 

692. TAXICABS... Imprinted paper strips can be attached to rear or side windows of taxicabs, facing out. Or, for benefit of cab passengers, imprinted cards, or paper strips, can be attached inside of cabs, perhaps to glass that separates the driver and passengers. 

Cards can carry lines: "Ride (company) cabs to (theatre) to see (attraction)." Parade of cabs can be arranged for opening day of • 302 •

an attraction, the cabs carrying banners, or cards attached to bumpers. 

693. THEATRE PARTIES... Perhaps theatre's attraction will appeal to some certain group or organization, and they might be interested in attending as a body. 

Social and fraternal organizations can be contacted well in advance. 

Large corporations and stores, or employee's organizations, might be interested in arranging a theatre party for employees. 

694. NEWSPAPER STORY... Frequently attractions carry a newspaper background or are based on the adventures of newspaper reporters and editors. 

For these, perhaps a corner of the lobby can be turned into a city room, with city editor's desk . . . and with man wearing an eye-shade at the desk, typing out "news". . . and accepting any news brought him. Sponsored by newspaper, one of the newspaper's staff might be assigned to cover the lobby, and might pick up many interesting stories. 

Journalists can be invited to select, among themselves, by popular vote, the best news story, or the best bit of reporting to occur on the local paper during the year. . . with a prize or trophy (from star of theatre's attraction) for the winner. And with attendant newspaper stories. 

Journalism classes of schools and colleges will naturally be interested, and should be contacted.

Newspaper can place copies of old editions, history-making editions, on display in their windows, with attraction panels. (See No. 739.) 

695. LOVE LETTERS . . . Handwritten "love letter" 

prepared, which begins by paralleling story in theatre attraction, and at finish goes into outright attraction copy. Cut is made up; and printed, the "letters" are folded letter-style and inserted in envelopes, which are sealed.

In distribution they are left on counters, dropped on floor in stores and business places where they will be picked up and read. 

Or, herald is made up to resemble folded note paper, with "love letter" printed on front page. Inner page carries ad on attraction. 

696. MERCHANT'S ADS SLUGS... In connection with a special “day," a theatre opening, or an outstanding attraction which may draw persons from out of town to city, perhaps the different merchants will be willing to permit a small cut, which carries copy on theatre's attraction, to be placed in their newspaper ads. Photographs or illustrations (perhaps cuts or mats) from the attraction, • 303 •

each different, can be supplied the various cooperating business places for ad illustration. 

697. WINDOW TAPPER 

With bell removed from an electric door bell, the tapper can be placed against the glass of a window, to attract attention to a display within the window. Dry cell batteries keep the tapper going. 

698. ANNOUNCEMENTS ... Arrangements can be made to have announcements made at many places where crowds gather, using amplification system where they are equipped. Swim pools, ballrooms, athletic competitions, any special affairs that draw crowds. 

Personal announcements from the stage of theatre about coming show will emphasize its importance. 

699. TOAST... Guest tickets might be offered for best submitted "toasts" to star of theatre's attraction . . . via newspaper contest or radio program. Newspaper might picture a different star each day for several days, with "toasts" to be prepared for each

Cleverness, appropriateness counting in determining winners. 

700. GRADUATES... School graduations and commence ment days suggest theatre parties, school nights, sorority and fraternity tieups, invitations to graduates, special school theatre parties. one.

Graduates might be invited as guests of theatre, or special price can be made them. Letters of congratulation should be sent graduates, calling their attention, incidentally, to attraction. With graduates attending on a designated night, perhaps school band will appear and play.

Large clock can be set up as center of a display, perhaps in a jeweler's window, with a name indicated at each minute around the clock. Where minute hand stops, indicated student will receive a special prize, perhaps a three months pass, and possibly a watch or other gift from jeweler. Tickets to see attraction (which receives display in window) might go to 20 names previous to one where hand stops.

If school's auditorium is not sufficiently large for graduation ceremonies, possibly the theatre might be rented, or loaned to school for morning exercises.

Perhaps arrangements can be made to have gold medal (named for star) presented to grammar school graduates having highest averages. 

Graduate nurses, too, should be sent letters of congratulation on their graduation. 

701. DOG RACE... Novel stunt for kids might be arranged 

• 304

by arranging for them to "enter" their pooches in a "race." At designated place and time, someone holds dog at starting line for each youngster . . . and from some short distance the kids whistle for their dogs, and they are released. 

Where real whippet or greyhound races are featured, it will be possible, on an evening when large crowds are attracted, to "name" a race after theatre's attraction . . . as "(attraction or star) Trophy

Race," with announcements over track's loud-speaking apparatus. 

702. LATE SHOW... Midnight showing of an attraction might prove effective on an occasional attraction . . . especially the evening before a holiday. Perhaps a special stage or screen show can be arranged for a midnight show. 

An outstanding screen attraction could be given a midnight showing a week or so in advance of regular opening date, with the attraction benefiting by consequent word-of-mouth advertising. 

Showing of the attraction should be preceded by a trailer, which announces opening dates, urges those seeing it to tell their friends about it. 

Arrangements might be made to have buses or street cars or other transportation operate late cars to take care of those witnessing the show. Or a special car on certain lines. (This in event cars do not run all night.) Coffee might be served patrons. Street should be brightly lighted for the "Midnight Premier," and perhaps all the embellishments of a regular "Grand Opening" might be used (see 11). 

Late showing of a mystery drama or thrill-show might be especially appropriate, billing it as a midnight thrill show. Could be made a society event, assuring (with the aid of society editor of the newspaper) a good attendance from the upper strata for the midnight showing. 

Paper might use pictures of celebs arriving, and pictures of debutantes pretending to appear frightened. 

703. IMITATORS... Where star of an attraction is wellknown by costume and appearance, and easily imitated, one or a group of imitators might travel about downtown streets. Resemblance should be as nearly perfect as possible. They might wear papier mache heads made up to resemble star. 

Imitator, or a group of them, can distribute heralds; or they might participate in a parade. Group of them visiting newspaper office may rate a story. Imitator can serve as sidewalk barker during showing of attraction; might possibly appear at a luncheon club. ... 

704. SIDEWALK PANELS . . . In some locations it might prove desirable to construct a panel, on the edge of the sidewalk in • 305.

front of the theatre. Outlined in lights, and selling current attraction on outside, inner side of the panel (which patrons would see on leaving theatre) is devoted to a coming attraction. The display might be made only shoulder high. 

Similarly, giant letters spelling out attraction title can be placed on edge of sidewalk. (See No. 94.) 

705. LAUGHED HIS HEAD OFF... Man strolling about town, wearing costume that carries collar above the top of his head (collar and tie resting on top of his head, rest of the costume in proportion), giving effect of man having no head. (Shirt front is thin cloth through which he can see.) He carries a dummy head under his arm. Copy on his back reads: "I Laughed My Head Off At (attraction)." 

706. ATTORNEYS. . . Since lawyers are always interested in an attraction that features a lawyer, their attention should be called to the showing of such attraction. Mailing letters to them, or calling on telephone might do the trick. Law students should also be contacted. ...

Perhaps, in connection with legal drama, it can be arranged to have some prominent lawyer, or group of lawyers, dispense gratis legal advice during showing of attraction . . . either appearing in theatre lobby, or the questions to be submitted to a cooperating newspaper. 

Tickets to be awarded daily to most interesting legal query received. (See 47, 349.)

Law school students might stage a "mock trial," as prologue to a trailer on a "court room" attraction. 

707. DEARTH'S LIGHT... Jean Dearth's mysterious light extension cord will win attention for any window display. A short extension cord (twisted cord; and about three feet long), is equipped with complete fittings (attachment plug on one end, socket and small globe on the other). Extension is coiled, as center of display, on a small square of velvet; and though the extension is apparently in no way connected up, a globe in the socket is burning. 

Operation is simplicity itself. Another twisted cord extension, which is connected with house current, extends under the velvet. 

An ordinary straight pin is forced through each cord of Dearth's extension, through the velvet, and into the two wires of the practical extension underneath. Heads of pins are camouflaged or covered by a coil of the wire, so they can't be seen. Contacts underneath taped. 

708. GIRL IN CAGE... If appropriate, a novel lobby flash • 306 •

. would feature a cage, or replica of a large cage. interior of the "cage" being equipped with boudoir furniture (dressing table, mirrors), and with pretty girl in lounging pajamas occupying the "cage." Panels on the "cage" carry copy: "She's Dangerous! . . . . (and into copy on the attraction)," and "Beware! Do not feed or 

Annoy," and "Captured in the Wilds of Civilization." Girl pays no attention to those who stop to stare at her, devotes her entire attention to beautifying herself. 

A cutout life-size figure of a girl might replace the girl when she isn't in the cage. Or, cutout might be used entirely instead of live girl. 

709 DEPARTMENT STORES... In merchandising attrac tions, the cooperation of leading department stores is almost essential; such cooperation can prove of much mutual value. Department store executives and advertising directors can and generally do deal out an alert and high-powered brand of showmanship themselves. 

They're merchandisers and can appreciate a clever or mutually advantageous advertising idea.

Cooperation can embrace window displays, one or a series; storewide sales events which tieup with attraction title; special cooperative newspaper ads, using scenes from attraction as illustrations; radio program tieups; fashion tieups, perhaps using photographs of theatre's stars; tieups with their various departments. 

Often an attraction will carry a number of national tieups, and the department store will be found to be the local dealer or distributor. 

710. JEWELS. . . If jewels are important to attraction, display may be arranged for jeweler's window, featuring scenes from the attraction, together with display of gems. Star's favorite jewel might be the basis of the display, together with star's photograph. 

Display of different kinds of stones in jeweler's window would win attention, perhaps together with rough material which the stones originally came from.

Perhaps duplicates or imitations of jewels worn in an attraction can be secured for display in jeweler's window. Studio may lend them; and even if imitation, they should be handled as very valuable, delivered to jeweler's by (bannered) armored car, perhaps with "guard" arranged to pace in front of window during time "jewels" are on display. Or, jeweler might secure reproductions of famous diamonds for display.

Plate of glass in lobby, spotlighted and part of display on attrac- • 307 •

tion, might have patrons invited to write their names on it with their diamonds. Offer tickets to those inscribing their names, if there aren't too many takers. 

711. SANDWICH MEN... This commonly used stunt can be made much more effective if the boards, which sandwich men carry, are made attractive and carefully lettered. (Boards are carried by means of straps over shoulders, one board facing front, one rear.) Variation is panel resting on shoulders, elevated above the head of the man carrying it. 

Grouping of sandwich men can add to their effectiveness. six or eight of them traveling together. Men carrying panels can be costumed as suggested by attraction. No. 96 might be adapted. 

Sandwich men, for an impressive effect, might wear papier mache "heads" (made to resemble star of attraction and fitting over sandwichman's head, resting on his shoulders). Occasionally available, the heads can otherwise be made up by school or college art class. 

Sandwich man might be equipped with a portable radio. 

712. MODELING... Contest can be based on modeling, from wax, wood putty, or clay; or even soap, in tieup with soap distributor.

Objects modeled would be suggested by attraction, or might be heads of stars appearing in attraction, or modelers can be given free rein to model whatever they wish. 

Tickets for best, and store might sponsor the idea. 

713. TATTOO ARTIST . . . Lobby display panel carries offer to tattoo picture of star of coming attraction on patrons "without charge" . . . and as center of display on the attraction, house artist is set up, equipped with a small water-color air-brush and a small stencil in which outline of star's face has been cut, which can be applied to patrons' arms. Display might refer to the designing as "Modern Tattooing," calling artist "Professor (name)."

Or, arrangements may be made with a regular tattoo artist, if one is available, to set up in lobby, with any tattooing to be the real McCoy... though any applicants for the designing should definitely be over 21 years of age and made to understand that the designing is permanent. 

714. DETECTIVES, MYSTERIES. . . Audience might be invited to attempt to "pick the killer" in a murder mystery. 

Show might be stopped for a minute, just before murderer is revealed, and patrons invited to try to pick the guilty party. Trailer, • 308 •

with explanatory copy, might be cut in, possibly showing pictures of suspects or of clues. 

Or, the stunt might be used only in connection with a special screening of the attraction, with newspaper critics, columnists, and local notables present. Perhaps Chief of Police, or Chief of Detectives might witness screening, and attempt to solve the "murder." (Chief might be advised in advance.) 

A reverse angle is newspaper or radio contest, inviting those who have witnessed the picture (or play), to submit their suggestion as to which of the characters in the story should have done it instead of the one shown to be guilty in the picture; and why. "Clues," or objects important to the plot of the story, can be adapted to display for lobby or window flash. 

Cobweb effect can be added to front or lobby displays if suggested by the attraction . . using silk cord, which might be gilded, gold metallics added. Cutout letters can be attached in the web. "Mystery Club" might be formed, inviting patrons to "register," handing them membership cards (which are numbered, and to be compared with good-for-tickets numbers posted opening night at box office).

During the last few minutes and the ending of a mystery picture, patrons should be held instead of seating them. Newspaper ads include copy advising that no one will be seated during final ten minutes of attraction. Trailer be made up carrying similar copy, and attached at end of regular trailer on attraction.

Patrons can be requested not to reveal the ending of a mystery attraction, "that perfect enjoyment of their friends might not be spoiled." Newspaper ads, and trailer following or preceeding the showing of the attraction carry the copy. 

715. BE A BEAUTY JUDGE... Novel feature for newspaper in connection with a girl show or musical would have newspaper carrying daily photographs of individual girls appearing in the attraction... with newspaper's readers invited to "be a beauty contest judge," to pick the winner.

Prize goes to person giving best ten-word reason for selection. If in connection with a stage show, some prize or honor might be arranged for the girl, too—perhaps a dinner in her honor at night spot or restaurant, or prizes from cooperating business places. 

Stars of the attraction in connection with which the contest is arranged should be pictured, each together with one of the girl photographs... with the girl described as the star's selection. • 309 •

ENCYCLOPEDIA OF EXPLOITA TI O N 716. INDICATED COLOR... Where a definite color is re ferred to in a title of an attraction, or important to theme or suggested by it, many tieups might be based on the color. Stores may feature merchandise of the specified color, with credit given attraction, in windows and ads dresses, cloth, hats, gloves, shoes, hose, bathing suits, men's ties, etc. 

Arrangements can be made with ice cream company to feature a special ice cream in the indicated color. Automobile dealer may be able to supply an automobile of the correct color for a street flash, properly bannered.

The color scheme of front and lobby displays would, of course, be based on the indicated color. 

717. HOLD-TO-LIGHT . . . Having copy set up so that it might be divided directly down the center without touching any type, a proof is run off, and half of the ad (dividing down center) is sent to engraver for a reversed cut. Light card is then imprinted with the remaining half of the type set-up on one half, and the engraving is imprinted on the reverse side of the card (and on opposite side of the card), so that they match up, though on different sides of the card, and when held to light the complete message is visible (the reversed type becoming legible when read through the card). 

Or same gag can be adapted to newspaper ad, buying space on reverse side of page so that, held to light, the imprint on the second page shows through and connects up with copy in the ad. Title of attraction might be printed on the second page, or an illustration might be used. 

718. BEST WIRE TO STAR... Newspaper invites readers to send in their suggestions for a 50-word, or less, telegram to be sent star, congratulating him on new attraction. Best wire submitted to be sent to star, and prize to go to writer. Additionally, arrangements might be made with star or studio, to have star "answer" the wire, sending the winner a personal letter or telegram. 

719. BEST TOWN... Newspaper or radio can announce star of attraction as interested in finding the "best town" in the country... and inviting readers to tell in 50 words or less, just why they believe the home town is "the best town in which to live." 

Assured of favorable response, the contest would be illustrated with photographs from attraction or of star. Winning essay should be reproduced by newspaper. Imaginary conversation between star and editor or secretary of Chamber of Commerce may be made into a feature story. • 310 •

720. ELECTRIC EYE... Photo-electric cell animation can be adapted to many displays for lobby or windows or elsewhere, breaking of a beam of light (by person walking through it), causing the display to become animated, starting mechanism of animated display.

Photo-electric cell can be harnessed to many novel displays. 

Games of skill employing the electric eye, as the photo-electric cell rifle (a beam of light serving as a bullet), might have tickets to see theatre's attraction going to those making best scores. 

721. PUZZLE STORIES . . . Basis for a contest for news paper or radio, and adapted to the attraction, the correct solutions to a series of puzzle stories win tickets, or the puzzle stories might be offered merely as an interesting feature. 

Several stories: Woman reports her husband (or lover) as having died. 

Explains that he suffered from a weak heart. . . that he dozed, was dreaming (something shocking that might be suggested by attraction or its locale), and that he was so shocked that his heart couldn't stand the strain, and he died without awakening. Police officers immediately took her into custody for murder. Why? (Answer: She couldn't possible have known what he was dreaming, since he died without awakening).

Ancient relic, represented as dating back thousands of years, is offered for sale. As proof of its age, person offering it for sale calls attention to engraving on marble base (or bronze), "Made for (some Roman or Chinese name)," 212 B.C. However, person to whom the relic was being sold knew immediately that relic (vase or statuette) was not as old as represented. How? (Age representation was obviously fraudulent, since being before Christ, it was, of course, not possible to date things before his birth).

Locking bathroom door, preparing to bathe (name) broke lock, being unable to then open the door which was airtight. Water was running in bathtub, and (name) tried to turn it off, and faucet broke so that it was impossible to turn off water. No windows in bathroom, door airtight, impossible to turn off water which was rising constantly. . how did (name) keep from drowning? (Simple. Just pulled the plug in bathtub.)

Man has a seven gallon pail and a three gallon pail. He must place five gallons of a liquid into the seven gallon pail. Having no measures, how is he to accurately put exactly five gallons into the seven gallon container? (He fills the three gallon container twice, emptying into the seven gallon container. Filling the three gallon container a third • 311 ·

Then emptying the seven gallon container, he pours the two gallons which remain in the three gallon container into the seven gallon pail; then fills the three gallon pail again, adding it to the two gallons. Total, five gallons). 

Man claims that money was stolen. Tells police that he remembers placing the money between pages 45 and 46 in a book. Police take into custody for taking money himself. Why? (Pages 45 and 46 would be the two sides of a single sheet. Could be between 46 and

722. MISSING . . . Where story features a person who disappears for any reason, or is "missing," newspaper teaser ads might announce him as missing (using character name from story). . . tieing in several days later with ads on attraction. Teaser ads might be headed: "Girl Missing," or "(name) Missing.' 99 Comedy classified gag would have classified ad asking for whereabouts of "Brother,” “just arrived from Scotland," and missing, and that when last seen he was following a small mole on a big blonde. 

Adding that he left home with a clean shirt and a five dollar bill and has probably changed neither. Next day, classified ad carries "reply" from "brother," advising that he is Not Missing-that is, that he is not missing a single performance of (attraction) at (theatre). 

That he'll be home as soon as the attraction ends its engagement. 

723. HOW TO BE POPULAR... Folder herald carries copy on front cover: "How to Be Popular. in one easy lesson . . .'

Inside folder is imprinted: "Take your girl to see (and into attraction copy)." 

724. POSE... Using life-size cutout, a tieup might be made with a photographer, inviting patrons to "pose with (star).” 

Attendant, equipped with camera, might snap their pictures. Tickets to be offered to those selected for display in photographer's window; or in lobby; or for most comical or most attractive. Panel near the figure carries copy on attraction. ...

Tieing up with newspaper sport page, all important games to be played on a specified date can be listed, with readers invited to attempt to correctly name the winners and scores. Lists to be submitted in advance of games, and tickets to go to those most nearly correct. During football season the stunt can be made a weekly event. Idea might be adapted to radio-sponsored sports program, perhaps including it in their time. For

729. CROWDS . . . Full value from ballyhoos can best be obtained, of course, by sending them to places where crowds of people are certain to see them, downtown streets, ball games, crowded beaches, etc. Where some scheduled event is sure to draw a large gathering, arrangements might be made to place a large banner somewhere nearby where it will be seen by every person attending. 

Or heralds can be distributed, or it might be possible to have announcements made. • 313 •

730. ROARING KITTEN 

Loud roars, such as a lion would make, emanate from a cage, for lobby or front flash, in which an ordinary house cat is enclosed. Roar is effected through recording of jungle roar, or lion roar (generally obtainable from broadcasting stations), sending it through amplification system, with speaker concealed behind the cage (or see 168). Lettering on cage says: "You'd Roar, too, if you couldn't go see (attraction);" or, "You'll 

Roar, too, with laughter, when you see (attraction).” 

731. STREET CORNERS... Busy downtown street corners afford a great spot for advertising. Cards might be attached to poles, or to trash-cans. Side of building may offer prominent location for a banner. Perhaps displays can be placed in windows of stores or business places located on prominent corners.
