732. ANIMAL CRACKERS. . . Ordinary animal crackers 

Ican be distributed in connection with attraction that is based on circus, animal or jungle story. Might be inserted in imprinted glassine sacks, or small envelopes, which carry copy on the attraction. 

For display purposes, where animal angle is emphasized, animal crackers can be coated with silver paint . . . the backs shellaced, then glued to display panels. They will appear to be miniature metal animal figures. 

733. SKIP WORDS... Message about attraction (which might be designed after fashion of regular movie "columns") is carried, but with many words missing (being filled in with underline and blank space). Tickets are offered to first so-many correctly filling in the skipped or missing words. Used as a newspaper feature, the paper subsequently carries the completed message. Missing words could be scattered through classified ads. 

734. MODEL HOME... Small model of the house or build ing where action in story takes place may be constructed by art department, or by manual training department of school, and would win attention in theatre lobby or a window surrounded by display material on the attraction.

Elaborate give-away, which could be worked out with cooperation of leading stores and business places, would be a model home- a real house and furnishings. Built under newspaper sponsorship, the cost would be shared by cooperating stores who also furnish it. On display for weeks in advance, the "home" campaign would extend over a period of months... the cooperating business places giving a ticket on the home with every purchase; drawing to be held at theatre. 

Newspaper might assume sponsorship and initiative in working out • 314 •

details. 

Real estate company interested in directing attention toward a certain section would supply the lot. 

Where newspaper builds a model home as a promotional proposition, without theatre tiein, newspaper may permit theatre to place framed and lettered stills of stars of coming attraction inside the house. With hundreds of persons looking the house over, they would prove well worthwhile. 

735. AIR BATTLE. . . For an aviation story, especially a war-time aviation story. An "aerial attack on (city) and battle in the clouds" is announced, including mention of an exhibition of stunt flying . . . in honor of the showing in (city) of (attraction).

Several planes, two or more, might go through various maneuvers at the specified time, engaging in a “dog-fight,” above airport, or near city (if river flows near city, above the river). One plane might tow a banner which carries attraction title, not engaging in the maneuvers. 

During aerial "attack," noise-makers, fireworks, etc., might be exploded on the ground. The "battle" might end with one of the planes giving an exhibition of smoke writing, or merely leaving a trail of smoke. One of the planes can drop a number of small parachutes in merchant tieup. (See No. 201.) Planes should tour city before the exhibition flying. Siren might be added to the equipment of one plane. Possibly flying service at the airport might present the airshow in exchange for display in theatre lobby. . . perhaps having a representative, in flying togs, on hand to hand out printed folders. 

736. REVERSED TITLE ... Small panel, at eye-level, placed in location where persons will generally be facing it (as at entrance to elevator), carries copy in reverse lettering. Smaller straight lettering carries message: "To read this, look over your shoulder." And on looking, they see a mirror, which reflects and makes legible the reversed copy (which is, of course, about theatre's attraction). 

737. SIDEWALK ROAD MAP... Couple, comedy "rubes," 

or girls, spread out giant "road map" on sidewalk (several maps attached together, folded closely). Final fold, a large one, reveals copy: "We're looking for (theatre). We want to see (attraction.)"

After use, map is refolded, and stunt repeated. 

738. INVITATION SCREENING... Here's one for a show that audiences will definitely like, but a show that may be a little light in ordinary box office appeal. Invitations to witness special advance showing of the attraction (a week or so in advance), are distributed carefully about town, one being placed in each store or • 315 •

large office or factory or business place, or even classrooms in high schools or colleges (with number of invitations distributed not to exceed house capacity). Those fortunate enough to be the recipient of one of the invitations will naturally be inclined to tell all their friends and fellow employees about the attraction, beginning a tremendous amount of advance word-of-mouth advertising. The screening might be held after last showing of regular attraction on a designated night, or Sunday before opening, or at any satisfactory available time. Invitations should be signed. 

739. NEWSPAPER HEADLINES . . . In connection with newspaper story, front pages of different newspapers, with large headlines, can be used for front panel backgrounds, and lobby displays. 

Imprinted paper strip, headline size, can read: "The Big News of the 

Year," and might be pasted over many of the heads on the papers used; or, "Headline" in red or other color, might be stenciled, directly across the attached newspapers. 

Where an attraction is topical, and follows closely on the heels of a similar real-life occurrence, use of newspapers with headlines on similar subject, make an effective lobby flash.

Newspaper contest can have readers jumble or mix-up headlines from various stories in the paper, to obtain a humorous effect, the headlines, clipped from paper are reassembled in humorous style (they might be cut into individual words). In connection with a comedy attraction, the jumbled headlines are supposed to be arranged "as (star of attraction) might arrange them." 

740. SILHOUETTE-CUTTER . In lobby in advance of. 

Silhouette-cutter might perform in theatre lobby in advance of attraction, offering to cut silhouettes of patrons. Outlining profile of patron in black paper, the silhouette is then pasted to a card which carries space for the silhouette and imprinted ad on theatre's coming attraction. . . an ad that will be carried away by patrons and shown to friends. 

741. REPRODUCE SCENE... Important or typical scene from attraction might be reproduced, for display purposes, for window or lobby display. Done in miniature, or in full life-size, depending on available display space. Dolls or dummies can be used for characters portrayed in the attraction. Copy on the attraction included in the scene. 

742. WHAT TO DO... Contest for newspaper or radio can outline experience of star of attraction in a certain point in story, asking contestants: "What would you do?" in similar circumstances. • 316 •

743. MEMO TO BOSS... Herald for distribution to offices be headed: "Memo to the Boss," and then in smaller type: "Ask your 

Secretary to read this for you." Message on attraction in shorthand follows. Shorthand "message" must be written out, with cut made up for printing.

Or imprinted memo sheet carries copy: "Dear Boss: Confidentially, I'd like to get off a little early today, as I want to see (attraction and theatre)." Space is underlined for signing. Copy at bottom of the sheet suggests to secretaries and stenographers that they sign and submit the memo to the boss, as the show is swell entertainment, and they will surely want to see it. 

744. DON'T DISTURB . . . Cards made after style of hotel 

"Do Not Disturb" cards . . . imprinting with copy: "Do Not Disturb. . . I'm resting up so I can stand the thrills (or laughs) in (attraction)." Attached to hotel doors and used for distribution. 

745. YOUNG AND BEAUTIFUL. . . Emphasizing youth and beauty of star or girls, tieups can be made for cooperative newspaper ads and window displays with beauty shops, druggists, clothing stores, jewelers, and on automobile, silk hose, pajamas, lingerie, millinery. Bakeries and dairies will go along for a cooperative ad on the health angle. Distributors of household labor-saving devices will cooperate on the "Keep young and beautiful" angle.

Beauty parade might be featured in the window of a cooperating department store, with young and attractive girls modeling dresses, bathing suits or lingerie. 

746. ARTS AND CRAFTS, HOBBIES... Displays of arts and crafts, articles manufactured locally by technical schools, can be arranged for theatre lobby or mezzanine, possibly with newspaper sponsorship, interesting students and parents alike (See No. 91.)

Hobby show would draw interested attention, with collections of various kinds secured for display (under lock and key, in showcases), with persons owning collections present to explain them. 

747. BAD WEATHER... Running into a period when in clement weather conditions can be expected (check with weather department), tieups might be worked out that will encourage patrons to come out despite the weather.

Stores can feature special values with cooperative ads urging shoppers to ignore the weather. Street car company (or other transportation line), might agree to take patrons back home free at certain times on certain day; possibly with transfer obtained when going downtown, and stamped at theatre serving as a return ticket. • 317 •

Theatre trailer and merchants' ads suggesting "the safe street car way" in bad weather might repay the street car company. 

Storage garage should make special rates, also delivering cars to theatre. Radio appeals might be made. 

During heavy snow fall, usher equipped with whiskbroom should brush the snow from entering patrons. Snow also brushed from shoes of patrons; and galoshes checked (an efficient system uses numbered spring clothespin, with tag bearing corresponding number. 

Clothespin is clamped on galoshes, tag handed patron. When not in use, tag is held by clothespin). 

748. RETURN SHOWING . . . Ballots might be handed patrons, asking them if they would like to have another opportunity of seeing one of the year's top attractions. Large paneled "Request for Return Showing" might be made up, with spaces provided for patrons to sign. Photograph of local celeb or stage star signing the panel might be good for newspaper space. 

Occasionally it occurs that a previously played picture ties in with a subsequent headline news-break, and might be brought back profitably. 

749. DEFINITIONS. . . Comedy definitions of words or phrases in story, or of title, can be made a contest basis. Illustrated with photograph of star and his suggestion for a comedy definition. 

750. NAME IT . . . Newspaper, reproducing scenes from attraction, pictures stars with a number of articles which readers are asked to name (a different photo with a different thing to be named each day), a dog that she is seeking a name for; or star is singing a song "which needs a title;" or other subjects pictured in available illustrations. 

751. KEYHOLE... Novelty herald has die-cut opening in front of folder in shape of keyhole, and carries imprint: "Through the Keyhole," scene from attraction being imprinted on inner page and part of it showing through opening. Opening the herald, the full illustration is revealed, together with copy. 

Shadow-boxed panel for window or lobby, might feature opening in shape of keyhole, through which display is visible. 

752. IN CHARACTER... Arrangements might be made to have newspaper critics or local celebs photographed in scene similar to one in attraction, or in pose suggested by attraction title. Or, with their permission, superimposing photo of critic on figure in still scene from attraction.

Intended for newspaper reproduction, the photograph, or an en- • · 318..

largement, can also be used for lobby flash (perhaps adding critic's review on the attraction).

Or, whiskers might be painted on faces of photos of motion picture critics for a newspaper ad or lobby flash (with their permission). 

Artist can air-brush long whiskers, carrying copy: "(Names) will have whiskers this long before they see another show as great as this one." 

753. TOURISTS... Billboards at city limits might invite motorists to stop over, to spend a night in a pleasant city offering fine hotels, fine food . . . and finest in entertainment at (theatre). 

Space provided for poster on current attractions. Hotel and restaurant might share the expense. can

Filling stations, hotels, restaurants, and tourist camps hand each of their tourist-patrons an imprinted herald which invites them to relax a while and see (attraction and theatre). Emphasize "come as you are." 

754. WALTZING MICE... Pet store can supply or secure a number of waltzing mice-mice that chase their tails, travel in circles... and they will draw attention to a window display. Panel might call them "(star's) Waltzing Mice."

Ordinary white mice will win some attention, especially if a spinwheel upon which they might run is included in their section of the display. 

755. UPRIGHT BANNER 

"Streamer" for front, banner extending from the roof of theatre, or top of upright sign, to the marquee. Banner might parallel (on outer edge) the upright sign from top to bottom, being attached at top to an arm or beam extending from top of electric sign. Banner lettered both sides, or two lettered banners, placed together back-to-back, so banner can be read from either direction. Guide wires should carry down sides of banner, through gromets in banner edges, from top to bottom, holding banner securely.

An animated version of the upright banner is a four-sided revolving affair. Four upright streamer banners are arranged in box formation, attached to small square frame (width of banners) at top and at bottom. Top is swiveled so that it can revolve freely. 

Banners (facing four ways) are made to revolve by use of slowly turning motor (situated at bottom of banner) which turns a connecting wire which goes through a small hole in the lower frame and up through center of the banners display, connecting with center of the top frame. Each of the four banners might carry a different star name, or different copy suggested by the attraction. Banners • 319.

to be width of sign cloth, and any height desired. Guide wires are unnecessary. Might be effectively spotlighted at night. 

756. DOOR... Regular door, or a reproduction of one, can be used as center of a display, with patrons invited to "open this door;" illuminated display on attraction coming into view when they do. 

Copy on panel invites patron to ring "doorbell," which animates the top panel of the door, so that blown-up scene from attraction comes into view through unopaqued mirror section (lights flashed behind). Or, silhouette might show against a panel of ground glass. 

757. TELEPHONE BOOKS... Novel lobby display features several pages from telephone book (changed daily) on which a number of names have been selected at random and circled . . . those identifying their numbers getting tickets. Or pages are placed in window as center of display on attraction. 

Telephone company may permit heralds to be distributed with the new telephone books when they are put into circulation. 

758. BARBER SHOP CEILINGS... Offer an unusual spot for effective displays . . . where barber shop patrons can read the ad when tilted back in the barber's chair. Novelty of the spot selected for the display, too, will cause some additional talk. Light display or lithograph should be attached very securely to the ceiling. 

759. FRUIT STANDS... Generally strategically located, fruit stands offer, as a rule, excellent spots for display panels or cards. 

Imprinted tissue paper can be supplied fruit stands which is used for wrapping oranges, apples, etc. Or imprinted paper sacks might be supplied; imprinted aprons might be supplied the proprietor. 

760. PAPIER MACHE... Art school or art department of technical school can supply name of person adept in constructing figures from papier mache.

Or theatre art shop might construct desired figures. First step in construction of papier mache figures is modeling of the desired figure in clay (brick company would have the clay). After finishing the figure, it is shellaced immediately with orange shellac. After the shellac dries, apply steric acid (from paint or art supply shop or druggist), or grease (applied thin). For a half-mask that can be lifted straight off, no tin-lines are required, but for a three-dimensional figure (as a complete head), tin-lines must be next placed in the clay so that the casting may be divided and may be removed (tin-lines are made up of short, thin pieces of tin which are inserted in a line, making a break in the casting). After tin-lines have been put in, • 320 •

and steric acid has been applied, the making of the casting beginsusing number one modeling plaster. First a thin coat of it is applied to the model (filling cracks and crevices), then after it sets for a few minutes, another coat is applied; when it is almost hardened, excelsior is mixed with plaster and applied, and after bracing properly, the casting is removed from the model. Then for the papier mache. 

Inside of the casting, or mold, is shellaced and steric acid applied. 

And then the paper is applied-in thin strips, using tissue paper for the first several coats. After about eight coats of paper (wall paper will prove effective), the papier mache is left to dry evenly and slowly. 

After removing the papier mache from the casting, all edges are trimmed and fastened together. Figure is then sanded down and painted. (See Special Page, Picture Section.) 

Figure of star of attraction might be used in many ways. Front panels can feature figures or heads of star (perhaps a caricature of a comedy star); they might be made a half figure attached directly against a display panel . . . effective in lobby or as part of front display. Small animated bodies can be attached beneath the larger papier mache heads. Gigantic papier mache figure of star might be used.

Head like that of star can be made up sufficiently big to slip over a man's head . . . the man wearing it on streets, at games, dances, and at "grand opening" of the attraction at theatre. 

Papier mache head of star can be used as center of a lobby or front display, with two-way amplification hook-up concealed in the head making it possible for questions asked the display to be answered (by a hidden operator at other end of the hook-up). 

761. TRAVELING STUDIO 

Float equipped with microphone and made to resemble a broadcasting studio, and carrying along entertainers, singers, dancers. Broadcasting station to pick up the "traveling studio" from a number of points about town through wire connections at various points; or short wave might possibly be used. ...

Stopping at various points (where crowds will be attracted), entertainers on the truck go through a song-dance-music routine. 

And the entire program is broadcast over cooperating station. 

Calling it the "(name of attraction) Traveling Studio," radio announcements and newspaper stories announce in advance the appearance of the "studio" on the streets.

Announcer can interview pedestrians, too, as a feature of the • 321 •

broadcast, talking about star or attraction. Truck might be used as a broadcast point for games or important events. 

762. GUARD FOR FILM ... A special guard arranged for the film (for newspaper photographs). Police may cooperate, or cadets, or National Guards; or, perhaps a couple of good looking girls in attractive costumes as "guards." 

Guard might escort the print to theatre for its initial showing. 

Or, armored money truck, such as banks use for delivering money may deliver the film to theatre on opening day . . . armed guards standing by while film is taken into theatre. Banner might be carried on truck, or merely can of film lettered with attraction title. 

763. WHAT WAS HERE? ... Picturing a present-day scene about town, an important business place, newspaper asks question: "What was here before this building?" with tickets to see theatre's attraction going to best descriptions of the scene previously. 

Newspaper might feature a series of ads, with stores reproducing a picture of the present fronts of their business places . . . with guest tickets to theatre offered for best letters describing the scene previous to their occupying it... and with portion of space devoted to theatre's attraction.

Used in connection with an up-to-date store, emphasizing that it is as up-to-date as modern business places. Or, with attraction that dates back, permitting the stunt to lend emphasis to that angle. 

764. WESTERN... Cowboy stories suggest horses and big hats; and a window display of Stetson hats should be a "natural.” 

Manufacturer may even supply the cooperating merchant with a number of the ten-gallon hats for display purposes. 

Group of "cowboys," on horseback, can "deliver" film to theatre on opening day, carrying lettered pennants. "Cowboys" or "cowgirls," on horseback, can ride about city, carrying flag on which attraction title has been lettered. Or, banner can be attached to saddles. ...

Kids dressed as cowboys on opening matinee, or on special morning matinee, might be admitted gratis . . . perhaps with cooperation of newspaper; kids parading from newspaper office to theatre. Prize might be offered kid with best Western costume. 

Display in lobby, or prominent window, of cowboy regalia arranged. Old muskets, and six-shooters, Indian relics. 

Trick roper might be available, and costumed as cowboy, staging exhibitions in front of theatre, and about town... displaying banner at conclusion of his routine. He can teach roping tricks to kids. 322.

Patrons can be invited to lasso cutout figure of a cowboy (or other figure as suggested by the attraction), that is part of a display in the lobby. Cutout display of cowboy might be animated, with arm pivoted and arranged to revolve. Short length of real rope, arranged lasso style, is attached to the hand; stiffened throughout its length with wire, the rope appears to twirl as the hand is animated. 

Horseshoe nails can be attached to card (for distribution) by inserting the nail in two parallel slits die-cut in the card. Card imprinted: "A (star) Lucky Horseshoe Nail. To make your Good 

Fortune Complete . . see (attraction).”

Actual horseshoes might be gilded or polished, and with card attached, sent to movie critics and local prominents. Card calls them "(attraction) Good Luck Horseshoes."

Old-time covered wagon, or stage coach, might be secured, bannered and sent about streets. Couple of good looking girls might ride along, handing out heralds. "Indians," on horseback, might ride with the coach.

Radio station should dedicate program of Western songs to attraction. Western songs contest might be staged. A singing cowboy can appear in lobby or out front; or atop canopy (using amplification).

Newspaper columnist can cooperate in seeking out (in advance) old-time Westerners or cowboys.

Dude Ranch Party might be promoted for opening night, with invited patrons coming dressed in Western costumes. Prizes announced for best.

Essay contest for schools might be based on a comparison of the Old West and that of today or upon some subject that the attraction suggests. 

Riding habits, scarfs, can be featured by a ladies' store. Boots, rifles, saddles, camping equipment, can be used in window displays. "Western" handkerchiefs might be secured in quantity cheaply nough to be given away, with imprinted sticker attached. 

Travel bureaus, railroads, bus lines, airlines, should go along for window displays, featuring Western scenes. 

Title of attraction, out front, might be outlined by using a lariat, spelling out the title with the rope (which is attached to the front panels). Or, of course, painted rope can be used.

Stencil, for sidewalk or street, might be made up to duplicate horse's hoofs . . . with copy on attraction. Trail leads to theatre. 

Auto dealer might buy newspaper space which uses an illustration • 323.

from the attraction or cut of the star, carrying copy to the effect that cowboys today prefer to "ride the range" in one of their new cars. (See Nos. 603, 891, 926, 983, 986.) 

765. OUR PRESS-AGENT... Display in lobby features a desk, equipped with typewriter and desk light. Dummy is obtained from clothing house, and placed in seated position at desk. Red wig might be added for a comical touch. Display panel carries copy: "This is Our Press-Agent. He's just seen (attraction) . . . And the 

Laughter Left Him Speechless, the Thrills Still Have Him Spellbound. But when he Snaps Out of It, there won't be Enough Adjectives in his Book to Describe the Sensations, Thrills, Laughs, Surprises and Romance in (attraction copy)." 

766. MUMMY... For Egyptian story (or possibly adapt able to campaign on other attraction), a “mummy" can be constructed by securing an old department store dummy . . . or even using some old clothes stuffed with cotton to resemble the form of a man, with a head, modeled from clay or papier mache, added... the figure then being wrapped with gauze, shellaced, then tinted a light green. "Mummy" is placed under a green light, perhaps in a "mummy case."

Attendant, costumed as an Egyptian, hands out heralds. 

By using a two-way amplification hook-up, placing speaker inside the dummy, and a microphone (with an attendant and a similar setup hidden from view at other end), the "mummy" can be made to "answer questions."

Live girl might be used for "mummy" display draped in gauze except for her face, which is made up with green make-up. Flooded with green spotlight, she holds pose until she is the center of attention, then slowly "comes to life." Display panel carries copy: "Even a 

Mummy would come to Life to see (attraction)." 

767. EASIEST JOB. . . Star says that easiest job was his appearance in (attraction) opposite (feminine star). Upon this, contest (illustrated for newspapers with scenes from attraction), invites readers (or radio listeners), to submit comedy suggestions for easiest job imaginable. Star suggests such answers as: "Shade Tree 

Sitter Underer," "Lip-Stick Tester," "Snake Catcher in Ireland," "Century Plant Bloom Trimmer," etc. ... 

768. FAMILY . . . Appeal should be made to entire family in connection with an especially commendable attraction. P.-T.A. endorsement will aid, calling it "recommended entertainment for the entire family."

In other than week-stand situations, an attempt might be made • 324 •

to book such an attraction on a certain day each week, establishing that night (an "off night") as "Family Night,"

Family Night might be based on price, too-making a special admission price for the entire family, no matter how large (as long as they have evidence that all are members of one family). Prize might be offered largest family. 

A "family" might be used for a street stunt, loading a dozen kids into an old automobile, which "breaks down" in prominent locations. "Father" gets out to fix car, and when attention is attracted, unrolls banner, lettered: "I'm taking the whole family to see (attraction)." 

769. PERFUME... Cooperating druggist can secure small bottles of perfume, samples . . . which theatre distributes in small envelopes, imprinted: "Romance as fresh and fragrant as (perfume) (and attraction)." Bottles of perfume distributed at special matinee . . . with store incorporating copy on event and theatre attraction in store's ad.

Or, card placed on perfume counter of drug store, which carries copy: "Romance . . . as sweet as fine perfume . . . (and into attraction copy)."

Perfume has been used to add "atmosphere" to a particular scene that pictured flowers in great abundance . . . the fragrance of perfume being drawn into the house at the desired moment through the ventilating fans. 

770. MAGNET... A ball bearing rolling around the edge of a small circular panel will draw attention for a lobby or window display. Can be arranged by use of electrically driven phonograph turntable to the edge of which a magneto magnet has been attached, under the circular panel. Panel should be of thinnest wood, or painted glass, and perfectly level. 

Small figures, perhaps cutout figures of dancers, can be made to dance about. Metal base (metal washer will do) is attached; and several magnets at various positions are attached to turntable beneath painted glass on which the figures are placed. A bicycle wheel, motor-driven, and with the magnets attached, might be used. In turning, the magnets cause the figures to hop about. 

Or, magnet can be attached to a pivoted arm which describes an arc, then returning, behind a mirror background, causing a ball bearing to appear to be bouncing continuously. Or magnet might be made to move up and down (horizontally). 

771. STAGE NAME... Newspaper features photographs of stars or girls in show, asking readers to submit suggested stage • 325 •

names, with tickets for best, cleverest. In connection with a stage show, newspaper might use photograph of girls checking through the entries. 

772. MAGAZINES IN OFFICES 

Back numbers of magazines secured and a herald attached as a cover, or to the cover, then placed in waiting rooms and doctors' offices, barber shops. 

773. HOT STUFF... Heat (temperature or emotional) can be indicated by use of red floodlights in illuminating front of theatre (though not in warm weather). Lights under canopy replaced with red.

Giant letters might be constructed from pine wood, and placed on beach, or other place where they will be seen and where they can safely be set aflame for a nighttime flash.

Thermometer as part of a panel can carry copy: "This is the temperature now, but watch it rise when (star) comes to town in (attraction)." 

774. HOUR GLASS... Displayed in jeweler's window, it is kept in operation, with display card carrying copy: "Time Flies! 

And it will be only (number) days until you can see (attraction)."

Numbers (for numbers of days) are changed each day as the attraction approaches. Jeweler would tie in watch and timepiece displays. 

Novel use for small hour glasses, would have doll heads attached, plus arms, and made to resemble dolls. Attached card advises number days, hours, minutes until attraction arrives, and they are delivered to newspaper critics and reviewers well in advance. 

775. WRITE STORY... "Inspired" by theatre's attraction, newspaper staff might agree to collaborate, writing a story similar to that of attraction, or suggested by it, each newspaper writer or reporter to write one chapter. Paper prints the story, mentioning attraction as inspiration.

Or newspaper readers can be invited to collaborate on a story. . . asking contestants to submit a suggested first chapter, publishing winner, then asking readers to write a concluding chapter. ... 

776. LUGGAGE, BAGGAGE . . . A "natural" for travel pictures, of course, is a luggage tieup. Either for a window display or maybe the store will go along for an ad, using star photographs showing luggage and star. 

Trunks can be adapted to a sidewalk flash . . . the trunks being placed on sidewalk in front of theatre (perhaps on a baggage truck), or in lobby. And placard or banner announces "the arrival of a new • 326 ·

star;" or carries copy: “(star) arrives in town! (and copy on attraction)." 

777. SAND ARTIST .. Where crowds are attracted to beaches, a sand artist might model figure of star of attraction, also lettering attraction title in sand. Sand artist, who is already making appearances, can include the design in his routine. Sand artist can work in a sand-box in lobby or on sidewalk in front of theatre. 

778. RADIO DEALERS... Stores selling radios should be especially willing to cooperate with window displays, ads, where attraction deals with broadcasting, or star is radio favorite, or song hits can be introduced.

Display on attraction may be used as center of window displays. 

As, life-size cutout figure of star, at radio "listening." Newspaper ads might be illustrated with picture of star. "Smallest radio" would make an attention-getter for radio store window or lobby... with copy on attraction tied in. 

779. MORGUE... A live "morgue" (paradoxically speaking) can prove an excellent theatre aid (a file of show-selling aids for later reference). Ad ideas, clipped from outside newspapers and trade papers should be filed away for later reference (a deal can be made with newsstands whereby a couple of passes might be exchanged for unsold "foreign" newspapers). Stills that may possibly be later used can be put away, with due regard for easy reference, in the "morgue." Similarly, especially valuable ad-mats or engravings, accounts of stunts, tieups and gags that might be later used. 

Also illustrations from magazines, press-books, papers that may have value at some time for theatre artist, in designing lobby displays or drawing up ad designs. Illustrations of front and lobby displays, from trade papers and other sources, should be placed on file and will prove invaluable when a hurry-up idea is needed. 

780. ELECTRIC COMPANY... Light and power company might permit an imprinted insert to be included with the light bills mailed out. Or, illustrating an electric company newspaper ad, a night time photograph of the front of theatre may be used (with current attraction billing visible in the picture). Electric companies will generally cooperate, too, with window displays and in other ways. (Check Lighting and Electricity Classifications.) 

With light company cooperation, and perhaps including oculists, a "Better Vision Exhibit" can be arranged for theatre lobby. New eye-saving methods of illumination are shown. Patrons might be invited to have their eyes tested. Light company and any co- • 327 ·

781. LAUGH PHOTOS... Photographer sets his camera up in front of theatre on opening day, copy on panel explaining that he is offering a pair of guest tickets for best laugh pictures. As patrons exit from theatre, photographer snaps a number of people, prominents if possible, in wide-open laugh poses. 

Photographs are placed on display in window or in theatre lobby. 

Panel carries copy: "One picture is worth more than a thousand words". . . and copy on attraction. "Comment panel" set up in lobby, carries the photographs, with questions asked above each photograph: "And how did you enjoy the show (name)?", the laugh picture placed directly below the lettered question being an eloquent answer. Or this angle can be adapted to a newspaper ad effectively. "Lighting" cartoonist might be stationed in lobby, drawing quick sketches of patrons in laughing poses. Paper he draws on is imprinted with copy on comedy attraction. Finished sketches given to persons who pose.

Another adaption for newspaper ads would be use of photographs of newspaper critics, carrying name of each critic, and then the question, above the photograph. A sock ad can be arranged if the critics will pose. Idea might be adapted to a trailer. 

782. CAMPS... With an army or navy base or encampment nearby, much valuable cooperation is possible. Drill squads, honor guards, searchlights, might be secured. Airplanes might fly as a tribute to the attraction.

Tickets can be presented those passing inspection with best rating, or to winning squad in drill competition. Announcements might be posted at camp. For an occasional appeal, newspapers imprinted or with a herald attached, can be distributed. Special group price might be made for a certain day, or certain hours. (For summer camps, see 908.) 

783. THROW THIS AWAY... Card for distribution carries imprint in large letters at top: "Throw this Away," and at bottom, also in bold type: "Don't Read It." Centered, between these two lines, in smallest type possible, is copy: "-If you are not interested in an entertainment that brings you thrills, laughs, romance (and into attraction copy)." 

784. 24-SHEET JIG-SAW ... Giant jig-saw puzzle made • 328

up, mounting a poster on compo-board, cutting it up (in large pieces) after style of a jig-saw puzzle. 

The jumbo jig-saw might be used at baseball or football games, before the start of the game, using costumed girls to assemble it. 

Bringing the pieces onto the field, they assemble it as quickly as possible. Can be used wherever large crowds are assembled, or in a large window, or possibly a street location. 

Another 24-sheet (or a 6-sheet) jig-saw angle would have a poster displayed in the lobby. The 24-sheet is ruled off carefully, with pencil, in small squares, which are numbered (some of which are numbered with red pencil instead of black). A duplicate poster is then mounted on cardboard, and carefully cut into squares identical with those marked off on the poster, those drawing a red-numbered square winning tickets. 

785. HOME TOWN STAR... Opening night of attraction can be dedicated to the player, inviting immediate family or relatives as honor guests. Special car should be sent for the family. They should be radio-interviewed about star from theatre lobby. 

Newspaper should sponsor the event, playing up the home-towner with stories, photographs. A round-robin telegram of congratulations can be made up, the telegraph company having a representative in the lobby to take the names of those who would like to have names (for a few cents) added to the wire . . . the telegram to be sent on to the star after being placed on display. Early local photographs may be secured for newspaper and window use. Perhaps newspaper can sell cooperative advertisements in which stores "welcome" star. 

Arrangements may be made to have player wire greeting to local editors, which they will use. 

Home town girl in attraction may have had sorority and school connections, all of whom should be contacted. Perhaps teachers who instructed her, dancing school teachers, or others, might be located for an interview. 

786. BADGES, BUTTONS. . . Pin-on buttons, imprinted with photo of star and coming attraction title, can be secured from a novelty printing company. Distributed well in advance to patrons, and worn by house staff. Will prove especially valuable in appealing to kids. Might be effectively distributed at fairs, carnivals, wherever crowds gather. 

Employees of large manufacturing plants and factories generally are assigned numbered badges which they wear. Numbers are . posted on bulletin board at plant, or on a banner placed near entrance • 329

Cutout letters spell out the word atop canopy, one letter added each day until all are up, simultaneous with running of similar teaser newspaper ads.
