AO ing scene from attraction, might require submitted proverbs to apply to the illustration. con- Or contest might be based on contradictory proverbs testants to submit list of proverbs with one contradicting the other, (as: "A rolling stone gathers no Moss," and "A rolling snowball gathers Snow).”

Comedy proverbs can be requested in connection with a comedy attraction (and a reproduced illustration), as: "Pride goeth before a

Fall . . . and then came Winter," or: "Many a True Word is Spoken in Jest (a Whisper)." Contestants can be asked to pick a proverb for the comedy star. 

880. ORCHESTRAS 

If attraction features music or song hits, bands will plug the numbers in their regular dance engagements and radio broadcasts, and possibly they will give theatre's attraction an announcement at the same time.

Free-lance orchestras, as well as those playing regularly in night spots, should be contacted. 

If theatre's attraction has no song hits, orchestra can dedicate a number to attraction, or attraction star. Orchestra can arrange a complete program of numbers similar to one featured in theatre's attraction (with similar theme or titles) . . . or a program of numbers suggested by attraction's title or theme. 

Perhaps an attractive display panel might be placed near or on the bandstand, which is naturally, the center of attention. 

It might be possible to arrange a competition (for dance spot, or stage), between orchestras, publicizing it as a "Battle of Music," with local bands competing for a title, prize or trophy (the trophy to be named after theatre's attraction or star). Or, a "Battle of

Music" (for lobby or radio) might be based on phonograph recordings of band coming to theatre or featured in theatre's attraction, and any other bands (with theatre's band given the preference in selection of tunes).

Arrangements might be made to have orchestras at several different places play a hit tune in succession, radio station picking up and broadcasting the different versions. 

Orchestra can present a hit tune from theatre's attraction by presenting it as other well-known orchestras might present it. . copying their style. "Request Cards" can be supplied orchestras, carrying space for request tunes to be written in and the name of person requesting it . . . and carrying copy on theatre's attraction at bottom. • 365 •

881. STREAMERS 

Imprinted paper streamers can be effectively used in connection with any merchandising tieup, being attached to windows of cooperating business places. 

A tieup with a bottler or cigarette distributor may be arranged, with streamers attached to windows of stores or business places handling the product. (Tieup line on streamer ties in the product and the attraction if possible. And most of space is devoted to the attraction.)

Ice cream might be named after the attraction; and might even possibly be molded in design suggested by the attraction. 

Almost any merchandise from gasoline to groceries, sold in a number of business places, offers opportunity for a wholesale tieup; and printed streamers offer an ideal way to economically deliver the message at a number of different business places. 

882. BEACHES... With time for opening of beaches and swim pools approaching, locations should be arranged for banners and display cards. Arrangements might be made to maintain displays, changing them with the attractions, throughout the season. 

Boardwalk wheel chair might be built up as a miniature float, with panels carrying copy on attraction, and pretty girl riding along. 

Or girl can be merely busily engaged in "reading" a large bookwhich carries attraction copy lettered across it. Lettered swim suits can be worn by boys, or preferably, by pretty girls. Comedy attraction might suggest use of an old-fashioned comedy suit, with appropriate lettering on same.

Playing stage shows, stars and the girls in the show should be taken to beach for photographs for newspapers. 

If theatre is near the beach, or bathing parties pass it going to beach, a bid might be made to get the bathers, inviting them to attend in their bathing suits (and assigning several rows of seats to them which are covered with oil cloth, or issuing an oil cloth cover to them as they are seated). 

Check "Beach," "Bathing Girls" and "Swim" classifications for additional angles. 

883. LETTERED SWEATERS... With shapely girls wear ing them, will command attention at football games, or where crowds gather; or, with girls distributing heralds on street. Sweaters can be lettered across the front as well as across the back. 

884. OIL PAINTINGS... House artist might paint several portraits of stars of a coming attraction, which might be outstand- • 366 •

ing enough to merit exhibition-in department store or prominent window (as an exhibit), if not in local art gallery. 

Or, perhaps newspaper will carry reproductions of them, together with a feature story. Used as a Sunday magazine feature, the paper may accord them more space, might use a portrait of the artist at work, in addition. 

When attraction comes along, the portraits can be placed on display in individual windows about town, with lettered card attached; or used for front display. 

885. EYE-TEST CHART . . . (Optometrist's chart) is placed at one side of lobby. . . above a full-length, or large mirror. 

Across the lobby, a display panel on a coming attraction features a slight elevation, and panel carries copy, "Men! Take the (name of attraction) Eye-Test. Stand here . . . and see what you can see...

When they step on the platform (which faces them toward the eye chart), their weight throws a switch which turns on a light behind the mirror . . . illuminating a life-size cutout figure of a girl, or the feminine star of the attraction, which is placed behind the mirror; the mirror is of the transparent type, not opaqued, which becomes as plain glass when a light is flashed behind it. (Any glass dealer can construct the mirror.) Display is so arranged that complete darkness is possible behind the mirror when light is not flashed. 

During rush hours, a live girl might pose against an attractive panel (which carries copy on the attraction) behind the mirror . . . and the light might be placed on a flasher, so that it will flash on and off when a person steps on the platform (otherwise remaining off). 

886. FOLLOW THE GREEN RIBBON... To direct special attention to a display on an attraction, a panel placed where patrons entering theatre must see it, carries copy: "Follow the Green Ribbon to the Most Important Announcement of the Year" (or similar copy). ...

Narrow green ribbon attached leads through lobby, over panels- (out of the way, but following along the route that patrons must follow), and terminating at an elaborate display panel on the coming attraction, end of ribbon being attached to the panel. The two panels, to be most effective, should be some distance apart. 

Gag can be used outside theatre, too, placing the first panel on a prominently located corner, with the ribbon (which is kept out of way of pedestrians) leading to a nearby window, which features a display. 

887. "MISS PROXY"... Campaign on an attraction can be built about the selection of a girl to represent the star of the coming • 367.

attraction... her selection in a contest to be based on her resemblance to the star; or votes, or other method of picking the winner might be used.

Cooperation of newspaper, civic clubs, organizations, might be secured, giving the star's "proxy" a welcome such as might be accorded the star in person (having her board train or plane at last previous stop). See No. 434 and No. 594.

Star can wire her congratulations to the winner (arranging with studio), with regrets that she must visit (city) by proxy and not in person, but appreciating courtesies shown her proxy. Wire might be read over radio, used in newspaper and blown up for lobby display. 

888. MAYOR'S COMMITTEE . . . In connection with an outstanding attraction, or a special week which theatre is celebrating, the Mayor might be prevailed upon to appoint a special committee, whose duty it becomes to see that orphans and deserving unfortunates see the attraction as theatre's guests (on an off day, or at a slow hour). Passes are supplied to Mayor, who passes them on to Committee, which he appoints. It is the duty of the committee, too, to arrange transportation, which they might do through arrangements with transportation company or civic club. 

Mayor takes credit for the stunt (which he should do, of course, and which reacts to his advantage). Committee does the work. 

And newspapers will undoubtedly give the stunt space, mentioning the attraction, perhaps using pictures. 

Stunt might prove most appropriate the week before Christmas (with a good attraction booked, that Mayor can afford to endorse); or just before Thanksgiving. 

889. DEBATE . . . Oratorical contest can be arranged in schools on subject suggested by theatre attraction. Trophy can be presented to the winner "with compliments of star of attraction."

Announcements might be carried on school bulletin boards, or made in class rooms.

Joint debate on controversial subject suggested by the attraction might be arranged between luncheon club members, with newspapers picking the stunt up for a story. 

890. BILLBOARDS. . . Strategically placed billboards, perhaps on main streets approaching downton section, can carry painted institutional copy in addition to space for 24-sheets. 

Talking billboard might be constructed by wiring amplification equipment into it. . . concealing speakers behind large figure of star of attraction which is the center of a display. A recording of song • 368 •

numbers from attraction is played on concealed turn-table, equipped with record-repeater, broadcasting through the speaker; or announcements might be made. Figure, too, might be animated. Naturally, to justify its use, the "talking billboard" should be so located that there is a large amount of traffic by it. 

Moving "billboards" might be constructed, to be towed, as trailers, by automobiles. Specially constructed, and not too high, the "billboards" can be of considerable length, and of just sufficient width to house the rear wheel. (Front end is attached securely to automobile bumper.) Might be lighted for a night flash.

Panels can be attached to street cars, buses. ... ... 

891. COSTUMES . . . House staff, week in advance and during showing can be costumed as suggested by the attraction. 

Contest for newspaper can be based on costumes. possibly for a fashion page feature, tickets being offered for the best costume designs submitted. Figure of star accompanies announcement of the contest, with designs to be drawn over the figure. Or, the costume designs might be made from cutout bits of paper pasted over the drawing or photographs; or from actual pieces of fabric which are pasted over the figure of the star. Best styled costumes might be basis of the contest, with added prize for most bizarre or unusual. 

892. NEWSPAPER PRINTS FOLDER... Newspapers, for added classified ad coverage, have on several occasions published weekly a small folder, which is devoted about fifty per cent to theatre news, and fifty per cent to classified ads which are lifted intact from the paper the day the folder goes to press. 

Theatre illustrations and stories lend it color and assure that it will be well received and read... the front page being given over to pictures and stories about theatre's coming attractions. Folder is distributed by theatre to patrons as they leave. 

893. INSURANCE... Tieup might be made with Insurance company to supply heralds on a laugh attraction-the herald possibly made up after style of a regular policy, insuring the patron against laughing himself to death; or against thrills. Or it might assure a specified or satisfactory number of laughs. 

Insurance idea might be adapted to a newspaper ad (consuming only small amount of space), guaranteeing, or "insuring" the most entertaining theatre experience, or the funniest laughs. 

894. LOOK THROUGH CARD . . . Carrying imprinted copy: "Try this Eye Test. Stand before a mirror, Hold this card before your Eyes, Look Through the Opening." Small narrow • 369.

opening is die-cut in the card, and other side carries copy that has been reversed (engraving made up), and an illustration (preferably a girl cut). 

895. OLD GENT. . . Wearing long white beard, man in chair is wheeled about town by attractive girl. Copy on chair: "You're never too old to laugh at (or, "to enjoy") (and into attraction copy)."

Variation is man in Buster Brown get-up (kid costume), and wearing long beard, with "You're as young as you feel" copy on his back. 

Heralds, as described in No. 441, might be distributed. 

896. SHORTEST SYNOPSIS... Prize (perhaps a theatre party for a group) might be offered person writing shortest synopsis of an attraction. Broadcasting station might sponsor the contest. 

Especially effective if the attraction is a lengthy one, or based on a lengthy book. 

897. STAR SHOT... Trick herald, with large screaming headline, after newspaper fashion, carrying copy: "Star Shot (and then in smaller type:) the 'works' to give you the greatest picture of his career . . etc."

Or gag is adaptable to trick newspaper ad setup after style of news paper story. 

898. PAPER PLATES . . . Secured cheaply enough in quantity, for distribution from house to house, paper plates might be imprinted with copy: "Don't bother to wash the dishes. Don't waste a minute. Use this paper plate so that after dinner you can rush right down to the (theatre) to see (attraction copy)." 

899. TESTS... Where story deals with characters who, in real life, would be obliged to pass certain tests, or requirements, these tests can be used as basis for local contests, newspaper or radio. 

At Annapolis or West Point, it is necessary to pass tests in higher mathematics. Or to secure a pilot's license (for use in connection with a story that deals with aviation), it is necessary to pass certain physical tests.

In lobby in advance, patrons might be invited to undergo one or two angles of the test (with qualified person in charge of the "test"). 

Different types of attractions would suggest different sorts of "tests." Local authority on such subjects might prepare the tests to be used. 

900. CIGARETTE GIRLS... Arrangements might be made to attach card to trays used by regular cigarette girls in night spots. 

Or, using sample cigarettes (from distributor of some popular • 370 •

brand, and which are generally supplied in miniature boxes of one or two), the cigarettes are inserted in small imprinted envelopes. 

Copy on the envelope ties in the cigarettes in catch-line at top, but most of space is devoted to theatre's attraction. Envelopes are then distributed about town (especially including restaurants and eating places), by girls who carry the cigarettes in the usual night club tray. 

Distributed in connection with a thriller or a mystery-story, copy imprinted on envelopes can say: "Quiet your nerves with a (cigarette) after you witness (attraction)."

Using single cigarettes, loose, for distribution, a small rubber stamp might be made up, and each cigarette stamped with attraction title and cast. 

901. SUBTITLE... Directing attention to attraction title, newspaper readers or radio listeners might be asked to submit an appropriate subtitle, required to be brief, descriptive, clever. 

Occasionally, too, a subtitle added to the title of an attraction and carried immediately under it, perhaps in parenthesis, might serve to illuminate the title or to add to its appeal. A point to consider when confronted with a bad title or one that carries little appeal. 

902. CHINESE YENS... Very cheap China coins, yens can be secured from a novelty company or an importing company. 

Or a bank might secure them. Imprinted tags are attached, or the "yens" are inserted in small imprinted envelopes. 99 Tags, or envelopes, are imprinted with copy: "Here's a new Yen for you...' Or: "Good Luck will ever be with you . . . carry this lucky coin... and see (attraction)." ... 

903. TELL YOUR FRIENDS... A number of good friends of theatre, or manager, or theatre employees might be asked to tell their friends about an outstanding attraction. A letter is sent out, signed by the manager, or by individual employees who are acquainted with the persons addressed, enclosing a pass to see a show which is described in glowing terms, asking them in return to make it a point to tell ten of their friends about the attraction. Letter can conclude with: "If this is inconvenient, you can, of course, return the ticket; and the deal's off; but it's really a great show, and we want everybody to know about it; and we will be grateful to you for your aid, and feel sure you would enjoy the show." 

Another similar angle would have an imprinted card, on the attraction, but with boxed space at top carrying copy: "Please do us a favor. Slip this card in an envelope and send it to a friend. We • 371 •

want everybody to know about this great show. Our thanks in advance, and your friends will thank you, too.”

Or a matinee admission can be offered to those who bring to the theatre, unsealed, six letters, addressed to friends, that praise theatre's attraction. Letters are sealed, stamped, mailed. 

904. LETTERED CURBING... A strip, some twenty-four inches wide, along edge of sidewalk in front of theatre, in advance of coming attraction, can be painted in, and lettered: "No Parking. 

Reserved for (name of attraction or star)."

Curbings about downtown section might be lettered, on vertical edge, with attraction copy. Or narrow printed poster can be posted on curb edge. 

905. STORY ON PROJECTION... Critic or movie editor of newspaper may be interested in using a story on methods of reproducing recorded sound on motion pictures. 

And, in getting the information first-hand from visit to theatre booth, he will also refer to the attraction being shown, or the film he inspects.

Or, the "interview" can be broadcast, radio station carrying a line into the booth, carefully planning questions and answers in advance. 

Or, in connection with a stage show, a story on backstage operation of the presentation will naturally include mention of the attraction and stars. 

906. AWNINGS . . . Merchants' awnings, especially in summer when they are in constant use, present excellent locations for attaching narrow strip banners. Either front or ends; though ends, usually nearer eye-level and a "head-on hit," will generally prove most effective. Stores might permit straight attraction copy to be carried, though they may require a tie-in line. 

Use of a canvas sidewalk canopy can lend swank to a special occasion, as a "grand opening" of an attraction, or a society premier. 

Canopy would extend (under marquee) from front doors to sidewalk edge. 

907. LEARN TO TAP... Display for a large and prominently located window features a small elevation which has a couple of small steps built around it (both sides and front). . . display panel carrying copy: "Learn to Tap! You'll be so happy you'll want to dance after you see (attraction) at (theatre). Come on in, we'll teach you free!"

Pretty girl in brief dance costume serves as the instructor, running through a few tap routines herself; and a number of "stooges" had • 372 •

best be arranged, including several attractive girls and a couple of amusing fellows, who will "volunteer" (periodically) to go in and take a "lesson." Radio or phonograph (playing hit tunes from attraction, if any), can be used for the music, and window amplification system can carry notes and taps to those outside the window. 

Frequent mention of the attraction is made by the dancer. 

908. RESORTS... Nearby summer places sometimes offer many potential customers if reached. . .. by heralds, or bulletins, or any other method. Sound truck can be sent around. Displays or cards might be placed in the various resort hotels. Small cards, carrying transportation schedules (into town) and theatre ad can be distributed to various resort hotels. 

Transportation is sometimes an important item. . . and arrangements might be made with trolley company to set schedules so that connections can be easily made. Small roadside (permanent) pointer signs can carry copy: "(Number) Miles to town and (theatre)."

Special rate for larger parties might be made, to attract them in groups . . . and such groups, including names, might be reported to the society editor for newspaper mention, names of all secured if possible. .. 

909. CAST THIS PICTURE . With names of players in a screen attraction given, together with names of characters portrayed in the attraction, a contest, for newspaper or radio, invites contestants to correctly "cast" the picture to attempt to line up correctly the names of the players opposite the names of the characters they portray in the picture. Names of all actors of any importance in the attraction should be carried. Newspaper would use photographs of the players whom the contestants are to "cast.” 

910. ANNOUNCING AN ANNOUNCEMENT . . . Small newspaper ads (on either theatrical or radio pages) and radio announcements ask all citizens of (town) and vicinity to tune in any local radio station at a specified time on a certain evening for an important announcement. (Important that all local stations be arranged.) 

The "important announcement," when the appointed time finally arrives, proves to be an announcement, delivered in a dramatic and enthused voice, of the booking of an important attraction at (theatre). 

The attraction should really be outstanding, too. 

911. DESKS FOR CRITICS... Small desks (one for each critic or reviewer attached to newspaper), are placed side-by-side in lobby (in advance) . . . large panel carrying copy: "These desks • 373

reserved for motion picture critics of (newspapers) . . They won't want to wait a minute to write rave reviews . . after they see (attraction)."

Desks are equipped with typewriters, copy paper inserted in machines, ready to write. Smaller easel cards carry names of individual critics (if more than one). 

Critics may be persuaded to express approval of an attraction in writing... attaching their letters to a lobby panel which carries heading, "The critics put it in writing!" Or newspaper ad might be headed that way, reproducing their letters. 

912. STEEL ENGRAVING... Folder herald is imprinted, on cover, "Free! Here's a Steel Engraving of Washington. Suitable for Framing." Opening the folder reveals an ordinary one-cent postage stamp attached to upper right hand corner of inside page. 

Opposite the stamp is the imprint: "We cannot tell a lie... here's the engraving," and copy: "And here's the honest truth about a great show (and into copy on attraction)." 

913. PAPER CUPS... Ad can be imprinted on regular flat paper drinking cups. Distributed, well in advance, to factories, offices, stores, swim pools, and wherever the drinking cups are used. 

Placed in container near drinking fountain or water container. 

914. WHICH IS BETTER? . . . Contest is based on comparison of previously played hit show and current attraction. Contestants to give reasons for selections, or comparisons. Serves to compare present attraction with a previously played outstanding attraction, establishing it as a show of same high calibre. 

915. BLACKBOARD... Used as the center of a window display. Attractively costumed girl writes a series of questions on the blackboard (questions suggested by theatre's attraction or about players), concluding the routine by writing the line: "Thrill to the answer to all these questions... when you see... (attraction)."

Or, finishing final question, but not writing attraction title, she pulls down a small window shade which has been attached at the top of the blackboard . . . the window shade carrying lettered copy on attraction. 

Giant blackboard can invite signatures under copy that welcomes star in newest film. Board can be divided into lined-off sections. 

Chalk is provided. Attendant asks patrons to "sign up." Board might be used in lobby; or adapted to street use, perhaps covering ver the front of some vacant store. Blackboard might be used to • 374 •

mask in the front of a new theatre under construction, with those passing asked to sign a "welcome."

Picture of Mayor or some celebrity signing the first name to the board might be good for newspaper space. 

916. STOCKS, BONDS, BROKERS. . . If the attraction appeals to them or their customers, display panels or cards might be placed in various brokers' offices. 

Stock teletype could be installed in lobby, connected in with regular stock quotations, and made part of a display on the show. 

Might advertise for old stock, worthless now, to use in "papering the lobby." Offer passes for it. Use it to back up display panels. 

Carry an ad on stock quotations page of newspaper, and arrange to have paper place ad immediately below or beside quotations. 

Folder herald can have front page designed after style of stock certificate, copy calling the show as "good as a gold bond... get your share of happiness," with words "bond" and "share" standing out. 

Inside spread and back page devoted in regular herald style to the attraction. 

917. WATER BOY... Some communities go in for picnics in the summer time to a great extent. In connection with these outings, the theatre can render a service that will prove a great investment in goodwill, at slight expense, as well as selling current attraction; it's this: a keg or barrel is secured, equipped with a spigot, thoroughly cleaned and kept clean. . . and when picnics occur, the keg is filled with ice-water and ice, and mounted on the rear of a light delivery truck, it is dispatched to the scene of the picnic (or political rally, or wherever crowds gather).

Neat frame is attached to the keg, and a card on the current attraction is inserted in the frame; name of theatre is lettered above. 

Paper cups (perhaps imprinted) should be supplied. 

918. CACHETS... Letters might be sent a special mailing list from abroad... arranging with film company to have their foreign representatives mail the letters . . . which are prepared and shipped to them, together with amount necessary for postage. 

Mailing list should be carefully selected, and including editors, motion picture critics, radio commentators and stamp-collectors. (Perhaps stamp-collectors boast of a local club, from whom a list of members might be obtained; or newspaper might conduct a philatelists' column which might have names). Letters should be imprinted on thinnest, lightest possible paper. Booking of the attraction must, • 375.

of course, be sufficiently far in advance to permit the letters to make the round-trip.

Foreign background or foreign star featured in a coming attraction might suggest use of the stunt. Cards can be mailed from place pictured in the attraction. Perhaps arrangements can be made to have the letters dispatched on a boat or plane that is making a first trip, with this noted on the envelope, or cachet, and being of added value to stamp-collectors. "Message," written in English, praises the attraction, and urges person receiving the letter to see it when they have the opportunity at (theatre); can be signed by star of attraction or character in story; should be dated continental style (date of month before writing month).

Critics, editors, radio commentators, would be impressed by the novelty of a barrage of letters from all points of the globe. With a list that is limited to a select few, letters might be prepared and sent to points throughout the world. . . either to exchange branch offices, or the Consul in the different countries, enclosing a coin for stamps, and asking that the letter be mailed, explaining that it is an advertising stunt in connection with an attraction. "Messages" can all be signed by same name and while all are different, the general tone would be the same "Everywhere I go, they're raving about (attraction). Be sure and see it when it comes to (city and theatre)." 

919. MEETING TONIGHT... Person in costume suggested by attraction distributes cards through business section . . . cards carrying copy, in big type, "Meeting Tonight;" and in smaller type, "The place (theatre). The subject (attraction). The time, Tonight. 

You are hereby notified that you'll miss a grand evening's entertainment if you don't attend the meeting. Signed by whatever name the attraction title suggests. 

Additionally, cards may be numbered and copy advises, "Bring this card with you when you come, and check this number. If it is posted in front of theatre you will attend as theatre's guest." In evening a group of numbers, arbitrarily selected, are posted out front. 

920. PATRON WRITES AN AD... Newspaper ad or herald reproduces what is ostensibly a letter from a feminine patron. 

Addressed to manager, it says: "Sometimes you get my goat. Your ads use all the adjectives in Mr. Webster's book in describing (star) in (attraction). Granted that it's a great show, are all the adjectives really necessary? I abhor adjectives!" Sign feminine name.

Then add postscript, "Dear Mr. (Manager).

Since writing the above I • 376 •

dropped into the (theatre) and saw (attraction). Why didn't you tell us that star (and into a rave on star and attraction that includes dozens of adjectives)." 

921. CAMERA RECORD... Photographs may be made of all important local events, as a "record." Photographs turned over to Chamber of Commerce for preservation, but first they are exhibited (same night as taken, if possible) in front of theatre or in lobby. 

And in shooting the picture, with all eyes naturally focused on the cameraman, banner can be displayed which says: "See this picture on display tonight in the lobby of (theatre) now playing (attraction)." 

Wherever crowds gather, photographs might be made; and perhaps arrangements can be made with photographer to have him make the pictures in exchange for mention on the banner and on the panel in theatre lobby where pictures are displayed. 

It's an excuse to get the attention of the crowd focused on the banner, and may bring some of them into the lobby and perhaps on into the theatre. 

922. RUNNERS. . . Couple of long-distance runners, in track clothes, will attract attention racing leisurely down main streets, signs on their backs carrying copy: "We're running to (theatre) to see (attraction)." Or, similarly, girls on skates.

Runners can be sent down the main streets ahead of a parade. Or in connection with a track meet, they might be sent around the track before regular races begin. "Hiking contest" can be staged, with a group of boys starting from newspaper office, or from city hall (where some official might "start" them), and racing to theatre (by a round-about course, if theatre is too near). Or group of girls might be used, perhaps the girls in a stage show. 

923. ROULETTE WHEEL... Or lucky number spin wheel, such as are used at fairs and carnivals, may be adapted for lobby use. 

Being made a part of a display on an attraction, free admission is offered patrons if the wheel indicates a certain number when stopping. 

Or, instead of numbers, copy lines might be used, as suggested by the attraction (as, in connection with a baseball story, "home-run" for the winner, and other spaces marked with baseball terms). Each patron is permitted a single spin. Or, wheel can be animated, by connecting to shaft which is driven by worm-geared motor. To start and stop the motor (and the wheel), a chain-pull socket is used to turn current on and off, an oscillating fan, to which the chain is • 377 •

attached, throwing the switch on and off as the fan turns. (Oscillating electric fan.)

Real roulette wheel, or other gambling paraphernalia might possibly be secured from police department. 

Though especially adaptable to an attraction having a gambling theme, a spin wheel might be used for any attraction. In connection with a girl show, indicator might be made in the shape of a girl; and similarly other attractions will suggest other designs. Wheel can be designed so that it flashes a series of lights when turned; certain light, or certain color light, winning free tickets if the wheel stops there.

If not motor-driven, attendant might keep the wheel turning, when patrons are not engaged in spinning it. 

924. INVITE PLAYERS... Local football or baseball team might be invited as guests on opening night of an attraction... or on night of big game, or evening before. Sports writers should be invited, too; or perhaps, the stunt might be arranged under newspaper sponsorship with attendant newspaper stories. Cheer-leaders might lead cheers from the stage, if teams are school or college teams. 

Boxes or seats reserved for the players should be decorated in school colors. Or, if both teams are invited, the colors are divided. 

925. SIDEWALK ARTIST . . . With easel, canvas, all embellishments, an artist, costumed in smock and beret, obviously painting a scene will attract much attention. Periodically, as the attention of a crowd has been attracted, the artist lifts the painting off the easel revealing an ad on theatre's attraction (which has been concealed under the painting). Or, artist might clown the action, knocking the painting off the easel apparently accidentally. Or artist might be actually painting a picture of the star of theatre's attraction, with copy on attraction already lettered in. 

926. ART EXHIBIT ... Mezzanine or lobby exhibition of paintings, or other types of art, may be arranged in a tieup with art school or art institute. Might be suggested by a certain attraction; perhaps certain type of art or type of painting (as westerns, or seascapes) might be suggested. Exhibition is tied into attraction copy and announced in ads and on front panels. An authority should be on hand to describe the paintings and to make certain that amateur Rembrandts do not draw penciled moustaches on painted figures. 

927. HANDSOME MAN CONTEST... A travesty on beauty contests might be effectively staged at a luncheon club, and will get a lot of attention from club members and supply an entertaining program . . . besides assuring constant mention of the at- • 378.

traction. Letter is sent secretary of club by theatre manager, advising that the manager has been requested to present guest tickets to the most handsome member of the club, with the compliments of feminine star. A postscript to the letter suggests that members vote to select most handsome member . . . assuring that the contest will become an interesting and entertaining fifteen minutes. 

Arrangements should be made in advance with the club secretary to assure success of the stunt. Newspapers might carry a photograph of the "winners," together with cut of the star and story on attraction. 

Stunt might be staged in connection with "personal" appearance of star of stage show at the luncheon club, with star presenting an autographed photograph to the winners. 

928. COMMUNITY WEEK... Dedicating each evening to a different nearby community, or to a different organization or civic club, those identified with the organizations or living in the different communities are urged to attend on the designated nights. Organizations are contacted. Leading citizens of various communities, or heads of community organizations, or mayors, might cooperate. 

Newspaper, in connection with community attendance, might sell a page of ads to merchants in the community. Radio programs or broadcast announcements can "salute" each community on the day assigned them (and selling spot announcements). 

Glee clubs, bands, marching organizations that the different organizations or communities may boast of, might be brought along on the different nights, perhaps marching to theatre, or playing in front of theatre or on stage. 

Special section might be reserved. Welcome panels in lobby. 

929. "IF IT RAINS"... Teaser ads in newspaper, beginning a week in advance, carry copy, "If it Rains (day) (town) is in line for a treat! Will it Rain? And What's going to Happen if it does? 

See (day's) paper for Details." On the designated day, newspaper ad announces that if it rains opening day, the first twenty-five persons reaching theatre box office after it begins to rain will be admitted free. 

Though especially adaptable to attraction that refers to weather in title or theme, will arouse curiosity and cause talk in connection with any attraction. 

930. PERFECT SCORE... Theatre can tie in with any game that may be popular, by offering tickets to see attraction for highest score of week, or for certain difficult shot or score. 

This goes for pin-ball machines, or golf courses, or shooting galleries -any game where competition or interest is keen. • 379 •

Plenty of display material for the theatre is, of course, incidental.

931. DESK TYPEWRITER WINDOW... Tieup with office supply store or furniture store, placing small desk in window, close against glass with desk facing away from window. Paper is in typewriter on the desk, and apparently a letter has been started in the machine addressed in fond terms to some male name and enthusiastically telling about theatre's attraction . . . and being left unfinished. (Desk is close enough for those outside the window to read the "letter"). Framed photo of star is on desk.

Or the desk and typewriter might be made the center of a display, with copy to the effect that everybody's talking about the picture, raving about it, writing about it. 

Paper in typewriter can be lettered, using typewriter style. 

932. READING ABOUT YOU... Some one employee, per haps a cashier or secretary, might be assigned the duty of daily checking through the columns of the local paper, clipping out every mention of some local person where the address can also be obtained (perhaps from city directory or telephone directory, if newspaper story does not carry it). Name, in the clipping, is underlined. 

These clippings are attached to folder cards, which carry space for address on the front fold, and the imprinted copy: "We've been reading about you!" On opening the folder, imprint at top of the inside spread carries copy: "Here's what we've been reading about you." Then there's a blank space (about half the total card space) where clipping is to be pasted. Beneath the blank space is the imprinted copy: "Now we hope you'll read about us." And beneath that line of copy is more space where person handling the clippings is to write in a brief message about theatre's attraction. With “Best 

Regards," theatre's name is printed at bottom of card. 

Naturally, only clippings used are those where the publicity reflects definitely favorably to the person mentioned. (Reporting of traffic fines and husband shootings are not used.) Neighborhood houses would only clip those names where addresses indicate that they might be potential patrons. 

933. BEACH UMBRELLAS Lettered with name of attraction and theatre name, might be supplied swimming pools and beaches, well in advance of attraction. 

Perhaps traffic police stationed in center of streets can use large umbrellas to protect them from the elements. Umbrellas are attached to stands. Permanent copy could be lettered on; or copy can be changed as attractions change; using oil paint. • 380 •

Newsstands on street corners might use large lettered beachumbrellas. 

934. BALLOONS... Large captive balloon, above theatre, will command considerable attention. Balloon is lettered, or carries banner, or cutout letters (from cloth) attached to light net. Rubber companies often have balloons available, and possibly use of one can be secured in tieup with tire dealer. Inflated with oxygen. Spotlighted at night. Attendant must be constantly in charge while balloon is in the air.

Blimps ... constructed and piloted about the country for advertising purposes by the Goodyear Rubber Company, might possibly be brought to town in tieup with local tire dealer, if arranged well in advance. Blimp can tow banner on theatre attraction . . . theatre running trailer in advance, heralding blimp's visit. Local critics, officials, should be given a ride.

Small captive balloons, of some size, yet small enough for a man to hold, or for several men to hold, inflated, lettered, might be led about town by costumed men. Balloon may be included in parades. 

Star's face might be painted on the balloon. 

See No. 382 for toy balloons. ... 

935. SCHOOL BUSES Perhaps arrangements can be made to have school buses (generally privately owned) bring in patrons from rural districts on a certain evening of each week. 

Drivers can advise prospective patrons of the planned trip, through the school children whom they transport daily. Or, in connection with an outstanding attraction, principals of rural schools might be contacted by letter, urging them to have school buses bring in the children for a special Saturday morning show. 

936. FAIRS... Where state and county fairs and expositions attract large crowds, arrangements may be made to install a booth on the grounds (fair authorities might permit it without charge in exchange for theatre cooperation; or concession fee might be made a nominal amount).

The booth offers visitors a place to rest. Interior is decorated with photographs and displays on current and coming attractions, and heralds are handed fair visitors urging them to include a visit to theatre to see (attraction).

Any incidental expense can be handled by arranging to place a stereopticon atop the concession, flashing slides across midway and on screen placed above another concession booth (or other location), and including (together with numerous theatre announcements) ads • 381.

for several merchants, who share the expense of the booth. Permission to operate the stereopticon should be included in making arrangements with fair authorities for the booth concession. 

Several attractive girls, costumed, invite crowds to come in and rest awhile. They serve ice water, direct attention to theatre's attraction. Radio should be installed. 

937. KID CHAMPS . . . With cooperation of newspaper and radio station, a championship marble tournament (or soap-box derby, or kite-flying contest, etc.) might be staged . . . with a trophy or medal ("from star of theatre's attraction," or named after the star), to be presented to the winner. Perhaps additional prize, maybe a trip, can be arranged.

Paper should carry stories, and also a photo of winner and trophy. 

938. IRISH . . . When characters in an attraction are definitely Irish, or title or theme of story suggests appeal to the sons of Erin, a green color scheme should be used in lobby panels and front displays, using shamrock designs (perhaps framing stills in mats cut shamrock-shaped). All printing should be done in green ink. 

Stores should feature green in their windows. 

Irish neighborhoods should be billed. Or, securing mailing lists from Irish organizations, cards might be sent them, calling their attention to the attraction. If the Irish in town are strong enough, perhaps an Irish Night can be arranged, with band from Irish organization (if there is one), parading to theatre. 

Irish jokes might be made the basis of a contest for newspaper or radio. Or, contest might select prettiest Irish colleen, or most handsome Irish cop... with winners to be honor guests opening night. ...

Boy and girl in Irish costumes will attract attention . . . perhaps distributing heralds on the attraction through the business section. 

Or, a couple of Irish (costumed) lassies, travelling about downtown section, could carry small green parasols, on which the attraction title is lettered. They might pin small green ribbons (carrying attraction imprint), on persons they meet on street. Shamrocks can be secured in quantity, too, and attached to small imprinted card and distributed (the small manufactured shamrocks ordinarily sold on St. Patrick's Day). 

Irish flags might be displayed. 

See 309, 603, 880. 

939. FRENCH . . . Paris "sidewalk cafe" can be set up for the front, with awnings and with attractive girls in brief Frenchy costumes serving promoted coffee or tea, or other drink. Perhaps • 382.

"sidewalk cafe" might be made a lobby feature in advance of showing of the attraction.

Perhaps a gendarme's costume can be secured from a costumer for the doorman or barker.

If style angle enters into the story, hat boxes may be used for an effective display, with title lettered on the boxes. For a street flash, a couple of girls dressed as French maids can carry hat boxes, on which attraction copy is lettered. (No. 569 can be adapted to hat box.)

Fashion angle may prompt presentation of a style show as a trailer prologue. (See 26 and 131.)

French consul should be invited to the opening, perhaps introduced over radio. Those of French nationality in the town should be reached; perhaps through a nationality organization or a language newspaper. 

Fashion shops and stores should be glad to tie up dress displays or style trends with the attraction, for ads or windows, and using illustrations from the picture. Florists and bakers offer logical tieup possibilities.

Herald made up partly in French, or on style of flashy, spicy French magazine, with attractive girl illustrations, might be used. 

940. STROLLING TROUBADOUR . . . Man (or girl), costumed, strolls about downtown streets strumming a guitar, or playing an accordion (possibly playing hit tunes from theatre's attraction). Or he might appear in theatre lobby, or visit restaurants and night clubs.

Ribbon across front of the strolling music-maker carries lettered title of theatre's attraction; or a sign on his back carries the copy. 

A small amount of cash might be turned over to paper for their pet charity, with the story that it was handed to the strolling musician by persons who had mistaken him for a street singer, not noticing that he was advertising (attraction). . . and with possibility of consequent story. 

941. LUCKY DAY... Folder herald, outer page carrying copy, "This is Your Lucky Day (and then in smaller type:) 

Read what the Stars Say . . ." Inside folder is copy, "IS this your the Stars say about (attraction) . . . and YOU can see it NOW!" Follow with quote of comment of motion picture players, or radio or stage stars, about production, and attraction copy on the attraction. 

Lucky Day... Just read what 

942. AUTHOR... Lobby or window flash, selling author • 383.

of story: Against a display panel, large cutout replica of a fountain pen is attached, at an angle away from the panel, with the "point" resting near the panel. Copy, in script style, connects up with the "point" of the pen, the pen apparently having written the message copy to the effect that the high-voltage pen of (author) wrote the story. 

Using battery, stepped up through a Ford spark coil; or 110 volt (house current) through a toy transformer and a Ford spark coil, wires are connected behind the "pen" and into "point". . . one wire in point, the other coming through the panel where the point touches . . . the two wires, almost touching (" apart), will spark.

Weight of person on carpet might press switch that turns the display "on." Display should be worked out by an electrician, and protected from patrons touching, as the spark will shock or burn. 

Miniature of the idea can be used for center of a window display, perhaps using real fountain pen which sparks continuously. 

Typewriter could be set up as the center of a lobby display with sheet of paper in the typewriter carrying message (lettered on typewriter-style, but several times larger than typewriter type), "(author) has written another master mystery (and attraction copy)." 

943. PIN TALE ON DONKEY... Old Hallowe'en game 

(of blind-folded person attempting to pin a detached tail, in as nearly the correct position as possible, on a large picture or cutout of a donkey) might be adapted to many displays, as inviting patrons to correctly pin a moustache on photo of star; or a cigarette (to be pinned as though in mouth of star). Or similarly other items. 

944. SWEET NOTES... Girls costumed in long black, formfitting dresses, of velvet or similar material, with a large, white musical note on each costume, might be featured on a float, or as center of a display which carries copy, "Sweet notes from (attraction)." 

If girls can sing or play, they might introduce attraction song hits at luncheon clubs, night clubs and over radio. 

945. DREAM GIRL... Tieing in star of a coming attraction as "The Girl of your Dreams," a display placed in theatre lobby features a "dream girl" in person-a personable young lady who is stationed in the booth, and who offers to analyze and interpret patrons' dreams. Display panels carry copy: "Ask the Dream 

Girl," and refers to attraction as "The show you've dreamed of."

Girl uses an ordinary "dream book" (from a book store), and concludes each "analyzation" with prophecy that the person will soon be much happier, when (attraction) is witnessed. • 384 •

946. ORGAN LIFT... Where theatre is equipped with an organ console lift, it might be effectively adapted to trailer-prologue stunts . . . raising the console just before trailer, with appropriate display, or person in costume atop the console. Action as suggested by the coming attraction might be presented, if using persons in the "prologue;" then blacking out spotlight, and hitting the screen with trailer on the attraction. 

947. BOY'S BAND... Newspaper, and theatre can cooperate in sponsoring a band. Useful especially in summer months when schools are not in session and school bands unorganized. Perhaps some sort of uniforms might be promoted, or benefit show staged to buy uniforms. Concerts to be held during summer, in park (at time when not competitive to theatre), or in theatre.

And, with the band organized, it can naturally be used for parades and grand openings, and other exploitation of theatre attractions ... also affording an easy, and in fact a welcome way, of crashing parades where ordinarily any kind of theatre advertising would not be permitted. 948. THANKS 

Inserts that will receive a pleasant reception, to be inserted in bread or packages, can carry picture of star, or full figure of one of girls from attraction. "Thanks for your

Patronage," is imprinted above the photograph; and below, the name of cooperating merchant. Reverse side of the insert is devoted entirely to ad on theatre's attraction. 

949. BOY SCOUTS... As feature of ceremonies attending 

"grand opening" of an attraction, group of scouts could parade to theatre, as a special "guard of honor;" they might be led by a scout drum and bugle corps, or band.

Scouts can be enlisted in securing dependable city-wide coverage with special heralds. "Boy Scouts Week" could be celebrated by having scouts "operate" the theatre for an evening. Scouts are appointed or are elected by Scout vote as "guest manager," "guest stage manager," and to all other posts. Those appointed are permitted to accompany the real employee, and observe, and perhaps being permitted to perform some duties that they can safely take care of. Newspaper should go along for stories, and perhaps photographs. A ticket sale benefit might be included in the arrangements, scouts selling tickets, receiving a percentage of the sales. 

950. JOKE BOOK... Regular paper-back joke book used in connection with a window display. The book is opened at an • 385 •

especially amusing gag, and attached to a display panel which carries copy: "Funnier than all the gags in all the joke books ever published (and into attraction copy)." 

Especially adaptable to some attractions: as an Irish joke book, to be used in connection with an Irish story that stresses comedy. 

Folder herald can carry imprint on front cover: "(Star's) Joke 

Book" (and attraction copy). Inside folder, several stories are printed, and they must be carefully selected, definitely clever and funny. Straight attraction copy on back page. 

951. ORIENTAL, DESERT, INDIA . . . Veiled harem cos tumes might be worn by usherettes, or by girls who distribute heralds through downtown office buildings and stores. 

Imprinted envelopes used for distribution contain a small amount of white sand or granulated sugar. Catch-line refers to sand, as, "Across the desert sands, comes (attraction copy)," or top line might say: "Let this Lucky Sand Guide your Destiny. It suggests that you will find two hours of Happiness . when you see (attraction)." "Arab" in lobby can tell fortunes for patrons from sand. 

Oriental atmosphere can be given front and lobby panels, featuring a minaret design (the pinnacled turret that tops a mosque). 

Arch in lobby through which patrons might enter can be constructed in the shape of a minaret. Used in advance it is lettered: "Enter here for Happiness. You will find it when you see (attraction copy)."

Perhaps a small group of Oriental musicians can be located, costumed and seated in lobby, playing on native instruments. 

Dancer, in Oriental costume, might periodically go through an Oriental dance routine to their music. 

Man dressed as a sheik might be used on the street, either walking or riding a horse.

Stores tieups can include perfume, jewelry, rugs, silk, dates, and figs, and, of course, Oriental shops.

Couple of "natives" carrying a sedan chair about town will attract attention a covered chair, carried along by means of parallel handles that extend underneath it... pretty girl in the chair, wearing half-veil and costumed, handing out heralds; or copy might be lettered on the chair. Chair might be "parked" at curb in prominent downtown spots while girl enters cooperating store.

Novel department store window can feature a fine carpet, which is held by wires in "flying" position. . . off floor, and slanting upwards towards back of window. Cutout figures of characters from • 386 ·

ENCYCLOPEDIA O OF EXPLOITATION 

attraction are placed on the rug. Card carries copy, "The Magic 

Carpet of Bagdad couldn't have brought you greater Happiness (and attraction copy)." 

952. MAGIC TELEPHONE... Display in lobby features a telephone. Panel carrying copy, "Lift the Receiver. . . and hear an important announcement" "Or lift the receiver and listen to the newest song sensation!" Lifting of the receiver can flash a light or sound a buzzer in theatre office, signaling someone there to make a brief announcement into the telephone or to start phonograph. 

Panel can carry copy: "Talk to London Free!" Person answering phone beginning with "This is Robert London, telling you about (attraction)." 

953. UPPER WINDOWS. . . Stores having second story, and located prominently, may permit upper windows to be lettered with attraction title, one large cutout letter in each window. 

Or if windows are sufficiently large (perhaps full plate glass windows) a large panel may be placed on display. 

954. DIALECT STORY-TELLERS . . . Basis for contest for stage, radio or newspaper contest . . . where theatre attraction suggests a certain nationality. Stories to be told in the dialect of the nationality suggested. 

955. LAUGHING HYENA . . . Secured from the zoo, in connection with a comedy, and used, in a cage, in window or lobby. 

Copy on panels to the effect that the laughing hyena has right to laugh, as he has seen (attraction).

Or, banner might be attached to hyena cage at the zoo. 

956. MOTORCYCLE PARADE Through motorcycle clubs, arrangements may be made to secure the services of members, having them assemble at some convenient point, riding to theatre together, as escort for film or star, or as a feature of a parade. If broadcast "grand opening" is staged, motorcyclists might be timed to arrive at theatre during the broadcast. 

Lettered panels, or cutout letters, attached to bikes in front row might carry name of attraction. Or banner might carry copy: "On our way to (theatre) to see (attraction)." If celebrity or personnel of stage show is being escorted to theatre, banners might be attached to sides of car or cars. Police motorcyclists should be set to lead the parade. 

957. LETTERED GIRLS . For a novel beach or swim pool flash, attractive girls can wear low-back bathing suits. Copy on attraction is lettered in water-color on their bare backs. (And girls • 387 •

to stay out of water as long as lettering is to remain on their backs.) 

Lettering might read: “Meet me at (theatre) . . . I'm going to see (attraction)." (See Photos.) 

958. COLOR CHANGES... Figure, or illustration, disappears if gelatine or cellophane of same color is made to cover it. 

Based on this, two illustrations may be painted on the same display panel, one over the other, one illustration in red and one in blue, with revolving wheel, half of which is red gelatine or cellophane, other half blue, in front of the panel. When illustrations are covered with red, the illustration done in blue will show . . . when the blue gelatine covers over the panel the illustration in red will show. Thus a change of character or dual role might be shown. 

Or, instead of a revolving wheel to change the colors, a panel, half red and half blue gelatine, may be made mechanically to move up and down in front of the display, so that the illustration is alternately covered by each of the two halves. 

However, animation is not necessary to get the effect. Two panels, with openings covered in with the desired colors of gelatine might be placed in v-shape, so that they meet in the center, in front of the display panel. Thus, a person moving from one side of the display to the other, views it through gelatines of different colors. 

Or a figure of a star, or other illustration or lettering used in a display panel, can be represented merely by outlines, the outlines being cut out, stencil-like, the openings being left as wide as the painted outline originally was. Back of the display a revolving disc is placed, half of which backs up the cut out lines with a contrasting color. Other half of the disc is painted same color as panel. When half of disc that is identical with panel background is back of the cutout opening, no figure is visible. (See Photo Section.) 

959. BEST HAND PAINTED SIGN... Offer of a cash prize of several dollars for the "best hand painted sign" on an attraction, to be brought to theatre unwrapped on opening day at a specified time, will assure a great many perambulating displays. Schools might cooperate. 

960. SMOKE... Comedy "Indians,” in full costume, and wearing "war-paint," can stop on prominent corners and proceed to make "smoke-signals" (using smudge-pot) in Indian fashion . . . then holding up the blanket, revealing lettering (inside the blanket): "Signaling to call your attention to (attraction)." "Indians" can clown the smoke-signaling business, coughing in the smoke, etc. 

One red man might beat a tom-tom. • 388 •

Or, tom-toms alone might be used... with one "Indian" squatting on corner, pounding the tom-tom while other savage war-dances. 

Then displaying inside of blanket which carries attached sign cloth, lettered: “We've left the reservation because we've got a reservation at (theatre) to see (attraction)." Or "We're making heap big noise for (attraction)."

Smoke for use in connection with displays can be chemically created. (See diagram page in Photos Section). Or, burning incense might be used. Dry ice in hot water can supply "smoke." Steam from radiator exhaust valve (where steam heating system is used), can be piped to front of theatre (as top of marquee for a display). 

961. VENETIAN BLIND ... Display can be made up after the style of a venetian shade; or a venetian blind might actually be used: Copy or illustrations being painted on each side of the blind, and the scenes changing as the panels in the blind are reversed (which might be done by use of a small motor). Also, an illustration or panel can be placed behind the blind, being visible through the blind when it is open... thus delivering three separate messages or illustrations. Oscillating electric fan can be hooked up to pull the shade as the fan swings, a small spring at the bottom of the shade returning it to first position with return swing of fan. 

Idea can be adapted to a large display, using larger panels which just meet, side by side, or horizontal and one above the other, swiveling at center of each panel, and animated together. (See Photos and Diagrams.) 

Panel for lobby or ... 

962. ANIMATED BLACKBOARD 

window display, is designed to resemble a blackboard. 

However, black cloth is used for the "board" . . . copy on attraction being lettered on with white water-color (in irregular style, resembling chalk on a blackboard). Figure on the board, apparently drawn on with chalk, is made to move... as a large face, with the eyes made to roll round and round, or a figure which continuously waves a hand. It's done by using magnets behind the cloth... which are attached to a small wheel (for a round-and-round motion), or to a motor-driven arm. The figure or "drawing" on the board is painted on with white paint, except for the part that is made to move, which is cardboard. Small piece of metal is attached to cardboard at point where magnet makes connection. 

963. LONG HANDLED UMBRELLAS . . . To add to their attention-getting value, the handles of lettered umbrellas used for • 389 ·

street bally can be lengthened, raising them several feet higher than an umbrella would ordinarily be carried. 

Long-handled umbrellas afford an excellent opportunity of getting advertising into a football game or other place where crowds gather. 

964. SAFETY. . . Cooperation of police department might be secured, if attraction stresses safe driving; or, dangerous driving portrayed in a story can be used as an object lesson and an argument for safe driving. 

Cards could be headed: "Drive Safely, and see (attraction)." Or attraction, or title, may suggest other safety tiein angle, or catchline. 

Title is included in copy. And because of the safety copy, cards might possibly be placed on poles, and in spots where ordinarily police permission would not be granted. 

Slips carrying similar copy might be printed to resemble police "tickets" (with police permission), and attached to windshields of parked cars.

Newspaper, possibly with police cooperation, might list each day, the license numbers of several cars, the drivers of which were observed driving carefully, and who are to receive guest tickets. Might limit it to safe women drivers.

Attraction should be screened for judge of local traffic court. 

Perhaps he will sentence speeders to see the film. . . thereby creating a news story. Prize can be offered for best safety slogan that ties in attraction title. Theatre's kiddie club might adopt a safety pledge. promising to cross streets carefully, to be careful when riding bicycles or skating, to avoid playing in streets, etc. Insurance companies should cooperate with heralds and newspaper ads that direct attention to the attraction. Taxi ads might urge the public to ride safely in one of their cabs to (theatre) to see the attraction. Tire, brakes, garages (for steering gear) offer "natural" safety tieups. (See 504.) 

965. INSURE PRINT . . On noteworthy production, insurance company might issue a policy (for the advertising), insuring the print while in the city. 

Arrangements may be made to store print in bank vault, bonding all who handle it, with police guard to and from bank. 

And, to make the gag effective, newspaper story is essential. 

966. HILL-BILLY BALLY... Mountain musicians, in cos tume and playing hill-billy tunes. . . using them as lobby flash, or in window or on truck. 

Panels, or banners are lettered, "No . . . There Ain't No Hill-Billys • 390 •

in (attraction) . . . but there's goin' to be Hill-Billys in (theatre) when (attraction) comes to town... 'Cause we're A-Goin' To See It. 

We hear as how it's a great show." 

And, of course, if its a hill-billy story, the mountain music bally can be used "legitimately." 

967. WHY I WANT TO SEE... Easiest of contest angles, for newspaper or radio, is based on these words, "Why I want to see (attraction)." Newspaper illustrates with scenes from the show. 

968. DIFFERENT ROLES... Photos of star in different characters played in his most popular pictures can be imprinted on cards (which can be distributed, over a period of several days), in tieup with bakery or laundry or store. Copy on current show is carried on one side of the card . . . with illustration of star in previously played role on the other side, with different photos from previous characterizations on different groups of the cards. ...

Imprinted copy offers ticket to see newest hit, with compliments of cooperating business place, to those collecting a complete set of the photos. (Controlling number by limiting one of the sets.) 

Or the several stars appearing in the same attraction might be pictured on different sets of the cards. 

Radio contest can present, throughout a program, "clues," to former roles played by the star of a coming show, with tickets for first so-many listeners phoning correct identification. "Clues" may be a line of dialogue from a previous hit, or the name of a character, or some fact pertaining to a previous film. Or, radio contest can be based on identification of star of a coming show, interpolating facts about the star through a program, asking "Who is he?" Best written identifications get tickets. 

969. BACK-DROP . . . Where a spacious lobby permits, a permanent display might be constructed to resemble a theatre stage, "proscenium arch," with shallow platforming back of it. 

Painted back-drop backs up the opening, being designed to carry a scene from a coming attraction, or a scene suggested by it. Lighting from the front is designed after fashion of footlights. Easels at sides of the "stage" can carry copy on coming attraction, and cutout or built up displays can be displayed on the "stage" against the painted background. Or entertainers may be featured. Should be well lighted in deep colors. 

Backgrounds can be designed, to remain for some time, with the attraction scenes and billing in front changing as the attractions change. In summer, a snow scene or beach scene could be used. • 391 •

Enlargement of a scene from a coming screen attraction might be centered against the space (as a motion picture appears on the screen), with display panels carrying copy on the show. "Scenery" can be stored and used again. 

970. MOVIE HERMIT 

.. • 

Person who has never seen a motion picture will prove to be good for an interesting newspaper story. Locating him (perhaps at old folks' home), he should be invited as newspaper's guest, being escorted to the theatre by a newspaper reporter. Attraction should be one that will prove definitely impressive, and a friendly newspaper man can build an interesting story out of it. 

Playing stage show, might have him meet the folks in the show, too, photographing him surrounded by show girls. 

971. DEPARTMENT STORE ANNOUNCEMENTS . 

Many department stores are equipped with amplification equipment that carries announcements to all parts of the store. Perhaps arrangements can be made to have announcements of theatre's attraction made several times daily in the store... possibly in return for a store display placed in theatre lobby, or in connection with some store-theatre cooperation. 

972. HUNTING, FISHING... Occasionally fishing or hunt ing plays an important part in an attraction, perhaps in a short film that might be worth "selling.' 99 Appeals to local fishermen, or hunters, follow naturally. Mailing lists can be obtained from sports goods stores, or from fishing and hunting license bureaus. Isaac Walton Societies and fishing and hunting clubs should be reached. 

Window displays in sports goods stores might feature displays of equipment and mounted fish (or stuffed animals). 

Well known local big-game hunters (or exponents of the rod and reel) might be interviewed, for newspaper or over radio (basing interview on attraction). 

973. PRINT PRESS ... Arrangements made with a printer to transport a small printing press to theatre lobby, where it is set up and operated, printing heralds on theatre's next attraction. 

Display panels carry copy: "Here's News' Hot off the Press""

Heralds are handed to patrons as they are printed. Serves as an ad for the printer, too, with his name being imprinted at bottom of the heralds.

For small town use, or where satisfactory printing is not available, a small hand press can be secured at nominal cost, together • 392 •

with sufficient type to meet ordinary requirements. Member of theatre staff might operate it. Regular circulars and handbills can be printed for distribution, and small cards which carry the week's program. Or a mimeograph might be made part of equipment. 

974. KITES... Occasionally some kite enthusiast appears who is capable of building a kite that can carry a light banner, name of attraction being lettered vertically on the banner. 

In making a bid for kid business, ordinary kites will prove of value, if seasonable, as prizes; or if possible to secure them cheaply enough, given to all kids attending. Theatre imprint on the kites. Or prizes might be offered for best kite models. 

975. CHINESE, JAPANESE . . . Stores can feature man darin coats, kimonos, Oriental rugs, Chinese sandals, pajamas, perfumes, incense; with tieup cards in the various windows carrying copy on theatre's attraction. "Coolie Hats" can be featured by a millinery store. (See 422.) Shops selling Chinese curios and merchandise will naturally be glad to cooperate with window displays. Chinese dolls featured by a toy shop. 

Tea tieups are, of course, a "natural." Arrangements might be made with distributor of tea to serve it to patrons in lobby, having a girl in Chinese costume (perhaps a Chinese) do the pouring. And perhaps the girl can "tell fortunes" from tea leaves . . . including information that person whose fortune is being told will soon have opportunity of witnessing (attraction).

City-wide tieup with grocers on tea and rice might be worked out. (See 301.)

Restaurant might feature a Chinese menu, “dedicating" it to theatre's attraction, or billing it as "inspired" by the attraction. 

And Chinese restaurants shouldn't be overlooked.

Rice may be used for distribution, a small quantity of it being inserted in imprinted envelopes. Perhaps a quantity of Chinese newspapers can be secured, and overprinted in English, for distribution. 

Jinrickisha could be drawn through the streets by a boy in costume. 

Girl, also costumed, rides in the 'rickisha, which carries lettered banners. ('Rickisha might be made up from a racing sulkey, or specially constructed, using bicycle wheels.) 

Girls in Chinese costumes, carry lettered parasols. They walk with parasols closed until attention attracted, then opening the parasols, disclosing a lettered ad. Costumed girl carrying a huge 

Chinese fan can ride buses, streets cars; and seating herself, she un- • 393 ·

folds the fan, revealing name of attraction lettered on the fan. She can also appear in downtown stores, restaurants. 

Boy dressed and made up as Chinaman carries a lettered cymbal about town, occasionally striking it. 

Fan idea might be adapted to a lobby or front display, an unfolding fan (motor driven) showing copy on attraction when it is open, revealing stills as it closes. 

Theatre front should reflect Chinese or Japanese atmosphereusing bamboo effect, Japanese lanterns. Display panels for box office might be constructed pagoda-style. Giant Buddha might be secured or made up, used in a display, with incense kept burning near it. 

Chinese musicians might be stationed in the lobby, playing on native instruments. 

Japanese lanterns can be placed in barber shops, beauty shops, restaurants, attaching over light fixture. Attraction title is lettered on a ribbon trailing under the lamp, or carried directly on lantern. 

Chinese "yens" (Chinese money) may be used (see 902). The yens might be used in a window or attached to front panels. 

Announcement might be made over radio by a Chinese (in Chinese), with English translation immediately following. "Teaser ads” feature Chinese writing (the symbols being prepared by a Chinese, and a cut made for reproduction), tieing in later with ads on the attraction. 

Chinese "makeup" contest can be staged, with prize for person appearing most Oriental. (See 891, 978.) 

976. YOU'RE THE PRESS-AGENT. . . Contest invites patrons to act as press-agents for an attraction . . . asking them, "What would you do to advertise (attraction)? What one outstanding stunt would you pull? You're the press-agent . . . send in your 'campaign.' The best ones win" .. Radio or newspaper, with newspaper illustrating with scenes from attraction. (And, incidentally, it is just possible that a couple of good ideas might roll in.) 

977. BRONZE TABLETS . . . For display purposes, the effect of bronze tablets can be obtained by using ordinary matrixthe ad-mats prepared and available on almost all attractions. The mats, of larger dimensions and carrying large type impressions, would be first gilded; then painted with green paint which is then immediately wiped away with a soft rag (leaving green effect in impressions, adding to the appearance of an engraved bronze tablet). 

978. HATS... Suggested by some attractions, hats might be obtained in sufficient quantity to letter and distribute. • 394 •

Imitation jungle helmets, aviation helmets, or football helmets, etc., may be used.

Properly lettered with name of attraction, the hats should be worn by house staff, newsboys on corners, and others. Or distributed to kids if bought cheaply enough. 

979. SPARKS AND FLASHES... Occasionally a display can be improved by the addition of electrical sparks . . . with contact of some sort, as part of an animated display, resulting in a spark. (Dancer, as center of a window display that is not too brightly lighted, might draw additional attention because of sparks flashing from her shoes as she dances; or striking of an article can result in sparks, as blacksmith pounding an anvil.)

Effect is secured by use of variable rheostats with which the objects are wired. And wiring should be done and the stunt should be supervised by a competent electrician to avoid danger. He should definitely know his business. Sparks from a dancer's feet would be secured, by having her dance on small platform which has been wired with one wire (using variable resistance), the other wire attached to metal plates on the heel and toe of her shoes; or, eliminating necessity of attaching wire to her shoes, two metal plates (to which wires are connected) could be attached, parallel, across platform, or sunken into wood of platform . . . so her shoes touch them both (and with metal strip connecting metal heel and toe of shoes), completing the circuit and causing the spark when she places a foot on both metal platform strips simultaneously.

Fuse should protect lines. There must be no grounds (no water pipes near, or other grounds). No tacks should protrude into shoes, and they should be rubber-lined. Or a sword could be waved in the air, with a trail of sparks following it (the sword being carried across a wire)... handle of sword being insulated, one wire being connected to the sword, and one to the wire which the sword strikes. Carefulness should be emphasized, and the stunt first tried with the variable rheostats stepped down, then brought up gradually to the point required, which should still be as low as possible. An electrician who isn't experimenting must do the job.

An easier way for dancers to produce sparks with their feet as they dance would be to have them dance on a 12" strip of medium coarse sandpaper. with flint taps on their shoes. Routine would have them tap and shuffle their feet across the sandpaper. Produces noise, too, similar to an electrical discharge. Window or display • 395

should be darkened. Mill supply house can supply the sandpaper. 

Luminous paint can be used on costumes for additional effect. 

Light and power company might cooperate in working out electrical stunts. They can also arrange high frequency displays in connection with an attraction, for front or window or lobby-long flashing, crackling waves of electricity, leaping from one object to another. 

Or electric supply house might supply a "static machine." However, such displays must be protected, and safely out of reach of any person, and should be handled by a person who is an authority on the subject. Best in a window, where patrons can't possibly touch. 

Continuous sparking for a display can be secured through use of battery and a Ford spark coil, or, 110 volts (house current) sent through a toy transformer and a Ford spark coil Wires are separated ". Must be out of patron's reach. 

980. NEGATIVE . . . Photograph of star made into an engraving as a negative (appearing exactly as a negative film appears, with shading and light in reverse) is imprinted on small card for distribution. "Instructions" imprinted above the negative photograph suggest that person receiving the card gaze intently at the center of the reproduced reverse photograph for a full minute, then closing eyes, when "your favorite star" will be seen (process supposedly makes photograph appear correctly before the eyes for an instant when eyes are closed). Imprint follows, "You're right! 

It's (and into star and attraction copy)."

Negative photographs can be used for a newspaper contest, reproducing them over a period of several days, asking contestants to identify them. In addition contestants might be required to describe "impression" the star registers with them. 

981. HISTORICAL... Stories dealing with historical events or incidents will generally receive the support of educational organizations.

Schools might permit announcements; or heralds or blotters can be distributed. Perhaps a study period, or an essay contest, might be based on the subject or period dealt with in the attraction. 

Endorsement of Parent-Teacher Association, D. A. R., and Better 

Films Council should be secured; also other civic organizations and clubs.

Newspaper feature could deal with days pictured in the attraction. With local historical points of interest tied in. 

Perhaps old files of local newspaper might date back to time of • 396.

attraction story, and if so, the paper might reproduce a photograph of the paper that reported some event in the attraction. 

982. TALISMAN... Rabbit's foot can be used as center of a window display (possibly a jeweler's window), with panels carrying copy, "You don't need your lucky rabbit's foot, because this is your lucky day... you can see (attraction and theatre)."

Especially adaptable, of course, if Lady Luck plays any part in the story or title. And further display of charms might also be used for lobby or windows-trinkets, lucky coins, ju-ju mixtures, and any other gadgets that are supposed to be bad luck antidotes. Perhaps newspaper will do a feature story on good luck charms. 

Perhaps "lucky" pocket-pieces, resembling a coin and bearing imprint on attraction can be stamped out; or they might be available for distribution. 

983. GIVE-AWAYS FOR KIDS... A pony (named after attraction), as first prize in a newspaper contest designed to appeal to youngsters will be certain to create tremendous interest in the contest. (Picture of the pony should be carried in the paper.)
