Similarly, a dog would be a very desirable prize in appealing to kids. (See 475.) Or a "(Star) Doll." Or a bicycle.

Contest might be based on best 50 words, or less, written about subject suggested by attraction. 

Also, samples of various kinds-gum, candy, cake, might be promoted for distribution to the kids at a matinee. Tops (in season) might be secured cheaply in quantity and distributed. Imprinted stickers attached. 

984. NEON... Effectiveness of displays can be increased greatly by use of neon lighting. Might be used for an occasional flash, outlining a panel or outlining letters, or supplying illumination for a display. 

Front and lobby panels can be effectively illuminated, indirectly, using neon, by concealing the neon tubing under the edges of panels (or cutout figures), that are extended forward some several inches from the background panel. 

Made up in any design for front or lobby display, and available in a choice of colors, neon will add to the attention-arresting value of any display. Floats, for a night-time flash, can be made doubly effective through use of neon outlining. Window displays can be outlined. Neon should be out of reach of patrons. 

Effect of neon can be secured by cutting slots in display panels, in desired designs, and inserting (edge-ways) strips of colored celluloid. • 397 •

Illuminated from behind, the celluloid strips will reflect the light through to the front. 

985. TIME CLOCKS . . . Regular time clocks, such as department stores and manufacturing plants use, can be placed in lobby as center of a display on a coming attraction. Panel carries copy, "Be on time next week . . . to see (attraction)." Copy on display panel urges patrons to "punch the time-clock," to keep the card, bringing it back when the attraction comes along. . . when a number of different time indications will be selected and posted in lobby which will entitle those having similar cards to receive free admissions. "Time cards," made exact size as regulation cards, carry space for time to be registered and devote rest of space to copy on the attraction. Those stamping a card will be inclined to carry the ad around with them until they attend the next week. 

986. INDIANS . . . Riders on horse-back (bareback), in

Indian costumes, can carry lettered banners. Teepee might be made part of lobby display, inhabited by a couple of "Indians." 

Float features a teepee; and several Indians (including several pretty squaws), beat tom-toms, hand out heralds, as float travels about town.

If there is an Indian reservation near, the services of real Indians may be secured. A group in full regalia may be invited to attend as theatre's guests on opening day (provided the attraction pictures them in a favorable light). Miniature Indian Village might be set up in town square or prominent spot about town. 

Displays of Indian relics can be arranged. Moccasins, arrows, tomahawks, head-dresses. Perhaps from local collector or a museum. 

Shoe store can feature moccasions, hat store an Indian head-dress.

Art shop might show a group of Indian subjects. 

Quantity of large feathers, with copy imprinted, can be distributed by boys or girls dressed as Indians. Newsboys can wear the feathers in their hats.

Indian, in Chief's feathers, might appear at theatre, schools, luncheon clubs, city hall. Could visit newspaper offices, smoking peace-pipe with the editor for a photograph. School essay contest might be based on Indian legends or myths. On opening day, Indian runners could bring a message from the Mayor that "officially" opens the show (they might work relay-style, one every few blocks). 

See 603. 

987. PAGE... Star of theatre's attraction can be "paged" in hotels, restaurants, dance places, in theatre during intermission, • 398 •

988. WIVES, WOMEN... “Which type of woman do men prefer?" Can be made the basis of a newspaper contest. Feminine star of an attraction portrays for the photographer several different types, and these are reproduced by the paper, one each day, together with stories on the contest. Types would include, "Demure," "Allure," "Sophistication," "Gay," "Exotic," "Clinging Vine."

Suggestions for a list of ten most famous women in history, might be used as a contest basis. 

Other angles: Merchant tieups with stores that specialize in women's wearing apparel. Stills of stars in stores' windows, ads. 

Heralds distributed with packages. Gifts for wives and sweethearts featured, appealing to men. Cosmetic counters and beauty shops.

Women might be invited to pick most handsome male, submitting their nominations of either screen stars, or locals. Winning male to be guest of honor opening night (if local). Tickets to women who give best reasons for their selections.

Men might be invited to tell what they believe to be the qualifications for a perfect wife. 

989. MAGIC CARPET... Man, or a couple of girls, possibly in costume suggested by picture, slowly unroll length of carpet down the sidewalk (towards theatre) . . . revealing copy: "The Magic 

Carpet"... leading the way to new marvels in entertainment . . (picture) at (theatre)."

After unrolling, carpet is rerolled, and the gag is repeated to a new audience.

Strip of carpet running from front doors to curb, in front of theatre, has been used to attract attention. Footman is hired to keep it dusted off, with attraction copy carried on his uniform, or on the carpet.

991. BEER COASTERS... Imprinted on heavy cardboard or blotting paper, rests for glasses can be supplied restaurants, hotels, taverns, all places serving beer. 

992. DRESS STAR... Newspaper readers may be invited to "dress" the star of theatre's attraction. From among the items advertised by stores in the newspaper (one issue or several), they are to select an outfit (clothes) "for the star of the attraction." Prizes for best suggested ensembles. 

Newspaper might include the contest in a cooperative page, with selection of articles to be confined to stores whose ads appear on the page. Stores would supply prizes for winner, perhaps a complete outfit. 

993. CARTOONS... When a cartoon character is featured both on theatre's screen and in a newspaper cartoon strip (or a similar character is featured), newspaper might place copy beside or above their strip, directing attention to theatre's screen subject featuring the character.

Appealing especially to kids (though adult appeal of cartoons must not be minimized or overlooked), kiddie clubs can be organized in the name of the cartoon "star" (if the cartoons are shown regularly). (See No. 280.)

Impersonators of the cartoon character might appear on the street to advertise the showing of one of the cartoons. Made up to resemble the character, with papier mache heads used to make the resemblance more nearly perfect. Might go along in parades, or wherever crowds gather. 

994. UNIVERSITIES. . . Students like to be considered, and generally appreciate any evidence of a desire to cooperate; though just how close this cooperation can be, depends, of course, on the individual schools. Most schools will generally permit announcements, usual school tieups, on commendable attractions. 

Benefit ticket-selling arrangements can occasionally be worked out with school organizations. Perhaps it might be desirable to make a special students' rate on a certain evening of each week. 

It's a good idea to welcome incoming freshmen each year, sending them a letter, perhaps including a little note-book or date-book, or something of the sort. Generally they're beginning four long years of residence in the town. Trailer welcoming back all students should be carried, too.

Possibilities include: 

Display cards in book shop; or cafeteria or restaurant. Cards in nearby restaurants and soda dispensaries. • 400 ·

Ads and stories, regularly, in college papers. Essay contests. Distribution of blotters, heralds, imprinted rules. Direct mail. Telegrams sent fraternity and sorority houses (requesting that the telegram be attached to bulletin board). Star made honorary member of a fraternity or sorority. Football team (in season) as guests on night of at-home games, designating it "Varsity Night." Tire covers which boost football team, carry name of theatre. Personal contact, friendship of students. 

995. DIPLOMACY ... This classification is lifted intact from Epes W. Sargent's swell Exploitation page in "Variety," because it illustrates a qualification that is so necessary an adjunct to ordinary good judgment in selling shows. "Some years ago Jack Rowley of Robb & Rowley wanted some girls to ride in an open car for 'Why Girls Leave Home.' He wanted the smart looking debs who couldn't be hired. It didn't seem to be so good for the sort he could pay." "He picked out a little group and offered to give them a box party if they had the nerve to pull off the stunt. That appealed to their sporting blood, and they went through with it where an offer of cash would have been fatal. Just diplomacy.' "Eli M. Orowitz wanted to put a billboard atop a one story taxpayer in an ideal location. He knew the owner of the store had turned down offers so he went around to see the man, but he didn't talk money. He told his listener that the low building looked dinky and pointed out how much better it would look with an addition, even if this were only a billboard. That convinced and Orowitz got the sign. Diplomacy again." "The Mayor of a certain town announced he would not have the streets cluttered up for advertising purposes. All street work was out. A manager knew His Honor was deeply interested in the local orphanage. He invited the Mayor to bring the children to a special showing, promising to provide transportation. This he arranged through Rotary. As a final touch he provided a brand new car in which the Mayor headed the procession. After that the Mayor could not very well crack down on prams or newsboy parades. More diplomacy." "There is always other than the grab method of getting something." 

996. SOUND TRUCK . . . A suggestion that must be included: Properly bannered or paneled truck, equipped with public address system, and with announcer supplied with good line of copy to • 401 •

announce (which should be brief), and playing a recording of hit tunes (if any) from the attraction.

Sound truck can make business section when crowds are on the street, factories at quitting time; at other times covering outlying districts and residential sections. Truck should go where crowds go. 

In summer time it might make the beaches on days when crowds are there. 

997. LIVING BILLBOARDS... A billboard display panel can be erected atop theatre marquee, made up after fashion of regular billboard, but with platforming in front of the billboard background. Girls promenade across the platform; or they might assume various poses. Some local celebrity can draw a curtain to "unveil" the living display as the highlight of opening night (with photos for the papers). 

Girls should wear brief dance costumes, or costumes suggested by the attraction. For a musical, girls and entertainers can sing or play, using amplification, presenting both a sight and sound flash. 

Or, "Guards" might promenade across in front of the display. Or savages beat tom-toms, in connection with a jungle picture. 

And, of course, a living billboard might be placed in a location other than the top of theatre marquee, if more attention would be attracted. 

Living billboard display can be effectively used, too, as prologue to a trailer on a coming attraction. Display panels constructed to resemble small billboards, with lettered name of attraction, etc., are set up in boxes, down front, or on sides of stage. Lights are arranged to dim-up on the "billboards," disclosing a girl posed (on narrow platform in front of the panel) pointing towards lettering, holding pose as lights slowly dim up. Then she walks across display to microphone to make prepared and memorized announcement. 

Using two panels at either side of the stage, and two girls, one girl might recite one line, the other girl the next line, until last line, which they recite together. Lights blackout fast on last line, and trailer hits the screen. Or, of course, only one panel and one girl need be used. Silhouette of girl's figure can be cut into the "billboard" . . . with girl posed in this opening, stepping out to make announcement.

Perhaps faint musical background might be supplied as girls recite. 

Instead of girl making announcements, entertainers, as suggested by the attraction can be used.

1001. CHECK AND DOUBLE CHECK... This classification doesn't really come under the head of show selling, except in the sense that any aid to better house operation can be interpreted as tending to attract additional business. These reminders, suggestions, will prove of value in checking for top efficiency. 

House Check: 

Front: Is it properly lighted? Clean? Neat? Are display panels attractive? (Only the current show should be billed directly in front of theatre.) Is attraction sign getting the attention it merits? Is sales copy for attraction sign carefully prepared? 

Are the letters clean? Do they need paint? Are lamps clean? Are lamps turned out in attraction sign where they are behind blanks and consequently not required? 

Check lamps in trough letters; borders; flashers; behind translucent letters; soffit (under marquee); in vertical sign; borders. Are lamps all of same wattage? Is neon lettering okay; or are letters out or flickering? Is curbing clean of debris? Sidewalks clean, clear of trash? Is front of theatre kept clear of parked cars, so that automobiles can load and unload? 

What is the condition of display frames? Do they need paint? What is the general impression the lobby presents? Are display posters inviting . . . do displays sell? Is spelling of words on display panels and in attraction sign correct? Banners, valancesare they neat, clean, attractive? Is brass polished? Glass in doors clean? Are swinging banners or signs definitely secure so that it is impossible for them to blow down? 

Is front lighting turned on at proper time... the time to be determined by, and varying according to the length of the days? Are lights turned off promptly when box office closes? Is front billing changed on final evening of attraction, late, instead of on opening morning of a show? 

Is cashier attractive, courteous, neat? Does she say "Thank You” with a smile when patrons purchase tickets? She should be well-informed as to schedules, current show and coming shows. She should answer the phone with a cheery "Good afternoon" (or "Good evening"), then giving the name of theatre. Cashiers should not eat candy or chew gum while in box office; or carry on extended conversations with patrons or with other employees. They shouldn't go in for too long telephone conversations.

Is there a sign displayed in the box office, when closed, telling opening time of theatre? Is theatre opened punctually? Are proper price signs displayed? Is box office neat, clean? Money kept off shelves, and out of sight? In what condition is the ticket register does it need repairs? Is box office door opened at any time (when theatre is open for business) without use of safety chain? Are curtains neat, clean, • 404 •

fresh? Glass clean? Brass brightly polished? Is cashier's number (if required) properly displayed? 

Is inner lobby devoted entirely to selling coming attractions? Are frames neat, clean, properly displayed? Is floor kept clear of ticket stubs, paper, debris? Is lobby lighting inviting? Check for dust on ledges and light fixtures. How about shadow boxes; rubber matting; ropes; brass; glass; sand urns; carpet; doors; door checks; door stops; chandeliers; mirrors; furniture; curtains and drapes; exit lights, lobby floors?

Is doorman neat, capable of handling any situation that may arise at his post? 

Is he cheerful, courteous to patrons? Does he accept tickets from patrons instead of grabbing them? Is he well informed as to schedules? Is ticket chopper in good repair? Are ticket stubs burned daily by manager or assistant?

Are ushers on the job? Do they present a good appearance, and do they really know how to usher? Do they realize the value of courtesy and a smile in handling people? And in “handling" patrons do they keep their hands off of them? (They should never push or touch a patron's arm.) Do members of the staff show special attention and consideration for the aged and infirm? Are ushers, quick, bright, interested? Is Aisle No. 1 kept covered at all times? Is there an usher on duty in the balcony at all times when it is in use? Is staff familiar with emergency requirements, and with fire drills? Are all accidents, no matter how slight, reported to manager immediately? In bad weather does the staff report early, so that the house may be opened, getting patrons in off the street and out of the weather? Are uniforms neat? 

Ushers clean, hair combed, shoes shined? Do ushers enter into conversation, either with patrons or other employees when on duty? Additional points to check can include . . . too many ushers on an aisle, or grouped together in conversation; ushers eating candy or chewing gum while on duty; ushers' room-uniforms should be hung up and kept in good condition when not in use, room should be kept clean, neat. 

When was last service meeting held? Were methods of improving the service discussed? Are meetings of employees held regularly? Are employees invited to suggest improvements in service, in house operation, in advertising? Is an attempt made to cultivate a keen interest in the operation of the theatre, no matter what the employee's position? 

Is house lighting too bright? Stray light? Annoying brightness in the line of vision? Or is there enough light? Are aisles well lighted-especially stepdowns? How about lamps in wall brackets, chandeliers, stand lamps? Are they clean, or will inspection reveal dust? Is the color combination correct, and is it in season (greens, blues predominating for hot weather; amber for winter). Are globes of higher wattage than necessary being used? Are lamps clean? Are lights turned on too early, or left on too long after show is out? To secure cooperation of employees in conserving electricity, it might prove a good idea to post small reminder cards near all light switches (where they are out of sight of the public) carrying copy, "Please turn out lights when not in use."

Check carpet carefully; are there any torn, worn or ripped places where a patron might catch a heel? Is brass clean, shined? Curtains, drapes clean? Are erit doors tried each day? Exit lights lighted at all times when house is open? dition of fire hose, or other similar equipment? Are door checks in good repairs, or do they permit closing doors to bang? How about restroom signs? Glass (clean)?

check? How about the auditorium floor-how long since it's been painted? Are floors mopped thoroughly and regularly? Does the theatre reflect good house-keeping? 

Does it smell clean?

What is the condition of the seats? Are they dusted daily, carefully, and turned up? Are they kept in good repair, with some member of the staff assigned the duty of checking them daily and keeping them in good condition? Are they firmly anchored to the floor or will a tug at the end seats show some of them to be torn loose from their anchoring? 

Are the cleaners on the job? Are they competent? Do they use work-lights, instead of house lights? Are supplies used by cleaners kept under lock and key?

Are supplies wasted? Is there any possibility of loss of supplies through their being stolen? Check for dust on ledges, bracket lights, grille-work, radiators, frames, draperies, seats, dark corners. Is glass and brass kept properly cleaned and shined? 

Will trash be found behind radiators? Is the room which cleaners use to store their equipment kept in good order; and do they turn the lights in the room out when they leave? Cleaners should be careful never to permit greasy rags to accumulate; if they must be kept, they should be placed in a heavy covered can. Booth and stage might check on this point, too, as greasy rags can cause spontaneous combustion. Is hose to vacuum cleaner carelessly dumped on the floor when not in use, or is it coiled up carefully? Are sidewalls (sides of auditorium) clean; or can soap and water be used to remove marks left by patrons' hands (without making the cleaning too conspicuous compared with space above which cannot be cleaned)? Tapestries should be brushed. 

Are rest-rooms clean? And are they kept clean? Well lighted? Is all equipment in good repair? Floor clean? Fixtures clean? Towels in container? Used towels in receptacle provided, instead of on the floor? Tissue supply? Soap? Are walls clean, or can they be cleaned; or do they need paint? How about light fixtures? 

Furniture? Carpet and equipment in lounges? Drapes, curtains? Rest room signs?

Framed panels can be provided in ladies' room, beside mirrors, in which blotting paper is inserted . . . and where the ladies can wipe lipstick, sparing the walls. 

Mezzanine . . . furniture; carpet; floor lamps; sand-urns; draperies; curtains; are all furnishings clean, neat, inviting? 

Is basement clean, free of valueless rubbish? Is stored material kept in order? 

Floor painted? Walls painted or whitewashed? Is basement swept and mopped regularly and kept free of accumulated dust? 

How about booth and projection equipment? Can the quality of sound be improved? Is the house checked for proper sound distribution? Is sound too loud, is it too low? Are horn units checked daily? Check projection for poor definition, unsteady projection, flicker, poor light, out of frame, out of focus, poor masking, bad change overs, dirty apertures. Does stage apron reflect light? How about the screen... is it dirty? Shaky? Bulging? Is it properly masked? Are projection and movietone lenses cleaned daily? Reflectors, too, should be cleaned daily, and brushed several times each day with cheese cloth. Is proper light and economy obtained from carbon? Carbon economy can be acquired through proper adjustment of the arc crater and by keeping the generator commutator properly cleaned and brushes correctly adjusted. Short carbons can be saved for short reels and screenings (rate of carbon burn per minute should be determined). Sound amplifying equipment should be kept free of all dirt; and make and break contacts, including tube prongs and contacts, should be thoroughly cleaned each week with nonabrasive material (rough brown paper can be used). Tubes must be kept in first class condition to assure sound • 406 •

EN CY CLOPEDIA OF EXPLOITATION 

transmission without interruption. Spare parts and replacements should include such items as tubes, horn units, generator brushes, motor brushes, main driving gear for projectors, spare reflectors for lamps, spare intermittents and film sprockets. How about the carbon supply? Is there an emergency supply held in reserve? Is the booth properly equipped with fire extinguishers and safety devices? Do the fire shutters work okay? Can they be closed by hand, and are they properly fused? How long since the fire extinguishers were refilled; check; they should be refilled annually, at least. Equipment should include a two-gallon soda extinguisher and two pyrenes. (Use of pyrenes in event of small blaze is preferable since less damage will be done machinery.) Separate fireproof containers should be provided for film, waste film and waste materials and for cleaning equipment. Is the exhaust fan in the booth working? Can noise from booth be heard in the house? Playing stage shows, how about cues? Are cues understood and properly executed for smooth continuity? 

Is the booth kept clean?

Roof: What is condition of roof equipment? Roof should be clear of all debris, to prevent stopping of drains and consequent leaks. Is the flashing in good repair? 

Skylights? Ventilating louvres (if automatic, do they work)? Revolving turret draft ventilators-are they in good repair, do they revolve freely? Are exhaust fans and power source in good repair and lubricated regularly? Are fire escapes to and from the roof safe?

Is stage kept clean, whether in use or not? Is equipment in perfect working order? 

If stage is not in use, are the stage ropes and rigging inspected regularly? Is the Asbestos curtain in perfect working order? Is unused scenery properly stored? Is the switchboard protected? Is sprinkler system regularly inspected and in proper working order? 

Fire Extinguishers should be stationed on both sides of stage. Stage manager should have an extinguisher convenient, near switchboard. Stagehands should know locations of extinguishers and exit doors. At least one light on stage should be kept burning at all times, night and day. Smoking on stage should never be permitted. 

Microphones used on stage should be kept covered with cloth cover when not in use, to prevent dust accumlating. 

Are dressing rooms backstage in good condition? If in use they should be cleaned daily. Even if not used, they should be kept clean and ready for instant use; should be kept locked when not in use, making certain, first, that no lights are left burning in them. How about other store-rooms and closets that are kept closed—is it possible that lights might be left burning in them?

Are electric switches guarded? Are they clean of dust and dirt (careful in dusting or cleaning them). 

Engine Room: If heat is being used, is heating unit entirely satisfactory? Is excessive amount of fuel used? Any way of saving? If gas is used, are meters okay?

In buying coal, can a deal be made with the dealer where he agrees to haul away the ashes, thus saving that cost? If winter is about over, coal or fuel oil should be ordered judiciously so that too large a supply is not left on hand. If heating equipment is not in use is it in condition to be put in use when required? Is it in need of any repairs, or cleaning? Have grates, fire-boxes, ash-pits, back connections, all oil-burning equipment been cleaned? Check for necessary adjustments, damper regulations, safety valves, gauges. Check, clean and replace flues or chimney boiler sections and tubes. 

Check, cement and repair any air leaks. Check pumps, leaking pipes, motors. Has boiler been inspected? Is engine room clean, painted, clear of all debris, and is brass brightly shined? • 407

ENCYCLOPEDIA EXPLOITATION 

O F If cooling plant is in use, is it running efficiently? Will it need repairs when it is shut down in the Fall? Had arrangements for repairs at that time better be made now? If plant is at present closed down, is it in shape to operate when it will be needed? 

When plant is operating, check temperatures hourly (should never be lower than 74 degrees dry bulb, with a relative humidity of 55 per cent; house temperature should never be more than twelve to fifteen desgrees lower than street temperature). Check water temperatures every hour; also oil temperatures, bearing temperatures, oil levels, motor amperage. Before starting machine each day check pressures on all equipment and check them every hour. Air washers should be thoroughly cleaned each week; or in very dirty surroundings should be cleaned every day (this will increase efficiency and will eliminate necessity of frequent cleani.ng of tubes in coolers). All strainers, oil or water, should be cleaned at least weekly If these practices are followed faithfully, possibilities of trouble will be largely eliminated, and any difficulty will be found before great damage is done.

A good indication of the way the cooling system is being operated is to watch the audience; if they're uneasily moving about in their seats, it's either too hot or too cold; they're not comfortable.

When cooling plant is closed for the winter, manufacturer's instructions (of the particular plant in use) regarding closing down of plant should be faithfully followed. 

As a general rule, after the cooling season is over, all condenser and cooler tubes should be cleaned, and a general check made on all equipment and bearings, and any necessary replacements made at this time. If plant is exposed to freezing temperatures all water should be drained from the machine in all places. When preparing to start plant, make certain plant has a new charge of oil, and a full charge of refrigerant. 

If cooling plant motors are operated out of season (as in testing in connection with repairs), arrangements must be made first with the power company, as starting the plant increases the demand (and the cost). 

How about fire escapes? Are they safe? Would they carry a load if called upon?

Are they tested regularly, kept in good repair, securely attached, painted at least once a year to prevent rust?

Fire extinguishers: When were they last filled? (Should be filled at least once a year.) Is location of fire extinguishers and fire fighting equipment known to those who would be required to use same in case of fire? If house is equipped with firehose, how long since it was tested under pressure? Is the hose okay, or has it deteriorated to such an extent as to no longer be of value? 

Fire and panic drill should be periodically practised and discussed with theatre staff. A routine should be worked out, so that every employee knows exactly what he is to do in an emergency.

Ushers should be instructed to remain at posts, to quiet excited patrons, and to set an example in this regard. If not necessary to empty the house, ushers should calmly inform patrons that there is no cause for worry, that the show will continue in a minute, asking them to kindly keep their seats. If it should be necessary to empty the house, effort must be made to impress the importance of orderly exit of patrons. In this event, ushers would open the exit doors nearest their posts, see that fire escapes are lowered, controlling the exit and restraining any rush. 

Patrons must be distributed to all exits. To get attention of crowds in an emergency, ushers and house staff must be in front of them, facing them . . . shouting behind them has no effect. Ushers would remain at posts as long as needed, then reporting to nearest point of confusion to assist. Ropes in lobby should be immediately removed if they hinder prompt emptying of house. Doorman should remove ticket chopper • 408 •

from exit, and notify cashier to stop selling tickets. Every effort should be made to control crowd, they must be controlled—persuading patrons to take their time. After house has emptied, check all aisles, restrooms, see if anyone has been left behind. 

Stage-hands would immediately lower asbestos in case of fire. Operators, in event of booth fire will, of course, drop fire shutters and attempt to extinguish fire. If fire is in house, operators will keep the picture on screen as long as they themselves are not in jeopardy. In the event of a booth fire in a magazine, operators should not open the door to the magazine. Ushers should know proper way to handle and carry injured persons, or fainted persons (two ushers joining hands, cross-hands, for a cradle effect; or "fireman's lift" may be used). Panic control: In event of a fire that is definitely of no danger to patrons, or fights, or drunks, or crazed persons, shots or confusion of any kind. . . ushers should assure patrons calmly that there is no danger, to remain seated, that the show will continue.

Disturbance: Ushers to get the help of manager or assistant in handling drunks, insane persons or morons. 

Uniforms: In summer winter uniforms should be cleaned, properly stored, and necessary repairs made so that they will be available and in good condition when needed. In winter . . summer uniforms cleaned, conditioned, stored. Uniforms in use to be kept clean, pressed; ushers to hang them up carefully when not in use. 

Is an inventory of house equipment available? Has inventory been checked, or made up lately? It's an excellent way to become thoroughly acquainted with every detail of theatre and equipment. 

Are lamps as well as other supplies (polish, cleaning supplies, carbons), kept under lock and key? Is an inventory of lamps kept? Are supplies reordered in sufficient time, so that they are not exhausted? 

Is house carefully and thoroughly checked before it is opened each day? Is special attention given to accident hazards . . . especially noticing hand-rails, carpets, aislelights, rubber mats. Does manager check safe contents the first thing each morning? 

Does he check first performance of every show?

Show Check: Pictures. . . Is program routined so that attractions will show to best advantage, building to a balanced program? Are too many trailers being shown? 

Is the projection all that it should be? (See check on booth and projection.) 

Show Check: Stage Show... Is show correctly routined at present for best results? 

Can a rearrangement of routining improve the show? Points to check include: Jerking curtains. Battens not properly masked with borders. Fouling of drops. Improper trims. Unsteady stage braces. Bad off-stage masking. Noisy traveler. Noisy working of ropes and drops. Too much off-stage noise. Torn places in scenery. Set off center. 

Visible wires. Platform not secure enough, or shaky. Borders not properly trimmed. 

Failure of draw curtains to come together. Dirty stage apron. Curtains too fast or too slow. Performers' entrances—are they clumsy or neat? Are girls in line properly in step, are they properly arranged for size? Dancers out of step. Lines (of dancers) crooked. Voices-are they heard? (Amplification loud enough and working properly.) 

Curtains not clean, heavy with dust. Miscues. Faulty makeup. Props missing. 

Too many bows. Numbers repeated too often. Unplanned encores. Stalling. 

Uncalled-for ad-libbing of actors. Performers visible when off-stage. Master of ceremonies, if show features one, failing to sell an act properly when introducing it; failing to subordinate himself to the performer after introduction; familiarity with audience overdone; lack of variety in introductions. Diction. Gestures. Speaking before applause has subsided. Stage lighting: Spots slow, or wrong size. Flood lights • 409 •

covering too much territory. Reflected glare from shiny surfaces. Dimmers not working properly. Spotlight halo. Footlights not properly sheltered from balcony. 

Poor choice of spotlight colors. Lights on behind scrims at improper times. Offstage lighting equipment not concealed from view. Bad contacts at stage pockets. 

Effect machines (too fast or too slow). Failure to properly spot performers. Can lighting and arrangements of lights be improved? 

Checking: Are checked articles properly cared for? Identification checks used?

Advertising: Newspaper: Viewing a finished newspaper ad, does it seem to invite reading? Has the ad touched an instinct-selfishness, fear, love and curiosity are four of the strongest. Is there too much copy in the ad; and is it interesting? Does the ad move to sales? Can it be read without effort? Has it a definite beginning and a definite ending, continuity? Are the illustrations good likenesses, and do they carry appeal? Does the copy used apply or connect up with the illustration used? Have the ladies been considered in the ad appeal? Is all necessary information included in the ad-program, play dates, theatre name or sig-cut, theatre address if this is important? Does newspaper properly set up the ads? Are the ads handed paper in sufficient time? Do they submit proofs in time for corrections? What kind of position is the paper according the theatre's ads? Check proofs for misspelled words. 

Ad Approach: Angles that might be applied to theatre advertising can include:

Behind-the-counter style (a direct, plain, talking-to-'em style). Institutional. Testimonial. Demonstration (pointing out values). Monologue (written in first person). 

Interview. Patron talking. Emotional. Humorous. Staccato (excitedly brief, and rather disconnected). Reading Notice. Comparison. Slang. Dialect. Fright. 

Curiosity. 1-2-3-4 Technique (listing points of value). Love. Behind-the-Scenes 

(ad-writer "stepping out of character" to comment). Open Letter. Sensational. 

Appeal to Adventurous instinct. News (tying to some topical subject). 

Advertising: Outdoors: Are cards and displays receiving proper distribution? 

Are old cards and displays permitted to "live" after attraction has played? Is posting covered over as soon as possible after attraction plays or on final day of engagement? 

Could better posting or card locations be secured? Are heralds receiving proper distribution . . . are they going into the homes or into the creek? or more.

Art shop: Footage of compo-board for fronts and displays should be figured out so that there will be no waste (unsalvageable small pieces). If scraps are left over, mats and letters should be cut from them. Interchangeable false fronts, constructed from a good grade of compo-board, can be washed off, and used again, a dozen times 

Use scrub brush, hose and running water in washing. Care should be taken to mix just the required amount of paint, since it's not likely that that identical shade will be required again. Paint, ordered from out of town, should be shipped before cold weather, since freezing spoils water colors. Brushes should be washed immediately after using. An air-brush will be found a good investment, since it requires less paint, less time. Display matter, stills, lithographs, photographs, should be kept in order when awaiting use. Art shop, or sign room should be kept clean. 

Engravings: Where more than one cut is to be used, as a series of ads on an attraction, can they be joined together in making up (later to be separated by newspaper), thus receiving the benefit of the rate which applies on larger cuts. All illustrations on drawings should be pasted down if possible, saving the cost of extra negatives. 

Artist should put benday on copy, where required, so that engraver doesn't have to add it. White line should be tooled around photographs for best effect. 

Routine: Typed up schedule of day's routine details, reports, etc., and of week's • 410 ·

routine reports, letters, regular details to be attended to, meetings, etc., can be prepared as a reminder and reference. 

Scales and Vending Machines: Do scales register correct weight? Are present locks sufficient safeguard? Are vending machines kept filled and in good repair? 

Are deposits made regularly?

Snow and Ice: Canopy and roof should be checked during and after every heavy snowfall, making certain they are not overloaded with weight of the snow. Ushers should brush snow from patrons entering, using a whisk-broom.

Spring: Spring cleaning from roof to cellar. Repainting where paints have faded. Or wash walls. Are summer uniforms ready? Inspect roof.

Summer: Seat covers? (Clean?) Cooling equipment in perfect working order? 

Cool valances, clean and repaired and in use. Summer uniforms. Lighting. Tieup with florist for flowers. (See "Summer" classifications.)

Telephone: List of names and telephone numbers of all employees, together with addresses, should be on file in office. List of numbers often called will prove convenient near phone. 

Tickets: Is present supply of tickets sufficient? Should an order be placed?

Local check: Newspaper rates; newspaper circulation; population; population within drawing radius; manufacturing plants, and how many employed; conditions; nationalities; seating of house and opposition houses; product; opposition of all kinds; outdoor advertising rate; license and tax information; protection over surrounding towns and distance to all nearby towns; carbons required weekly; train and plane schedules; type of equipment in house-booth (projectors, sound), heating, cooling; figures-past and present, and year to date; expense in various departments-advertising, rent, heat, water, payroll, maintenance, electricity and power rates. 

Final Check: The suggestion that every exploitation idea be accorded thorough consideration before it is put into use. There should never be an opportunity for an exploitation stunt to boomerang and in any way damage the theatre or offend patrons or potential patrons. Every stunt should call attention, and definitely favorable attention, to the theatre and its attractions to justify use, and should be reasonably sure of sufficient box office returns to justify the expense. • 411.

First step is the construction of the armature, or wooden frame upon which the clay form is modeled. (Fig. 1.) Shape of armature depends upon the figure to be modeled. The clay model is then built over the armature, using ordinary brick clay, modeled to desired shape (Fig. 2). Model is then cleaned up, smoothed down, and shellaced. After the shellac is thoroughly dry, a thin coat of stearic acid (from wholesale druggist) is applied. Next, insert ti line (3-A), which divides the casting into desired sections (Can be separated down the middle of the face (as in Fig. 4). or down the sides). Then begin to construct the mold. applying plaster. Four coats of plaster are upplied, permitting plaster to set and thicken between applications. First cost is applied very thin, filling in lines and crevices. Final cost is mixed with excelsior to strengthen it, soaking the Ocelsior in the plaster before applying. Then the braces (Fig. 4-0 and 5) are installed, holding them in place with plaster. Number one molding plaster (from lime and coment company) is used in constructing the mold. In mixing, it is sprinkled into the desired amount of water until it appears above the surface. Don't stir until all plaster is in the water, and after stirring don't add plaster. 

In applying plaster (to form the mold), one side of the casting is completed, up to the fa-line (4-8), which divides It. After first half of casting is completed and set (about 20 minutes), tin-lines are removed. Edge of the completed half of the casting (4-A) is shellaced and a coat of stearic acid applied; and thin coat of dark show-card color is applied, to make the division visible. Then the second side (4-C) is completed. Molds are removed in sections (Fig. 4), then cleaned, repaired where needed, and the actual papier macho construction begun. Paper is applied in thin strips (6-A), using ordinary well-paper paste. Use thin strips of paper for first several coats, pressing to exactly fit the shape of the mold, then applying about eight layers of well-paper (in strips), carrying paper over the edges of the mald (Fig. 6-8). Paper remains in mald until thoroughly dry (about 24 hours), and is then carefully removed from the mold (Fig. 7). Edges are then trimmed, and the separate parts sewn together (Fig. 1), using burlap needle, and small, strong card. (If heads are small, stitching isn't necessary: paper will hold it). Cost of thin paper is applied over the stitching: and after it is dry, the entire figure is smoothed with sand-paper. Figure is then completed (Fig. 9) and ready for painting.

plays (as Fig. 10), attached against display panels. Animation is possible with papier mache figures (as making eyes rall, lower jaw move) in construction of a head (Fig. 12 and 14, 15).

Eye that meves up and down, with lid, giving effect of opening and closing eye, is constructed in one piece (Fig. 11), and placed behind eye opening in papier mache head (12-A), with motor-driven eccentric moving it up and down, Lower jaw can be made to move

up and down with same motion that drives oyas (12-C). (Bottem jaw ia over-lapped by extension of chook (12-D).) Loud speaker can be con cealed inside papier mache head (Fig. 12-8), voice sont through amplification causing the head to "talk" Two-way amplification makes possible answering of questions. Relling eyes (Fig. 14) are enclosed in a com structed housing (IS-A). Extensions behind the eyes (15-F) are attached by means of a ball socket (16-0) to an arm (16-H) that connects offconter to a motor-driven wheel (1-E). Any other desired movement of a figure can be worked out in similar fashion. Large papier mache heads can be worn by street belly mon (Fig. 13).
